title: Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger review – mammoth tour movie brings the joy and poignancy of reunion | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Gallagher brothers’ comeback concerts are given the full fan-worship treatment, but it’s impossible to begrudge the euphoria they have created
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The Gallagher brothers’ comeback concerts are given the full fan-worship treatment, but it’s impossible to begrudge the euphoria they have created
Content: Brothers in arms … Oasis: Don’t Look Back In AngerPhotograph: Simon EmmettView image in fullscreenBrothers in arms … Oasis: Don’t Look Back In AngerPhotograph: Simon EmmettMoviesReviewOasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger review – mammoth tour movie brings the joy and poignancy of reunionThe Gallagher brothers’ comeback concerts are given the full fan-worship treatment, but it’s impossible to begrudge the euphoria they have createdPeter BradshawSat 5 Sep 2026 15.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Hello … hello … It’s good to be back.” With these words – and the unfortunate possibility of a royalty payment to a certain disgraced ex-pop star – this highly enjoyable fan-worship documentary revives the memory oflast year’s staggering and already mythic Oasis reunion tour. It also recollects how effortlessly funny the Gallagher brothers are, like a great comic double act. There’s a big laugh in the tense scene in the rehearsal room, when Liam finally shows up after Noel and everyone else had been there for hours – and the very first thing that comes out of his mouth is a fierce and magnificently sullen objection to the baffles on the drum kit: “They’re giving me the hump.”Yet to the surprise of many who did not believe, and these biblical echoes are strangely appropriate, Liam and Noel did not fall out; the resulting stadium tour put a fresh coat of paint on the word “phenomenon”. Middle-aged and elderly people together with young people sporting bucket hats, some accompanied by their pets in bucket hats, sang their hearts out as if it was the 90s again and Manchester City had just won the World Cup 10-0 (although this film was evidently completed beforeWonderwall’s moment at this year’s World Cup).We see again theOasiscongregation engaging in colossal Dionysian events of mass joy – but of course, the poignancy of time passing and the irresistible narrative of the brothers’ public reconciliation give a new layer of emotion to the songs. Noel now looks like the silver-fox dad of the band; Liam, with what looks like a ridge or a scar on his nose that I don’t remember from before, looks more like a bloke whose pint you do not want to spill, a pint around which you want to put a 10-metre exclusion zone. But this was always the case. Noel’s songs always combined, in a distinctive way, euphoria and sadness, moods which seem to float free of meaning in the strictest sense. Now they and all their fans have got something to be euphoric and sad about.As for the brothers’ togetherness, I think the film shows it is sincere and real in public, and real on stage, where it counts. Noel and Liam are rarely interviewed together; here mostly it is Noel solo. I wonder if, like Mick Jagger and Keith Richards, they now come together to make music after reaching an accommodation. Whatever wound each other up has not magically vanished, but is being managed. Part of the problem was that Noel’s songwriting credits made the big money – not Liam. Perhaps the lawyers have hammered something out here, but it is not shown in the film.The documentary begins with an extended montage of the 90s glory days leading to the ugly falling out in the 00s, and how the non-Oasis years coincided with an era of inept politicians and terrible sadness all round. Then we see Keir Starmer chortlingly agree how great it is that Oasis reunited on his watch. But this film misses out one of the most famous moments of their career:Noel’s 1997 handshake with Tony Blair at the Downing Street victory party, which came to capture the zeitgeist of Cool Britannia. The film does not includeNoel’s earlier comment at the Brits: “There are seven people in this room tonight who are giving a little bit of hope to young people in this country. That is me, our kid, Bonehead, Guigsy, Alan White and Tony Blair.” Noel is not asked about Blair here, but both him and Liam reject any notion they are “rightwing”.From here we are immersed in the gigs themselves, on the face of it no bigger in scale than many other band’s live shows, but with the specific tearful ecstasy that U2 or Metallica or the Stones cannot manage. As Liam says, they just stand there, rooted to their mic positions; they don’t do Jagger acrobatics, it’s very relaxing and they can keep doing it for years. It was always difficult to be cynical about Oasis and now it’s impossible.Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger screened at theVenice film festivaland is out on 11 September in the UK and USExplore more on these topicsFilmOasisDocumentary filmsMusic documentaryVenice film festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Box review – no one knows what’s going on here … least of all Gary Lineker | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: In this bizarre new gameshow, you will encounter John Bercow doing topless karaoke while tossing glitter at pensioners and Joey Essex pounding on the walls of a shipping container. Why? Who knows!
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: In this bizarre new gameshow, you will encounter John Bercow doing topless karaoke while tossing glitter at pensioners and Joey Essex pounding on the walls of a shipping container. Why? Who knows!
Content: Gary Lineker on The Box.Photograph: ITV/Two Four/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGary Lineker on The Box.Photograph: ITV/Two Four/ShutterstockTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewThe Box review – no one knows what’s going on here … least of all Gary LinekerIn this bizarre new gameshow, you will encounter John Bercow doing topless karaoke while tossing glitter at pensioners and Joey Essex pounding on the walls of a shipping container. Why? Who knows!Sarah DempsterSat 5 Sep 2026 16.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat is The Box? It is easier, perhaps, to list the things The Box is not, if only to give ourselves something to cling to when the more recognisable trappings start to wobble, the floor gives way and we find ourselves in a tent with Joey Essex, watching in silence as a topless John Bercow hurls glitter at an audience of braying pensioners.So. Some things The Box is not: a sitcom; a medical drama; a property show presented by sockless men with teeth that follow you around the room; a thing about badgers. Beyond this, however, we are on our own. The opening titles do little to assist. “10 BOXES” booms a caption as the camera swoops over a collection of giant yellow containers strapped to the back of a flatbed lorry. “10 CONTESTANTS” it continues, as a montage of coming attractions reveals footage of Graeme Souness squinting at an egg and a member of JLS running towards some trees. And, finally, a distinctly disobliging caption that is nevertheless pivotal to the wilfully befuddling modus operandi of this six-part series: “NO HELP”. Bloody hell. Or rather, “bløødy hell”, because The Box is a Norwegian format so something may have been lost in translation. Anyway, shh, because it’s episode one and here isGary Lineker.“Boxes,” he says, peering through his binoculars at 10 yellow boxes. Inside them, we learn, are a corresponding number of trembling minor celebrities. “Remember,” adds our host, chuckling mildly in a jumper the colour of patio, “the celebrities have no idea where they are or what they’re supposed to be doing!”Tiny cameras capture the mood of the interned stars as they sweat and fidget in their metal tombs. “I don’t like surprises,” gulps broadcaster Ranvir Singh. “I’m in a state of unparalleled uncertainty,” confesses the former speaker of the House of Commons, John Bercow. “I’m Joey Essex,” bellows Joey Essex, pounding on the walls of his box like a distressed navvy trapped in an overflowing portable toilet.Finally, the doors of the containers slide open and they – and indeed we – are off. But where? And to what end?As the opening captions state, there is no help and few instructions for the contestants. Instead, they must “work together” to “solve challenges” such as finding hexagons to fit into hexagon-shaped holes and completing an egg and spoon race in a set amount of time. Then they are divided into teams before being sent back to a custom-made house. Then one of them is eliminated. There is no prize.View image in fullscreenThe Box’s contestants, from left: John Bercow, Sara Davies, Graeme Souness, Danny Aarons, Joey Essex, Ranvir Singh, Jenny Ryan, JB Gill, Ellie Taylor and Shakira Khan.Photograph: Two Four/ITV“One thing’s for sure,” gasps JLS singer JB Gill, “The Box is absolutely unknown!” Alas, this is balls. The only certainty here is that the boxes are pointless, their sole purpose being to briefly conceal contestants from their location, a task that could just as easily be achieved with a blindfold made out of old tights.This would, however, deny us the sight of Essex bursting out of his box like a frightened horse at Epsom, or a boxed-in Danny “I’m a content creator” Aarons shouting about how he “can’t hear the skies” while frantically thrashing his horrifying Norman-era bowl cut from side to side like a one-man Battle of Hastings. So boxes it is.Unlike, say, Taskmaster, where chaotic things happen for a reason, here, chaotic things happen for no reason and continue to happen long past the point at which either their chaotic methods or pointlessness would make some sort of sense on a conceptual level. The second episode, for instance, ends with a genuinely harrowing sing-off that climaxes with Bercow performing a rendition of Pink’s So What, while a tentful of holidaymakers aggressively demand he remove his shirt.The Box isn’t so much a gameshow as a sustained howl of existential confusion. A gameshow that scoffs in the face of convention yet seems bewildered by the bedlam that such showmanship inevitably unleashes.A gameshow in which John Bercow bellows “Orderrrrrr!” while showing us his nipples.I commend it to the house.The Box aired on ITV1 and is on ITVX now.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionGary LinekerGame showsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t have any friends’: why do young people today have fewer mates? | Loneliness | The Guardian
description: Social media, mental health problems, the pandemic and financial instability all contribute to the phenomenon
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Social media, mental health problems, the pandemic and financial instability all contribute to the phenomenon
Content: Tess Lavanda: ‘I think there’s a lack of drive for people to go out and meet people, and when you do go out, people are on their phones so it’s harder to approach them.’Photograph: Tess LavandaView image in fullscreenTess Lavanda: ‘I think there’s a lack of drive for people to go out and meet people, and when you do go out, people are on their phones so it’s harder to approach them.’Photograph: Tess LavandaLoneliness‘I don’t have any friends’: why do young people today have fewer mates?Social media, mental health problems, the pandemic and financial instability all contribute to the phenomenonJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentSat 5 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Tess Lavanda’s YouTube channel there is one video with substantially more views than the rest: it is titled “I don’t have any friends” and has been watched more than half a million times since she posted it a month ago.Over on Instagram she has posteddozens of reelswith titles like “I turned 22 alone”, “Living alone in London” and “Feeling alone this summer is OK”, each garnering thousands of views and hundreds of comments, many from people feeling the same way.A quick search for terms like “solomaxxing”, “loneliness influencer” and “no friends aesthetic” brings up hundreds of videos and posts from people – many of them teenagers and young adults – talking about what life is like without friends.“I think people feel relieved it’s finally being spoken about,” says Lavanda, 22. “No one felt brave enough to speak about it because there is this culture where people think being alone is embarrassing and wrong.”Number of young people with no close friends has soared since 2014 in EnglandRead moreNew research from the Institute for Public Policy Research published this week found the number of young people in England with no close friends has risen fivefold since 2014, now standing at one in 20, and a growing number saying they are not happy with the friends they do have.Lavanda says: “I think there’s a lack of drive for people to go out and meet people, and when you do go out, people are on their phones so it’s harder to approach them.”She has always struggled with making friends but it was only during the pandemic when “that lack of a genuine friendship really hit” and she started to feel isolated. “I had no one to talk to and I went into quite a dark place,” she says.Then one night when she was about to head out alone feeling “so scared and awful”, she put on her camera and started talking.Lavanda says: “I had no intention of posting it. This was just purely a video for myself, about how I was feeling to try and hype myself up, really. But then I thought maybe this will help someone, so I posted it.“I was fully expecting to be judged and bullied but the response was overwhelmingly positive. People were sharing their own stories, and I realised that so many people feel the exact same way.”View image in fullscreenTess Lavanda: ‘It’s more important to just be honest and speak up.’Photograph: Tess LavandaShe says there is a growing trend for solo life to be “aesthetic or romanticised” but her videos are more about showing people without friends they’re not alone. “I think people take comfort in the fact there’s now a voice about this topic,” she says. “It’s more important to just be honest and speak up.”There has been growing discussion around why young people today report having fewer friends than previous generations – a combination of social media, mental health problems, the Covid pandemic and financial instability are all often thrown into the mix.Pamela Qualter, the UK’s leading scientific expert on child and adolescent loneliness, says there are no straightforward answers. But it is clear that, as a society, we’ve stripped back places where young people can practise basic social skills like saying “hello”.“We’re really lacking those very simple conversations you have each day with somebody you just bump into,” she says. “More people are working from home, and people have less disposable income at a time when there are very few free or cheap places for people to come together.”Qualter says it is these “weak ties” – small interactions with acquaintances – that form the building blocks and social skills that can build into solid friendships.But she emphasises there is not much evidence to suggest young people are actually getting lonelier: those aged 14 to 24 report the highest levels of loneliness in the UK but this has always been the case.“Maybe our expectations of friendships are changing. Maybe those people with fewer close friends are happy with that,” she says.However, there is also evidence to suggest young people are increasingly dissatisfied with the friendships they do have.Jodie-Leigh Foster,atraining and development officerat UK Youth, teaches youth workers about youth loneliness and isolation, as well as empowering teenagers to launch their own projects tackling the problem.She says it is the quality of friendships that many young people struggled with. “These are friendships that often play out on social media and group chats, which can quickly turn to bullying and harassment,” she says. “That leads to them becoming isolated and withdrawn.”Money is also often an issue: some young people reported not being able to afford to get transport to see people outside school. Others struggle with large crowded spaces, especially since the pandemic, which increased levels of anxiety.Foster says: “People make assumptions about being a young person, that it’s a carefree time in their lives, and the whole world’s at their fingertips. But for some young people, that’s actually really overwhelming and daunting. It’s a tough time to be a young person.”Explore more on these topicsLonelinessYoung peopleSocial mediaCoronavirusDigital mediaMental healthHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Uefa legal case may be beginning of the end for Infantino as Trump’s support evaporates | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The order of discovery related to Fifa’s failed plan to sell the World Cup will worry the American president, a situation that tends to end badly for the culprit
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: The order of discovery related to Fifa’s failed plan to sell the World Cup will worry the American president, a situation that tends to end badly for the culprit
Content: Gianni Infantino already looks to be running out of support in the light of being accused of ‘criminal mismanagement’ by Uefa.Illustration: Cameron Law/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino already looks to be running out of support in the light of being accused of ‘criminal mismanagement’ by Uefa.Illustration: Cameron Law/The GuardianFifaUefa legal case may be beginning of the end for Infantino as Trump’s support evaporatesBarney RonayThe order of discovery related to Fifa’s failed plan to sell the World Cup will worry the American president, a situation that tends to end badly for the culpritSat 5 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 06.34 EDTShare“Tell Mike it was just business. I always liked him.”“He understands.”“Tom, can you get me off the hook? For old times’ sake?”“Sorry can’t do it.”I never believed it would actually happen. Not really. Not until this week, when, for the first time, there was a sense, as The Godfather makes so abundantly clear, that you really can get to anyone.Fifa calls Uefa’s legal threat a ‘smear campaign’ in US federal filingRead moreGianni Infantino is beleaguered.Gianni Infantinois re-beleaguered. Gianni Infantino has been beleaguered for almost six weeks, since news emerged of his grotesque undercover plan to sell off, for related personal gain, the shared global property he’s employed to preserve, protect and safely pass on.There has been hopeful talk in that time of toxic status attained, a base being hollowed out,a rival presidential candidatenext March. But power runs deep. Entrenched dictatorial power runs even deeper. Time passes. The doorway narrows. Infantino is already the man who sold the world, not once, but twice, most recently to Donald Trumpin return for a peace prize, a scrunchie and a fawning presence around the sub-table of power.Give it a month. Chuck in a Football Jesus turn at the lighted lectern a few weeks from now, arms whirling like a street magician, reeling off the usual stuff about caring and sharing, égalité, fraternité, fiscal stimuli. Look deep into those weirdly flat painted-on eyes, cold and hard behind the papier-mache mask of power. You don’t buy me out. I buy you out.But something has shifted this week. It was never going to be the gnats around his ankles that did for Infantino: another thundering newspaper column, the latest stern denouncement from – whoah, hang on – former Manchester United utility defender Mikaël Silvestre.Hard power is something else, however. And two things have now happened, both responses to thethreat of a Uefa lawsuit, which I believe has no really serious notions of ultimate victory, but which may turn out to be an expert chess move, a zugzwang that leaves the king having to go somewhere, but with no safe spaces left to hide.View image in fullscreenJosh Kushner said he ‘would not have gotten involved’ in Fifa’s plans had he known the full picture.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersThe first response was Josh Kushner’s statement this week after being named as a party to discovery in Florida. Kushner was the money guy behind theFifaForward fiasco. Nuts isn’t it? The person you come to for finance and macro-favour just happens to be, by an accident of talent and destiny, the brother of the president’s son-in-law.Kushner said he “would not have gotten involved” in Fifa’s plans had he known the full picture. He said this was all regrettable. Ostensibly mild and reasonable words, but with a sense of distance being carved out, of a cutting loose from the protective apron.Kushner has also hired a nuclear option lawyer, Alex Spiro, who defended Elon Musk when he called a caver “a pedo” and Alec Baldwin when he accidentally shot someone. It’s a serious defensive move. As is, to a more rattled degree,Fifa’s counter-filing this week, which dismisses the whole episode as a “smear campaign”, then says the quiet thing out loud. Specifically, Fifa mentions discovery and a very urgent intention to resist it.This is the real point. No one on the Infantino side wants discovery. Which is, to be clear, the sharing of related documents, from internal memos down to relevant emails sent from your smartphone on the golf course after lunch.This, as Gianni knows, is always a worry to those in power. And you really don’t want to be a worry to anyone in any way connected to Trump. This is why, behind the sabre rattling, there is for the first time a sense of a thinning out, of nobody there on the ward, no cops on the doors, of the old man up there unprotected.Even Trump’s early support for Infantino was a little over-juiced in the media. The president Truth Socialed his assurances in early August. It still felt a little qualified. “If for any reason” Fifa got rid of Infantino, well, this would be really bad. And nothing since.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is a vague sense of a shrug here, of an amble away from the stage. We remember the good times for the Gianni-Trump bro-tocracy, laughing together like men in a Brooks Brothers senior knitwear advert, the gleaming bald impresario to power and his tolerant daddy-patron looking as ever like a giant man-size unit of American food, as though something deep-fried, honey-glazed and dished up at an out-of-town hotel conference buffet has somehow learned to walk around in a baggy suit and say things like “a very tall, very handsome man”.View image in fullscreen‘Zip it’: Fifa will want to avoid discovery to protect Gianni Infantino’s relationship with Donald Trump.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAThis is always brittle. Trump will walk you in, remember your name, glad-hand you by the stairwell. But once you’re gone you really are gone. There is no loyalty, and logically so, because Trumpian politics has no core belief, no substance, just a cold, hard matrix of winners and losers.And if you lose, or look like you might, then by coincidence bad things tend to happen. The Guardian published a list a while back of Trump enemies whonow find themselves subject to charges, exile, security clearances revoked, mortgage fraud investigated. And that list does include some pretty high-profile one-time golden boys.Michael Cohen, the fiercest of Trump loyalists, who famously stated he would “take a bullet” for the big man? Legal difficulties and fallings-out intervened. Cohen has since been imprisoned, disbarred and sent into exile. The former US attorney general Jeff Sessions was among the first to call Trumpism “a movement”. He’s now not only out of the game, but has apparently been described by Trump, variously, as weak, confused, dumb, an idiot, a disgrace, and “mentally retarded”. There is a pattern here. If you’re in then you’re in. But don’t fly too close to those flames.The decision of the court on allowing discovery could well be key. Make no mistake, Uefa is accusing Fifa and Infantino of “criminal mismanagement”. The key issue is an alleged undervaluing in the sale of the World Cup. Unrelated, and arguably standard industry practice, Infantino also stood to take a huge personal salary from all this.It is a clear attempt to peer inside and see what, if anything, is in that box. Uefa wants discovery from Fifa, Thrive Capital and the Trump donor and deal adviser Greg Maffei, all of whom will have paper trails from that period when Infantino was granted intoxicating access to the halls of power. It puts you in mind of the Club World Cup trophy, a weird, frightening-looking thing, all razor-sharp odd nooks and crannies, the secret little drawer full of human toenails. Do you really want to know what’s in there? Is it safe to look?“Please Mike, don’t do this, don’t do this to me”“Today I settle all the family business. So don’t tell me you’re innocent.”How is this going to play out? Infantino is doing what he can, touring his outer provinces and pressing the flesh. Saudi Arabia has offered qualified backing (“at this time …”). There’s a Fifa congress in November. Really, though, you wonder about votes, and to what extent votes are the thing here. It is hard not to muse on how it ended in football for Sepp Blatter and Michel Platini. That one-shot illegal payment allegation really did come out of the blue.For now the process will simmer on. Legal challenges often fail or melt away. Uefa just needs to keep pressing, to make it clear that coals will be raked. Keep the pressure up and you never know what may fall out, or from where. Mr president, you can have my answer now. Our offer is this. Nothing.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: How posh are you? Do you have a therapist? What would you say to Trump at a party? Marina Hyde answers readers’ questions | Politics | The Guardian
description: We asked you what you most wanted to put to our Guardian columnist. You responded in droves, querying her ‘beef’ with Burnham, who she thinks is this generation’s Hugh Grant, and what she really thinks about Richard Osman ...
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: We asked you what you most wanted to put to our Guardian columnist. You responded in droves, querying her ‘beef’ with Burnham, who she thinks is this generation’s Hugh Grant, and what she really thinks about Richard Osman ...
Content: Marina Hyde: ‘What drags you out of bed in the morning? Insomnia’s pretty helpful.’Photograph: Jay Brooks/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMarina Hyde: ‘What drags you out of bed in the morning? Insomnia’s pretty helpful.’Photograph: Jay Brooks/The GuardianPoliticsHow posh are you? Do you have a therapist? What would you say to Trump at a party? Marina Hyde answers readers’ questionsWe asked you what you most wanted to put to our Guardian columnist. You responded in droves, querying her ‘beef’ with Burnham, who she thinks is this generation’s Hugh Grant, and what she really thinks about Richard Osman ...‘There is light at the end of this tunnel. But the tunnel is filled with sewage’:an exclusive extractfrom Marina Hyde’s new bookMarina HydeSat 5 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 05.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat are your bunker plans?James, PortugalMasses of things to read, incredible food and an unethical doctor with an insane war chest of interesting pills. The second that bunker door closes, the doors of perception are opening.Will Restore gain more tractionby the next election and genuinely split the rightwing vote?Natasha,LondonThey won’t split it in some 50‑50 way, but they could peel off a bit more from Reform’s right flank. Nigel Farage is looking vulnerable. In the Woody Allen film Deconstructing Harry, Robin Williams plays an actor who literally goes out of focus. Having once been sharp and clear, his nervous system is so shot that he becomes a physically blurred and imprecise distortion of himself. Metaphorically, something similar has happened to Farage in recent months.Who do you think is this generation’s young Hugh Grant(iewitty, funny, sexy, intelligentand gorgeous)?Anna, New ZealandIt’s being done as a job share between Jude Bellingham and Cole Palmer.Are the men of the manosphere right about anything?Kate, LondonI saw Clavicular say, “My life is a horror story”, which feels about right.I have noticed a more serious tone in your columns this year. In light of recent events, here and abroad, are you finding it increasingly difficult to maintain your humorous disposition?Tim, LondonNo. I’m sorry, I must have been tired when I wrote those ones. It’s always more effort to be funny than serious.If you met Andrew Tate, Elon Musk and Donald Trump at a hideous dinner party,how would you greet and say goodbye to each of them?Becky, Bristol“You must try the beef bourguignon. I hear our hostess foraged the mushrooms herself.”What would you have said to Margaret Thatcher’s face if you’d had a whole two minutesalone with her?Eamon, IrelandSo much is known and has been written about her that new lines of inquiry can feel hard to come by. But I would have liked to find a way of getting her to reveal how she felt about being the object of so many men’s crushes. Both those who worked around her and what Norma Desmond called “all those wonderful people out there in the dark”. She knew, of course, and would most certainly have had Inner Thoughts about the phenomenon. However, I have to say, it would be quite difficult to build the rapport required to get them out of her in two minutesWhy are journalists failing to make the case to the public that rightwingerssuch as Nigel Farage,Richard TiceandStephen Yaxley‑Lennonare dishonest, self‑serving and not terribly bright?Alexis, KentI really don’t think the vast majority of people pay the slightest direct attention to journalists at all. There are still some heavily invested continuity Corbynites out there who will imply that two or three critical columns I wrote about their absolute boy had something to do with him losing his second general election on the bounce in 2019. To which my reply would be: “Yes, dear, I’m sure they talked of little else but my columns on the doorsteps of the ‘red wall’. Yet, if we were to humour your notion that the whimsical musings of some silly cow in London make one nanoparticle of difference, how come I wrote 937 critical articles about Boris Johnson and he still won a landslide?” On the rightwingers front, however, I would point out that it is journalists and not anyone else who have been exposing, for example, Farage, Tice and Yaxley‑Lennon’s financial arrangements, and I’m very grateful to them for their work.The citations in your columns have taken me down some scurrilous rabbit holes I would not otherwise have encountered. How much of yourresearch is spent in corners of the web you would rather not be? And do you have a therapist?!Ian, Aylesbury, BuckinghamshireHahahahaha. Someone once told me they found out about edging videos from something I wrote about Theresa May’s endlessly inconclusive Brexit votes in the Commons. I can only apologise. Personally, I love the fact that I can spend my days wading through the more recherche bits of contemporary culture, and if anyone sees me, just say, “It’s for my WORK????” As far as the last part of the question goes, I don’t have a therapist. It’s so unfashionable, of course, but I have to say I’m a big, big believer in pushing it all down. I know, I know – I consistently note people’s looks of distaste when I tell them that. But I’m just putting the counterpoint out there.Your articles usually speak to power. Have you ever felt fear of the potential consequences?Chris, near Brighton, East SussexThe most credible politically motivated threats I have faced have been from the far right and the far left – and always from supporters rather than any publicly known figures. But – so far! – I’ve always found the bigger danger to be lone men who develop obsessions of one kind or another.Do you work on resilience?Mary, DublinNot particularly consciously. But I valorise it. The older I get, the more I see that it is an endlessly useful kind of freedom. But that’s easy for me to say, because I’m so lucky. The resilience it takes to be, say, a woman in Afghanistan or a little girl in Congo is quite simply utterly inconceivable to me. I basically think that everything I have, and everything that I have achieved, is overwhelmingly the result of luck and good fortune, and not remotely to do with any kind of exceptionalist skill.If you had to spend a month on a desert island with a group of footballers, politicians or celebs, which would you choose and why?Charlie, SwitzerlandHot footballers, let’s face it.Will Andy Burnham’s plan for a No 10 North in Manchester be a stroke of genius or his undoing?Patrick, LaSalle, CanadaNeither (the most versatile answer in politics).Clearly, politicians are worse than useless. Who would you pickas prime minister?Eric, Newton Abbot, DevonJK Rowling.View image in fullscreen‘He’s funnier than me’: Hyde co-hosts The Rest Is Entertainment podcast with Richard Osman.Photograph: Goalhanger PodcastsWhat’s always off-limits to critique? And what would feel important enough to make you reconsider your own boundaries?Josh, Palm Springs, USIn general, I think everything can and should be written about, as long as you get the right tone. Anything involving children is always what I’d be most cautious about.Do you have a writing routine?Michael, Gijón, SpainI try to be at my desk at 5am, because I’m definitely a lark. Something that takes me five minutes at 5am will take me an hour at 5pm. So the morning is definitely my best writing time. As far as column-writing goes, I tend never to start with the first sentence. I just put a few things down in a Word document and move them all round till some kind of column starts to stagger out of the primordial soup. I mostly don’t know what I think until I’ve gone through the act of writing about it, so the conclusion can often be as much of a surprise to me as to anyone kind enough to read it.Which ludicrous situation involving a UK PM has made you laugh the most during your career?Richard, NSW, AustraliaTony Blair having someone at the Foreign Office during the Iraq war whose official, ask-at-reception job title was “head of story development”. That was quite a mirthless laugh, obviously. David Cameron? Either leaving hisdaughter in the pubduring a “troubled families” initiative week, or theshagging-the-pig’s-headthing. Theresa May calling a general election and the exit poll coming out at 10pm showing she’d lost her majority. Boris Johnson hiding from the media in abig fridge. Liz Truss spending her entire career wanging on about the infallibility of free markets, then getting her arse handed to her by them in about 10 minutes. Rishi Sunak calling the election in thedriving rain, and then not realising thatbinning off Normandy D-daycelebrations for a media interview would play badly. Keir Starmer calling for the return of theGaza sausages. Andy Burnham: TBC, but it’s coming, I assure you.The 1970s was a time of revolution, with so many groups up in arms. I sensed the same energy atJune’s Dublin Dyke March: outrage, we’ve had enough … Do you think young people today have revolutionary energy?Ger, DublinNot at all, I have to say. I think as long as people have smartphones in their hands, they will be too narcotised to rebel. There’s a kind of dropout energy in a lot of young people, which is as completely understandable as it is completely sad. I really feel for them.What is your favourite meal?Douglas, GermanyHonestly, my next one. At home, I make a huge amount of schnitzel in all kinds of ways. And multiple types of apple pie. Very pleased (and culinarily jealous) to be giving this answer to someone based in Germany.Celebrity culture and AI promise a world where some people are valued and others deemed worthless. What human qualities do you most value?Sean, Swinford, County MayoCompassion, tolerance, wisdom, kindness, bravery, strength of character. And GSOH.Across your articles and podcasts, I noteyou consume a huge amount of news and media. How onearth do you find the time? And do you have to take comprehensive notes in case you need to make connections between people or events at a later date?Simon, Windsor, BerkshireI love the idea of notes, but, no – I have never taken any! Maybe I need to get Stacey Solomon to do an episode of Sort Your Life Out in my memory palace. The truth is my brain just works quite associatively, so something in politics will always remind me of something in sport or music, and it often ends up feeling more illuminating to me that way.View image in fullscreenSet design: Victoria Twyman. Fashion styling: Hope Lawrie. Hair and makeup: Celine Nonon at Arlington Artists. Suit: Emilia Wickstead. Jewellery: Marina’s ownPhotograph: Jay Brooks/The GuardianI’m intrigued by your somewhat startlinganimus towards Andy Burnham. What is driving this?Ricardo, Carshalton, south LondonListen, I’ve been hurt before. Meet you back here in two years?How posh are you?Rob, New ZealandI guess I can hold my own.What’s the worst thing about working withRichard Osman on The Rest Is Entertainment?Katie, DublinHe’s funnier than me. Also, he only pretends to support Fulham. That second one might not be true – I just wanted to say something in a public forum that would incense him but where he wouldn’t be present to reply. (Try writing to the letters page, Richard – see how you get on.)Are you still on X? If so, why?Caroline, SwitzerlandYes, I am. I don’t use it much at all as I find social media a massive time‑suck. I hear Bluesky is truly ghastly, but have never visited.What’s your favouriteBrooklyn Beckhamcareer?Martin, Weston-super-Mare, Somerset2042 chairman of the Federal Reserve.You often draw equivalence between Labour and the Tories: “They’re all as bad as each other.”Do you ever worry thatyou’recontributing to an anti‑political climate thatis one of the factorsrendering Britain ungovernable?Shaun,Punta del Este, UruguayI hope I’ve never used that phrase, Shaun. However, when any side falls short of the standards we should expect in public life, it massively undermines trust inallpoliticians. That’s happened a lot since the turn of the millennium. But I don’t think Britain is ungovernable, and I fundamentally believe that politics is still the best way we have of making people’s lives better.Will art save us?Steven, LondonUnclear. Still, what a way to go.What usually drags you out of bed in the morning?Peter, PerthInsomnia’s pretty helpful. But I’ve usually got lots to do and I love a new day.Does anyone care if Prince Harry is in or out? Are the people ahead of the papers on this one?Paul, LondonI definitely think stories abouthim and Meghando a lot of traffic, which is why he gets written about so much. I think a lot of people claim they’re not at all interested and yet still read huge amounts about him. I’m like this about The Rock’s multiple business ventures. Could not care less about them; have read 23 articles this week about them.What makes you feel hopeful and optimistic?Pauline, BristolLove, human ingenuity and listening to pop music.What’s your favourite word in the English language?Rick, ManchesterCocktailhour.What a Time to Be Alive!
