title: Why the Bayeux tapestry and Franco-British relations are natural bedfellows | Bayeux tapestry | The Guardian
description: Tapestry’s loan to UK is just another chapter in the love-hate relationship that has spanned the centuries since it was created
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: Tapestry’s loan to UK is just another chapter in the love-hate relationship that has spanned the centuries since it was created
Content: Andy Burnham (left) said the loan, overseen by Emmanuel Macron, was a ‘tremendous demonstration of goodwill’.Illustration: Anais Mims/Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham (left) said the loan, overseen by Emmanuel Macron, was a ‘tremendous demonstration of goodwill’.Illustration: Anais Mims/Guardian Design/GettyThe Saturday readBayeux tapestryWhy the Bayeux tapestry and Franco-British relations are natural bedfellowsTapestry’s loan to UK is just another chapter in the love-hate relationship that has spanned the centuries since it was createdEsther AddleySat 5 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 01.01 EDTShareFive British prime ministers ago – and six French ones – when Emmanuel Macronfirst confirmedthat France would return the Bayeux tapestry to Britain after 1,000 years, hetold an audienceat Sandhurst and Theresa May – the No 10 seat-warmer of the day – that when it came to France and Britain there were “two things that nothing can change, be it a vote or a political decision: our history and our geography”.It was January 2018, 18 months after the UK had voted to leave the EU, and relations between the near neighbours were not good. The French political establishment had been shocked and angered by Brexit; personal relations were frazzled, and cross-Channel government contactsmeasurably dwindling. This was not a rupture that a piece of embroidered medieval linen, however perfectly it represented that tangled history, was going to solve on its own.It took only eight and a half years and many, many changes in personnel, but this week Macron finally made good on that pledge with the unveiling of the tapestry at the British Museum in London, inscenes of suchamitiéthat one could almost forget the bilateral chill that had gone before.No one pretends that the Bayeux tapestry alone has been responsible for stitching together two nations whose connections had visibly frayed. (When it comes to the tapestry, as every commentator this week has shown, the needlework metaphors are hard to resist.) But the French president’s single-minded commitment to drive through a loan that he haspreviously called“seemingly impossible” illustrates that, in diplomatic terms, the London exhibition is not just a decorative sideshow.View image in fullscreenKing Charles, alongside Queen Camilla, speaks to Emmanuel Macron as they view a section of the tapestry at the British Museum in London.Photograph: Adrian Dennis/PA“It is much more than just a linen canvas embroidered with wool,” Macron told an audience at the museum on Wednesday. “It represents a whole chapter of French, British and European history.”In that context, it was notable that he speculated that people “decades or even centuries from now” would look back not only on the tapestry itself but on “what we did here today” – the very fact of its loan to theBritish Museum– as being a significant marker in the long span of Franco-British relations. “Two countries which, after centuries of shared history, [chose] to forge a bond as close as the threads of this thousand-year-old embroidery,” he said.The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earthRead moreThe latest UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, agreed in language tailored to suit his own political project. As a “tremendous demonstration of goodwill”, he said, the loan “says so much about the friendship of our two nations … It shows the power of collaboration to lift people’s lives.”TheBayeux tapestry, of course, was always a highly political artefact, even before it acquired its status as a foundational text for the English nation (1066, the date of the Battle of Hastings, is “the nation’s pincode”, the British Museum chair, George Osborne, noted drily on Wednesday).Much remains unknown about the circumstances of its commission and creation, but a vast artwork showing a clash of kings and wholesale invasion of a nation is not a neutral object. “It was definitely designed with a political purpose in mind when it was first made,” says the historian Dr David Musgrove, who has written a book,The Story of the Bayeux Tapestry, with Prof Michael Lewis, the curator of the exhibition.“That political purpose was essentially to legitimise the invasion of William the Conqueror, to explain why he did it, why he chose to send his fleet across the Channel,” argues Musgrove, who is the content director ofHistoryExtramagazine and podcast. The “crux scene”, he argues, is not the famous bit where Harold takes an arrow to the eye, but an earlier portion that shows the then English earl Harold making an oath to support William’s future claim to the English throne.View image in fullscreenMost historians believe the tapestry was made in Canterbury.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianHarold reneges on this later when he has himself crowned king of England. “So he perjures himself and that gives William the reason to invade,” Musgrove says. “My take is that the tapestry is entirely predicated on making that justification. So it’s very modern in that sense; people trying to justify military action today is kind of the same thing. It’s a retrospective justification for what happened.”Most historians believe it was made in Canterbury, but “just about everything around [the tapestry’s creation] is a little bit uncertain”, according to Leonie Hicks, a professor of medieval studies at Canterbury Christ Church University. She says historians’ “best assumption” – based on the internal evidence of the embroidery itself and other contemporary documents – “is that it was likely commissioned by Bishop Odo, who was William the Conqueror’s half-brother, bishop of Bayeux and also earl of Kent after the conquest. Or somebody very close to Odo.”Odo and Willliam had fallen out, so an elaborate narrative wall covering at Odo’s Norman cathedral celebrating the new English king could be seen as an attempt to regain favour. But if the tapestry undoubtedly flatters William, it is not a piece of crude propaganda, argues Hicks, and the politics of its depiction are nuanced. “It’s not a straightforward piece of ‘Yay, aren’t the Normans great, they dumped the English and took the throne.’”Among the most intriguing details, she notes, are the depictions in the margins of the human cost of war – all stitched, most likely, by English women who may have lost husbands and sons in the battle. “We have the scene where a house is being burnt and a woman is holding a child’s hand and leaving the house. [There are] very graphic depictions in the margins of decapitated soldiers, and bodies being looted. It does give that sense that war is horrific and terrible.”It is context which, we can assume, was lost during the tapestry’s long afterlife. History records nothing about it until it turns up inan inventory of the Bayeux Cathedraltreasury in 1476. The tapestry, it noted, was hung around the cathedral for a few days each year. During the French Revolution it was narrowly rescued from being used as a wagon cover.It would not be long, however, before the tapestry’s political usefulness would again be recognised. Napoleon, planning an English invasion of his own in 1803, displayed it in Paris where “it was quite a sensation”, says Musgrove. “I think Napoleon probably thought it was useful to have an artefact which showed a previous cross-Channel invasion by forces fromFranceinto Britain.” When the invasion plans foundered, the tapestry was quietly returned to Bayeux.The Nazis were “obsessed” with the tapestry – “they basically saw it as part of their worldview of Aryan Teutonic supremacy”, says Musgrove – and in the days before the liberation of Parisplanned to whisk it awayto Germany. They were, however, frustrated by the French resistance, who had been alerted by codebreakers at Bletchley Park.Eight quiet decades followed before the renovation of the museum where it is housed in Bayeux prompted its removal from display. But if that immediate circumstance opened the possibility of the artwork being loaned to Britain, there was certainly no inevitability that this would happen.Britain first made a request almost a century ago, in 1931. A request to borrow the artwork in 1953 to mark Elizabeth II’s coronation wasinitially agreedby France, before it reversed the decision over conservation concerns. Another attempt in 1966, to commemorate 900 years since the battle, foundered in the face of local and national French opposition. Another bid in the 1980s came to nothing.View image in fullscreenThe Labour MP Lisa Nandy, accompanied by the British Museum chair, George Osborne, views the tapestry.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianMacron could easily have come to the same judgment, not least because there wasplenty of oppositionin France to the loan, including fromartistsand conservation experts. Why, then, such commitment to making happen a loan which, heonly half jokedlast year, had been more complicated to negotiate than the Brexit withdrawal agreements?ToHelen Drake, a professor of French and European studies at Loughborough University London, making the loan happen fits with Macron’s view of himself as a cultured international statesman – but also with the value he attaches to repairing the Franco-British relationship in the face of mutually threatening global forces.“Macron is a French president who has pulled the maximum levers that the constitution give him to operate on the international stage, and that will probably be his legacy. So from that perspective it would make sense to him to be seen to be behind the transfer of the tapestry.“But he has also very much made it part of his mandate to be at the forefront of ameliorating France’s relations with the UK.” On Ukraine, defence and security, migration and Trump, British and French shared interests have become ever more pressing, she says. “The external environment, to put it bluntly, has pushed the two together.”But for all the genuine bonhomie over a dazzling piece of history, Drake says, neither side has any illusions about the dynamic tension that has always characterised theirlove-hate relationship. “The fact is that France habitually plays hardball with the UK in its negotiations with the EU post-Brexit,” she says. “You can have all the warmth you like in the British Museum, [but] the Quai d’Orsay will still drive a hard bargain. The two co-exist and they’re not even contradictory – they’re just part of how we see the Franco-British relationship.”

title: ‘I wasn’t even listening,’ Farage says of donations scandal meeting  | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Reform UK leader maintains innocence in overseas funding controversy on last day of party conference
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Reform UK leader maintains innocence in overseas funding controversy on last day of party conference
Content: Farage’s party had been hoping to move the focus to policy announcements as Reform’s conference closed in Birmingham on Saturday.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFarage’s party had been hoping to move the focus to policy announcements as Reform’s conference closed in Birmingham on Saturday.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianNigel Farage‘I wasn’t even listening,’ Farage says of donations scandal meetingReform UK leader maintains innocence in overseas funding controversy on last day of party conferenceBen QuinnandPeter WalkerSat 5 Sep 2026 12.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage has claimed that he “wasn’t even listening” during a meeting at the centre of a controversy about whether his party considered evading the law on accepting donations from overseas.TheReform UKleader also claimed he knew donation law “better than anybody” during interviews as he sought to salvage the final day of his party conference from the fallout that has already cost him two of his closest aides.The two-year trail of financial controversy dogging Reform and FarageRead moreFarage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes andReform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigationappearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.The undercover reporters from a group called Verbatim posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party when it was published in national newspapers.The Reform leader himself remains under pressure over a separate clip in which he was heard saying “it’s all above board” after one of the reporters who was posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy US backer told Farage he had been in discussions with Jukes and Orr for some time.“I’ll be the registered donor,” the son says. “But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that’s done and all those conversations are had the money is available.”In an interview on Saturday, Farage told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that “of course” he knew it was illegal for foreign firms to donate to UK parties, adding he was told the money was being given via a UK family office.When challenged by Kuenssberg that while in Farage’s presence, one of the undercover reporters had said they “run an American family office”, the Reform leader said: “I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton byelection. I turn up. I frankly wasn’t even listening.”He added: “I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore. The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have come from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.”Farage’s party had been hoping to move the focus to policy announcements, including on tax cuts, as Reform’s conference closed in Birmingham on Saturday.View image in fullscreenReform MP Robert Jenrick addresses the conferencePhotograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianIts Treasury spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, gave a keynote speech in which he pledged to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 within the first 100 days if the party were to take office. The threshold has been set at £12,570 since 2021 and is due to remain there until 2031.But in interviews given earlier in the day to trail the policy, he also found himself forced to deflect from the donations controversy. “That’s been dealt with,” he told GB News. “The two individuals concerned have gone, and we’re here today moving forward. The language that they used was clearly inappropriate, that was very disappointing.”In an interview with Times Radio he said Orr and Jukes had been “permanently suspended”, appearing to differ from the latest party line that they had “stepped down pending outcome of an investigation”, indicating a possible way back.Farage meanwhile accused “the establishment” of trying to derail Reform UK, when challenged by ITV’s Robert Peston on thestring of allegations related to his and the party’s finances.“And it will go on. You come back and see me in six months, there’ll be five more investigations. It won’t end. This won’t end,” he said.Farage said he had some “thoughtful” moments over the summer, claiming his family had been asking him to “walk away” from politics amid pressure on them and him.Despite Reform’s efforts to insulate Farage, the Met police are now assessing evidence after a complaint that the Reform leader, as well as Orr and Jukes,may have broken political funding laws. They all deny wrongdoing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe final day of the conference also coincided with an appeal by West Midlands police for a woman, who was among climate activists who were removed from the hall on Friday as they heckled Farage’s speech, to come forward after footage emerged over her allegedly being assaulted.The police initially responded on X to a clip that appeared to show audience members pulling her hair and grabbing her head as she was carried out of the conference hall. West Midlands police later said in a statement that they were aware of a video circulating from the Reform UK conference showing an incident with a protester, and had asked the woman to come forward.The activist group Climate Resistance, which claimed responsibility for the protest during Farage’s speech , said the protester was considering whether to speak to police.View image in fullscreenA heckler is carried out during Nigel Farage’s keynote speech on the second day of Reform UK Annual Conference at NEC in Birmingham, Britain, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPANadine Dorries, a former Conservative MP who has joined Reform, said sensitivities were “heightened” in the aftermath of the killing of the Reform spokesperson Ann Widdecombe in July.“They tried to completely derail the speech. It was an organised sting again,” she said in an interview with LBC when asked about the incident.Also speaking on Saturday was Suella Braverman, the party’s education spokesperson who, like Jenrick, is another defector from the Conservatives.Her speech announced a planned cut of 20% to the number of student loans given, with funds only granted to university courses that can demonstrate good economic returns, with exceptions for some courses “of strategic or cultural importance”.View image in fullscreenThe Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, closed the conference with some final comments.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianFarage ended the conference with closing comments to the main hall, where sections of seating were unoccupied and the mood was more subdued than earlier in the event, by telling the Reform faithful that “there would be good days and bad days”.“Sometimes we will get things wrong and get a bit of a kicking, but what this conference has shown is that whatever you throw at the leadership, whatever you throw at you, the people’s army, we immediately stop, pick ourselves up and start all over again,” he said.Get in touchContact Guardian Politics about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject you can contact the Guardian's UK Politics team confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Scroll down and click onSecure Messaging. When asked who you wish to contact please select thePolitics (UK)team.EmailFor encrypted email correspondence you can create a free Proton Mail account and email us at guardian.politics.desk@protonmail.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKnewsShareReuse this content

title: Putin begins talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on ending war with Ukraine | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Moscow and Kyiv vow not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during negotiations
Author: William Christou
Headline: Moscow and Kyiv vow not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during negotiations
Content: The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, welcomes Jared Kushner (left) and US envoy Steve Witkoff (second left) to the Kremlin.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/Kremlin/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Russian president, Vladimir Putin, welcomes Jared Kushner (left) and US envoy Steve Witkoff (second left) to the Kremlin.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/Kremlin/EPAUkrainePutin begins talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on ending war with UkraineMoscow and Kyiv vow not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during negotiationsWilliam Christouand agencySat 5 Sep 2026 18.13 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 10.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussian presidentVladimir Putinbegan talks with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the Kremlin on Saturday – aimed at ending more than four years of war in Ukraine, ahead of the pair’s first visit to Kyiv expected on Sunday.Both Russia andUkrainevowed not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during the negotiations, as Washington tries to revive US-led talks to end Europe’s worst conflict since the second world war.The visit came asDonald Trumpsuggested on Friday a new proposal to end the war, without providing any details on what his new plan might be. Trump made ending the war a priority early in his second term, but little has changed so far.Trump said his son-in-law Kushner and business ally Witkoff were bringing “a proposal to end the war”.“Dear colleagues, I warmly welcome you to Moscow. The situation is, of course, not simple,” Putin told the envoys in a grand Kremlin hall in footage aired by Russian TV. “But before we begin to address it, I would like to ask everyone to convey their best wishes and words of gratitude to US president Mr Trump.”The talks come as the grinding war, launched by Russia in 2022, saw increasing civilian deaths and attacks this summer. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine. The war has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.Russian strikes on Ukraine on Saturday killed at least seven people, including in the Kyiv suburbs, Ukrainian officials said.The Kremlin said it would not strike Kyiv from midnight on Saturday, while the Ukrainian president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he would halt strikes on Moscow “from now” until Monday.“The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight tonight not to strike Kyiv for three days,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said.Zelenskyy, who had offered a truce during the US visits, later said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow,” he said on social media.He said he had spoken to the US officials and that he expected them in Kyiv on Sunday.Europe would not be able to sustain war of attrition with Russia, defence officials sayRead moreLarge gaps remain between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the war. On Friday, the Kremlin said it was sticking by the position Putin set out two years earlier – that Ukraine should give up four regions claimed by Russia and not join Nato. That position is intolerable to Ukraine.As peace efforts floundered in recent months, with US attention turned to its war with Iran, the conflict has intensified.Ground troops have been locked in a grinding stalemate along the 775-mile (1,250km) frontline with little advances on either side. Both sides have intensified their aerial attacks in recent weeks, hitting increasingly distant targets.Ukraine has carried out long-range strikes on Russian military facilities,oil refineriesand e-commerce warehouses, to try to degrade Russia’s war effort and economy. Its strikes on Russian oil refineries have led to fuel shortages and rising prices at the pump.On Friday, a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), one of the agencies responsible for carrying out deep-strike operations in Russia. Zelenskyy has vowed to retaliate. Russia has also increased its attacks on Kyiv and other cities with waves of bombardments, stretching Ukraine’s air defence systems.Officials visiting Ukraine have largely done so by train, as Ukrainian airspace has been closed since 2022 due to the war.Russia had earlier struck Kyiv suburbs, reportedly killing two people in the Bucha district. Another attack on the Dnipro region killed five people and wounded five more at a factory, according to the local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha.He said those killed were employees working at the factory who were “doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives”. A 62-year-old man was injured and several homes and a building were damaged in another attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said.Russia also struck a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging the building and injuring a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl. Emergency services said they were repeatedly forced to withdraw because of the threat of more strikes.Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 drones overnight, including jet-powered UAVs. Ukrainian air defences disabled 128 of the drones, the air force said.Russia’s defence ministry said it had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.Explore more on these topicsUkraineJared KushnerUS foreign policyTrump administrationRussiaVladimir PutinUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thousands of jobs to be cut at Jaguar Land Rover after slump in profits | Jaguar Land Rover | The Guardian
description: As many as 4,000 positions could go over two years after cyber-attack and US tariffs take toll
Author: Angus Thomson
Headline: As many as 4,000 positions could go over two years after cyber-attack and US tariffs take toll
Content: A technician works on the production line at Jaguar Land Rover’s factory in Solihull.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenA technician works on the production line at Jaguar Land Rover’s factory in Solihull.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersJaguar Land RoverThousands of jobs to be cut at Jaguar Land Rover after slump in profitsAs many as 4,000 positions could go over two years after cyber-attack and US tariffs take tollAngus ThomsonSat 5 Sep 2026 17.42 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of workers atJaguar Land Rover(JLR) will be offered redundancies after Britain’s largest car manufacturer had its revenues slashed by falling sales, a cyber-attack and Donald Trump’s tariffs.JLR informed workers and their union on Saturday that the company would be opening a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members, the BBC and Sunday Times reported.As many as 4,000 jobs would be cut over two years, the Times reported. JLR told the BBC it was yet to confirm the number but the company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years.Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, told the BBC she and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would meet JLR’s chief executive, PB Balaji, next week, after a weekend of intensive talks to mitigate job losses.About 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK. Most of them work at 14 plants across the West Midlands, where the company is one of the region’s largest employers.Range Rover launches its first electric vehicle, with starting price of £154,070Read moreThe job cuts will be unwelcome news for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who has pledged to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” andreindustrialise Britain.Under his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Labour said it wouldunderwrite a £1.5bn loan guaranteeto JLR after it halted production for several weeks last year in response to a cyber-attack.The attack led to a 27% drop in overall production and cost the company about £200m. It was one of several factors contributing to JLRposting a profit before tax of just £14m– down from £2.5bn the year before.Tariffs on vehicles imported into the US – whichTrump raised to 25%before agreeing adeal for 10%for the UK – also caused turmoil for the carmaker, which is attempting to push more luxury cars to the US market. This contributed to the company’s retail and wholesale volumes – sales via dealerships – falling by about 70,000 and 90,000 respectively.“These challenges arrived with the global automotive industry already under continued pressure from cost inflation, slower-than-expected uptake of electric vehicles, and the deterioration of market conditions in China,” Balaji said in the company’s annual report published in May.The carmaker this week launched its first electric Range Rover in an effort to appeal to climate-conscious fans of the luxury SUV – at a starting price of £154,070.Explore more on these topicsJaguar Land RoverAutomotive industryRedundancyWork & careersnewsShareReuse this content

title: London Paddington fire causes rail chaos as Heathrow trains cancelled | Public transport | The Guardian
description: Blaze causes electricity supply failure and disruption of services to airport and Reading
Author: Angus Thomson
Headline: Blaze causes electricity supply failure and disruption of services to airport and Reading
Content: Passengers in Paddington station, London after a fire near a train track in the area caused major disruption.Photograph: Mathilde Grandjean/PAView image in fullscreenPassengers in Paddington station, London after a fire near a train track in the area caused major disruption.Photograph: Mathilde Grandjean/PAPublic transportLondon Paddington fire causes rail chaos as Heathrow trains cancelledBlaze causes electricity supply failure and disruption of services to airport and ReadingAngus Thomsonand agencySat 5 Sep 2026 18.18 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 14.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of passengers were evacuated from a train, and services to Heathrow airport were cancelled, after a fire near tracks in theLondonPaddington area caused major disruptions to London’s rail network.The fire caused an electricity supply failure which left all lines between Paddington and the airport blocked, National Rail said on Saturday afternoon.Photographs on social media showed large plumes of smoke rising from the Paddington area.London fire brigade was called to the grass fire near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington, just after 4pm on Saturday, with six fire engines and 40 crew tackling the blaze.Fire crews were also called upon to help evacuate 380 passengers left stranded on an Elizabeth line train.The Elizabeth line was suspended between Paddington and Heathrow Terminals 4 and 5, and between Paddington and Reading, while the line to Abbey Wood also experienced severe delays.Passengers travelling to the airport were advised to use the Piccadilly line, although that line also experienced severe delays between Heathrow and Acton Town. There were minor delays along the rest of the line due to an earlier trespasser at Hammersmith,Transportfor London (TfL) said.Heathrow airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys.Great Western Railway (GWR) services to Reading were cancelled, and disruptions were expected until the end of Saturday.Explore more on these topicsPublic transportTransportLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Black-clad protesters in balaclavas block road at port of Dover in Kent | Kent | The Guardian
description: Port authorities say access roads ‘free flowing’ again after large group forces road closures in both directions
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Port authorities say access roads ‘free flowing’ again after large group forces road closures in both directions
Content: Balaclava-wearing protesters blocking a road in Dover on Saturday.Photograph: SWNSView image in fullscreenBalaclava-wearing protesters blocking a road in Dover on Saturday.Photograph: SWNSKentBlack-clad protesters in balaclavas block road at port of Dover in KentPort authorities say access roads ‘free flowing’ again after large group forces road closures in both directionsDonna Ferguson,Priya Bharadiaand agenciesSat 5 Sep 2026 15.57 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 04.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDozens of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road at the port of Dover inKent, forcing closures in both directions on Saturday morning.Kent police said they were were in attendance and engaging with the protest, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. No arrests were made during the incident. Responsibility for the demonstration appears to have been claimed by an anti-immigration group with links to the far right.The behaviour of the participants and the travel disruption they have caused has been condemned by the government. Traffic in and out of the port on the A20 was stopped, causing delays of up to 30 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways.Videos shared online showed a large number ofmasked people in black marching on the road in a large group as lorries waited in traffic next to police cars.By lunchtime, the protesters had dispersed and access roads to the port were “free flowing”, according to the Port of Dover. Ferry operators pledged to put those who had been delayed by the disruption on to the next available sailings.View image in fullscreenMasked people on the road in Dover.Photograph: Ay_audits/YouTubeThe number of people involved was not immediately clear. One livestreamer estimated he was marching with hundreds of people but police did not give an official estimate.Social media videos showed demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20 and chanting “stop the boats”and “England till I die.”A group called Patriot Platform, which styles itself as having “a fierce love for our homeland”, claimed responsibility for the blockade.The far-right activistTommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, reposted videos of the blockade, highlighting a live stream of the protest that directed viewers towards Patriot Platform.In his post, Robinson encouraged more to join, saying: “Get there to support them.”In another post, he wrote: “Simultaneously at different locations across Dover patriots have mobilised to close down the port. There are 3 plus locations that patriots have shut down so far with many more planned to be closed. People wanted action I’m guessing there are 100,000s of men willing to fill their shoes.”Map including DoverThe founder of Patriot Platform, Danny Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, wrote on social media “live Dover somethings [sic] happening” and posted a live stream.In a video posted on 2 September, he told his followers he was meeting with “a huge group [of] top, proper patriots” to prepare for a message he was planning to send to the government.“Very, very soon, we are going to send a message that will make sure they understand that we will not go down without a fight. We will not allow our nation to be plagued in the way that it is.“And when you see it and when you feel it, I guarantee the whole thing will change for the better. Because once the message is sent once, imagine the sheer numbers that will be sent on the second, the third, the fourth message.”In further comments, he said: “From the hills of Scotland to the fields of Wales to the streets of Northern Ireland and to the towns and cities of England, we are building something that’s never been built before.“And when you’re part of it and you see what’s about to go down, you will understand … we’re about to show you what can be done when men and women of this country, who have the blood that runs through them like their grandfathers, get off their asses and do something about it.”View image in fullscreenBalaclava-wearing protesters gather earlier on Saturday.Photograph: Ay_audits/YouTubeOn Saturday morning, the Port of Dover confirmed in a statement that the disruption was affecting “all routes” in and out, as well as around the town.Nathan Ditchburn, who was on his way to work when he saw the group arrive at about 6.45am, told KentOnline: “I would say there are around 300 men, maybe more. Nobody will speak; they just handed me a piece of paper to look at. They have blocked off every entrance and exit of the Dover port area.”One woman, who asked to remain anonymous, said: “I was at Dover port this morning, trying to get on a ferry to France. In the end we left and returned home – it wasn’t worth our while, we were only going to Lille for the day.“But the headlines calling it a ‘protest’ suggest something very different to what took place – which looked like a highly organised event.“Masked teenagers in black clothes were coordinated by walkie-talkie and I directly witnessed an older man, not in black, on an electric bike – coordinating in plain sight and being applauded by the masked teenagers as he gave them the thumbs up for their ‘good work’.“The guy on the bike then went to the nearest police stop, [he was] obviously monitoring and reporting police activity.“There were no banners and no slogans, just pure intimidation. It was a demonstration only in the sense that they wanted to demonstrate their power and to intimidate.”Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, criticised what he described as “idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption”. In a post on Facebook, he said: “Parkrun cancelled and port access disrupted. I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption.“I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossings are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess. Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.”Chris Vinson, the leader of the Conservative group on Dover district council, said the protest appeared to be “illegal migration-related”, but said the demonstrators did not appear to have placards or banners.“I’m not aware that there’s been any violence, although clearly, having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating, especially when it’s not clear why they’re there, and the police weren’t aware and so haven’t been able to warn people in advance and make sure that they are made to feel safe.”A Home Office spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused.“We appreciate the frustration of those who have been impacted today. Access to the port is now restored and traffic is flowing. Those travelling to the port are advised to allow for extra travel time and to follow guidance from providers.”The shipping company DFDS and P&O Ferries said they would offer customers whose journeys were disrupted access to the next available departure.Explore more on these topicsKentTransportProtestTommy RobinsonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Prince William to represent King Charles at funeral of Norway’s King Harald V | Monarchy | The Guardian
description: Duty falls by precedent to William to attend service of late monarch, alongside Princess Royal, who is godmother to new king Haakon VIII
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Duty falls by precedent to William to attend service of late monarch, alongside Princess Royal, who is godmother to new king Haakon VIII
Content: Members of Norway’s royal family including Queen Sonja (left), King Haakon VIII and Queen Mette-Marit (foreground) lay flowers in Oslo’s Palace Square on 31 August, three days after the death of King Harald.Photograph: Cornelius Poppe/EPAView image in fullscreenMembers of Norway’s royal family including Queen Sonja (left), King Haakon VIII and Queen Mette-Marit (foreground) lay flowers in Oslo’s Palace Square on 31 August, three days after the death of King Harald.Photograph: Cornelius Poppe/EPAMonarchyPrince William to represent King Charles at funeral of Norway’s King Harald VDuty falls by precedent to William to attend service of late monarch, alongside Princess Royal, who is godmother to new king Haakon VIIIPress AssociationSat 5 Sep 2026 18.11 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Prince of Wales is to represent his father at the funeral of King Harald V ofNorwaynext week, Buckingham Palace has announced.William, the heir to the throne, will be joined by his aunt the Princess Royal, who is attending in a private and personal capacity as godmother of the new king, Haakon VIII.Norway has seen an outpouring of grief for the much-loved late monarch, who died on 28 August at the age of 89.Harald has been hailed as an inclusive “people’s king” who modernised the Norwegian monarchy during his 35-year reign.View image in fullscreenKing Harald of Norway escorting Princess Catherine, then Duchess of Cambridge, to a dinner at the Royal Palace in Oslo in February 2018.Photograph: Ntb Scanpix/ReutersHis funeral will take place on 9 September at Oslo Cathedral, with mourners including his widow, Sonja, now the queen mother.In keeping with precedent that the sovereign does not attend funerals of other heads of state, the duty falls to William, a future king, to represent his father and pay his respects at the service.Charles paid a touching tribute to his “dear cousin” and “much-loved kinsman and friend” after the news of Harald’s death was announced.In a message of condolence, he praised Harald’s “unwavering dedication” and his “kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades”.The late Queen Elizabeth II and King Harald were second cousins. They shared the same great-grandparents, King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra.View image in fullscreenKing Harald V’s coffin is carried to Oslo’s Palace Chapel by members of the royal family including (at front) Haakon VIII and Queen Mette-Marit.Photograph: Ole Berg-Rusten/EPAIn April last year, William represented his father atthe funeral of Pope Francisin the Vatican.William and the now Princess of Wales carried out an official tour to Norway in 2018, dining with King Harald and Queen Sonja at the Royal Palace, where Harald described them as “family” and praised their support of the then Queen.The Norwegian sovereign processed into the banquet arm in arm with the pregnant Catherine, who was expecting Prince Louis and wearing a flowing Alexander McQueen gown, with the gesture mirrored by Sonja and William who walked behind them.William and Kate also spent time visiting the ski slopes with the then Crown Prince Haakon and Crown Princess Mette-Marit, now the King and Queen.Explore more on these topicsMonarchyNorwayPrince WilliamEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime | Egypt | The Guardian
description: Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs
Content: Sarah Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and an event production company.View image in fullscreenSarah Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and an event production company.EgyptEgyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crimeSarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugsAFP in CairoSat 5 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 19.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.The verdict is subject to appeal.Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.Explore more on these topicsEgyptAfricaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Ministers plan to slash paperwork rules for small UK businesses | Small business | The Guardian
description: Business secretary looks to simplify corporate reporting rules and exempt some SMEs from certain form-filling
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Business secretary looks to simplify corporate reporting rules and exempt some SMEs from certain form-filling
Content: The business department said it was ‘nonsensical’ for small businesses to have to conduct detailed paperwork when they should be focused on their day-to-day trade.Photograph: Reeldeal Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe business department said it was ‘nonsensical’ for small businesses to have to conduct detailed paperwork when they should be focused on their day-to-day trade.Photograph: Reeldeal Images/AlamySmall businessMinisters plan to slash paperwork rules for small UK businessesBusiness secretary looks to simplify corporate reporting rules and exempt some SMEs from certain form-fillingPress AssociationSat 5 Sep 2026 18.39 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe amount of paperwork businesses are required to regularly carry out could be slashed, the business secretary has announced.Jonathan Reynolds said he plans to simplify corporate reporting rules and exempt some small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) from the need to carry out certain form-filling exercises altogether.The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said the corporate reporting changes could save businesses across the UK £450m.It added that it was “nonsensical” for small businesses, including cafes, hotels and furniture makers, to have to conduct the detailed paperwork when they should be focused on their day-to-day trade.The department claimed the average annual report and accounts of some businesses now run to 98,000 words, and compared it to the length of JRR Tolkien’s fantasy novel The Hobbit, which is more than 95,300 words.The average count is said to be even higher for FTSE 100 companies, at 152,000 words.“No one goes into business to fill out forms,” said Reynolds.“For years, hardworking firms in this country have been weighed down by pen-pushing paperwork and frustrating costs, ticking boxes that do nothing to help them grow their business.“We’re stripping back outdated bureaucracy and building a commonsense system fit for a 21st-century economy.“This will cut the cost of doing business, giving breathing room to bosses across the country and free them up to focus on what they do best, creating jobs and growth.”A consultation into the plans begins on 7 September.Explore more on these topicsSmall businessEconomic policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Richard Osman lets slip Celebrity Traitors season 2 launch date | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: Presenter reveals ‘absolutely embargoed’ start date during live podcast, and describes new series as ‘quite intense’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Presenter reveals ‘absolutely embargoed’ start date during live podcast, and describes new series as ‘quite intense’
Content: Richard Osman (seen here at the 2026 Bafta awards) was speaking at a live edition of his The Rest Is Entertainment podcast.Photograph: Tristan Fewings/Getty Images for BaftaView image in fullscreenRichard Osman (seen here at the 2026 Bafta awards) was speaking at a live edition of his The Rest Is Entertainment podcast.Photograph: Tristan Fewings/Getty Images for BaftaThe TraitorsRichard Osman lets slip Celebrity Traitors season 2 launch datePresenter reveals ‘absolutely embargoed’ start date during live podcast, and describes new series as ‘quite intense’Press AssociationSat 5 Sep 2026 18.51 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe TV presenterRichard Osmanhas appeared to accidentally reveal the launch date for series 2 of The Celebrity Traitors.During a live edition of The Rest Is Entertainment podcast, which he hosts with the journalist Marina Hyde, at London’s Southbank Centre on Saturday, the 55-year-old said the new series of the BBC reality gameshow would begin on 23 September.The pair were joined by a special guest, the former Celebrity Traitors finalist Joe Marler, who when speaking about the advice he would give new contestants, said: “What is it, September 23, the next series?”To which Osman confirmed: “By the way, to point out, it’s absolutely embargoed that it starts on September 23 … let’s talk about what we call the events of September 23 this year … the cat’s out of the bag isn’t it? Not to repeat it.”Osman also said that from what he had heard from those involved, the new series “sounds like it was quite intense”.Marler added: “I believe it was a slightly different emotion than our experience. Ours was very laugh-led, and everyone was sort of enjoying catching up, you know, pratting about to the point where they went: ‘Guys, we’re trying to play a game.’“It’s not just for the laughs – ‘Oh, do you remember going to that party, darling?…’“Whereas this lot really want it from the start, and then I guess they see how well the first series has gone and there’s a little bit of pressure on them to be like: ‘Oh I’d quite like a bit of that.’”Official lineup confirmed for second series of The Celebrity TraitorsRead moreThe Celebrity Traitors will return to screens with a new batch of 21 celebrities who will face one another for the chance to win a cash prize of up to £100,000 for a charity of their choice.Set in a Scottish castle in the Highlands, the game follows the celebrity contestants – the majority of whom are known as faithfuls – as they try to seek out the murderous traitors among them, who kill off players in the middle of the night.The first series of The Celebrity Traitors aired on the BBC last autumn, with its nail-biting finale hitting a peak of 15.4 million viewers, according to the broadcaster.It featured a star-studded cast including the actors Celia Imrie and Nick Mohammed, the singer Paloma Faith, the author and actor Stephen Fry, the broadcaster Jonathan Ross and the comedian Alan Carr,who went on to win as a Traitor.The spin-off series brought in an average audience of 14.9 million people during its run – the biggest TV audience of 2025.The BBC has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsRichard OsmanTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Grief becomes a routine’: Farhana lost five babies. A ‘culture of silence’ exacerbated her pain  | Miscarriage | The Guardian
description: A first-of-its-kind study shows the prevalence of miscarriage in Australia, but experts fear multicultural groups remain underrepresented
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: A first-of-its-kind study shows the prevalence of miscarriage in Australia, but experts fear multicultural groups remain underrepresented
Content: ‘Maybe miscarriage isn’t the worst thing that’s ever happened to anyone ever, but it was the worst thing that had ever happened to me’ … Farhana Laffernis at her home in western Sydney.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Maybe miscarriage isn’t the worst thing that’s ever happened to anyone ever, but it was the worst thing that had ever happened to me’ … Farhana Laffernis at her home in western Sydney.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianMiscarriage‘Grief becomes a routine’: Farhana lost five babies. A ‘culture of silence’ exacerbated her painA first-of-its-kind study shows the prevalence of miscarriage in Australia, but experts fear multicultural groups remain underrepresentedFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAchol ArokSat 5 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a quiet street in westernSydney, Farhana Laffernis races her curious English staffy and boisterous three-year-old daughter in the front door.Inside, her three-year-old wears a pink tutu and excitedly babbles as she cuddles her toy doll. The family life Laffernis has built did not come easy.The 34-year-old has experienced five miscarriages. For someone who “always wanted to be a mum”, the experience “completely shattered” her.“Grief almost becomes practised or like a routine. You still feel the sting of it every time it happens,” she says. “It’s almost like your mind and your body know the drill.”After several miscarriages – each with its own trauma – my husband and I were forced to cobble together a new life | Tess PryorRead moreLaffernis isn’t alone. Three in 10 women who gave birth in 2022 had previously experienced miscarriage, meaning pregnancy loss before 20 weeks’ gestation, according to the Australian Institute ofHealthand Welfare. One in 10 had experienced two or more.The data comes from a first-of-its-kind study in Australia,heralded for helping create better understanding of the prevalence of early pregnancy loss. The study came about after a years-long push by Isabelle Oderberg, founder of peak advocacy group the Early Pregnancy Loss Coalition (EPLC), who was concerned about substandard care for women who had miscarriagesafter experiencing seven losses herself.Currently, there is no requirement for doctors to report miscarriage, meaning the data is not collected.But while the new study has been welcomed, experts fear the data does not capture large groups of women, particularly those from multicultural backgrounds – like Laffernis. And they say the lack of data could mean diverse families are missing out on services they desperately need.‘The worst thing that had ever happened to me’Laffernis’s first miscarriage occurred eight weeks into her first pregnancy. It was during the height of the Covid-19 lockdowns, and she couldn’t have her partner with her at any of her appointments and scans.“It was the first time in my life that I’d ever experienced anything like that, or felt real grief and loss before,” she says. “I was getting all of this terrible news pretty much on my own and having to kind of process that and figure it out.”That was the first of two miscarriages Laffernis had before successfully conceiving her daughter through IVF. She remembers being “so terrified the whole way through”.“It seems like everywhere you turn, someone is having this, like, blissful ignorant pregnancy where nothing can possibly go wrong … I could not have that, I just could not be that blissful, relaxed, unaware pregnant woman.”Another three pregnancy losses after her daughter’s birth marked “the end of the road” in her attempts to have more children.For Laffernis, who comes from a migrant Indian family, the pain of the miscarriages was exacerbated by a reluctance within her family to talk about what was happening.“When I was talking to my own family about my losses, the first one was sort of ‘bad luck’, the second one was like ‘Oh, that’s a little bit of extra bad luck’… but then it happens like five times and you kind of just like stop telling people at that point.“I think in a lot of migrant families, or at least in my experience … there is that sort of mentality in a lot of our communities where our parents have come over [to Australia] from less than ideal circumstances,” she says.“Maybe miscarriage isn’t the worst thing that’s ever happened to anyone ever, but it was the worst thing that had ever happened to me.”After years to trying to avoid conflict around the “deeply upsetting” interactions, she had to confront her family about the support she needed.“I went for a long time just sort of trying not to have the argument before it all just honestly got to me. I did have to have some really hard conversations with members of my family about exactly what it was that I needed from them at this time in my life,” she says.View image in fullscreenFarhana Laffernis says she hopes to see greater awareness filter through the medical system, normalising conversations about pregnancy loss.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianThat reluctance to talk about miscarriage within migrant families is something Dr Fatima El-Assaad has seen many times before.“It’s something that’s considered very icky to talk about,” says El-Assaad, who founded Sydney-based The Still Nest, a platform supporting diverse families affected by infertility, pregnancy loss, birth trauma and infant loss.She says cultural and religious practices tied to a women’s fertility journey “may make them feel like it is not in the public arena” and “like it’s something that is meant to be kept behind closed doors”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile she is encouraged to see data on miscarriage come to light, she questions how representative it is of culturally and linguistically diverse families – and worries that a culture of silence, compounded by the way the data is collected, could be contributing to “a number of holes in the picture”.double quotation markI don’t think there’s anything that can prepare you for what happens … it’s what happens next that makes the differenceFarhana LaffernisThe data was collected using existing surveys and clinical registries compiled by midwives and other birth attendants. El-Assaad says flaws in the system could be leading to significant gaps and inaccuracies in the data.“Are [surveys] primarily in English? Is there a translator that is trauma-informed? … How was the survey conducted? … Where was it captured? Was it in a clinic? Was it at home on a personal device? Was the place safe?” she says, listing factors that can affect the process.“And we’re also asking culturally and racially marginalised people, and culturally and linguistically diverse people, to just voluntarily answer a survey on top of all the other issues that they’re currently dealing with.”The problems with the gapsAlthough miscarriage is “the most common pregnancy complication”, there’s a lack of healthcare and social support – and Australia is “so far behind”, Oderberg says.Allanah lost her son when she was 22 weeks pregnant. Now she’s helping others through the grief of stillbirthRead more“We had no idea how many people in Australia were experiencing miscarriage, whether it was going up, down, sideways,” she says. There was also a lack of information about high-priority groups, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women, newly arrived migrants, people whose second language is English, people from lower socioeconomic demographics.Oderberg says data directly helps governments understand what kind of support services the community needs and where.Assoc Prof Jade Bilardi fromMiscarriageAustralia says efforts to be inclusive must “go beyond” simply translating resources into different languages.“That’s a great first step, but it’s to work more with women, pregnant people, partners, family members, and support services that work directly with people from Cald backgrounds so that we can better understand what their needs are,” she says.Laffernis says she hopes to see greater awareness filter through the medical system, normalising conversations about pregnancy loss.“No one had really talked to me about the risk of miscarriage until it was already looking like that was what was happening. And then, once they had talked about the fact that it was likely to happen, it became about the fact that this happens to so many people and it’s so common,” she says.She also holds hopes to see a dedicated focus on post-miscarriage support, including mental health services, for all women.“I don’t think there’s really anything that can prepare you for what happens. I think it’s more what happens next that makes the difference.”In Australia, thenational maternal and perinatal mental health hotlineis 1300 726 306, and support for people who are grieving is available fromGrieflineon 1300 845 745. In the UK, thePandas foundationoffers support via Whatsapp on 07903 508334. In the US, call thenational maternal health hotlineon 1-833-852-6262.Explore more on these topicsMiscarriageHealthSydneyPregnancyWomen's healthHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Then who or what did we cremate?’ Daughter’s horror at finding bones in British wildfire victims’ car | UK news | The Guardian
description: Danielle Gillam-Kirton claims police botched investigation into her parents’ deaths in Spain and is demanding answers
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Danielle Gillam-Kirton claims police botched investigation into her parents’ deaths in Spain and is demanding answers
Content: Charred earth after a wildfire near the municipality of Bédar in Spain’s Almería province in July.Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCharred earth after a wildfire near the municipality of Bédar in Spain’s Almería province in July.Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty ImagesUK news‘Then who or what did we cremate?’ Daughter’s horror at finding bones in British wildfire victims’ carDanielle Gillam-Kirton claims police botched investigation into her parents’ deaths in Spain and is demanding answersHelena HortonSat 5 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 14.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Danielle Gillam-Kirton’s parents, Pete and Fran Gillam, were killed in July’s Spanish wildfires, she felt her nightmare could get no worse. The much-loved couple had built their home in Bédar in Almería after retirement, becoming part of a tight-knit community. Fran, a former headteacher, loved to organise quiz nights to raise money for the local school and the couple enjoyed playing padel at a nearby sports club.Spanish police told Gillam-Kirton that the vehicle in which her parents died had been “inspected meticulously” and no possessions had been found. But Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, was sure her parents must have been wearing their wedding rings when they died.She was invited to search the vehicle herself, which was parked in a police compound in Mojácar. “You won’t find anything,” she was told.Fran Gillam with her daughter Danielle Gillam-Kirton.Photograph: Danielle KirtonShe describes crying out in shock when she looked through the door of the burnt-out car. On the front seats was what appeared to be a human hip bone. “I honestly can’t describe what that felt like. I remember staring at what was in my hand, and the slow realisation of what I thought I was looking at hit me. I shouted out in shock,” she says.MapShe and her partner searched the car and found more bones, which appeared to be the remains of the couple. They also found her parents’ mobile phones, sets of keys, jewellery, money and other personal effects.The Gillams wereamong 14 people killed in the fires, including Belgian, French, American and Spanish nationals. Some of the bereaved familiesare now searching for answersand claim the Bédar authorities have botched the investigation into their deaths.View image in fullscreenThe names of villas amid Béjar’s burnt landscape.Photograph: Jorge Guerrero/AFP/Getty ImagesThere has already been a funeral for the Gillams. “It makes you wonder: who or what did we cremate?” Gillam-Kirton says. She is demanding answers from the Spanish government and asking the UK Foreign Office to hold the authorities to account.The bones she found have been sent for DNA testing after weeks of delay from the Bédar local authority. Forensic scientists who have looked at pictures of the bones have told Gillam-Kirton they appear to be human.“The whole sequence is incredibly difficult to understand. We were told there was nothing left, and yet when we were finally able to look ourselves, we found significant personal belongings and what appeared to be human remains,” she says.“We were initially told it was probably animal remains.” She says she had to push the Spanish authorities to send them off for DNA testing. “The bones were big. I can’t see how a large animal like a cow would have climbed into the passenger seat of the vehicle during a fire.”View image in fullscreenA Bédar house after July’s wildfires.Photograph: Ana Beltran/ReutersGillam-Kirton says she helped another family who were told their loved ones died while attempting to escape the fires on foot and that their remains had been cleared by a forensic team. She arranged for a search party – including a police officer and one of the victim’s relatives – to travel to the hillside on which they died. There they found what appeared to be human bones lying in plain view along with various personal belongings.“These were people who were caught in the same horrific fire as my mum and dad,” she says. “They lost their lives in terrifying circumstances and they deserved dignity and respect, in the way they were treated at the time and afterwards. And for us and the other families, those personal belongings aren’t just objects. They’re the last physical things connecting us to the people we have lost.”Pete Gillam with Danielle Gillam-Kirton (right).Photograph: Danielle KirtonGillam-Kirton has previously criticised the Spanish authorities for failing to alert her parents to the danger of the fire in good time. Though the fire alert came at 4.30pm, the evacuation order did not come for another three hours and was delivered by a lone police officer, who was “frantically driving from house to house”. Thirteen residents from the Gillams’ village died.Gillam-Kirton says she wants the UK government to “keep pressing the Spanish authorities for proper answers”. She adds: “Eight British people died in this fire, including my mum and dad, so I think it is really important that the UK government continues to take an interest in what happened. After all, we are talking about the treatment of British nationals – the deceased and the living.”She and the other families are asking the Spanish authorities for “a proper, thorough and transparent investigation … and I mean the whole thing, not just what caused the fire, but what happened during the emergency response, what warnings were given, when they were given, who received them, what evacuation arrangements were in place and what happened to the victims afterwards”.View image in fullscreenA burnt-out car after the wildfire in Bédar.Photograph: Ana Beltran/ReutersInitially, theSpanish authorities blamed the victimsfor not understanding or following the evacuation instructions. However, it later emerged that no such instructions were given.“I think that’s one of the things we’ve found hardest,” Gillam-Kirton says of the police response. “At the beginning, there seemed to be a lot of emphasis on the idea that the victims had ignored instructions or hadn’t evacuated when they were told to. And that was incredibly painful for us. And now, months later, we’re still asking basic questions.”She adds: “That, along with what appears to us to have been a lack of proper search-and-preserve procedures at the scene, has left us feeling that there has been a real lack of empathy towards the victims and their families.”View image in fullscreenPolice block access to Bédar after the wildfires.Photograph: Ana Beltran/ReutersThe families hope that if there is a proper investigation into the deaths of their relatives and the behaviour of the authorities afterwards, others will not have to go through the unbearable situation they have had to face.“Wildfires are becoming more frequent and more severe, and communities are going to face these situations again,” Gillam-Kirton says. “There will be another fire somewhere, and there will be other people who need to be evacuated.“If you don’t properly investigate something, you can’t learn from it. We don’t want Mum and Dad to simply become two names in a list of people who died in a wildfire. We want to understand what happened to them, and if something went wrong, we want the lessons to be learned.”The Foreign Office said that any investigations were the responsibility of the Spanish authorities. A spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British couple who died inSpain, and our thoughts are with those affected by the devastating wildfires.”The Bédar local government has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsUK newsSpainWildfiresEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The chancellor is in a bind’: is No 11 at odds with Burnham’s big vision? | John Healey | The Guardian
description: MPs applaud PM’s ambition and optimism but John Healey has yet to show he can match leader’s radical perspective
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: MPs applaud PM’s ambition and optimism but John Healey has yet to show he can match leader’s radical perspective
Content: Among Burnham’s closest allies, there have been mutterings that Healey could fall into the trap of being ‘captured’ by the Treasury.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/ReutersView image in fullscreenAmong Burnham’s closest allies, there have been mutterings that Healey could fall into the trap of being ‘captured’ by the Treasury.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/ReutersJohn Healey‘The chancellor is in a bind’: is No 11 at odds with Burnham’s big vision?MPs applaud PM’s ambition and optimism but John Healey has yet to show he can match leader’s radical perspectivePippa Crerar,Heather StewartandJessica ElgotSat 5 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUntil now, Andy Burnham has been a lucky prime minister. In office for just over six weeks, no major domestic crisis derailed his plans over the summer, Reform has beenon the back foot, and he arrived back at Westminster with his personal approval ratings soaring and optimism undampened.But underneath the sense of relief that manyLabourMPs are feeling that their high-stakes gamble of ousting Keir Starmer appears – for now – to have paid off, there is an unease that Burnham’s premiership is yet to make contact with economic reality.In their early weeks in office, his team were able to point to some inherited green shoots: below-forecast inflation figures, sustained growth, signs that sluggish productivity could be starting to turn around. All despite the economic turmoil unleashed by the Iran conflict.Why the Bayeux tapestry and Franco-British relations are natural bedfellowsRead moreThis week, all that changed. With the end of summer recess came a global bond sell-off amid anxiety over oil prices, sticky inflation and pressure to ramp up defence spending, which pushed government borrowing costs to their highest since the 2008 financial crash.It makes the backdrop to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor a difficult one. Economists reckon about half of the £24bn fiscal breathing space his predecessor Rachel Reeves had built up at her spring forecast has since been wiped out by higher inflation and interest rates, severely limiting Healey’s room for manoeuvre.Among the more experienced hands in government, there is a firm view that the new administration cannot return to the days of slim headroom given Reeves’s experience last year, which led to more brutal proposed welfare cuts and ultimately a backbench rebellion last summer.Healey has just returned from the G20 finance ministers’ meeting in North Carolina and is acutely conscious of factors beyond his control that will hit the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, including the rising cost of oil after bombing resumed in Iran.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and John Healey visit the Hare Inn in Harlow, Essex, in July.Photograph: Richard Pohle/ReutersIt is little surprise, then, that he has repeatedly stressed that fiscal responsibility is the “bedrock” of his approach and he will stick to Reeves’s fiscal rules.But his cautious tone jars uncomfortably with the prime minister’s large – and costly – policy vision: more public control of utilities, reform of the broken social care system and a mass social home building programme.“[Healey] is in a bind,” one Treasury source said. “His instinct is to keep things steady, especially while the OBR does its snapshot, but that’s not Andy’s gameplan for his first week back.”Indeed, Downing Street has been eager to ensure Burnham’s vision stays front and centre. In a mammoth three-and-a-half-hour Commons session on Tuesday, he repeatedly promised to deliver the “much more substantial change” the country was crying out for.Among Burnham’s closest allies, there have been some mutterings that Healey could, like chancellors before him, be in danger of being “captured” by the Treasury and its more orthodox arguments. “John did not exactly show in the Ministry of Defence that he was good at questioning internal departmental wisdom and pressures,” one government aide said.The friction between the two operations burst into the open last week when Healey suggested in a television interview that Burnham was running a “continuity” government.No 10 insiders pushed back hard. “Nobody listening to Andy and his plans for growth could think he is just about continuity,” said one senior figure. “He’s going to change things.”A timely report that suggests Manchester’s economic success – one of Burnham’s biggest legacies – could be replicated across England to unlock untapped growth potential of up to £80bn is released this weekend.Mandala Partners, a global economic research consultancy that was led by Nick Williams – a former Downing Street economic adviser who is now working for the first secretary, Louise Haigh – found that housing, transport and health devolution would be crucial to achieving the prime minister’s aim of “growth in every postcode”.Of these, the impact of following Manchester’s housing investment model is most striking. The report found that an £8.5bn programme of revolving public risk capital across mayoral strategic authorities could unlock almost 100,000 additional homes, crowd in more than £20bn of private investment and support more than 70,000 jobs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile not commissioned by No 10, Mandala’s study nevertheless bolsters Burnham’s central growth argument that learning from the success of Manchester’s devolution model could deliver far-reaching economic benefits and release the country from its low-growth chokehold.The chancellor has privately acknowledged there is room for modest additional borrowing to fund investment given Reeves’s rule change in 2024, which allowed the Treasury to offset financial assets against government debt.However, there is little sense of a radical new perspective emerging from the new regime at No 11. On Monday, Healey will give a speech on the government’s mission for growth, which is expected to stress the importance of devolution and public investment – both themes Reeves repeatedly returned to.The chancellor will emphasise the need to give the private sector the confidence to invest – raising doubts about whether he is likely to go ahead with one of the big revenue raisers that progressive economists and the TUC have called for: a windfall tax on banks.Treasury sources have declined to say whether Healey will stick to Reeves’s intention of holding only one major “fiscal event” each year, with the spring forecast a much more low-key affair. That would leave open the possibility of using his 28 October statement to fund the gaps in the defence investment plan and make more progress on tax devolution, while leaving the weightier tax and spending decisions until the spring.Labour MPs are anxious for change as quickly as the government can deliver it. They applaud Burnham’s ambition and the sense of hope he fosters but worry that the economic realities will drag him down.Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the Commons defence committee, summed up the mood when he suggested at PMQs that “vibes alone just will not be enough”. While he was referring to military spending, the sentiment is shared across the backbenches.Burnham has repeatedly said he will be relentless in fulfilling his priorities. But some of his MPs are already worried that his promise to repair the crumbling state and offer “breathing space” on the cost of living could be hard to reconcile with promises of fiscal responsibility.Downing Street sources argue, however, that it is only by improving infrastructure and devolving power that the British economy can grow as fast as Manchester’s. They cite Burnham’s visit to Cornwall this summer, where businesses told him it was taking them a year to connect to the grid.Healey’s economic instincts are less clear. When asked what would be the main difference between him and his instinctively prudent predecessor, one adviser said: “To be honest, I think he will actually be more cautious.”Despite his apparent wariness, government aides insist the chancellor is fully onboard with Burnham’s vision. One said: “There will always be tensions between the different parts of government, but John is aligned with Andy’s agenda. And he knows who is boss.”Explore more on these topicsJohn HealeyEconomic policyAndy BurnhamLabourEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content
