title: Arteta v Alonso, part one: a desire for control and the theory behind the chaos | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso prepare for an intriguing tactical battle in the first Premier League meeting between these two old friends
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso prepare for an intriguing tactical battle in the first Premier League meeting between these two old friends
Content: Mikel Arteta (left) and Xabi Alonso grew up in the same youth ranks, but have different managerial philosophies.Composite: PA, ReutersView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta (left) and Xabi Alonso grew up in the same youth ranks, but have different managerial philosophies.Composite: PA, ReutersChelseaArteta v Alonso, part one: a desire for control and the theory behind the chaosJonathan WilsonMikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso prepare for an intriguing tactical battle in the first Premier League meeting between old friendsSat 5 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 15.02 EDTShareControl v chaos. On the one hand, the forces of order, regimented, playing in precise patterns and, on the other, something darker, more visceral, a method that acknowledges the imperfection of the human soul, the unknowability of football in all its randomness; better, that second way says, to attempt to ride the fury than to believe it might be harnessed.When it began, a decade ago, that’s how the Pep Guardiola v Jürgen Klopp rivalry appeared. Apollo v Dionysius. Two fundamentally opposed ways of seeing the world. But in time, the two crept towards each other. Klopp moved away from the heavy metal of his Borussia Dortmund years to something more conservative. Guardiola experimented in multiple directions, slowly abandoning the possession-oriented idealism of his past to something less radical but also less predictable.‘Reverse bucket list’: Arteta channels Wenger in defence of Arsenal windowRead moreThe temptation, after the first two weeks of the season, is to cast Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso in a similar light. Arsenal are yet to concede a goal. They dominated the Community Shield from the first minute,beat a shambolic Manchester City 3-0and gave the sense that they could easily have won more comprehensively had they been minded to do so. They were no more troubled inbeating Coventry by the same scorelinein their opening league game and, while they were rather less dominant,they were still extremely comfortable against Aston Villa on Mondayand had been slowly increasing the pressure when Bukayo Saka gave them the lead just before the hour.Arteta has become more controlling over his seven years atArsenal, not just in his micromanagement but in his demands from his team. Tactical plans are sophisticated and negotiable only in the final details. In their third successive season of finishing second he spoke repeatedly of the need to reduce, to zero if possible, the xG of the opposition. If they have no chances, they cannot score, and if they do not score, they cannot win.Last season it was a refrain heard less often; Arsenal did reduce their opponents’ opportunities, conceding seven goals fewer than they had the previous season. There were those who criticised them on aesthetic grounds, bemoaning their reliance on set plays and occasional bouts of excessive pragmatism, but it worked. They were the best team and they won the league, in the end, fairly comfortably. All else is taste, subjective.Might, it will be asked, there be a more expansive approach this season? Might, with the burdens of yearning and doubt lifted, the insistence on control lessen? Might this be a breezier, a freer and easier, Arsenal? Might that even make them more effective in Europe, more capable ofbeating Paris Saint-Germain?View image in fullscreenBukayo Saka scores Arsenal’s winner at Aston Villa on Monday.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersProbably not. Arsenal played as they did in the Champions League final out of necessity, not choice. They were exhausted. Only three PSG players had played more than 2,000 minutes in the league last season; nine Arsenal players had – and given the relative strengths of the Premier League and Ligue 1, theirs were harder minutes. In such circumstances an open game is impossible.Accepting the role played by fatigue, in fact, has been one of Arsenal’s great strengths; last summer’s business was characterised by the accumulation of squad depth over acquisition of the very highest quality. This summer has been about upgrading where possible. They’ve seemingly done that well in midfield and at the back, although losing three players who can operate from the left wing while signing only Christos Tzolis seems a risk, even with Max Dowman likely to be more involved. It’s possible, likely even, that a more relaxed outlook will allow Arsenal to play with a greater freedom but it would be a surprise if the tactical emphasis were not still on control.Chelsea’s case is more complex; the sense of chaos of Alonso’s opening two games has surely not been deliberate. He is no Kloppite; his heritage is of John Toshack and Rafa Benítez, Vicente Del Bosque and Guardiola. Like Arteta, four months his junior, he came through the youth ranks at Antiguoko in San Sebastián; they are not so different in their formation. When Alonso won the league at Bayer Leverkusen, they had 62% possession. Although they pressed hard, they were not part of the high-tempo, high-turnover Bundesliga trend. Yet inbeating Fulham 3-2, Chelsea had 38% possession, and inbeating Brighton 4-3they had only 26%.Game state is partly responsible. In both games,Chelseahad the lead early and could afford to allow their opponents the ball. The front three of João Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers have excelled playing on the break. There have been glimmers of the sort of interactions Leverkusen produced, the modifications that prevent Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 from experiencing the blockishness that means the formation is more often a tool for counterattacking sides, most notably when Maxence Lacroix advanced from central defence to set up Rogers’ goal against Fulham. But they take time to develop; perhaps the idea for now, as patterns are assimilated, is to lean into the basic simplicity of shape, the security the two screening midfielders in front of the back three should offer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenChelsea have won their opening two Premier League games this season.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Nigel French/Apl/SportsphotoThe problem is, it hasn’t yet worked – although that may in part be down to personnel. Having sold Enzo Fernández without signing another central midfielder, though, Chelsea look short in midfield (in as much their bloated squad can look short of anything). If Roméo Lavia can remain fit, and if Reece James’s minutes can continue to be rationed, the issue should not be insoluble, but Moisés Caicedo’s knee problem complicates things, especially with Alonso seemingly unwilling yet to trust the 22-year-old Argentinian Valentín Barco from the start. Without Caicedo, that is not a midfield that is going to create much, and may struggle even with ball retention.Chelsea hit bullseye with Morgan Rogers as Arsenal rue what might have beenRead moreIt’s possible that on Sunday, in a game Chelsea are not expected to win, it is easier to maintain shape and discipline, that a destructive pairing works more naturally. Only by making the game a midfield slog to be decided by which team’s forward line can best exploit breakdowns can Chelsea feel they have an edge. That may end up looking like control against chaos, like possession against turnovers. It may even be so. But for Alonso that is a matter less of ideology than of expediency.Explore more on these topicsChelseaXabi AlonsoArsenalMikel ArtetacommentShareReuse this content

title: Lewis Hamilton urges Ferrari to put full weight behind F1 title challenge | Ferrari | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton said Ferrari needs to stay hungry for success and back his F1 title push, warning that light at the end of the tunnel was ‘getting dimmer’
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton said Ferrari needs to stay hungry for success and back his F1 title push, warning that light at the end of the tunnel was ‘getting dimmer’
Content: Lewis Hamilton was mystified by his car’s lack of pace during Q2 qualifying at the Monza track.Photograph: Anna Szilagy/Pool EPA/APView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton was mystified by his car’s lack of pace during Q2 qualifying at the Monza track.Photograph: Anna Szilagy/Pool EPA/APFerrariLewis Hamilton urges Ferrari to put full weight behind F1 title challengeLight at end of tunnel is ‘getting dimmer’Team needs to show hunger and ‘passion’Giles Richardsat MonzaSat 5 Sep 2026 14.56 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 16.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton has suggested it is time his Ferrari team put their full weight behind his efforts to challenge for the Formula One world championship if he is to have a shot at the title, and warned his chances were diminishing with every race.Hamilton trails Kimi Antonelli, the championship leader, by 59 points with 11 races to come. Having qualified in fifth for the Italian Grand Prix, one place behind hisFerrariteammate Charles Leclerc, who is 87 points off the lead, Hamilton was asked if it was time Ferrari gave him priority as their best chance for the title.Pierre Gasly takes shock pole for F1 Italian GP as Alpine stun big gunsRead more“Yeah, there’s light at the end of the tunnel, but it’s getting dimmer the further we get through,” he said. “The team is doing an amazing job in bringing upgrades and pushing us forward, I always want to make sure that I acknowledge them and recognise them for that.“I want them to continue to push and I want them to stay hungry and keep that passion on fire. But also at the track we need to come correct and act. We need to make sure we get the results we need.”Hamilton had very nearly been eliminated during Q2 in qualifying, struggling for pace and questioning Ferrari’s decision-making in trying to give both drivers a chance of a tow at a high-speed circuit where it is vital for a quick lap.“I don’t really fully understand why we were lacking so much pace in Q2, because we should have had pace like we did in the first one, but everyone just advanced forward, so I don’t know if that’s tyre pressure. I’m not quite sure, I need to look into that.“I think at the end, the team was solely focused on trying to get an equal tow for each driver and we just stumbled.“We were supposed to do a push, cool, cool, push [sequence of laps]. But because everyone was waiting and Charles didn’t want to go out first, we had to wait, wait, wait, and then we only got one push. It made it pretty challenging for us.”Quick GuideItalian F1 GP qualifying resultsShow1Pierre Gasly🇫🇷Alpine1:21.8762George Russell🇬🇧Mercedes1:21.846†3Oscar Piastri🇦🇺McLaren1:21.9664Charles Leclerc🇲🇨Ferrari1:22.0045Lewis Hamilton🇬🇧Ferrari1:22.0116Max Verstappen🇳🇱Red Bull1:22.070*7Kimi Antonelli🇮🇹Mercedes1:22.0938Franco Colapinto🇦🇷Alpine1:22.2209Lando Norris🇬🇧McLaren1:22.25610Arvid Lindblad🇬🇧Racing Bulls1:22.286Q2 eliminations11Gabriel Bortoleto🇧🇷Audi1:22.51712Oliver Bearman🇬🇧Haas1:22.75613Nico Hülkenberg🇩🇪Audi1:22.779*14Liam Lawson🇫🇷Red Bull1:22.82115Carlos Sainz🇪🇸Williams1:23.45316Esteban Ocon🇫🇷Haas1:23.454Q1 eliminations17Yuki Tsunoda🇯🇵Racing Bulls1:23.755*18Alexander Albon🇹🇭Williams1:24.35619Valtteri Bottas🇫🇮Cadillac1:24.36420Sergio Pérez🇲🇽Cadillac1:24.59521Fernando Alonso🇪🇸Aston Martin1:25.15022Lance Stroll🇨🇦Aston Martin1:25.22† Piastri given a three-place grid penalty for impeding Lawson. *Antonelli, Lawson and Albon all relegated to the back of the grid for taking new power unit elementsWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Alpine’s Pierre Gaslytook a remarkable pole positionfor the race, with Mercedes’ George Russell, who is equal with Hamilton on points – 59 behind Antonelli – in second place. With the Mercedes looking formidable in race pace and Antonelli starting from 20th after an engine-change grid penalty, Russell is in a strong position to make points back, and Hamilton emphasised this was a potentially crucial moment for Ferrari.“We’re at a point in the year where 59 points is a huge deficit to recover from, especially when Mercedes continue to be the leaders in speed,” he said. “So yeah, we do have to work as a team.”Leclerc and Hamilton will start from third and fourth respectively on Sunday after McLaren’s Oscar Piastri was given a three-place grid penalty.Explore more on these topicsFerrariLewis HamiltonFormula OneFormula One 2026Motor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ingebrigtsen sorry for calling 1500m rivals ‘losers’ but maintains Hocker ‘acted cowardly’ | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen has issued a part-apology for calling his rivals ‘losers’ and a ‘bunch of cowards’ after a spicy men’s 1500m Diamond League final on Friday
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Jakob Ingebrigtsen has issued a part-apology for calling his rivals ‘losers’ and a ‘bunch of cowards’ after a spicy men’s 1500m Diamond League final on Friday
Content: Jakob Ingebrigtsen (right) was unhappy with how most of his fellow competitors approached Friday’s 1500m, in which he finished fourth.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAView image in fullscreenJakob Ingebrigtsen (right) was unhappy with how most of his fellow competitors approached Friday’s 1500m, in which he finished fourth.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAAthleticsIngebrigtsen sorry for calling 1500m rivals ‘losers’ but maintains Hocker ‘acted cowardly’Fiery Diamond League comments partially walked backOn Hocker: ‘Cole and I talked it through after the race’Sean Ingleat the Stade Roi BaudouinSat 5 Sep 2026 15.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe double Olympic champion Jakob Ingebrigtsen has issued a part-apology for calling his rivals “losers” and a “bunch of cowards” after aspicy men’s 1500m Diamond League finalon Friday.However, Ingebrigtsen has continued to maintain that he was still right to accuse the Olympic 1500m champion Cole Hocker of cowardice – because he asked for a strong pace and swapped in his own pacemaker only to then hide behind others in the race.Audrey Werro fends off Femke Broeders-Bol’s charge in Diamond League final 800mRead moreIn a statement issued on Saturday, Ingebrigtsen, who finished fourth behind Australia’s Cameron Myers in a tight finish in 3min 30.52sec, said: “I shouldn’t have called anyone losers. I apologise for that. It was beneath me, regardless of the adrenaline and emotions. But I stand by what I said about Cole and his team acting cowardly.“They told the other athletes and the organisers that they were targeting a specific pace and were bringing in their own pacemaker to set that pace, but then they did something completely different.“When you promise the crowd a fast race, you have a responsibility to follow through – at least in my view. This isn’t about me losing. I wasn’t good enough. It’s about taking responsibility for the commitments you’ve made to the meeting organisers, the crowd and your competitors.”Ingebrigtsen, who returned to racing in August after 11 months out after an achilles sheath injury, ended up following the pacemakers himself after no one else went with them.But despite running a season’s best time, he was bluntly honest about his “shitty, terrible and extremely disappointing” run afterwards – before criticising his fellow racers.On Saturday Ingebrigtsen insisted that he had talked to Hocker afterwards and the matter was settled. However the row flared up again when Hocker’s agent Ray Flynn accused Ingebrigtsen of whining.“Jakob now appears as a whiny runner who blames others,” Flynn wrote in an email to the Norwegian newspaper Dagbladet. “It is embarrassing to see a great champion complain and blame other runners when he doesn’t win. It is completely disrespectful to his competitors, who now regularly beat him in the 1500 metres.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever Ingebrigtsen said that his broader comments were good for the sport as he returned fire on Flynn.“Cole and I talked it through after the race,” the Norwegian added. “As far as we’re concerned, the matter is settled, so I don’t really understand why his agent is getting involved in all of this now. If you’re not allowed to show a bit of passion after a race, you should find a sport that doesn’t want an audience.”The pair could renew acquaintances next week at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest, when Ingebrigtsen is down to run the 1500m and 5,000m. However, according to Dagbladet, the Norwegian is now likely just to focus on the 5,000m.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Glasner claims VAR was ‘guessing’ after Forest are denied winner against Spurs | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Neco Williams had a goal disallowed for handball as Nottingham Forest drew 0-0 with Tottenham, and Oliver Glasner argued the evidence was unclear
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Neco Williams had a goal disallowed for handball as Nottingham Forest drew 0-0 with Tottenham, and Oliver Glasner argued the evidence was unclear
Content: Neco Williams had a goal disallowed for handball in the second half.Photograph: Chris Radburn/ReutersView image in fullscreenNeco Williams had a goal disallowed for handball in the second half.Photograph: Chris Radburn/ReutersPremier LeagueGlasner claims VAR was ‘guessing’ after Forest are denied winner against SpursBen Fisherat the City GroundSat 5 Sep 2026 13.59 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 12.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOliver Glasner argued there was insufficient evidence to disallow Neco Williams’s goal against Tottenham, accusing the video assistant referee Peter Bankes of guessing that theNottingham Forestdefender handled and said ruling it out weakens the officials’ authority. Midway through the second half, Williams stooped to head in on the goalline as Sandro Tonali attempted to hook the ball clear after Morgan Gibbs-White’s deflected effort bobbled towards the net.Glasner conceded at least one angle showed Williams appeared to handle the ball, seemingly to protect himself as Tonali went to clear the ball with his left boot, but said the footage was too unclear to disallow the goal. “I don’t think VAR can intervene when he’s guessing,” said Forest’s head coach. “It was not clear and obvious. We had a briefing before the season that the threshold for VAR intervention should be very high and this is why it was a wrong intervention for me.Chilwell seals Crystal Palace comeback win after Mitchell double at FulhamRead more“I’ve watched five or six different angles and to be fair, from one angle you can guess that the ball touched the arm because the shirt [of Williams] moves a little bit, but it’s not clear whether it’s [because of] the ball or Tonali on the goalline. I know refereeing aPremier Leaguegame is really difficult – refereeing a training session is sometimes really difficult – but we are told to support the referee, to keep the threshold for VAR intervention very high, to strengthen the referee’s decision and they didn’t do that today. With these kinds of situations, you weaken the referees.”Bankes checked the goal and then the referee, Craig Pawson, took to the mic before awarding a Spurs free-kick amid a chorus of boos from the home support: “After review, the ball touches the hand of Nottingham Forest’s No 3 before the goal is scored.” Williams was adamant he did not handle the ball. “I headed it in between my arms,” said the Wales defender, who this week signed a new four-year contract. “If you’re going to pause it, it’s going to look like it hit my arm but it didn’t. I have seen all the images and at not one moment can you tell that has clearly hit my arms because it never. I knew straight away I’d headed it down in between my arms.”The disallowed goal was undeniably the moment of an underwhelming contest. For the third successive league match, Tottenham failed to score and this time they did not even muster a shot on target. Dominic Solanke heading on to the roof of the Forest goal, 88 minutes on the clock, was as threatening as they got. Omar Marmoush wellied a shot wide after Spurs countered at speed. Mykhailo Mudryk was brought off the bench for his first competitive minutes for 645 days after a doping suspension but Spurs were blunt. Aside from a5-1 win against a Charlton B teamin the Carabao Cup, their season so far reads: five goals against and none scored.View image in fullscreenSpurs’ Mykhailo Mudryk came on as a late substitute for his first competitive appearance for 645 days.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersApart from Gibbs-White’s effort in the buildup to the disallowed goal, Forest’s only other shot on goal was a daisy-cutter from James McAtee. TheSpurs league debutant Sávio, a £75m arrival from Manchester City, showed a few neat touches but he and Destiny Udogie were withdrawn after an hour on the advice of Tottenham’s medical department. “I’m not happy when we have the plan but it is for my advantage, my business, the management of the players after their injuries,” said De Zerbi, who accepted his team lacked quality in the final third. “We have to make better decisions, to keep more calm when we are very close to do something important.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNo wonder both teams remain winless. Spurs’s date at home to Everton next weekend has taken on another layer of significance and the same applies to Forest’s trip to Aston Villa. Vinai Venkatesham, the Tottenham chief executive in attendance, could be forgiven for wondering when Spurs will see the fruits of their £300m-plus spend, much of the focus on sharpening their attack. They turned to Mudryk, who thrived under De Zerbi at Shakhtar Donetsk, after the failure to sell Richarlison halted moves for preferred targets Cody Gakpo and Iliman Ndiaye. This was not the desired result. “We bought very, very good players but you can’t just build the team with the names like in Football Manager,” De Zerbi said.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueNottingham ForestTottenham HotspurVideo assistant referees (VARs)match reportsShareReuse this content

title: Francisco Cerundolo roars back from brink to stun home hope Taylor Fritz at US Open | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Francisco Cerundolo beat No 9 seed Taylor Fritz 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4 after the US player had three break points in the final set for a chance to serve for the match
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Francisco Cerundolo beat No 9 seed Taylor Fritz 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4 after the US player had three break points in the final set for a chance to serve for the match
Content: Francisco Cerundolo overcame the odds to make his way into the next round at Flushing Meadows.Photograph: Brian Hirschfeld/EPAView image in fullscreenFrancisco Cerundolo overcame the odds to make his way into the next round at Flushing Meadows.Photograph: Brian Hirschfeld/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Francisco Cerundolo roars back from brink to stun home hope Taylor Fritz at US OpenArgentinian beats No 9 seed 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4Fritz had three break points for chance to serve for matchTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsSat 5 Sep 2026 17.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs his last, desperate backhand soared far past the baseline inside Arthur Ashe Stadium, Taylor Fritz instantly held his face in his hands, unable to hide the agony of squandering such a great opportunity.For much of his afternoon, Fritz was cruising. He had established two sets to love lead against Francisco Cerundolo before breaking serve in the opening game of the third. One unfocused service game was enough to shift the momentum and once Fritz had lost control, he spent another two hours failing to retrieve it. His US Open ended with an excruciating 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4 third-round defeat by a courageous Cerundolo.US Open tennis: Gauff and Swiatek go through; Cobolli, Fritz and Keys tumble out – liveRead moreAny early loss at a home grand slam is incredibly difficult to accept, but Fritz’s timing was fatal. Having been ranked as high as No 4 last year, he is the most successful American male player of his generation. In 2024, Fritz became the first American man to reach the US Open singles final since Andy Roddick in 2006, a breakthrough run sandwiched between two quarter-final losses to Novak Djokovic in 2023 and 2025. The 28-year-old is a tremendously committed and diligent competitor who, despite his own athletic shortcomings, has eked so much out of his game. There has always been a far superior tennis player, usually an all-time great, standing before him and the major titles.This year’s US Open, however, presents a completely different challenge for most of the men’s field. Jannik Sinner, the world No 1 and four-time grand slam champion, is absent due to injury and the now 39-year-old Novak Djokovic wasdramatically defeated in the first round. Carlos Alcaraz, the seven-time grand slam champion and defending champion, is competing his first tournament back from a four month injury layoff.View image in fullscreenTaylor Fritz later said of his defeat: ‘I don’t really want to talk to anybody … I don’t know how I let that happen today.’Photograph: Brian Hirschfeld/EPAIn the absence of an obvious favourite in obvious grand slam-winning form, this tournament is such a great opportunity for any player with aspirations of winning a grand slam title. Fritz, who was high up on the list of names hoping to take advantage, was understandably disgusted with the way he let this opportunity slip. In the deciding set he had three break points for a 5-3 lead and the chance to serve for the match.“I don’t even know what to say,” he said. “I don’t really want to talk to anybody, see anybody. I kind of just need to get out for a couple days and then just get back to work. I don’t know how I let that happen today.”At the beginning of the day, seven American men remained in the singles draw: Ben Shelton, Fritz, Frances Tiafoe, Learner Tien, Tommy Paul, Alex Michelsen and Michael Zheng. In the bottom half of the draw, where the fourth-round berths were decided on Friday, there is an American man in each of the four matches. Fritz’s defeat is a warning to any of his compatriots with hopes of becoming the first American man since Roddick at the 2003 US Open to win a grand slam title. More opportunity means more pressure. The coming week will reveal so much about the character of every player in the men’s draw.Saturday proved a challenging day for American players as a whole. Two days after Madison Keys completed one of the more dramatic comeback victories of her career, saving five match points en route to her tight three-set win over Anna Bondar, she suffered one of her worst ever collapses. Keys led Zheng Qinwen 5-0 in the final set of their third-round match before collapsing in the final set as she lost 1-6, 7-6 (3), 7-5. “I think she started playing better; I started playing poorly,” Keys said. “Then I felt like I couldn’t play tennis any more, and it just was – it just felt like it was a much bigger deal than just playing a tennis match all of a sudden.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenZheng Qinwen set up a last-16 match against Iga Swiatek after fighting back to beat Madison Keys in three sets.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APKeys,the 2025 Australian Open champion, said she believes a result like this had been coming for some time and will force her to address certain issues she has been dealing with. “I just feel like I’ve been struggling for a while now and I feel like I was able to kind of play through it for a bit,” she said. “I’m sure everyone could kind of see that I was struggling a little bit, but inside it felt probably even bigger than that. Some weeks are easier than others, and this week is obviously one of the harder ones just because you care so much. Yeah, I’m going to have to make some changes.”For Zheng, however, this was an enormous win. Havingwon the Olympic gold medaland reached the top 10 in 2024, the Chinese player has fallen down the rankings since her return from elbow surgery and the 23-year-old was forced to come through qualifying here just to compete in the main draw.“Tennis sometimes feels like a rollercoaster,” Zheng said. “You see many times that people have a match point, but at the end [their opponent] makes a comeback. Like today was just happening. So this also gives me a lesson that in a tennis match you always have to be there. It doesn’t matter if you are winning or losing, you have a match point or you don’t have a match point – you just need to be concentrated for every single point as long as you can.”Amanda Anisimova, whose incredible breakthrough summer of 2025 included runners-up finishes at Wimbledon and the US Open alongside a career-high ranking of No 3, will fall out of the top 10 after tamely losing 6-2, 7-5 to the 24th seed Anastasia Potapova. Iga Swiatek, meanwhile, brilliantly saved three set points in her second set before working her way to a tough 7-6 (3), 7-6 (3) win over Marie Bouzkova. Swiatek faces Zheng in the fourth round on Sunday.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Katie Taylor bows out from boxing as undisputed champion after dominating Flora Pili | Katie Taylor | The Guardian
description: Irish fans at Croke Park saluted their retiring hero as Katie Taylor overwhelmed Flora Pili, as reflected in scorecards that read 110-90, 110-90 and 98-91
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Irish fans at Croke Park saluted their retiring hero as Katie Taylor overwhelmed Flora Pili, as reflected in scorecards that read 110-90, 110-90 and 98-91
Content: Katie Taylor beams in the Croke Park ring after what she describes as ‘a dream end to a dream career’.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKatie Taylor beams in the Croke Park ring after what she describes as ‘a dream end to a dream career’.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesKatie TaylorKatie Taylor bows out from boxing as undisputed champion after dominating Flora PiliIrish fans dazzled by showcase of skills in huge points winScorecards read 110-90, 110-90 and 98-91 in her favourGuardian sportand agenciesSat 5 Sep 2026 18.18 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKatie Taylor signed off her storied career in style by outclassing Flora Pili on points as an 80,000 crowd at Croke Park celebrated her fairytale farewell.With the gaze ofIrelandupon her, the country’s great became a three-time undisputed world champion by overwhelming the previously unbeaten Frenchwoman 100-90, 100-90, 98-91 on the scorecards.Boxer Thomas Carty falls out of ring after 92 seconds in bizarre no-contestRead moreTaylor dominated through her hand speed and movement and never looked in danger as she added the vacant WBC title to her WBO, WBA and IBF belts to begin the party at GAA headquarters.As the final seconds before retirement approached, the Olympic gold medallist ended the 10th round by trading with Pili against the ropes knowing victory was assured.The victory completed a remarkable journey for Taylor, who began boxing at a time when girls were barred from amateur competition in Ireland and sometimes entered bouts simply as “K Taylor”.She went on to win Olympic lightweight gold at London 2012, when women’s boxing made its Games debut, before turning professional four years later.Taylor finishes her professional career with 26 victories and one defeat, having won world titles at lightweight and super-lightweight.Her farewell also brought top-level boxing back to Croke Park for the first time since Muhammad Ali defeated Al “Blue” Lewis in 1972.View image in fullscreenKatie Taylor’s speed and ringcraft told from first bell to last as she left Flora Pili well outclassed.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesFollowing the fight, she placed her gloves in the centre of the ring to mark her retirement, while her team assisted her in assembling her belts around them.Addressing the buoyant crowd, she said: “Croke Park! We did it,” said ‌Taylor as she saluted the crowd. “I don’t know of any other country that ​would sell 80,000 tickets.”She later added: “The people of Ireland gave me a dream end to a dream career. Nothing can top this.”Explore more on these topicsKatie TaylorBoxingIrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Premiership: Celtic’s Yang completes fightback to see off St Mirren | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: Celtic came from behind to win 2-1 at St Mirren, while Rangers lost Lawrence Shankland to injury but Ryan Naderi scored in a 1-0 victory against Motherwell
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Celtic came from behind to win 2-1 at St Mirren, while Rangers lost Lawrence Shankland to injury but Ryan Naderi scored in a 1-0 victory against Motherwell
Content: Yang Hyun-jun slots home to put Celtic 2-1 ahead of St Mirren.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PAView image in fullscreenYang Hyun-jun slots home to put Celtic 2-1 ahead of St Mirren.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PAScottish PremiershipScottish Premiership: Celtic’s Yang completes fightback to see off St MirrenCeltic come from behind to win 2-1 at St MirrenRangers beat Motherwell 1-0 but lose Shankland to injuryPress AssociationSat 5 Sep 2026 17.36 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYang Hyun-jun scored the winner asCelticcame from behind to beat an impressiveSt Mirrenside 2-1.St Mirrenwere heading for the top of the Premiership when Nikolas Agrafiotis netted from the spot midway through the first half.Liam Scales conceded the penalty with a handball but made amends when he headed home six minutes after the break. And Yang finished off a counterattack midway through the second half after good pressing from Camilo Durán.The victory in Paisley made it five wins from five league games for the champions and inflicted St Mirren’s first Premiership defeat. Martin O’Neill’s side were made to work all the way by a Saints side who played with tempo, invention and managed 19 shots at goal.O’Neill later lamented the unavailability of Yang for some crucial games – the 24-year-old will now fly to Japan for the Asian Games and miss the midweek trip to St Johnstone and two games againstRangers, plus the Europa League opener against Ferencvaros.“We are going to miss him. He’s in really fine form at the moment,” the manager said. “But he’s signed off with a brilliant goal. He’s in great form and he’ll work for you going backwards. He doesn’t mind doing the hard graft.”Rangersstriker Ryan Naderi accepted a gift to score the only goal againstMotherwellat Ibrox, but they fear their captain Lawrence Shankland faces a lengthy spell on the sidelines after a hamstring injury suffered early on in the game.Naderi, who came on for Shankland in the eighth minute, dispossessed Alex Paulsen as the Motherwell goalkeeper attempted to dribble the ball past him outside his box and the German had the simple task of rolling the ball into the net to score what proved to be a 12th-minute winner.Motherwell dominated possession and created several chances but Rangers were more effective in the final third and should have added to their lead. Kim Min-su missed a first-half penalty and the debutant striker Kevin Kelsy was among those to pass up good opportunities after he came off the bench.View image in fullscreenLawrence Shankland leaves the pitch unaided but his manager later revealed the club fear his hamstring injury is significant.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PARangers ultimately saw out the game without any late scares as they recorded a third consecutive Premiership victory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOf Shankland, the Rangers manager, Derek McInnes, said he fears the injury is similarly significant to the one that kept him out for two months early in 2026. McInnes said: “He has a similar feeling to the hamstring injury he had at Hearts last January. We don’t want to speculate too much but he says it feels similar, in the same area, so we’ll get him scanned on Monday.“He says he felt fine going into the game and there was nothing really that he did in the game that he was aware of, he just felt it pull up. It’s a shame for the boy because he was obviously in good form, getting himself moving and enjoying some of that attacking threat we’ve had over the last few games, and we’ve waited long and hard for that.”Michael Forbes scored an added-time equaliser forDundee UnitedagainstFalkirk, who had led at Tannadice thanks to Jacob Murrell’s fourth-minute opener, whileKilmarnockpicked up their first point but are still waiting for a first Premiership win of the season after a 0-0 draw atAberdeen. Kilmarnock’s Aaron Tshibola was sent off for a second yellow card after 83 minutes but the hosts could not find a way past the 10 men.Explore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipCelticRangersMotherwellSt MirrenAberdeenKilmarnocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Kriel and Marx tries help South Africa power past All Blacks to take series lead | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: Second-half tries from Jesse Kriel and Malcolm Marx inspired South Africa to a 29-24 win against New Zealand and a 2-1 lead in the four-Test series
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Second-half tries from Jesse Kriel and Malcolm Marx inspired South Africa to a 29-24 win against New Zealand and a 2-1 lead in the four-Test series
Content: Jesse Kriel races clear to score South Africa’s third try against New Zealand.Photograph: Siphiwe Sibeko/ReutersView image in fullscreenJesse Kriel races clear to score South Africa’s third try against New Zealand.Photograph: Siphiwe Sibeko/ReutersRugby unionKriel and Marx tries help South Africa power past All Blacks to take series leadSouth Africa 29-24 New ZealandAll Blacks captain Ardie Savea out of final TestGerard MeagherSat 5 Sep 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere have been moments over the past couple of weeks that have made us question South Africa’s status as the standard bearers in world rugby. After this helter-skelter third Test victory that ensures they cannot lose the series, we have an emphatic answer. The Springboks’ power is unrivalled. The All Blacks’ panache has taken them mightily close but South Africa remain on their perch.A consolation score for New Zealand at the death rescued some pride but flattered the All Blacks – and afterwards it was confirmed that their captain Ardie Savea will miss the final Test. A second-half masterclass from the Boks, the relentless kind that leaves even opponents as worthy as these suffocated, gasping for air, confirms what was taken as read before this series started – South Africa remain the hot favourites for next year’s World Cup.South Africa v New Zealand: rugby union third Test – liveRead moreThere is a fourth Test next week in Baltimore but the reality is it is a money-spinning appendage to the three matches in South Africa. TheSpringboks lost the firstbut haveroared back on home soil. They take a 2-1 lead in the series and are unofficial winners of the best-of-three contest in South Africa. The All Blacks have failed in their quest to emulate the class of 1996.No individual performance was more significant than their collective ability to put on the squeeze but Ox Nché’s 56 minutes at the coalface were exceptional and it is no coincidence that Siya Kolisi, who now has more Test wins than any other Springboks captain, sat out the one Test South Africa have lost this series.Quick GuideSouth Africa 29-24 New Zealand: teams and scorersShowSouth AfricaKolbe (Libbok 10); Arendse, Kriel, De Allende; Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Reinach (Van den Berg 42); Nche (Steenekamp 56), Marx (Esterhuizen 67), Louw (T du Toit 50), Etzebeth (De Jager 56), Nortje, Kolisi (capt; Fourie 56), PS du Toit, Wiese (Hanekom 61)TriesArendse, penalty, Kriel, MarxConsFeinberg-Mngomezulu 2PenFeinberg-MngomezuluSin-binFeinberg-Mngomezulu 10.New ZealandMcKenzie; Jordan, Tupaea (Lienert-Brown 42), Barrett; Carter (Moorby 67); Love, Roigard (Preston 66); Bower (Numia 45), Aumua (Taukei’aho 61), Lomax (Newell 45), Vaa’i, Darry (Holland 61), Lakai, Jacobson, Savea (Sitit 31)TriesSavea 2, Jordan, Taukei’ahoConsTaukei’aho, McKenzieSin-binLove 36Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The All Blacks showed their class for much of this contest, which hinged on Jesse Kriel’s decisive second-half score just after Will Jordan had struck for New Zealand. From that moment on, South Africa smelled blood and capitalised with the ruthless streak that has crowned them consecutive World Cup winners.The All Blacks are evidently their closest challengers and matched the Boks’ four tries with four of their own. They possess a remarkable running game but eventually South African power has caught up with them. They will rue losing Savea to a shoulder injury late in the first half – “He won’t travel now,” said head coach Dave Rennie of the captain’s chances of making the Baltimore Test – and some key mistakes after the interval. Perhaps Ruben Love’s two missed kicks at goal too. Savea’s early withdrawal was certainly a setback but it is no excuse, not least because Cheslin Kolbe lasted all of 10 minutes before going off in another Test match of remarkable intensity. South Africa’s head coach Rassie Erasmus later revealed Kolbe had broken his jaw.A breathless first half began with a statement of intent by the All Blacks. First the Springboks’ maul was stopped in its tracks, then South Africa’s bulldozing No 8 Jasper Wiese was knocked back in the tackle. A mesmerising run up the middle by Jordan demonstrated the All Blacks had come to play too and the Springboks were rattled when Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu was sent to the sin-bin for a deliberate knock-on.View image in fullscreenArdie Savea charges over to score New Zealand’s first try.Photograph: Siphiwe Sibeko/ReutersFrom the resulting lineout move, Savea had space to pounce for the opening try and to compound matters for South Africa, Kolbe had been taken off with a head injury. South Africa’s foothold came from the set-piece superiority, however, and shortly after Feinberg-Mngomezulu’s return, Kurt-Lee Arendse was over on the right.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe All Blacks were at this point struggling at the breakdown but have showcased throughout this tour an ability to strike on the counter. Again Savea was the beneficiary for their second try which owed much to some nifty footwork from Tupou Vaa’i and plenty to their innate ability to stay patient and keep the ball alive.For the third week in a row South Africa finished the first half the stronger and the All Blacks were dealt an almighty blow when Savea was taken off in clear discomfort. Manie Libbok proceeded to go close after an astonishing pickup by Nché but Love had infringed on his own line and became the second fly-half to be shown a yellow card. A dominant Springboks scrum yielded a penalty try and parity at 12-12 at the break.The second half took a while to ignite but Love’s missed penalty lit the touch paper. Jordan started and finished the All Blacks’ third try with a fine chip through to Leroy Carter, who popped the ball up off the floor to his fellow winger. Almost immediately, however, the Boks responded when Kriel slipped past Carter far too easily and sped to the line. Feinberg-Mngomezulu converted whereas Love had missed his effort to nose South Africa ahead.It was sloppy by Carter and the same can be said of Jordan, when his overhit kick led to a Springboks scrum. The inevitable penalty was kicked to the corner and a ferocious rumble by South Africa was finished off by the irrepressible Malcolm Marx. A Feinberg-Mngomezulu penalty pushed South Africa’s lead to 12 with 10 minutes to play and though the All Blacks had finished the stronger in both previous Tests, they could only muster a pushover score by Samisoni Taukei’aho with the clock well into the red.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSouth Africa rugby teamNew Zealand rugby union teammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Own goal and inspired debut from keeper Akane Okuma earn Villa point at Chelsea | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Veerle Burman turned the ball into her own net to secure Aston Villa a WSL season-opening 1-1 draw at Chelsea, who took the lead through Lauren James but were thereafter frustrated by Villa’s new goalkeeper
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Veerle Burman turned the ball into her own net to secure Aston Villa a WSL season-opening 1-1 draw at Chelsea, who took the lead through Lauren James but were thereafter frustrated by Villa’s new goalkeeper
Content: Akane Okuma produced nine saves to keep Aston Villa in the game in their season opener at Chelsea.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenAkane Okuma produced nine saves to keep Aston Villa in the game in their season opener at Chelsea.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersWomen's Super LeagueOwn goal and inspired debut from keeper Akane Okuma earn Villa point at ChelseaSuzanne Wrackat Stamford BridgeSat 5 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 12.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Veerle Buurman own goal punished a profligate Chelsea at Stamford Bridge, securing a point for Aston Villa in a frustrating start to the hosts’ push to win back the WSL title.How Villa came away with a point having conceded 65% possession and having amassed just seven shots to Chelsea’s 34 and five touches in the opposition box to the home team’s 57 is somewhat inexplicable.Alexia Putellas begins WSL ride as London City outclass Manchester UnitedRead moreChelsea were creative and Lauren James was at her free-flowing best, but they could not convert their many chances, and the new Villa goalkeeper Akane Okuma’s monumental performance was a big part of that.“If you analyse the performance today and the statistics of the game you can say that’s crazy we couldn’t win the game,” said the Chelsea manager, Sonia Bompastor. “You need to make sure you kill the game because when you are only one-nil up, you are always exposed. That’s what happened today and I think at the end of the game we are all frustrated because it’s not a good result.”View image in fullscreenAlmost every Villa outfield player joined the celebrations for their equaliser.Photograph: Katie Chan/Action Plus/ShutterstockChelsea’s summer has been one of change after a somewhat transitional season that broke a run of six consecutive WSL titles, and spirits have been high about their potential. However, they have a problem up front: with the new signing Melvine Malard, whocame off the bench and scored twoin their Champions League qualifier home leg against Real Sociedad, out with an injury, and Mayra Ramírez yet to make her return from a long lay-off, Aggie Beever-Jones failed to make the most of the opportunity to lead the line.“In football, some of these things are also about mentality and mindset when it comes to being ruthless, being critical in the box,” said Bompastor. “The best teams don’t need to have many opportunities. So, that’s something we need to work on and find solutions for.”Ushering in a new era in front of 7,900 fans at Stamford Bridge, where they will play all their WSL home games for the first time, Chelsea’s aggressive and relentless pressing in the opening half-hour caused all sorts of problems for Natalia Arroyo’s team, forcing error after error.View image in fullscreenLauren James gave an early sign of what she is capable of with a finish that left the Villa keeper helpless.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersIt was no surprise when that physical effort yielded results. In the 11th minute when pressure caused confusion between Okuma and the target of her pass out from the back, the loose ball was worked to James who glided into the box, shifting her weight as she went, before lashing the ball into the roof of the net. It was a statement goal from a statement player.This was always going to be a tough opening game for Villa, who had lost all 12 of their previous WSL games against Chelsea and were startingfive of their eight summer signings,. They only began to look a little more comfortable and structured as the home team’s pressure eased off towards the end of the first half.“We just need to go through that and understand that when you’re in the middle of the jungle or whatever, at some point, you arrive at a point where there’s no more trees and I think that’s what we do at the end of the first half,” said Arroyo. “We get the energy back in the changing room and we talk about how to avoid these moments.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChelsea’s profligacy in front of goal was the big frustration for Bompastor, and Villa were clinging on for large swathes of the game with Okuma, signed from the Japanese champions INAC Kobe Leonessa, key to keeping the margin to one goal.View image in fullscreenNoelle Maritz’s (centre) shot led to Veerle Buurman’s own goal.Photograph: Katie Chan/Action Plus/ShutterstockAt no stage had it felt like the visiting team would be able to take something from the game. They were patient, but Chelsea were the masters of their own downfall, and in the 79th minute the ground was silenced when they failed to clear Lynn Wilms’ cross, Noelle Maritz swiped it goalwards from eight yards out, and Hannah Hampton’s block sent the ball bouncing off Buurman and over the line.The home side pushed hard for the winner but Okuma was equal to every attempt. “We gave her some nice tests this week trying to know where she was at, if she was nervous, if she had any doubt and in which ways we could help her,” said Arroyo. “She’s still settling in here, she’s still trying to learn the language to be able to communicate with all the players, but we were surprised to see that she was safe in some of the actions, she read the game really well.”On the final whistle the Japanese goalkeeper was enveloped in the hugs of her teammates as the players in blue digested how they had ended up with only a point from such a dominant performance.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueChelsea WomenAston Villa WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: When Dad asked me to edit his novel, I wanted to say no – but ran directly towards the lion’s den | Anna Spargo-Ryan | The Guardian
description: My father doesn’t ask for help from just anyone. And yet he asked for mine. He believed in me
Author: Anna Spargo-Ryan
Headline: My father doesn’t ask for help from just anyone. And yet he asked for mine. He believed in me
Content: ‘My dad was asking me to teach him something new, and I realised he wasn’t perfect at everything first go; he was perfect at persevering.’Photograph: Lesia Larionova/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘My dad was asking me to teach him something new, and I realised he wasn’t perfect at everything first go; he was perfect at persevering.’Photograph: Lesia Larionova/AlamyOpinionFather's DayWhen Dad asked me to edit his novel, I wanted to say no – but ran directly towards the lion’s denAnna Spargo-RyanMy father doesn’t ask for help from just anyone. And yet he asked for mine. He believed in meSat 5 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 19.56 EDTShareMy dad and I believe in many of the same things: cheesecake; the Geelong football club; my mum. And that we should immediately be experts at anything. First try. No practice. No revision.He taught me this in kindergarten. Every day he pushed me to be brilliant. We played spelling games in the car and did maths workbooks for fun. Before I started school I had “published” a library of my own books, complete with copyright information. I had become – and I’m assuming this is true of most Guardian writers – a precocious kid who irritated everyone around her by being boisterously, aggressively right about everything all of the time. Just like my dad. (Obviously I’ve grown a lot since then.)The kindness of strangers: After losing my wife and son, I ate alone one Father’s Day – and another diner paid my billRead moreSo when he asked, at age 77, if I would edit the novel he’d been working on, I responded with what I’ll generously call abject terror. I knew, from teaching hundreds of later-life would-be writers, that there would be feedback. Good Lord, would there. And I also knew, from a lifetime of being explicitly told, that we always got things right the first time. No exceptions.I wanted to say no. I wanted to tell him, Dad, our relationship is too precious to me. “I’m not sure I have time,” I said, because I am the worst daughter on Earth. But, after my life had flashed before my eyes, I took a beat. The truth is: his outrageous self-belief is well founded. Most people are worse than him at most things. My dad doesn’t ask for help from just anyone. And yet, he had asked for mine.He didn’t just believe in cake and footy and my mum. He believed in me.So I did a 180. I ran directly towards the lion’s den. “Sure,” I said, impaling myself on the sword of my dad’s validation, “I would love to edit your novel.”He sent me the manuscript and I sent him some ground rules: everything was open to suggestion; he wasn’t allowed to yell at me; critiquing his work wasn’t the same as critiquing who he is as a person (writers know this is a lie). He agreed. I opened his document with fear in all four chambers of my heart and started reading.View image in fullscreenAnna Spargo-Ryan and her father, David RyanI had a lot of feedback. He had written a gorgeous story about young men and football and friendship, but like most new writers, his dialogue clanged. His characters’ actions didn’t ring true. He told too much and showed too little. Nervously, I added comments. At first they were like, “Hi Dad, I love you so much!!!!!! I would maybe consider removing this word ONLY IF YOU WANT TO! Shall we get a coffee?” I sent him a chapter at a time, waiting for him to call and tell me I was out of the will and also a live shark was on its way to kill me.But he didn’t. Mum sent secret photos of him bent over his laptop, writing and rewriting.Around page 260, I noticed something. Inside this story about vulnerable young men was a vulnerable older man. As his characters trained and competed to be better than before, so did he. With his 80th birthday in the near distance, my dad was asking me to teach him something new, and I realised he wasn’t perfect at everything first go; he was perfect at persevering. When I was little and frustrated at not being the best, he didn’t show me I didn’t have to try. He wasn’t teaching me I could get things right the first time but that I should never stop believing I might.The tables turned. “This doesn’t make sense,” I wrote. “She would never do this.” I began to lean on what I knew about him. “You know how the wind comes through Norwood Oval and it brings the pie smell? Show me that.” I had a shorthand for everything. A common anecdote. A memory we shared.Familyfolklore, in-jokes, people we’ve known. “WHY is this character behaving like Simon from the fruit shop???” Sometimes I just called him and made him explain himself, rationalise his choices, workshop a problem until it was solved.Dad made revisions. The harder I challenged, the better he wrote. Each chapter he returned was an improvement on the last, with people and scenes and conversations busting out of the pages. Not on his first go, or even second go, but on his ninth and 10th goes. “Thank you,” he said, over and over. “This is so helpful.”The more honest I was, the more he appreciated it. He did not yell at me. He did not think I loved him less.When Dad published his book this year, we did apodcastabout father-daughter editing. He spoke about how much it meant to him that I said yes. I ordered my copy the minute it went live, and when it arrived, I shelved it alongside my own books. Our little library – not of getting it right first time, but of learning to believe you might.Anna Spargo-Ryan is the author of A Kind of Magic, The Gulf and The Paper House, and a winner of the Horne prizeExplore more on these topicsFather's DayOpinionParents and parentingFamilyAustralian bookscommentShareReuse this content

title: Losing a parent is a bewildering, lonely experience. Here are the things I wish I had known before | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: There’ll be exhaustion, love tinged with occasional rage, even moments of black humour. But my mum would want me to tell you: don’t be afraid, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: There’ll be exhaustion, love tinged with occasional rage, even moments of black humour. But my mum would want me to tell you: don’t be afraid, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Illustration: R Fresson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: R Fresson/The GuardianOpinionBereavementLosing a parent is a bewildering, lonely experience. Here are the things I wish I had known beforeGaby HinsliffThere’ll be exhaustion, love tinged with occasional rage, even moments of black humour. But my mum would want me to tell you: don’t be afraidSat 5 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 12.22 EDTShareMy mother’s house looks exactly as she left it.Two novels sit by the armchair, their pages neatly marked for book group. Pinned to the noticeboard is a shopping list in only slightly shaky writing, with “FRUIT!” in urgent capitals, and “make soup” underlined. The sole outward signs of something missing are her cats twining needily around me – loneliness having finally overcome their innate horror of visitors – and the one thing I can’t bear to look at, which is the empty hospital bed marooned bleakly in the sitting room. Delivered by social services when it was deemed she could no longer manage stairs, it is now stripped bare, awaiting collection. Another family will be needing it.This is not my childhood home – my parents moved here only a few years ago – but it’s the one, I suppose, where childhood formally ended. Washing up at her kitchen sink a fortnight ago, looking out at the same scarlet fuchsia I remember blazing in the garden when my father died, it struck me for the first time that soon I would no longer be anyone’s daughter. What I didn’t know then was that the loss of both parents would feel less like the end of a relationship and more like its transition to a new stage, of finally being able to see them clearly as people in their own right.I thought I’d nailed that years ago, but of course I was wrong. When news spread of her diagnosis – an aggressively fast-moving cancer, erupting from nowhere to overwhelm her in six weeks – my mother’s friends descended in hordes, bringing soup and cake and clove-scented sweet peas from their gardens. But they also brought stories I hadn’t heard before. Though my father was the outwardly gregarious one and my mother more self-effacing, evidently she was the one who watched and listened and caught what others missed. I already knew that for a while she’d channelled that into volunteering as a Samaritan – her way of dealing with the suicide of a close family friend – and training as a Relate counsellor. I was vaguely aware, too, that in retirement she’d founded local hillwalking groups, a social club for widows – and who knows what else. But stupidly, I hadn’t realised what the things we took for granted – “there goes Mum, on one of her missions again” – meant to others. She had been the author of small kindnesses remembered for decades.double quotation markHave a baby and the world falls over itself to offer advice. But losing a parent remains a private, bewildering, lonely affairWhy wait for a funeral, one of her friends argued, to say nice things? There was talk of a pre-party, a wake Mum could actually join in, abandoned when it became clear she was already too tired. But the urge to invent new rituals makes sense. With modern medicine rendering heart attacks and strokes more survivable, death increasingly announces itself to elderly people not suddenly overnight but slowly, and with plentiful warning. The creeping degenerative diseases of old age allow more time to say goodbye, or make amends if necessary. But they also force us all to look death squarely in the face, and that takes no little courage.Fiercely independent at 84, my mother dreaded going into a home. So when she was given less than three months to live, my sister and I promised to nurse her at home, despite having no real plan for managing that alongside jobs and teenage children, beyond somehow basically winging it. Have a baby and the world falls over itself to offer advice. But losing a parent remains a private, bewildering, lonely affair. Here, then, are a few things I wish I’d known at the beginning of summer, in case – like that empty bed – another family can use them.That care for the dying will trigger the instant muscle memory of caring for small children, if you had them: the same broken nights, same constant vigilance, same exhaustion after a day in which you can’t name a single thing you actually did, and the same unmistakable feeling of love tinged with occasional rage. Then as now we wouldn’t have coped without understanding employers, good friends and neighbours, an army of often overworked NHS and care staff, and things my sister learned from training as a midwife. (For the love of your lower back, get a professional to show you how to move a bedbound patient safely.)That there are moments of unspeakably black humour to be found even in dying, if you’re that kind of family.That there are times when your role is to argue with their doctors, and times for shutting up and listening, and you may never be wholly certain which is which.That if an old person in beady possession of all their marbles goes seemingly mad overnight, test for an underlying infection causing delirium. Antibiotics work miracles.That you should keep the bad photographs, because afterwards they’re the ones you invariably want to look at: anything where the kids were scowling, the haircuts sorely regrettable, the beach day rained off. It’s the life actually lived, not the one curated for Instagram, that you miss.That death can trigger an overwhelming urge to put one’s house in order in ways that make sense to the dying, but absolutely nobody else. (My mother had to be dissuaded from getting the sitting room repainted; a friend’s father insisted on alphabetising his CDs.) Within reason, don’t fight it. Like the manic nesting phase of late pregnancy, it’s all part of the process.That if you find old letters, you should read them only when feeling resilient. Your parents had lives before you existed and secrets they may not have shared.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat death itself is different for everyone, but that even the most peaceful kind looked to me like a form of work. The best way I can describe it is like a reverse childbirth: you can comfort the person going through it, but you cannot be in it with them.That it wasn’t nearly as frightening as that may sound.That grief doesn’t always wait for death. Dementia meant I lost my father in some ways years before he died, and a wise friend said that nursing my mother might feel, in retrospect, like starting to work through bereavement in advance. She wasn’t wrong.That adrenaline may power you through initially, and kindness may undo you.And lastly, what I think my mother would have wanted me to say: that if this is something you have yet to face, don’t be afraid. But if you’re already there and struggling, then you are nowhere near as alone as you think.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBereavementOpinionDeath and dyingFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: Catastrophic dangers await Burnham’s push for English devolution | Phillip Inman | The Guardian
description: Like France, the UK has always been centralised – and imposing a new political structure brings huge risks
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Like France, the UK has always been centralised – and imposing a new political structure brings huge risks
Content: In most countries where devolution works well, the establishment of local structures was organic rather than imposed.Photograph: Adrian Weston/AlamyView image in fullscreenIn most countries where devolution works well, the establishment of local structures was organic rather than imposed.Photograph: Adrian Weston/AlamyDevolutionCatastrophic dangers await Burnham’s push for English devolutionPhillip InmanLike France, the UK has always been centralised – and imposing a new political structure brings huge risksSat 5 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShareDevolution in England is going to be messy and slow, and brings with it huge risks thatAndy Burnhamignores at his peril.The prime minister’sdevolution pushwill be messy because Whitehall’s ingrained anxiety about handing over money and power will lead to piecemeal deals, starting with a deal for Cornwall that will lack the much-promised driving force of a newly minted mayor.And there is every prospect that it will be slow now that thereappointed housing secretaryAngela Rayner’s reorganisation of local government, creating hundreds of unitary authorities where counties and districts once ruled, is mired in judicial reviews. Some councils have run up huge debts in the last decade and it’s not clear how these debts will be divided among the new entities.There are claims that plans to divide some existing county councils into three, four or even five unitary authorities is politically motivated and thatLabourhas become seduced by the prospect of retaining a presence in local government through gerrymandering.Last week, Hertfordshire county council and Newcastle-under-Lyme borough council became the latest local authoritiesto send letters to Rayner, seeking clarity on how the government reached its decision in their areas.A week earlier, Lincolnshire county council did the same. Farther south, Essex county, which is to be divided into five unitary authorities, found that the recommendation of Whitehall officials for just three new authoritieswas overruled by Rayner.Supposedly, all this infighting will be resolved by Christmas andEnglandwill be ready for an entirely new map of local authorities by next May when fresh elections will be held.Surely these councils and combined authorities, many of which are also embryonic, will struggle to become public institutions with verve, drive, knowledge and experience, able to make good decisions in time for the next election in 2029.When devolution is the prime minister’s big idea, one that will energise Britain’s spirit of enterprise, how it works is going to be crucial. He cannot risk Reform UK and the Tories crowing about another broken promise; or how it shows the British state is clogged with officials waiting for their generous pension, and in need of a Trumpian deep clean.Rayner’s plan is rooted in a belief that local government has failed to work properly and that structural reform is the answer, saving much more over the longer term than the estimated £2bn initial cost.It is a belief that has no basis in academic study. It would be a relief to all of those involved in local government and devolution to know that somewhere in the world there was data illustrating how this kind of structural change improves services, saves money and, as Burnham would have it, supercharges economic growth.Unfortunately there isn’t any such evidence. It is, to use a well-worn cliche, just re-arranging deckchairs. And it is not just because the same people will be taking up the same roles in new offices (and yes, there will need to be five head offices instead of one in Essex).As the Institute for Government says: “Structural reforms can be necessary, and useful. But there isnothing inherently valuableabout them.”What improves services are reforms to the way public officials work, and that means difficult discussions with trade unions. There needs to be a level of accountability that is absent in significant areas of the public sector. And it will be crucial to change how public organisations relate to each other, how they work together, breaking down old silos and protective practices. It involves giving more information to local people and including them in decision making going forward.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGeoff Mulgan, a University College London professor and the former boss of the Nesta thinktank, saysdevolution must answer basic questionspeople should know, such as how private and public services are delivered and who determines the outcome, from broadband to banking.“Otherwise it will remain entirely legitimate for populist politicians to say that people have lost control and to claim that they are the answer,” he says.In most countries where devolution works well, the establishment of local structures was organic, not imposed. Germany grew out of mini-kingdoms. The US started as a collection of states. The Länder in Germany, and US states, agreed to a federal government while retaining a good deal of power for themselves.The UK is more like France. It has always been centralised, and gained in many ways from that and lost out in others. So we should not underestimate how difficult it will be to impose a new political structure on England that devolves money and power to brand new councils and mayors, or in the case ofCornwall, a cabinet committee.The public will rightly be sceptical when so many councils under the current system have fallen for the idea that they can raise themselves up if only they borrow lots of money and “invest it” in new stuff. A new high street with hotels and leisure facilities wasWoking borough council’s dreamuntil it crashed, £2bn in debt.To say there are huge dangers in the world of finance when local council leaders are let loose, armed with a mission to generate growth, is to understate the situation. There are catastrophic dangers waiting.Explore more on these topicsDevolutionLocal governmentEconomicsPublic services policyAndy BurnhamCornwallLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Booyakasha! Ali G is back – but even he can’t match the absurdity of modern Britain | Jason Okundaye | The Guardian
description: Sacha Baron Cohen’s character once exposed the contradictions of an emerging multicultural nation. But nearly 30 years on Britain has changed – and so has the joke, says assistant Opinion editor Jason Okundaye
Author: Jason Okundaye
Headline: Sacha Baron Cohen’s character once exposed the contradictions of an emerging multicultural nation. But nearly 30 years on Britain has changed – and so has the joke, says assistant Opinion editor Jason Okundaye
Content: A still from the forthcoming film Ali G: Who Iz I?.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosView image in fullscreenA still from the forthcoming film Ali G: Who Iz I?.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosOpinionSacha Baron CohenBooyakasha! Ali G is back – but even he can’t match the absurdity of modern BritainJason OkundayeSacha Baron Cohen’s character once exposed the contradictions of an emerging multicultural nation. But nearly 30 years on Britain has changed – and so has the jokeSat 5 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 07.04 EDTShareAnd so the nostalgia machine grinds on, dragging another pop culture corpse back into the light: yes, it’s the return of Ali G. Respeck.Sacha Baron Cohen’s skull-cap-wearing, “rudebwoy” wankster is staging a comeback with Ali G: Who Iz I?. The new film, premiering next month, is amockumentarythat sees the character starting a family with long-term companion Julie (thinking his approach to fatherhood will be “absent”) and embracing TikTok, all while donning new fake dreads and a rastacap.It’s taken little time for this revival to enter Britain’s terminal “ARE U OFFENDED, SNOWFLAKE?” culture-war cycle. The Telegraph’s chief film critic, Robbie Collin, wrote that Ali G would save us fromcomedy’s offence police: “We need a good dose of this sort of puerile needling more than ever.” And now there is apressure campaignasking cinemas not to screen Baron Cohen’s “racist caricature”, which has accruedmore than 46,000 signatures.The old hits never die. Yet I think this reboot, however tedious, prompts some worthwhile reflection about the changing state of Britain. Since Ali G’s debut in 1998, there has been disagreement over who the joke is on. Erstwhile defenders viewed the character’s absurdity as a reflection of society’s soft bigotry, a satire of white liberal elites’ prejudices.Ali G’s initial premise was interviews with unsuspecting public figures while posturing as a low-educated wannabe, and lobbing inane questions that reliably wrongfooted the interviewee. With a few exceptions, these interviewees were white, from Noam Chomsky to Newt Gingrich to Donald Trump (who walked out). The socialist MP Tony Benn, victim of such a set-up on the 11 O’Clock Show,admitted in 2000that “at no stage during our talk did I suspect for a second that it was other than a genuine programme”. The idea then was that you were laughing at the gullibility of the liberal middle classes.View image in fullscreenSacha Baron Cohen in Ali G Indahouse (2002).Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyBut some viewed this interpretation as apologia for something sinister. Black British comedians in particular viewed Ali G as a straight-upracist caricature. Comedian Felix Dexter was candid: “I feel that a lot of the humour is laughing at black street culture and it is being celebrated because it allows the liberal middle classes to laugh at that culture in a safe context where they can retain their sense of political correctness.”I think the most interesting intervention worth revisiting is that of the sociologist Paul Gilroy, who saw the comedy as a reflection of multicultural Britain’s coming-of-age.Writing in 2002, after the premiere of the film Ali G Indahouse, Gilroy posited that the character provided “a satirical Rorschach blot in which even the most neurotic scrutineers of the national psyche can discover their fears and hopes”.That interpretation fit with Gilroy’s theory of cultural hybridity: Ali G’s incoherence as a “shapeshifting” white English man performing a pastiche of Black urban street culture embodied the cultural mongrelisation that had been shaping Britain under New Labour. Ali G represented a cartoonish version of the very real destabilising of racial categories that was happening at the time. Some were optimistic about cultural diversity, while others were anxious. In particular the influence of nascent “yardie” culture, American hip-hop and conspicuous consumption was sometimes viewed as a social contagion impeding British youth.The salient question for me, then, is less whether it’s OK to find Ali G funny, or if it’s offensive, but rather what the character’s function and purpose is in 2026. His particular cultural bricolage is now being thrown into a far more charged political environment.Cultural boundaries remain porous, but the political boundaries around national belonging have hardened. Ali G emerged from a politics fascinated by cultural change and mixing, and returns to a politics dominated by a more severe policing of who gets to be British. The anxiety Ali G once represented is now a far more antagonistic struggle; just take a look at the ubiquitous“yookay”meme, the idea that multiculturalism has socially corrupted the UK.The mediums through which we absorb culture have also changed. Ali G’s racial politics were originally mediated through television: editing, scheduling and official channels for regulation meant that, however controversial, Baron Cohen and his collaborators could control its message. Online, that control disappears. You can easily imagine an Ali G scene now being clipped and shared as an anecdote of Britain’s decline.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd so Ali G arrives from the analogue world into one that is far more racialised, online and politically volatile. But the character has become obsolete because it is no longer transgressive: the cultural mix that once made Ali G ludicrous is now mundane. The seemingly exotic language Ali G parodies has for a long time now been understood asMulticultural London English.There is also the problem of Baron Cohen himself. His original approach had an incredibly effective comedy mechanism, using interviews to make powerful establishment figures reveal themselves. But Baron Cohen is no longer the outsider performing the outsider role, he is now a very famous 54-year-old multimillionaire attempting a last-gasp revival. Will anyone be duped, and what exactly could he reveal now anyway?It’s easy to dismiss the furore around Ali G’s return as political correctness. But it’s not that Britain has become too sensitive for the joke, it may be that the joke simply doesn’t work any more. And so what returns with Ali G is little more than the same old stereotype in a new costume, detached from the time in which it meant something more.Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the GuardianDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
