title: The pressure on Burnham to appease the right is huge. But now is the time to step out of Reform’s shadow | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: A scandal-besieged Reform still has a loyal base that won’t budge. That should free up the PM to deliver some home truths, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: A scandal-besieged Reform still has a loyal base that won’t budge. That should free up the PM to deliver some home truths, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Attenders at the second day of the Reform UK conference in Birmingham, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenAttenders at the second day of the Reform UK conference in Birmingham, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionAndy BurnhamThe pressure on Burnham to appease the right is huge. But now is the time to step out of Reform’s shadowAndy BeckettA scandal-besieged Reform still has a loyal base that won’t budge. That should free up the PM to deliver some home truthsSat 5 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 11.42 EDTShareDespite the bright start to Andy Burnham’s premiership, and Reform UK’s sudden disarray, a shadow still hangs over British centre-left politics. Labour has a smallpoll lead, a cautious air of confidence and a leader who seems energised rather than overwhelmed by trying to solve the country’s problems. Meanwhile, Reform is having a terrible 2026: mired in deepening funding scandals, losing winnable byelections and, thanks to the drama and novelty of Burnham’s leadership coup and new government, no longer the freshest story around.Yet Reform UK’s support has either held up or fallen only slightly in most polls since Burnham entered Downing Street. Even in the Makerfield byelection, where he beat it more decisively than expected, Reform’s vote share and total supportactually rose. Nigel Farage may have spent the year uncharacteristically avoiding journalists, or in his prickly rather than jolly public mode, but the overwhelming majority of Reform supporters, almost a quarter of the electorate, remain faithful. “Power is within our grasp!” insisted Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesman, at its party conference in Birmingham on Friday, and they applauded with determined gusto.Meanwhile, their preoccupations continue to shape politics and how the media processes it. Immigration, crime, the benefits system, “wokeness”,net zero policies: all are constantly presented as out of control and contributing to national decline. From our overcrowded prisons to our almost exhausted North Sea oil- and gasfields, what are widely considered to be the most politically realistic options for the government are generally what most Reform voters would like to happen. The likelihood that permanent crime crackdowns and further large-scale fossil-fuel drilling – which the government looksincreasingly likely to approve– will bedisastrous for a country with an ever more obvious climate crisis and unprecedentedlylarge prison population, by historical and European standards, does not disturb this deep-rooted rightwing consensus. The pressure on Burnham to go along with it as prime minister will be never-ending.Yet the risks of governing under Reform’s shadow, while less discussed, are much larger. So far, Labour’s fragile poll recovery has mainly been built by taking support back from the Greens and Lib Dems, as the dip in their poll ratings since a Burnham premiership became likely has demonstrated. This change would almost certainly be undone if Burnham decided to follow a Reform-defined agenda. Keir Starmer’s abrupt announcement that he will leave parliament is the ultimate result of him making exactly that mistake in Downing Street – and has given the Greens’ leader, Zack Polanski, a chance to reverse the momentum shift from his party to Labour bystanding as a byelection candidate.Meanwhile, with Reform, Restore and the Tories all competing to be the most rightwing, and this country’s many reactionary media outlets doing the same, many right-leaning voters are even more convinced than usual that noLabourgovernment is acceptable. So the appeasement of conservative Britain, designed by Morgan McSweeney and carried out by Starmer, not always with conviction, was never likely to win many converts for long. In a deeply divided country, the days of Labour premiers attracting and holding on to large numbers of rightwing voters, as Tony Blair, Harold Wilson and Clement Attlee once did, are gone, at least for now.As a politician unusually keen by modern standards on cross-party collaboration and broad coalitions, Burnham could waste much of what may not be a long premiership trying to build bridges with the right. But there are some early signs he may pursue a more streetwise strategy. His debut contributions as prime minister in parliament this week mixed consensual catchphrases such as “problem-solving over point-scoring”, which made the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, sound rigidly confrontational in response, with sweeping attacks on areas where the right is vulnerable. Austerity, Brexit, privatisation and the centralisation of power in London have dwindling electoral support and even less credibility, however loudly the Tories and Reform defend some or all of them, because for decades these old-fashioned rightwing remedies have clearly failed to revive the country.“Far from ‘taking back control’, the combination of those policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain,”said Burnham, deftly turning a key promise of populism back against the rightwing populists. He knows that while Margaret Thatcher is still revered by Farage and Badenoch, the sometimes brutal economic changes that she and her Conservative successors drove through are not popular with all Tory and Reform voters. They may never switch to supporting Labour, but could support parts of Burnham’s programme, such as stronger public control over “the essentials of life” currently provided at excessive cost by toxic Thatcherite creations such as Thames Water.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAndy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations | George MonbiotRead moreThe approval, tacit or otherwise, of usually hostile voters on a specific issue can provide useful political cover for a government – especially an unpopular one, which Burnham’s is likely to be, however he performs, given the number of parties arrayed against him in our fragmented political landscape. He may well need that cover if his government is going to restructure the economy even half as ambitiously as he promises. The shareholders, financiers, lawyers and corporate executives who have done extremely well out of privatisation are not going to give up their gains and privileges without a fight.A temporary coalition of leftwing and rightwing voters may be the only way to overcome them. The economy is not democratic – much to the disappointment of generations of radical leftists – but in a democracy, powerful interests can be curbed or even defeated if they are challenged by a premier acting with broad public consent, as Attlee and Franklin D Roosevelt once did against some of the 20th century’s most entrenched economic elites.Yet if Burnham is to govern with anything like those legendary reformers’ effectiveness, then in other policy areas his government is going to have to stand up to Reform supporters. New research about them by King’s College London and UK in a Changing Europe shows that, despite this summer being the UK’s hottest ever, almost two-thirds “want to scrap the 2050 net zero target”. Meanwhile, anew Ipsos pollshows that immigration remains the number one public issue, particularly for Reform and Tory voters, despite the fact that immigration israpidly falling.Sooner or later, Burnham is going to have to use his celebrated communications skills to tell Britons some home truths, whether rightwing voters want to hear them or not. Otherwise, Reform’s shadow will chill his government for good.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourReform UKImmigration and asylumPrisons and probationClimate crisiscommentShareReuse this content

title: The US attorney general is fretting about a ‘pandemic’ of gender transitions in schools | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Todd Blanche’s remarks are part of a totally-not-invented moral panic that stretches the limits of the imagination
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Todd Blanche’s remarks are part of a totally-not-invented moral panic that stretches the limits of the imagination
Content: ‘Our intrepid attorney general, Todd Blanche, is on the case.’Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Our intrepid attorney general, Todd Blanche, is on the case.’Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersOpinionTodd BlancheThe US attorney general is fretting about a ‘pandemic’ of gender transitions in schoolsArwa MahdawiTodd Blanche’s remarks are part of a totally-not-invented moral panic that stretches the limits of the imaginationSat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 17.32 EDTShareBeing a public school teacher in the US these days is tough. You’ve got topayfor a lot of your own supplies, deal with smartphone-addicted children and perform gender-affirming surgeries on your lunch break.Luckily our intrepid attorney general, Todd Blanche, is on the case. Blanche appeared on Fox News this week todecrya “pandemic” of gender transitions in schools across the US. “There’s not a parent in America, no matter where you live, that would want their school to change and call their child by a different name and not expect to be told about that. We partnered with the Department of Education recently to combat this very trend and, really, pandemic that’s happening in some school districts around the country,” Blanche said. He seemed more concerned with name changes than with surgery, but the president himself has suggested on severaloccasionsthat schools are furtively doing surgery on children. During a campaign speech in 2024, for example, Donald Trumpsaid: “Can you imagine … your son leaves the house and you say: ‘Jimmy, I love you so much. Go have a good day in school,’ and your son comes back with a brutal operation? Can you even imagine this?”No, I can’t even imagine this. The public schools near me can’t affordair conditioning, so I’m not sure where they are getting all these operating theaters and surgeons from.Still, don’t let my lack of imagination stop you from getting outraged over this totally-not-invented moral panic, which is consuming valuable government resources. Blanche’s Fox News interview came shortly after the justice departmentfiledwhat itdescribedas a “first-of-its-kind lawsuit” against a Kansas school district, aimed at stopping itfrom“facilitating secret ‘gender transitions’ for children at school without their parents’ knowledge or consent”. The district, which denies wrongdoing, risks losing almost $70m in federal funds if it is found to have violated federal law.While this all sounds terribly dramatic, the substance of the Kansas public school lawsuit is actually rather mundane. It seems what is riling the Trump administration up are some extremely reasonable internal school guidelines, never adopted asformal policy, whichstate, according to the justice department complaint, that if a transgender student doesn’t want their parents notified about their preferred names and pronouns “that request will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis”.There’s certainly a sensible conversation to be had about whether teachers should inform parents if their child wishes to be known by a different name. And Blanche might actually want to ask the vice-president to weigh in on that matter, considering JD Vance has changed his own namemultiple times. But let’s not pretend that Blanche and Fox News are interested in sensible conversations. One suspects they just want to whip viewers up into a frenzy about trans people, a favourite boogeyman, in order to distract from the fact that the Trump administration is pillaging the country for personal gain.Let’s also not pretend that the attorney general, who wasconfirmedlast month, is in his job because he is deeply invested in the wellbeing of America’s young people. Blanche was Trump’s personalcriminal defense lawyerbefore he was brought into the White House; he eventually became attorney general following the ousting of Pam Bondi. He is a Trump loyalist who oncesaidhe’d tell the president: “Thank you very much. I love you, sir” if Trump nominated someone else for the job. He’s got his job, I’d wager, because he’s made it clear he’ll protect the president and advance Trump’s agenda. Indeed, one of the very first things that Blanche’s justice department did after he was confirmed as attorney general was to issue an opinion stating that the president’s “executive privilege” can extend to advisers whodon’t work for his administration. Which makes it harder for Democrats to investigate Trump in the future.But maybe I’m being uncharitable here. Maybe the attorney general isn’t just interested in advancing his own career by finding ways to give Trump carte blanche to do whatever he likes. Maybe he really does care about vulnerable young people. In which case, may I suggest he focus some of his attention on revisiting theJeffrey Epsteinfiles? I’m sure that I don’t need to remind you that theonly personin jail right now because of their connection to the late sex offender is Ghislaine Maxwell. An awful lot of powerful people seem to have successfully dodged any accountability.One would think an unpunished international pedophilia ring might worry Blanche more than schoolkids experimenting with their names in Kansas. However, Blancheseemsa littleresistantto taking the investigation much further – possibly because Trump is named in the Epstein files thousands oftimes. The attorney general also made sure to stress on Fox News earlier this yearthat“it isn’t a crime to party with Mr Epstein”.Still, it doesn’t matter how much Blanche tries to distract us with culture wars – he can’t escape the ghost of Epstein. This week, the outgoing congressman Thomas Massie, a staunch Trump critic, noted that millions of Epstein files have yet to be publicly disclosed andurgedthe Department of Justice to launch an immediate investigation into 14 named Epstein associates, including the billionaire Leon Black. “Perhaps hearing these names will shame the Department of Justice into delivering justice,”he said. One would hope so. But it’s hard to shame the shameless.Trailblazing feminist Gloria Steinem dies aged 92“Steinem, unlike some of her contemporaries, never recanted or modified her many causes, which included civil rights, violence against women, and the struggle for equality,” Yvonne Roberts writes in the Guardianobituary. “She continued to argue that every economics course ought to start not with production but with reproduction, and an understanding of the patriarchal instinct to restrict a woman’s right to contraception and abortion.”Eighty-nine percent of Americans believe there’s ‘widespread corruption’ within US governmentThat’s according to a newGallup poll, which found perceptions of corruption are at their highest level in 20 years. Gosh, I wonder why.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTennessee is about to execute its first woman since 1819Christa Pike isdueto be executed at the end of the month for a murder she committed with two others when she was 18. Pikesufferedchild sexual abuse, neglect and violent rape growing up; according to one psychologist she “experienced more severe adverse events than 99% of the US population”. Her case raises troubling questions, Austin Saratwritesin the Guardian: “For women as well as men, capital punishment offers no solution to the problems that give rise to the most serious crimes.”Israel ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’Anyone paying attention could seethis wasalways the plan.Health department accused of using fake AI studies to justify teen pregnancy cutsThe US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)canceled53 teen pregnancy prevention grants earlier this year and wants to direct millions in funding to organizations that emphasize “body literacy” and abstinence instead. This is despite (or perhaps because of) studies that have shown abstinence-only approachesincreaserates of teen pregnancy. There’s now a lawsuit over this, and the HHS has defended its decision with references todubiousstudies. In anopiniongranting a preliminary injunction, the judge said: “On the topic of body literacy, the notices (remarkably) reference public health studies that appear either not to exist or not to support the propositions for which they are cited – a hallmark of AI-generated citations.” This is on-brand for the HHS secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, whose team released a report on children’s health last yearfull of fake citations. It’s almost as if the man is dangerously unqualified for his job.JD Vance is OK with his work leading to the ‘end times’“While I wouldn’t be shocked if we are living in the end times, what I’m trying to focus on is doing as much of God’s work as possible right now,” the vice-presidentsaidduring apodcastinterview with Bryce Crawford, a young Christian evangelist. Vance added: “And if that leads to the end times, OK.”Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsTodd BlancheOpinionGenderTrump administrationDonald TrumpJeffrey EpsteinUS politicsKansascommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrike | Israel-Gaza war | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Guardian investigation reveals targeting of World Central Kitchen convoy was result of widely used military tactic
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Exclusive: Guardian investigation reveals targeting of World Central Kitchen convoy was result of widely used military tactic
Content: Top row, from left: Britons James Henderson, James Kirby and John Chapman were killed in the April 2024 Israeli strike on their aid convoy. The other victims were, bottom row, from left: Damian Sobol, Lalzawmi Frankcom, Jacob Flickinger and Saifeddin Abutaha.Composite: World Central Kitchen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTop row, from left: Britons James Henderson, James Kirby and John Chapman were killed in the April 2024 Israeli strike on their aid convoy. The other victims were, bottom row, from left: Damian Sobol, Lalzawmi Frankcom, Jacob Flickinger and Saifeddin Abutaha.Composite: World Central Kitchen/Getty ImagesIsrael-Gaza war‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrikeExclusive: Guardian investigation reveals targeting of World Central Kitchen convoy was result of widely used military tacticDeath on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted WCK aid workersMatan Cohen in Jerusalem, andJulian BorgerSat 5 Sep 2026 07.08 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven aid workers killed in an airstrike in Gaza were marked as targets under an Israeli military practice of establishing guilt by association, a Guardian investigation shows.A top Israeli military prosecutor announced last month that he would not pursue criminal proceedings for the April 2024 incident in which drones fired missiles at three clearly marked World Central Kitchen (WCK) cars soon after they had escorted a food aid delivery toGaza. Three British humanitarian workers along with an Australian, a Palestinian, a Pole and a dual US-Canadian national were killed.The official Israel Defense Forces (IDF) version of events pointed to specific mistakes made by a handful of officers. The victims of the strike were also blamed for hiring armed guards to protect a food aid convoy and for allegedly “deviating” from their agreed route.Death on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted World Central Kitchen aid workersRead moreHowever, interviews with senior Israeli officers involved in the incident or familiar with the official Israel investigation suggest it glossed over the role played in the killings by a common IDF practice used to designate targets, which endangers aid workers and civilians in general, especially when combined with the army’s open-ended mission to end Hamas’s civil control in Gaza.More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military in the three years of the Gaza war. The army’sown internal datasuggests more than three-quarters of the dead have been civilians.The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, said the WCK workers became potential targets after they had a brief encounter, lasting just minutes, with armed guards assumed to be from Hamas (an assumption later shown to be groundless).He deemed them to have “mixed together” with alleged Hamas militants, where mixing together was defined as being “near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on”. Asked whether the presence of armed men made the entire convoy a target, Mendel replied: “Certainly.”He concluded: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.”View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the Israeli airstrike on the World Central Kitchen convoy in Gaza. Military prosecutors have ruled out criminal charges over the attack that claimed seven lives.Photograph: Ahmed Zakot/ReutersMendel was referring to a general policy ofhaflala, “incrimination”, which gives commanders in the field wide discretion on designating someone as a “terrorist”, including those “incriminated” by association. The manner in whichhaflalais to be applied in a given sector is often conveyed in a commander’s mission brief delivered verbally to other officers.He said his unit had been commended by the army hierarchy for its involvement in several strikes on what were deemed to be Hamas's attempted commandeering of aid. “They applauded us and were pleased with our action,” he said. The difference in the WCK incident was that foreign nationals were killed, he said. “That’s the whole difference. Not a substantive difference.”First location map and timelineWhen the WCK convoy was destroyed, it was nowhere near Israeli troops. Several Israeli officers familiar with the incident said the strikes were not ordered on the basis of an imminent threat to Israeli lives, but to fulfil the mission to thwart Hamas attempts to control aid deliveries.2nd location map and timelineAn IDF statement said the airstrikes were a result of an “erroneous assessment that Hamas military operatives were present in the vehicles, rather than from an intention to target the organisation’s personnel”.The statement added that “this assessment was compounded by serious failures to comply with applicable orders and procedures”. However, it said: “Following an in-depth examination of the findings and in light of the standards applicable under criminal law, it was determined that, despite the aforementioned failures, the circumstances of the incident did not give rise to a reasonable suspicion of a criminal offence warranting the opening of a criminal investigation.”The WCK said the Israeli decision not to pursue criminal proceedings was “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. “At the time of the lethal attacks, our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody,” the WCK said. “The IDF had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”Britain, Australia and Canada denouncedthe prosecutor’s decision as “shameful”, saying they would “continue to seek answers” on behalf of the slain aid workers. The UK opened an inquest in 2024 into the deaths of the three British team members: James Kirby, James Henderson and John Chapman.Saifeddin Abutaha, a Palestinian,Australian Zomi Frankcom, Damian Sobol, a Pole, and a dual Canadian-US citizen, Jacob Flickinger, were the other victims. The UK inquest was adjourned pending the outcome of the Israeli investigation.View image in fullscreenThe funeral in Bristol of James Kirby, 47, in May 2024.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesMendel, who is the only officer of such high rank to have been dismissed for his actions in the Gaza war, has been portrayed in army command briefings as a rogue operator. Questions have been raised about a political motive. Mendel is a settler who is reported to have been one of the 130 signatories of a 20 January 2024 letter to the IDF calling for the flow of aid to Gaza to be restricted.However, the way the Israeli army operates in Gaza – rules of engagement are made contingent on local circumstances and passed on, often verbally, down the chain of command – gives officers at Mendel’s level wide discretion in subjective judgments as to who is a “terrorist” and therefore a target.The IDF statement said its activity in the Gaza Strip was “regulated by a broad range of binding written orders and standing directives governing the use of force, the approval processes for strikes, strikes against sensitive sites, and other matters” and that these incorporated “the rules of the laws of armed conflict, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precautions in attack”.The statement said that “a person does not become a lawful target merely because they are in the vicinity of an armed individual, come into contact with them, or travel alongside them”.The IDF said: “Carrying a weapon may be a relevant factor in such an assessment, but is not sufficient on its own without meeting the definitions described above. In particular, and in the context of the incident in question, security personnel hired to protect a humanitarian convoy from looting do not become lawful targets merely because they are armed.”An IDF officer familiar with the WCK killings said that given the circumstances and the standing IDF procedures, the overwhelming majority of officers would have acted in the same way. “There were armed men next to them,” the officer said. “If you took qualified people and put them on the call, in 90% of cases this is what would have happened,” the officer said. “In my guess, 99% of the time the first bomb would have been dropped; 90% of the time the second; 80% of the time the third.”Reserve Brigadier General Oren Solomon, the battle manager of Gaza Division, said that a mistake had been made in determining that an armed man had entered one of the vehicles, but added that once that error had been committed, the incrimination procedure led inevitably to the three missile strikes.“If I incriminated this vehicle beforehand as Hamas – anyone who escapes from it and enters another vehicle: death comes,” Brig Gen Solomon said. “Together with him they will die. That meets the incrimination rules, no problem.”A senior officer involved in the initial Israeli military investigation into the WCK case, argued Mendel overstepped in interpreting the rules of incrimination.“You can’t incriminate 20 people if there’s one armed,” he said. The officer argued that the first strike could have been justified by the initial misidentification, even at the cost of civilian casualties, but not the subsequent missiles.“You struck someone you suspected, a vehicle you suspected had an armed man in it. The moment two people came out, nobody with a weapon, the second and third strikes are contrary to orders because you don’t know whom you’re striking,” he said.The other systemic factor that contributed to the deaths of the seven aid workers, and potentially countless more civilians, was one of the missions given to the army in Gaza by Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government: to destroy Hamas’s influence and control. That meant anyone deemed to be involved in – or assisting – the Hamas administration, including by distributing aid, could find themselves in the sights of an Israeli drone operator.“I remind you that part of our mission was to crush Hamas’s ability to govern,” Mendel said. “Part of the mission was to hit that [Hamas-controlled aid deliveries], and we hit it.”Interviews with IDF officers suggest there was a widespread belief in the ranks that Hamas had wrested control of the bulk of aid deliveries into Gaza. That assumption was unfounded, later analysis showed. It was a period of widespread hunger caused by an Israeli blockade, when food convoys were being mobbed by desperate civilians, criminal gangs and Hamas militia.The belief that Hamas hijacks were widespread meant that the appearance of armed men in proximity to the WCK vehicle in April 2024 fitted a “pattern of activity” that helped incriminate the whole convoy in the eyes of Mendel and his unit.The IDF officer familiar with the incident said it was common practice to designate any armed man in Gaza as Hamas or a “terrorist”, as Mendel did. The officer added: “How you define that it’s Hamas – he’s in proximity to weapons, and because he touches the trucks, and because he does all sorts of things that look as if he’s going to take over the trucks.”The role of the incrimination principle in the WCK killings shows how it has become a factor in the historically high proportion of civilians killed in the Gaza war. This sits alongside the routine acceptance of high “collateral damage” in the targeting of Hamas militants, the designation of large and shifting areas as free-fire zones, and the deliberate levelling of neighbourhoods to prevent the return of Palestinian communities.The common factor is that constraints on targeting were minimised in the interests of an open-ended mission. Since the start of the war in 2023, no Israeli soldier has been convicted of wrongful death or war crimes in Gaza operations.“I came to defeat Hamas,” Mendel said. “If such an event came before me again, I would do exactly the same thing.”He also dismissed the significance of the killings. “I think it’s an idiotic side event,” Mendel said. “It really isn’t a serious event.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsIsrael-Gaza warIsraelGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahunewsShareReuse this content

title: Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flash flood disaster | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation
Author: William Christou
Headline: Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation
Content: Rescuers in Nepal find two more people aliveNepal-Tibet flood disasterRescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flash flood disasterChinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operationWilliam ChristouSat 5 Sep 2026 07.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 14.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmergency responders have rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hitNepal.The Nepali military said on Saturday a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India,China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.Two Nepali workers wererescued from another tunnelin a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.Rescue of Nepal hydropower workers ‘triumph for humans and humanity’, tunnelling expert saysRead moreExperts have said the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapseon 26 August.Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalChinaTibetSouth and central AsiaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Drone attack blamed on guerrillas kills at least three soldiers in Colombia | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Officials accuse National Liberation Army of launching strike followed by clash inside military compound
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Officials accuse National Liberation Army of launching strike followed by clash inside military compound
Content: Colombia’s minister of defence, Jorge Mora (centre), looking at the site of a guerrilla drone attack, at a military garrison in Ocaña, Colombia, on 5 September 2026.Photograph: Javier Cassela/Colombian ministry of defence/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenColombia’s minister of defence, Jorge Mora (centre), looking at the site of a guerrilla drone attack, at a military garrison in Ocaña, Colombia, on 5 September 2026.Photograph: Javier Cassela/Colombian ministry of defence/AFP/Getty ImagesColombiaDrone attack blamed on guerrillas kills at least three soldiers in ColombiaOfficials accuse National Liberation Army of launching strike followed by clash inside military compoundAssociated Press in BogotáSat 5 Sep 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn attack involving explosives dropped from drones followed by a clash inside a military compound in north-easternColombiahas killed at least three soldiers and wounded four, Colombia’s army said on Saturday.Local authorities blamed the attack – which took place late on Friday – on the rebel National Liberation Army (ELN).It targeted a military unit in the municipality of Ocaña, in the Norte de Santander department, which borders Venezuela. Two soldiers died at the site and a third after receiving medical attention, Colombia’s military said on X.Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, condemned the attack. “For every police officer or soldier murdered, we will bring the full weight and legitimate force of the state down upon the criminals,” he said.Much of ELN, an armed group active since 1964, is based in the Catatumbo region, which includes parts of the Norte de Santander and Cesar departments. ELN also harbours dissident factions of the now defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) that did not join the peace agreement a decade ago.Both groups are vying for control of the strategic region, which connects to the porous border with Venezuela and is one of Colombia’s primary coca-producing areas.In August, an explosion outside a police station in Cucuta injured 11 police officers and killed a police dog. Officials also blamed that attack on the ELN.Earlier this week, at least one civilian was killed and 11 other people were injured after a car bomb exploded outside a police station in north-eastern Colombia.Explore more on these topicsColombiaAmericasDrones (military)newsShareReuse this content

title: More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican | US news | The Guardian
description: Latest data from Gallup, showing 49% leaning Democrat and 39% Republican, marks sharp reversal from 2024
Author: Roque Planas
Headline: Latest data from Gallup, showing 49% leaning Democrat and 39% Republican, marks sharp reversal from 2024
Content: A polling station in North Carolina on 3 March.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersView image in fullscreenA polling station in North Carolina on 3 March.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersUS newsMore voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves RepublicanLatest data from Gallup, showing 49% leaning Democrat and 39% Republican, marks sharp reversal from 2024Roque PlanasSat 5 Sep 2026 17.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves Republican, according to thelatest quarterly data published by Gallup.Some 49% of voters surveyed leaned Democrat, including independent voters asked to pick one party or the other. Only 39% of respondents leaned Republican.That 10-point spread marks a sharp reversal from the four-point advantage that Republicans held over Democrats in the fourth quarter of 2024, when voters sent Donald Trump back to the White House and Republicans swept both houses of Congress. Democrats are seeing their most sizable advantage since 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president,according to the New York Times.The data offers the latest evidence that Trump’s second term has proved unpopular with voters, driving a potential backlash.Trump’s approvalrating stood at 52%at the time of his second inauguration in January of 2025, according to an average of polls published by the New York Times.But his popularity dwindled immediately, as he cleaved the federal workforce, imposed price-inflating tariffs, passed a profligate spending bill and launched a rudderless war with Iran. Some 58% of voters now disapprove of his performance, with only 38% approving, according to the Times.Democrats are hoping to take advantage of Trump’s tanking popularity. Liberals are likely to retake the US House of Representatives in midterm elections this November. The party is much less certain to retake the US Senate, though polling is giving Democratsreasonstofeel optimistic.A growing share of American voters have not identified with either party in recent years. Back in 2002, roughly a third of voterssurveyed by Gallupidentified as either Republican, Democrat or independent. By last year, 45% of respondents called themselves independents, with only 27% identifying as either Democrat or Republican.Explore more on these topicsUS newsDemocratsRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge orders Trump administration to reveal who set up $1.8bn ‘anti-weaponization fund’ | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Judge issues order as part of discovery process in lawsuit brought by non-profit into now defunct compensation fund
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Judge issues order as part of discovery process in lawsuit brought by non-profit into now defunct compensation fund
Content: Todd Blanche proposed the compensation fund before his confirmation hearing for US attorney general, then dropped it after bipartisan outcry.Photograph: Samuel Corum/EPAView image in fullscreenTodd Blanche proposed the compensation fund before his confirmation hearing for US attorney general, then dropped it after bipartisan outcry.Photograph: Samuel Corum/EPATrump administrationJudge orders Trump administration to reveal who set up $1.8bn ‘anti-weaponization fund’Judge issues order as part of discovery process in lawsuit brought by non-profit into now defunct compensation fundEdward HelmoreSat 5 Sep 2026 11.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 16.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal judge has ordered theTrump administrationto reveal who set up the structure of a controversial $1.8bn “anti-weaponization fund” to recompense victims of so-called political lawfare that was reportedly dropped by the justice department last month.Ivan Davis, the US magistrate judge for the eastern district of Virginia, issuedthe ordercompelling discovery materials from the government as part of alawsuitbrought by the Democracy Forward non-profit on behalf of plaintiffs including a fired prosecutor and a college professor acquitted of assaulting federal agents at a protest against an immigration raid inCalifornia.“Today’s order granting discovery is a significant step in getting to the bottom of the slush fund,” said Aman George, senior counsel at the non-profit. “We will continue to meet the government in court until our investigation is complete and the slush fund is permanently halted.”Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US militaryRead moreLast month,Todd Blanchesaid the fund he proposed before he was confirmed “is dead”. The US attorney general told Fox News Sunday: “The fund is dead or whatever word you want to use. It never started. So, it’s not as if the fund is coming back.”Democrats maintain that the proposed fund would have been used to compensate prosecuted and since-pardoned January 6 rioters, among others. Blanche said that Trump “believes the justice department was weaponized against a lot of Americans” under the Biden administration, adding: “It really hurt them financially.”The proposed compensation scheme was set up as part of the settlement Trump reached with the IRS regarding a lawsuit over the leak of his tax returns. The agreement shielded the president and his family from future tax audits.In July, another federal judge found that the parties had never truly been in conflict and Trump’s $10bn lawsuit against the IRS had only ever been a pretense for setting up the fund.“There was never adverseness between the parties; there was never a case or controversy; and there was never a question as to who would prevail,” the US district judge Kathleen Williams said in a ruling, adding that the lawsuit had been brought “for an improper purpose – to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy for a ‘settlement’ that had no viable basis in law or fact”.The proposed fund drew bipartisan criticism in Washington, including opposition from two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and it put Blanche’s confirmation for attorney general at risk.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCritics of the program have noted that the document demanded by lawmakers did not include signatories to the initial agreement, suggesting that it could be revived. Blanche has said that “there were never commissioners” in charge of the “payout pot”. But Senate Democrat Cory Booker said the agreement guaranteed “nothing … no guarantees whatsoever that this slush fund still can’t go forward”.Trump has rued the abandonment of the fund and has not ruled out another avenue to compensation. “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t,” he said of the fund at a cabinet meeting in July. “To be honest with you, I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationDonald TrumpTodd BlancheRepublicansLaw (US)US politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform continues to cast doubt on climate science. Do its supporters agree? | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Climate scepticism is common at the Reform party conference, but many also criticise Labour for failing to protect Britons from hot weather
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Climate scepticism is common at the Reform party conference, but many also criticise Labour for failing to protect Britons from hot weather
Content: A Greenpeace protest banner was unfurled during Richard Tice’s speech on Friday.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Greenpeace protest banner was unfurled during Richard Tice’s speech on Friday.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersReform UKReform continues to cast doubt on climate science. Do its supporters agree?Climate scepticism is common at the Reform party conference, but many also criticise Labour for failing to protect Britons from hot weatherFiona Harveyin BirminghamSat 5 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 08.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the second day of the Reform UK conference,in the wake of an undercover investigationalleging party officials plotted to evade the law on foreign donations, the deputy leader, Richard Tice, addressed the audience. Within minutes, a banner appeared behind him reading: “Collect £5m, burn the planet.”It was taken down promptly and Tice, who has repeatedly called on people toenjoy the summer’s five successive heatwaves and record drought, rolled on. As Reform members at the Birmingham venue applauded Tice, there was plenty of agreement with his views. “I enjoyed the heat this summer,” said Jeanette Bowden, of Bexley. “I don’t think people need telling to take care of themselves.” Her partner, James, added, without scientific backing: “Carbon dioxide was much higher in the past, it was 10 times higher than this during the ice ages. It’s not a human problem.”11:20Reform donations scandal: is this the final blow for Farage? - The LatestAmid stalls offering simulated helicopter rides, gold as an investment, tattoos and discounts on rum, climate scepticism was common. “It’s overhyped,” said Yvonne, who did not wish to give a surname.“I don’t believe the predictions,” said Jim Langford. “They told us Norwich would be underwater by now and it’s not Atlantis yet.” Ed Rennie, a former Labour councillor from north London, said theIntergovernmental Panel on Climate Changehad reduced some of its higher predictions.But many of the same people who, like Tice,cast doubt on climate science, also criticised the government for failing to protect people against the hot weather. Bowden pointed to new-build houses. “They have really small windows,” she said. “That might be good in winter, but in summer it must be too hot, you can hardly open them. The government should not force this on people.”Yvonne added: “The government were all on their holidays in the summer, not doing their jobs [to help people during the heatwaves]. Government should ensure there is clean water and sewage, but they’re not even doing that.”Nicholas, another delegate who did not wish to be named in full, said air conditioning should be installed in all hospitals, schools, libraries and public buildings, and made more easily available for homes.View image in fullscreenRichard Tice speaking at the Reform UK conference in Birmingham.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersLangford said the government was “absolutely not” doing enough to help people cope with the impacts of extreme weather. “They’re not preparing us at all, they’re just wasting resources.” Beryl Kingsbury said people should take responsibility for their own safety during hot weather, but farmers needed help. “They should have more support, but this government seems to hate farmers.”For Mark Henderson, a facilities manager who works mostly outside looking after three large yards, the government’s role should be to apply common sense to health and safety. “I wear a helmet all the time, which was very hot [in the heatwaves], but I don’t need it all the time. You should be able to relax those rules in hot weather, to make them task-specific,” he said.The confusion among Reform supporters, explained Michael Jacobs, an emeritus professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, was to be expected given the party leadership’s peddling of “myths and lies” over the climate. Voters often say they want contradictory things, such as high standards of social care without tax rises to pay for them, Jacobs pointed out. But on the climate, they face an even more intensebombardment from contradictory viewpoints, asparties of the right try to turn the issue into a culture war.“It’s really incoherent to be in favour of adaptation but not [cutting greenhouse gas emissions], but it’s not surprising people think that, given what they’ve been told,” Jacobs said. “Tice and Farage have claimed net zero would be economically ruinous, which is simply wrong. They try to say the UK is acting alone in cutting emissions, also untrue. These are pernicious myths. They have obscured the scientific fact that net zero is the description of where you need to get to, to stop the climate crisis getting any worse.”Party activists of all stripes – the people who come to conferences – also tend to have stronger opinions than a party’s voters. Polls consistently show that Reform voters are muchless likely to deny climate science than their leaders, and large majoritieswould like to see renewable energy sited near them, despite opposition to renewables from the party leadership. And although Reform has railed against “net stupid zero”, a significant minority,roughly a quarter by some polling, remain in favour of the target. In contrast to the leadership’s stance, which is to scrap the North Sea windfall tax,about 70% want higher taxes on fossil fuels,according to a poll taken last year.View image in fullscreenProtesters from Climate Resistance brandished a ‘Resist Reform’ banner in the building where the conference is taking place.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersLabour’s climate minister, Katie White, said Reform was out of step with voters. “After the summer we’ve just had, outright climate denial is a pretty lonely corner of British politics,” she said, noting that the government was investing in flood and coastal defences, and in strengthening the response to wildfires.“My plea to Reform members, MPs and their leadership is a genuine one: please don’t turn climate change into another culture war. Britain has always been at its best when we lead, invent and build. I want our country developing the technologies the world will need, backing British businesses and innovators, and protecting the people and places we love.”Dissenting voices were hard to find among delegates, but there were occasional flashes of doubt. One younger Reform member, a 25-year-old candidate to be a councillor in the north-west, was unusual in being less certain of the leadership’s stance. “I’m not sure what they should be doing on the climate,” he said. “But I know I and my generation will have to live with it.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKClimate crisisNigel FarageClimate science scepticism and denialIntergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)Richard TiceClimate sciencenewsShareReuse this content

title: After overtourism besieged Big Sur, the worst finally happened: ‘People kept saying someone is going to die’ | California | The Guardian
description: The coastal community in California had already been devastated by landslides and wildfires before a fatal crash
Author: Andrew Gumbel
Headline: The coastal community in California had already been devastated by landslides and wildfires before a fatal crash
Content: Bixby Bridge in Big Sur, California, on 30 May.Photograph: Myung J Chun/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBixby Bridge in Big Sur, California, on 30 May.Photograph: Myung J Chun/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesCaliforniaAfter overtourism besieged Big Sur, the worst finally happened: ‘People kept saying someone is going to die’The coastal community in California had already been devastated by landslides and wildfires before a fatal crashAndrew Gumbelin Big Sur, CaliforniaSat 5 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCalifornia’s rugged Big Sur coastline is often called a slice of heaven, 120 miles (195km) of unspoiled rocky promontories, sandy beaches and redwood forests at the foot of the Santa Lucia mountains. This year, it has endured a long summer of hell.Wildfires, road closures and repeated disruptions to the local hotel, restaurant and campsite businesses all have posed significant challenges in an era of climate change and unpredictable weather patterns. One large fire broke out in the highlands east of Big Sur in early August and is still less than 25% contained. A second fire erupted 30 miles to the south two weeks later and is so inaccessible to firefighters that it has grown bigger than the first and is barely contained at all.Residents of the area have long known that the threat of natural catastrophe is part of what it means to live in a remote and beautiful place. But for many, the events of this summer have renewed questions about the sustainability of mass tourism in the area, particularly in the age of Instagram.The tourist industry accounts for about 90% of the local economy, so visitors are certainly welcome. But nobody feels comfortable with chaos on the roads, tourists who leave their messes behind or a pair of recent traffic deaths that have plunged the community into mourning. Like other global hotspots, from Italy to the Galápagos, Big Sur is asking: how many is too many?Henry Miller once described this coast as a place imbued with “the peace of God, and the serene security created by a handful of good neighbors living at one with the creature world”. But many coastal residents worry that sort of peace is rapidly eluding their grasp.A reopening marred by selfie-snappersThe disruptions began at the beginning of the year with the long-awaited reopening of Highway 1, a two-lane road that provides the only vehicle access to Big Sur from the Monterey peninsula in the north to Cambria in the south. For three years, the route had been cut in two by extensive repair work in the wake of heavy landslides, another abiding natural threat. The region lostabout 20%of its tourists over that time, at a cost of millions of dollars a month. Hearst Castle, on the southern end of the peninsula, lost as many as 40%.The reopening immediately caused visitor numbers toshoot back up, but residents and local officials noticed that along with the nature lovers and the hikers came many more tourists interested almost exclusively in snapping selfies at a handful of well-advertised locations before moving swiftly on.View image in fullscreenTourists take photos at Bixby Bridge on 14 January.Photograph: Myung J Chun/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesSuch visitors weren’t shy about stopping in the middle of the road to take pictures at the spectacular, arched Bixby Bridge, even if it meant snarling traffic for miles in each direction. Local media was filled with stories of visitors trampling on plants, camping illegally and tossing their trash in all directions. In July, a selfie-ruining banner appeared on the Bixby Bridge that read: “Overtourism is killing Big Sur.” But it made little difference.“Visitor behavior has changed so much,” said Kate Daniels, who represents Big Sur on the Monterey county council and successfully pressed for aparking moratoriumat the Bixby Bridge that went into effect last month. “This is one of the most beautiful places you’ve ever seen, yet people have decided their goal is to take a picture of themselves on a bridge … It’s really difficult and dangerous, and that road cannot handle it.”‘It was a nightmare’For many residents, the low point came in mid-August, when Monterey county hosted its annual Car Week extravaganza, featuring thousands of vintage and exotic cars and a line-up of events in and around the city of Monterey and the golf courses of Pebble Beach.Some of the event’s 100,000 visitors repurposed the Big Sur coastline as a playground for their souped-up coupes and convertibles. They had done much the same the previous year, but now the Timber fire was raging, every change in the wind was apt to carry the smell of burning forest and the community had no patience for it.Even as fire trucks were trying to set up defensive lines in an effort to save buildings and people, car aficionados were filmed making high-speed dashes down the straightest stretches of Highway 1,doing doughnutsat traffic intersections and gathering dozens of vehicles for group photographs.Photos and videosposted online showed fire trucks struggling at times to move on a highway clogged with brightly painted sports cars.“It was a nightmare,” Daniels said. “Car Week has been going on for decades and it never used to be like this, but now it’s this hyper-masculine racing culture thing. People kept saying that someone is going to die.”By the end, people did die.View image in fullscreenCrews put out spot fires from the Timber fire in Big Sur on 13 August.Photograph: Nic Coury/APOn the final weekend, a 20-year-old out-of-towner at the wheel of a Dodge Challenger coupe plowed into Brian Roberts, a popular figure in Big Sur who went by the nickname Brewski and, according to his friends, had spent many of the previous days railing against the behavior of the Car Week attendees. Accounts differ about how the accident happened – some of Roberts’s friends say he was crossing Highway 1 to admire the sunset, while others say he was in the road yelling at cars after he found them blocking the turn-off to Palo Colorado Road, where he lived.Days later, an 80ft skid mark was still plainly visible, along with circular burn marks where vehicles appear to have been doing doughnuts. One of Roberts’s friends, Brendon Shave, arrived on the scene shortly after the accident and found bloodstains smeared across the median line and on the tarmac.The following day, another 20-year-old visitor from outside San Francisco smashed a silver BMW convertible into a tree a few miles north of Big Sur, killing one of his passengers and injuring himself and two other friends. Police said the driver recorded a blood alcohol level of 0.13, well above the legal limit, and they were investigating the death as gross vehicular manslaughter.Traffic deaths are a fact of life in Big Sur, with news reports suggesting that one occurs every few months, either because drivers go too fast along the windy, narrow road or because they become distracted by the natural beauty and plunge off the side.Still, Roberts’s death has moved people to particular outrage.View image in fullscreenThe Plaskett fire burns on a hillside in Big Sur on 27 August.Photograph: Ethan Swope/AP“The community felt disrespected because the land was on fire,” said Lindsey Kirk, a friend of Roberts’s from the San Francisco Bay Area who spends as much time as she can spare in Big Sur. “It’s crazy that the fire services couldn’t get through because of all the cars they brought in.”Shave, who runs a hair salon in Carmel, a 20-minute drive from where Roberts died, blamed authorities in Monterey county who, he said, used the beauty of Big Sur as a draw for big events – marathons and golf tournaments as well as the annual car show – but did little to look out for its residents. “People live here,” he said, “to get away from all the stuff that Monterey county keeps sending our way.”See Monterey, which promotes tourism in the region, has repeatedly urged visitors to Big Sur to stick to the speed limit and park legally and put out one statement headlined: “Big Sur Deserves Big Respect.”But the organization also encouraged Car Week attendees to explore far and wide, including the Big Sur coast. Eleven days after Roberts’s death, See Monterey put out a statement proclaiming “abanner year”, with hotel revenue up, visitor spending exceeding $100m and more than $4m raised for charity.View image in fullscreenThe lunch crowd at Nepenthe restaurant in Big Sur on 30 May.Photograph: Myung J Chun/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesLeft unmentioned were the many area businesses that closed for the week or threw up metal fences and hired security guards so their parking lots would not turn intoimpromptu, days long motor sports rallies.The visitors noticed. The driver of a McLaren supercar denied entry to an In-N-Out Burger attractednational attentionwhen his brother protested on his behalf: “That’s profiling! That’sracism towards cars.”‘We lost a good human being’Days after the last Lamborghinis and Porsches left town, a flare-up in the Timber fire sent cascades of sparks and ash down from Mount Manuel and prompted what many Big Sur residents felt should have happened much sooner: a comprehensive closure of Highway 1 encompassing most of the hotels and restaurants and some of the most heavily visited spots, including Pfeiffer Beach and McWay Falls.Authorities gave residents 24 hours either to stock up on essentials or leave town. Roberts’s mourners cheered – “Tourism is a problem, not a boon,” said Ivy La Velle, who described herself as his best friend – but others acknowledged it was never easy to make such a call.When the community shuts down, many of the hourly workers at the restaurants and hotels lose their source of income. If the fires force them to evacuate – dozens of them are housed by the resorts and campsites that employ them – their problems are compounded by unexpected housing and other expenses.Ryne Leuzinger, board chair of the Community Association of Big Sur, said his organization had been cutting $300 checks to help the neediest community members get by, and another group, the Big Sur Big Share, had spent the last several weeks making sure that people temporarily without an income had enough to eat.View image in fullscreenA memorial for Brian Roberts.Photograph: Andrew Gumbel/The GuardianBig Sur prides itself on its communal spirit, which was on vivid display the night before the closure, when 200 mourners crowded on to the back patio of the River Inn resort to pay homage to Roberts’s life, surrounded by flowers and crystals. Roberts worked as a maintenance worker and gardener at the Alila Ventana resort but also helped with firefighting efforts in the final weeks of his life and enjoyed a wide circle of friends.“Brian was a big member of the community,” Shave said. “We lost a good human being.”Speakers recalled how he would park a motorbike in the same spot at the River Inn, one of his favorite haunts, and spend his nights smoking and drinking rum and Cokes. “He had terrible taste in cocktails,” La Velle said afterwards, laughing. “It wasn’t even good rum.” Roberts’s parents, who had driven out from the midwest, did not pay for anything because his friends raised money to pay for their lodging, meals, funeral expenses and a $1,200 bill incurred when police towed his parked truck after the fatal accident.The next day, even as a bedraggled parade of dirt- and ash-covered cars and trucks made their way north before the closure deadline, mourners gathered at the makeshift memorial on the side of Highway 1 near the spot where Roberts was hit.Kirk, the friend from the San Francisco area, laid some lapis stones and a bouquet at a shrine that also featured a pack of American Spirit cigarettes, Roberts’s favorite brand, and an empty bottle of Sailor Jerry rum. “He was always around for anyone who needed anything,” she said. “He was a wonderful guy.”Sarah Sweeney, who in less uncertain times sells sushi from a truck, said Roberts embodied a certain Big Sur ethos now under threat, because he was passionate about a community that rejects the ordinary rhythms of modern life and, perhaps, wants to run away from them. “I call this place Neverland,” she said, “and we’re all Peter Pan. Or the lost boys. There are a lot of lost boys around here.”Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaOvertourismCalifornia wildfiresLandslidesWest CoastWildfiresExtreme weatherfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beekeepers warn of Asian hornet threat and call for UK awareness campaign | Insects | The Guardian
description: Experts say invasive species are creating ‘pollinator deserts’ and could have serious impact on food security
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Experts say invasive species are creating ‘pollinator deserts’ and could have serious impact on food security
Content: An Asia hornet marked with green for identification purposes by the government’s Animal and Plant Health Agency as part of efforts to track and control the species.Photograph: Emma Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn Asia hornet marked with green for identification purposes by the government’s Animal and Plant Health Agency as part of efforts to track and control the species.Photograph: Emma Khan/The GuardianInsectsBeekeepers warn of Asian hornet threat and call for UK awareness campaignExperts say invasive species are creating ‘pollinator deserts’ and could have serious impact on food securityNatalie WintSat 5 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish beekeepers have called for a national awareness campaign about the impact of Asian hornets as they warned the invasive species was creating “pollinator deserts” and threatening food security.Native to south-east Asia, the yellow-legged hornet is thought to have arrived in Europe in 2004 and has continued to spread ever since, its numbers probably boosted by increasingly warm springs and summers.The end of summer is a crucial time in Britain’s fight against the species. As colonies mature and nests reach maximum size, the hornets produce fertile new queens that will leave, mate and seek places to survive winter. The following spring, they establish new colonies, resulting in more nests across a wider geographical area.Asian hornets are an invasive species that prey on other insects. “Yellow-legged hornets cause significant damage to native pollinators, including our much-loved honeybees,” said Kate Wilson, the head of the National Bee Unit (NBU), which is responsible for bee health in England and Wales and sits within the government’s Animal and Plant Health Agency (Apha).Graphic showing comparative size of Asian hornet and common waspBut as well as threatening bees and making honey production difficult for beekeepers, the “real cost” of Asian hornets also concerned human safety, pollination and biodiversity, said Lucie Chaumeton, a trustee of the British Beekeepers Association (BBKA) and the vice-chair of its committee on the yellow-legged Asian hornet.“Asian hornets leave behind pollinator deserts, with a serious impact on food security and agricultural economy,” said Chaumeton, who is also a beekeeper.The government has been aware of this threat to biodiversity since it completed a risk assessment in 2011, which prompted the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Welsh government to develop a contingency plan for dealing with the species.Britain’s strategyis based on destroying nests to prevent the hornets from becoming established. Missing a single nest sustains an already established colony and risks the establishment of new colonies. One indication of the strategy’s effectiveness is the number of nests that are found. In 2025, the NBUdestroyed a record 161 nests.But there is still some evidence of establishment. Genetic analysis of nests found in 2024confirmedthat queens had successfully mated, survived winter and established new nests the next year. This means the period when queens emerge from hibernation is an important intervention point.Apha said the public and beekeepers played a key role. Public sightings and reports are used to identify suspected hornets, whilevolunteer teamsfrom the BBKA help confirm sightings, track nests and undertake spring queen-trapping. Once a nest is confirmed, the NBU is responsible for its destruction.Chaumeton said: “The National Bee Unit’s response is extremely effective. But this relies entirely on members of the public reporting sightings.”Post-it notes and tiny trackers: behind the race to stop Asian hornets thriving in the UKRead moreThe scale of public participation is significant. In 2024,nearly 30,000 reports were submitted, resulting in the identification of 24 nests.Modelling of the British invasionsuggests that public reporting is essential to controlling the species; eradication depends on how quickly new incursions are detected and dealt with.Despite this, Chaumeton said Asian hornets were still seen as a “beekeeping issue” as opposed to a threat to national biodiversity involving the whole country. “Beekeepers cannot do this on their own. We urgently need more government-led national awareness campaigns so everyone in the country understands the threat,” she said.Apha has been testing technology to make capacity go further. In 2025, it trialledradio transmitters attached to hornetsto help locate nests. Researchers are also testingVespAI, an artificial intelligence system to identify Asian hornets visually.So far, the approach has resulted in the destruction of identified nests, but the number found last year raises a question about whether a system involving volunteers can continue to scale up. “We need a clear multi-year commitment from successive governments that eradication will continue,” said Chaumeton.Wilson added: “We encourage the public to remain vigilant and continue to report any potential sightings using the Asian Hornet Watch app and online.”Explore more on these topicsInsectsAnimalsWildlifeClimate crisisBeesBiodiversityConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK subsidence claims surge after hottest summer on record | Insurance industry | The Guardian
description: Insurers in England and Wales tell of busy August with one reporting near-140% jump in claims
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Insurers in England and Wales tell of busy August with one reporting near-140% jump in claims
Content: A cottage affected by subsidence in Shropshire. The most vulnerable areas include London, Essex, Kent and a tranche of land from Oxford to the Wash.Photograph: David Bagnall/AlamyView image in fullscreenA cottage affected by subsidence in Shropshire. The most vulnerable areas include London, Essex, Kent and a tranche of land from Oxford to the Wash.Photograph: David Bagnall/AlamyInsurance industryUK subsidence claims surge after hottest summer on recordInsurers in England and Wales tell of busy August with one reporting near-140% jump in claimsJulia KolleweSat 5 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK insurers are experiencing a surge in the number of homeowners making claims for subsidence afterthe hottest summer on record, with Hastings Direct reporting a near 140% jump to an all-time high for August.Insurance firms have been overrun by calls and online queries, as well as a rise in claims during the five heatwaves that followedthe warmest spring ever recorded in England and Wales.Subsidence claims typically peak during late summer and autumn, but this year they jumped in number during the summer.Millions of homes are at risk of subsidencebecause of the worsening climate crisis, the British Geological Survey has said.Ashotter, drier summersbecome more frequent, the ground under houses can shrink and drag down a property’s foundations. Older properties are more at risk. The most vulnerable areas for subsidence include London, Essex, Kent and a tranche of land from Oxford up to the Wash on England’s east coast, according to scientists.Hastings Direct, which has 4.8 million home and motor insurance customers, said it had had a significant increase in subsidence claims over the summer and received a record number in August, almost 140% more than in the same month last year.After two unusually dry summers, subsidence activity has increased significantly, the company said.Hastings predicted the large volume of claims would continue into the autumn even though temperatures had returned to more normal levels and there had been some rainfall in recent weeks.“We expect claim volumes to remain higher than normal through to around October unless sustained rainfall helps restore soil moisture levels,” the insurer added.Signs of subsidence range from diagonal cracks around doors and windows that often widen over time; windows or doors that stick or will not close properly and uneven or sloping floors. Wallpaper creasing or rippling can also be a sign of subsidence, as well as damp.The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a record £20,000between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, up from £60m in the same period last year.About £297m in total was paid out on claims in 2025, up 6% from the year before, and 89% higher than in 2022, the ABI said.Charlie Inwood, the general insurance policy adviser at the ABI, said: “Following this summer’s hot weather, it’s likely we’ll see more subsidence claims over the coming months.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAviva, which completed a£3.7bn acquisition of its rival Direct Linein July, and dominates the UK home insurance market, has also reported subsidence claim numbers had increased in recent months. “This is likely to continue unless there is significant rainfall,” it said.Amanda Blanc, the chief executive of Aviva, said last month that the company was reviewing the reserves it had set aside for subsidence claims, and would also look at its pricing models and exposure management. The insurer is also investigating what homeowners can do to prevent property damage from subsidence and flooding.Small shrinkage and movement cracks were normal after hot dry weather, Aviva said, while diagonal cracks that were more than 2.5cm wide, roughly the diameter of a £1 coin, could be a sign of subsidence.Axa, another home insurer, said it expected a “surge year” but could not say whether it would be a record year for subsidence claims.Adam Holland, the head of retail underwriting, fraud and pricing governance at the French company’s UK arm, said: “The Met Office’s announcement about summer 2026 being the hottest on record in the UK puts the impact of climate change into sharp focus … and we expect to see an increase in weather-related property damage this year.”Explore more on these topicsInsurance industryHome insuranceInsurancePropertyExtreme heatExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Police seize £200k Lamborghini under tightened antisocial driving laws | Police | The Guardian
description: Officers seize supercar in Southend after reports of it being driven at up to twice speed limit
Author: Angus Thomson
Headline: Officers seize supercar in Southend after reports of it being driven at up to twice speed limit
Content: The Lamborghini Huracan seized by Essex police. Certain Huracan models are valued at above £238,000.Photograph: Essex Police/PAView image in fullscreenThe Lamborghini Huracan seized by Essex police. Certain Huracan models are valued at above £238,000.Photograph: Essex Police/PAPolicePolice seize £200k Lamborghini under tightened antisocial driving lawsOfficers seize supercar in Southend after reports of it being driven at up to twice speed limitAngus ThomsonSat 5 Sep 2026 15.23 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 17.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice have seized a Lamborghini potentially worth more than £200,000 under tightened laws introduced to crack down on dangerous driving.Essex police confiscated the Lamborghini Huracan on Saturday afternoon after receiving reports of the supercar being driven dangerously in Southend. The car was travelling at speeds suspected to be more than twice the limit, police said.“Antisocial driving can pose a danger to other people using the road and cause misery to residents,” a force spokesperson said.“The safety of our communities will always be our priority and we’ll take action against those who risk the safety of others.”The online marketplace Autotrader estimates the total retail value of the Lamborghini Huracan at £238,195, depending on the model.The vehicle was seized under section 59 of the Police Reform Act, which was strengthened earlier this year to allow police to immediately confiscate a vehicle causing – or likely to cause – alarm, distress or annoyance to the public.Previously, drivers received a warning under which their vehicle could only be seized if they were involved in another antisocial driving incident within 12 months.Officers can still choose to give a warning at their discretion. The law allows officers to stop and seize vehicles, or enter premises where they believe the vehicle is being held – and “use reasonable force where necessary”.Wheelspins and burnouts, drifting in public places, racing in residential areas and repeated revving “causing nuisance” were all reasons for which vehicles could be seized, the Essex police spokesperson said.The Metropolitan police last year seized 72 luxury cars worth more than £6m in acrackdown on antisocial driving in London.The vehicles – which included Ferraris, Lamborghinis and Bentleys – were either unroadworthy or being driven illegally, the Met said.Last month, a police officer drove a Ferrari Monza SP2 worth £3.7m after the open-top limited-edition supercar was seized in aseparate, record-breaking crackdown.Explore more on these topicsPoliceMotoringSouthend-on-SeaShareReuse this content

title: Mental health groups have ‘failed to acknowledge’ risk of violence, says Mind chief | Mental health | The Guardian
description: Sector has avoided issue because of stigma fears, expert warns ahead of closure of Nottingham attacks inquiry
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Sector has avoided issue because of stigma fears, expert warns ahead of closure of Nottingham attacks inquiry
Content: Ian Coates, Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, who were killed by Valdo Colocane. He was later diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.Composite: Nottinghamshire PoliceView image in fullscreenIan Coates, Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, who were killed by Valdo Colocane.
