He was later diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.Composite: Nottinghamshire PoliceMental healthMental health groups have ‘failed to acknowledge’ risk of violence, says Mind chiefSector has avoided issue because of stigma fears, expert warns ahead of closure of Nottingham attacks inquiryNeha GohilMidlands correspondentSat 5 Sep 2026 16.43 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMental health organisations have “failed to acknowledge” the risk of violence from a minority of people with severe mental illnesses, the chief executive of Mind has said ahead of the closure of the inquiry into the Nottingham attacks.Dr Sarah Hughes, who has led mental health charity Mind for four years and has worked in the sector for almost four decades, said charities had shied away from addressing the risk of violence due to the fact it had increased the stigma and harassment around people with mental health conditions.The inquiry into theNottinghamattacks is examining the events leading up to 13 June 2023, when 19-year-old students Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, and 65-year-old caretaker Ian Coates, were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, who was later diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.In 2024, Calocane was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order after admitting three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility and three counts of attempted murder.The public inquiry has heard evidence from various local authorities, including health professionals and police officers, as well as Calocane’s family, in order to assess the “events, acts and omissions” that led to the killings.The inquiry heard how Calocane had committed a string of violent incidents in the years before the attacks, repeatedly refused to take medication, and was sectioned four times in the space of two years. During her evidence, Calocane’s mother described the mental health system as “so broken”.View image in fullscreenDr Sarah Hughes, chief executive officer of Mind.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The GuardianSpeaking exclusively to the Guardian, Hughes said charities specialising in mental health had to become “more comfortable” with discussing the risk of violence that could exist from a minority of people with mental health illnesses.Hughes’s comments come after the charity Mind held a roundtable with experts in Westminster to discuss the role mental health services needed to play to keep the public and patients safe.“We, as a charity sector, have failed to acknowledge that violence does happen in some circumstances,” she said. “As a sector, [we] have held the narrative that the majority of people don’t commit violent crime. However, some do and the consequences are grave.”Hughes added: “My feeling is that we haven’t always been able to articulate the topic of violence and mental health well to the public and ultimately, we have softened the truth. Stigma and discrimination are incredibly harmful, however our efforts to reduce them have, at times, meant that some of the most difficult topics have been brushed under the carpet. That’s why it’s so important to bring together a wide range of experts and experiences to have an open and honest conversation.”NHS trust investigated for corporate manslaughter after Nottingham attacksRead moreEmma Webber, whose son Barnaby was killed by Calocane, said she welcomed the statement by Hughes. “I do feel like danger to others has been almost deliberately quietened down in the conversation in the past,” she said.Webber said there had not been enough acknowledgment from mental health organisations of the risk of violence.“It could be a really powerful voice for the charities to have that difficult conversation, and to not be fearful of saying about the risks of violence toward others, and that people that are mentally ill, like Calocane, can and do go on to kill.“Obviously the vast majority of people with mental health issues in this country are completely safe … but if somebody’s dangerous, they’re dangerous.“Had the risks in Calocane’s case been understood, then I genuinely believe we wouldn’t be having this conversation today.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCeleste Calocane giving evidence to the inquiry in May.Photograph: The Nottingham Inquiry/PASeena Fazel, a professor of forensic psychiatry at the University of Oxford who attended the event by Mind, said a minority of people with mental illnesses perpetrate violent acts and high-quality research on schizophrenia had “converged on the same picture”.“People with schizophrenia do have an elevated risk of violence compared with the general population, even after accounting for socioeconomic factors, but the absolute risk is small. Only a minority will commit a serious violent act,” he said.“That risk increases when other factors are present, particularly drug or alcohol problems, a history of violence, or having been a victim of violence themselves. The important point is that treatments we already have, and which are widely available, can bring that risk down.”Hughes, who said she had experienced violence when she was a mental health practitioner from people experiencing psychosis, said many in the sector feared that addressing such issues could increase stigma and discrimination, and that could lead to dangerous health outcomes.“We are incredibly frightened of deepening that stigma and discrimination because we know how dangerous it can be,” she said. “This could risk going back to a more restrictive approach. My view is that’s not the answer, but stigma creates a pathway to that as being the only solution to this problem.”Hughes said this meant the sector had “shied away” from difficult conversations around violence. “The public, I think, are more ready [and] we’ve got to get our act together,” she said. “Even within Mind there was a reluctance internally and we had to really talk it though.”Hughes said the UK government’s upcoming mental health strategy must improve support and treatment for those with severe mental illnesses, as well as address matters of public safety.This includes ensuring an adequate number of beds in hospitals, assertive outreach, and accountability and communication with services.“I hope that by us having these conversations openly we can both make sure that the people we’re advocating for know that we’re doing this safely with their consent, but equally, the public and families and victims know that we recognise that we have to come together to solve this problem,” Hughes said.“Crucially, there is a role for Mind – and the sector as a whole – to show that patient and public safety are not mutually exclusive. Both are possible if we want to change our mental health system so people can get the right care before or after reaching crisis point,” she added.Explore more on these topicsMental healthCharitiesEnglandHealthNottinghamnewsShareReuse this content

title: John Healey warns of tough first budget as Middle East war puts pressure on economy  | Economic policy | The Guardian
description: Chancellor says he wants to ensure country has ‘buffer’ against uncertainty as global bond yields hit 18-year high
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Chancellor says he wants to ensure country has ‘buffer’ against uncertainty as global bond yields hit 18-year high
Content: John Healey says he is in ‘lockstep’ with Andy Burnham in determination to stay within fiscal rules.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersView image in fullscreenJohn Healey says he is in ‘lockstep’ with Andy Burnham in determination to stay within fiscal rules.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersEconomic policyJohn Healey warns of tough first budget as Middle East war puts pressure on economyChancellor says he wants to ensure country has ‘buffer’ against uncertainty as global bond yields hit 18-year highGeraldine McKelvieSat 5 Sep 2026 07.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 07.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chancellor has indicated that the UK will face atough budget next monthdue to Trump’s war in the Middle East.In an interviewwith the Financial Times, John Healey said the conflict in Iran would probably have a strong influence on his first budget on 28 October.Healey, who succeeded Rachel Reeves when Andy Burnham became prime minister in July, told the newspaper he wanted to ensure the country had a robust “buffer against uncertainty” amid increasing global instability.However, economists have predicted that Healey will need to raise taxes or implement significant cost-cutting measures to protect the £24bn fiscal headroom that Reeves had after her March statement.“What’s happening in the Middle East ishitting inflation, it’s hitting growth, it’s hitting borrowing costs,” Healey said. “It’s part of a more dangerous world that is more uncertain and it’s one of the challenges we have to meet in this country, but have to meet with other [countries].”Healey declined to say how much headroom he aimed to have, but insisted he and Burnham were “in lockstep in our determination to meet the fiscal rules”.The newspaper said he planned to stick to Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledges not to raise taxes on “working people”, such as income tax, national insurance contributions or VAT, and was also not expected to raise the rate of corporation tax.The public finances are under pressure from soaring global bond yields , which hit an 18-year high earlier this week. Bond yields have a significant impact on government spending plans, as higher yields drive up borrowing costs.Healey has faced criticism for failing to commit to the goal ofraising defence spendingto 3% of GDP by 2030. In June, he resigned as defence secretary because he was unable to get the Treasury to commit to the target, in what was seen as a fatal blow to Keir Starmer’s government.Acknowledging tough economic conditions, Healey said: “The country’s under pressure. People are under pressure with the cost of living. Households are feeling that. We’re concerned about the cost of living, and we’re concerned about the cost of business.”He also said he was committed to cutting the welfare bill. “We must cut the cost of welfare, we have to get more people back into work,” he said. “I know that some of the decisions I must take – and will take – will show the benefits in years to come.”Jim O’Neill, the cross-bench peer and economist who advised Burnham as he prepared to enter Downing Street, has suggested that the prime minister could reassure the bond markets by taking “credible actions” to rein in the “excesses” of welfare spending and the pensions triple lock.Speaking to Times Radio earlier this week, he said: “If you have the markets carrying on doing what they’re doing globally … eventually they’re going to have absolutely no choice [but to cut spending] because the penalty of the debt servicing cost and the knock-on effect to other markets including mortgage rates will be too severe for a government to resist.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe triple lock, introduced in 2010, means that state pension increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5% – whichever is highest. It has led to an increase of about £16bn in the state pension bill.On Saturday morning, Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the government could consider an Australian-style system.He suggested that the state pension could increase in line with workers’ earnings, with an inbuilt “temporary lock” to safeguard against a decline in average wages due to recession or high inflation.“It’s a reasonable way to increase the state pension over the long run that’s not as expensive but still generates increases,” he said.Reform UK has said it would cut £80bn of public spending within five years by reducing welfare payments, net zero investment and overseas aid. Speaking at the party’s annual conference in Birmingham, its economic spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, also pledged to reduce the number of civil servants.Explore more on these topicsEconomic policyJohn HealeyBudgetDefence policyTax and spendingInflationLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I could watch her for hours’: the woman who rescued a bee and created a buzz | UK news | The Guardian
description: After bringing queen Phoebee home, Gilly McArthur expected her to die within a day or two, but she’s bumbling on
Author: Amelia Hill
Headline: After bringing queen Phoebee home, Gilly McArthur expected her to die within a day or two, but she’s bumbling on
Content: Gilly McArthur in an Instagram video with Phoebee.Photograph: Instagram/@gillymcarthurView image in fullscreenGilly McArthur in an Instagram video with Phoebee.Photograph: Instagram/@gillymcarthurUK news‘I could watch her for hours’: the woman who rescued a bee and created a buzzAfter bringing injured queen Phoebee home in July, Gilly McArthur expected her soon to die, but she’s bumbling onAmelia HillSat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifty-two days ago, Phoebee was lying by the side of a road in the blistering sun with a broken wing. Today, she’s clambering up the arm of Gilly McArthur, around the nape of her neck and disappearing into her hair.“I couldn’t leave her by the roadside,” McArthur says. “So I bought her home and made her a bed of flowers. I thought she’d be dead in a day or so.”Instead of dying, Phoebee did something McArthur didn’t expect: she went viral. McArthur says: “A few days after I rescued her, I was due to go on a sailing trip for a week. I couldn’t leave her here, so I took Phoebee with me – and put aposton my Instagram account of her enjoying the trip.”The following morning, McArthur woke to find messages from around the world. “It was amazing: there were so many posts from people across the globe telling me their lovely stories of capturing bumblebees or helping butterflies with broken wings – and the stories kept coming.”Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueMcArthur, an author, is touched but slightly baffled by the furore. “I think it might be because the world is in such a polycrisis at the moment, and everyone is wanting to pull back to something authentic and kind,” she says.“Perhaps Phoebee reminds people of a time when bumblebees were more prolific, in a world that isn’t on fire: lots of the messages said the videos helped them feel more grounded in a world where the algorithms are usually so grounded in clickbait and violence.”Britain has 24 species of bumblebee and more than 240 species of solitary bee. Most bumblebees live for just one year. New mated queens have a bit more of a lifeline: they hibernate in the autumn and emerge in spring to establish colonies of their own.Phoebee has not mated. While McArthur does not know what that will mean for her, she is stalwart in the face of possible tragedy.“If I check on her one day and she’s not moving, I’ll check her bum. When she sleeps, her bum goes up and down very slightly,” she says. “If her bum is still, I won’t give up – I’ll put her in a quiet room and hope she’s hibernating. But her lifespan is her lifespan.”For now, McArthur spends a lot of time watching her. “She’s fascinating: she spends a lot of time cleaning herself like a cat. And I could watch her putting her long tongue out and getting the nectar out of the flowers for hours.”Andy Benson, of the Bumblebee Conservation Trust, has watched the brouhaha with similar bemusement. He thinks passions would have been cooler had Phoebee not been a buff-tailed bumblebee, the biggest and fluffiest bee, and a queen, “the biggest and fluffiest of them all”.View image in fullscreenA bumblebee on a purpletop flower in Weymouth, England in late July.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesBenson says that while McArthur’s heroic salvation of a single bumblebee is heartwarming, the advice is to gently place lost bees on a flower and let nature take its course.“A third of British wild bees and hoverfliesare in declineand a quarter of European species are at risk of extinction because of the loss of their natural habitat, climate change and bee-killing pesticides,” he says.This matters because one in three mouthfuls of our food depend on pollinators such as bees, with the crops that depend on pollination – including apples, beans, squashes and almonds – being five times more valuable than those that do not.Benson says if people want to help bees, they don’t have to take them into their home, or on a sailing trip, or let them nestle in their hair. “We can instantly help hundreds of bees in the smallest of spaces by simply planting a few flowers in their garden,” he says.McArthur knows she hasn’t stayed the plummeting bee numbers by prolonging Phoebee’s short lifespan. But she hopes she may have made a difference in another way.“Maybe this is something nice that people can pull back to and just go: ‘Oh, maybe I won’t blow my leaves away this winter – maybe I might plant more plants for pollinators – maybe I might just stop and look at the smaller things with more curiosity’,” she says.“And maybe Phoebee’s videos will help people realise that looking at the smaller things in more detail can make the bigger things feel more manageable.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsBeesInsectsWildlifeAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US military says it struck three Iranian tankers after American warships came under missile attack | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Officials said US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided attacks before three Iranian tankers were struck by the US
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Officials said US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided attacks before three Iranian tankers were struck by the US
Content: A US Centcom image of a US military strike on an Iranian oil tanker off the in the Gulf of Oman on 5 September 2026.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA US Centcom image of a US military strike on an Iranian oil tanker off the in the Gulf of Oman on 5 September 2026.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesUS-Israel war on IranUS military says it struck three Iranian tankers after American warships came under missile attackOfficials said US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided attacks before three Iranian tankers were struck by the USMarina Dunbarand agenciesSat 5 Sep 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 17.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS militarysaid Saturday it struck three Iranian oil tankers after US navy warships came under missile attack, further escalating tensions in the region and warning it would “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet”.According to the military, a US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided “multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks” while patrolling the region. No US personnel were injured.Two of the Iranian oil carriers were “permanently disabled”, the Pentagon said, while a third tanker, which was unladen, was destroyed.Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US militaryRead moreThe US said the vessels were part of a shadow network that helped finance Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards and armed proxy groups operating across the region.“We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet,” the head of US Central Command, Adm Brad Cooper, said in thestatement.The announcement followed an earlier report from Iran that the US had attacked an Iranian tanker near Kharg Island in the Gulf. Tasnim, a semiofficial news outlet affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps,reportedthe strike happened on Saturday morning. It said the tanker’s crew survived and was being evacuated.The US said one tanker was struck off Kharg Island, while another was hit near Jask. The unladen tanker was struck in the Gulf of Oman. The US statement also shared what it described as video footage of the strikes.Iran’s state broadcaster said later Sunday that Iran targeted three oil tankers and three American vessels in response to the US strikes. This could not be immediately confirmed.The latest attacks came nearly a week after the US and Iran resumed strikes after about a month of relative calm in the on-again, off-again war that began with US and Israeli attacks in February. Attempts at negotiations have collapsed.One of the strikeshit a weddingin southern Iran on Tuesday, killing four people, including a child, and injuring dozens, according to Iranian officials.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe US vice-president, JD Vance, said “sometimes things happen” whenaskedon Thursday whether an US strike was responsible for killing people at the wedding celebration.The renewed strikes have also brought fresh scrutiny to a 28 February US attack in Minab thatstruck a school compoundand killed at least 156 people, most of them schoolchildren.A preliminaryUS militaryinquiry reportedly found that the attack resulted from a targeting error after outdated coordinates identified the school as part of a nearby Revolutionary Guards naval base. The Pentagon said at the time that it was investigating. A full report has not been made public.Associated Press contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranUS militaryUS foreign policyIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Alzheimer’s trial to test drug on people without symptoms to see if it can be prevented | Alzheimer's | The Guardian
description: Healthy middle-aged people deemed to be at higher risk of developing condition among those eligible to participate
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Healthy middle-aged people deemed to be at higher risk of developing condition among those eligible to participate
Content: About 1,600 people aged 55 to 80 from around the world will be screened on Monday by the Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS foundation trust.Photograph: Alamy/PAView image in fullscreenAbout 1,600 people aged 55 to 80 from around the world will be screened on Monday by the Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS foundation trust.Photograph: Alamy/PAAlzheimer'sAlzheimer’s trial to test drug on people without symptoms to see if it can be preventedHealthy middle-aged people deemed to be at higher risk of developing condition among those eligible to participateDonna FergusonSat 5 Sep 2026 07.36 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 10.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople without memory loss will be offered an experimental Alzheimer’s drug that could stop the development of the condition before dementia symptoms emerge.Healthy middle-aged people deemed to have a higher risk of developing the condition will be eligible to participate in the trial, which is being run by an NHS trust as part of an international clinical trial aiming to prevent dementia.The first European participants in the trial, which is recruiting about 1,600 people aged 55 to 80 from around the world, will be screened on Monday by the Surrey and Borders PartnershipNHSfoundation trust.Participants from across the UK will be tested to check that they have no memory problems, before being offered a blood test to assess whether they have p-tau217, a biomarker that can predict cognitive decline and the development of Alzheimer’s.Previous research found people with the highest levels of p-tau217 had an estimated 78% chance of developing cognitive impairment within 10 years.Research has also showed that blood tests measuring p-tau217 could identify Alzheimer’s disease with up to 95% accuracy.The phase III trial, called the PrevenTRON study, will investigate whether prescribing a new drug, trontinemab, to participants who have elevated levels of p-tau217 and meet the trial criteria can stop dementia from developing in the first place.Trontinemab, which was developed by the Swiss pharmaceutical company Roche, attacks amyloid plaques, a toxic protein that builds up in the brain and slows down – and eventually kills – brain cells.Alzheimer’s blood test can spot people with early symptoms, study suggestsRead moreIt has been hailed as a groundbreaking drug after early research found that it cleared amyloid plaques in nine out of 10 people with early-stage Alzheimer’s or mild cognitive development within 28 weeks, meaning that one of the key characteristics of Alzheimer’s was removed.Prof Ramin Nilforooshan, consultant psychiatrist and chief investigator for the PrevenTRON trial, said the study demonstrates how researchers are shifting their focus from cure to prevention: “For decades, research has focused on treating Alzheimer’s disease after symptoms appear. PrevenTRON addresses a different question, whether we can act earlier, before symptoms begin.”Through research and trials such as PrevenTRON, he said there was the potential to help millions of people affected by Alzheimer’s.However, he stressed in an interview with the Telegraph the experimental nature of the treatment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I’m not saying this trial is magic. It’s an investigational medicine. We need to wait and see: will it work or not?” he said.At least 15 hospitals and clinics across the UK are expected to take part in the study by the end of the year, with recruitment led by the Surrey and Borders Partnership trust.The trial is expected to last four to six years. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either trontinemab or a placebo, and will then be monitored to see how quickly they develop any signs of dementia.Alzheimer’s disease is thought to develop inside the brain up to 10 years before people typically seek treatment for memory problems.It affects around one in 14 people over the age of 65 and one in six people over the age of 80.Those interested in being screened for the trial can contact the Surrey and Borders Partnership research team on 01372 216584 or at research@sabp.nhs.uk.Explore more on these topicsAlzheimer'sDementiaNHSMental healthHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Civilians among at least 60 killed in Yemen as ground fighting escalates | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Houthi rebel offensive against government forces on west coast leads to some of deadliest clashes in years
Author: William Christou
Headline: Houthi rebel offensive against government forces on west coast leads to some of deadliest clashes in years
Content: Forces loyal to Yemen's Saudi-backed government ride along a road in the Hays district, south of Hodeidah, on Saturday.Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenForces loyal to Yemen's Saudi-backed government ride along a road in the Hays district, south of Hodeidah, on Saturday.Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty ImagesYemenCivilians among at least 60 killed in Yemen as ground fighting escalatesHouthi rebel offensive against government forces on west coast leads to some of deadliest clashes in yearsWilliam ChristouSat 5 Sep 2026 09.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClashes between Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel movement have killed more than 60 people, including civilians, as theHouthispushed forward with a military offensive on Yemen’s western coast.Twenty-six government troops and 31 Houthi fighters were killed during several hours of fighting in the country’s south-west on Saturday, medical and military sources told Agence France-Presse (AFP). A missile strike also killed six civilians and injured seven others travelling by bus in the city of Taiz.The killings were the latest in a series of bloody clashes in recent days as the Houthis continued an offensive in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah along the Red Sea coast. On Friday, 129 were killed in fighting between rebel and government forces, according to an AFP tally.Iran-aligned Houthis claim they attacked oil refinery in Saudi ArabiaRead moreThe fighting is some of the deadliest in years, after thecollapse in Julyof the 2022 ceasefire. The truce fell apart after an Iranian plane attempted to land in Houthi-controlled Sana’a, triggering attacks by the Yemeni government on the airport.The Houthis are trying to beat back governmental troops to capture strategic hills overlooking Bab al-Mandeb in order to advance towards port cities on the coast. So far, they have managed to capture areas in western Taiz.In Taiz, a government military officer said the “coming hours will be decisive” as the Houthis had taken positions near the city a day before. They added that reinforcements had been arriving from Aden to try to stem the Houthi advance.On Friday, government forces said that they had recaptured the al-Khazan and al-Makahna hills west of Taiz, two strategically important areas for controlling the region.The Houthis had previously controlled the port city of al-Makha overlooking Bab al-Mandeb, before being pushed out by government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition.The Bab al-Mandeb strait is a crucial maritime chokepoint for ships heading to the Suez canal. About 10% of global maritime trade passes through the strait.Saudi Arabiahas been using the strait to export oil for months after the start of the US-Iran war.If shipping is disrupted in Bab al-Mandeb, it will only further raise the cost of global goods, which has already rocketed as a result of the virtual closure of the strait of Hormuz since March 2026.If the Houthis manage to recapture the port city and take key areas along the Red Sea coast, it will help them control naval traffic in the Red Sea. In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, and they have repeatedlydisrupted trafficin solidarity with Gaza since the start of the war there in October 2023.Yemen has been embroiled in a civil war since 2014, when the Houthis and allied forces took the capital city of Sana’a and pushed the then government out of power. A Saudi-led coalition then began a military intervention to support the Yemeni government and fight the Houthis, a strategic ally of Iran.At least 150,000 people in Yemen have been killed in the fighting, and hundreds of thousands more have died from related causes such as hunger and diseases. About 4.5 million people have been displaced by the fighting and more than 18.2 million are in dire need of humanitarian assistance,according to the UN.Explore more on these topicsYemenSaudi ArabiaHouthisIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Robin Morgan, child star who became feminist, poet and editor, dies aged 85 | US news | The Guardian
description: Leading second-wave feminist co-founded Women’s Media Center with Jane Fonda and Gloria Steinem
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Leading second-wave feminist co-founded Women’s Media Center with Jane Fonda and Gloria Steinem
Content: Robin Morgan at the Milford readers and writers festival in Milford, Pennsylvania, on 16 September 2017.Photograph: Zuma Press Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenRobin Morgan at the Milford readers and writers festival in Milford, Pennsylvania, on 16 September 2017.Photograph: Zuma Press Inc/AlamyUS newsRobin Morgan, child star who became feminist, poet and editor, dies aged 85Leading second-wave feminist co-founded Women’s Media Center with Jane Fonda and Gloria SteinemAssociated PressSat 5 Sep 2026 14.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobin Morgan, a child star of the 1940s and 50s who grew up to become an all-American radical as a poet, essayist, editor and second-wave feminist, has died. She was 85.Morgan’s death was confirmed Saturday by the Women’s Media Center, an organization she co-founded with Jane Fonda and the celebrated author and activistGloria Steinem, who died Wednesday.During the 1960s and 70s, Morgan embodied and inspired historic changes in how women lived and thought. As she was happy to point out, the one-time “ideal American girl” and adored “little Robin Morgan” was a rule breaker and justice seeker with a notable list of achievements, along with a prison record and an FBI file.Julie Burton, president of the Women’s Media Center, called Morgan “one of the architects of the contemporary women’s movement”, hailing her writing and “global leadership for justice and equality”. The statement didn’t specify the location, date or cause of Morgan’s death.Morgan was at the center of some of the defining moments of what came to be called second-wave feminism, expanding upon the achievements of the suffragists a half-century earlier. In 1968, she was among the organizers of the first protest against the Miss America pageant, joining fellow activists in tossing their bras (soon mythologized as burning) into a “freedom trash can”. The 1970 essay anthology she edited, Sisterhood Is Powerful, is considered one of the essential texts of the modern women’s movement.Robin Morgan, age 75, on voting for a female presidentGuardianHer legacy was one of deeds, words and images. Morgan is widely credited with coining the term “herstory”, the feminist reworking of “history”, and popularizing the clenched fist/female symbol icon of the liberation movement. Her poem Monster, with such lines as “I want a women’s revolution like a lover/I lust for it” was quoted at feminist rallies and beyond. Her poem Arraignment helped capture the movement’s embrace of the late Sylvia Plath and condemnation of her husband, poet Ted Hughes, whom Morgan and others blamed for Plath’s suicide in 1963. Morgan’s rhyming couplet “I accuse/Ted Hughes” inspired the title for Sonic Youth’s song J’Accuse Ted Hughes.Labeled an “anarchist housewife” in one government report, Morgan confronted the establishment, left and right. In 1970, she and fellow protesters were arrested and jailed after occupying the offices of the avant garde Grove Press, whose owner, Barney Rosset, was fighting employees’ efforts to unionize. In the widely reprinted 1970 essay Goodbye to All That, she called out activists and libertines from Abbie Hoffman and Hugh Hefner to Dave Dellinger and the music group the Fugs.View image in fullscreenMorgan, then the editor-in-chief of Ms, celebrates the magazine’s spring comeback in her New York office on 28 February 1990.Photograph: Susan Ragan/APIn her personal life, Morgan had male and female lovers and was married for more than 20 years to the gay poet Kenneth Pitchford, with whom she had a son, the musician, activist and record company executive Blake Morgan. She once described her marriage as a “two-member commune” and was so resistant to labels that she remembered being “straight-baited” by feminists who thought she should be a lesbian and chastised by conservatives who assumed she was a lesbian.In her 2001 memoir Saturday’s Child, she expressed joy and amazement at how her life had turned out and how she was able to retain “a threadbare, somewhat surreal sense of humor”.“Put that in your apple pie and smoke it,” she wrote.Besides Saturday’s Child, she completed more than 20 books, including The Word of a Woman: Feminists Dispatches and the poetry collections Monster and Dark Matter. She followed Sisterhood Is Powerful with Sisterhood Is Global (1984) and Sisterhood Is Forever (2002), featuring such contributors as Steinem, Simone de Beauvoir and Eve Ensler. For several years, she was editor-in-chief of Ms magazine.In 1984, she was a founder of an early feminist thinktank, the Sisterhood Is Global Institute. In 2005, she, Steinem and Fonda launched the Women’s Media Center, which has a mission to support “the visibility, viability and decision-making power of women and girls in media”.View image in fullscreenMorgan at age five, in New York on 8 August 1947.Photograph: Robert Kradin/APMore recently, she hosted a syndicated radio show and remained active despite being diagnosed with Parkinson’s, which inspired several poems and a TEDWomen talk in 2015.In a different era, she might have been just another forgotten child star. Born in 1941 in Lake Worth, Florida, and raised in New York, she never saw her father while growing up and was told – falsely – by her mother that he was dead. Her mother also shaved a year off her age, claiming she was born in 1942, to make her early public career seem even more impressive.She would meet some of the era’s biggest stars, from Abbott and Costello to Sal Mineo, and was popular enough to inspire such commercial tie-ins as Robin Morgan dolls. Magazines described her as “unspoiled” and “courteous” and “the ideal girl-next-door”, immune from “violent outbursts of antagonism against established society”.As she recalled in Saturday’s Child, producer Dan Ehrenreich squeezed her shoulder so hard that Morgan could feel his fingernails. He turned her microphone away and eventually placed his hand over her mouth.“I realized that I loved and respected that child who fought back in what was the first political act I recall ever daring to make,” Morgan wrote.Explore more on these topicsUS newsActivismWomennewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models
Content: With every increase in the power of AI, there is a potential increase in risk. Illustration: Just_Super/Getty ImagesA spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced modelsByRobert BoothUK technology editorSat 5 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePicture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium.These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence.Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAIclaimedthe technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI – artificial general intelligence – with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra.That claim came as the company prepared for a potential $850bn (£630bn) stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.The tasks it claims Astra can automate include designing circuit boards, filling out tax returns, building video games, financial modelling, engineering design and helping assemble legal documents. The threat to some white-collar jobs is implicit.View image in fullscreenOpenAI launched its latest AI model this week, GPT-6 Astra.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockYet, the AGI claim coincides with rising fears about AI risks among safety experts and political leaders, whose nerves have been jangled by the increasing power and impenetrability of AI models this summer and a spate of serious safety accidents viewed by some as possible final warning shots.“We’re heading through the rapids and we’re really hoping there isn’t some kind of drop in front of us and we don’t really know,” said Trager. “We’re plausibly close to crossing the line to what’s called recursive self-improvement, where [AI] systems improve themselves. That kind of recursivity is actually the definition of an explosion.”The latest worry came on Friday, just hours after Astra’s launch, with reports that a swarm of AI agents had repurposed a German website as a message board to share tactics to cheat on tasks,according to Reuters. OpenAI said it was reviewing the matter but would not characterise it as a hack.Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn dealRead moreThere is a sense of an awakening among politicians. On Thursday, the US senator Bernie Sanders cited this summer’s alarming breakout of a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents whichhacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store, when he called for “an immediate pause on advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence”.He said countries around the world must “work together to prevent this nightmare scenario”, which he defined as “an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control”.View image in fullscreenA swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockConcerns currently focus on AIs mounting cyber-attacks that could cripple real-world social and economic infrastructure, but future concerns include their ability to create biohazards and control military hardware.Across the Atlantic, a cross-party group of UK parliamentarians has called for AI “kill switches” to be required by law to prevent disastrous loss of control, citing “a recent spree of rogue AI incidents”.Darren Jones, an MP and former chief secretary to Keir Starmer, is also urgently attempting to set up a body to help legislators grapple with the technology. “AI is developing at such a pace that neither government nor parliament can keep up,” he warned. And next week a bill will be proposed by the Labour MP Alex Sobel toprohibit superintelligent AIdevelopment in the UK.The increasing anxiety comes amid a torrent of new AI models. Already this year, 67 have been released by the leading US companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, and their Chinese rivals Moonshot, Z.ai and Qwen,according to one count.With every increase in power, there is a potential increase in risk. OpenAI’s rivalAnthropic, which is targeting a $2tn stock exchange listing, this week admitted its own AIs were “not perfectly aligned” with human values and said there had been a “failure of operational security” in July hacks by its own model, Claude. It said the incidents had “stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defences is even higher than we previously believed”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe ability to monitor what AI models are thinking as they advance is another growing source of safety fears.Illustration: Yuichiro Chino/Getty ImagesAI’s double edge – opportunity and risk – was on show when OpenAI launched Astra on Thursday. Itsmarketing videofocused not on the risks but on the breezy convenience that AI could offer to a certain kind of customer. It showed an upmarket San Francisco woman simultaneously booking a tennis court and designing a presentation for her high-end rainwear collection; a thirtysomething man being helped to build his dream space invaders game and order a takeaway; a law firm executive being helped to draft some contracts.Yet only weeks ago, this was a model whose training had to be partly paused because of safety concerns after the Hugging Face incident. An independent safety researcher drafted in to investigate, Ajeya Cotra,said it was“more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover”.Astra also has whatOpenAIcalls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability – the first time it has given a model such a label. It means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”. The company’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, insisted the model was properly aligned not to do that, but added that “as these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder”.The ability to monitor what AI models are “thinking” as they advance is another growing source of safety fears. This week it was reported that OpenAI had been training Astra to reason not only in natural language, but in a more opaque manner that is faster and more efficient – and can make models’ chains of reasoning harder to follow. It means a model’s internal calculations may not always be written out as directly readable words – as if it was thinking in its head, rather than showing its working. Some experts fear this could help AIs covertly conspire against their human overseers.OpenAI confirmed Astra “shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models” and Pachocki said “as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging”.View image in fullscreenOpenAI’s Sam Altman: ‘We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time.’Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersThe company played down the development, but the increase in opaque reasoning sparked concern from AI safety researchers. Ryan Greenblatt, the chief scientist at Redwood Research, a nonprofit examining AI safety and security, called it “extremely concerning”. Gary Marcus, an influential AI sceptic, compared it to kicking away an already “rickety scaffolding before we have something better”.OpenAI’s chief executive,Sam Altman, said this week he felt conflicted about the advances of AI models. He admitted OpenAI’s security had “failed” in the Hugging Face incident and called it “a legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure”.“We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us,” he said in a tweet. “We know it is much more discordant for other people.”His rationale for releasing OpenAI’s most powerful model so soon after a safety crisis appears to be that the world needs to see how AIs perform in the real world to understand where AI is heading. He said: “An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.”And yet he can see the risks. On Tuesday he addressed the G20 ministerial summit in North Carolina in the US and told politicians that “some things are going to go very wrong with cybersecurity unless people act quite urgently”.He added: “There will be other challenges in the next five years. People talk about biosecurity and the things we are going to face there. There will be bigger ones yet to come.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingOpenAIAnthropicBernie SandersSam AltmanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Please find daddy’: the haunting missing posters of September 11 | Art | The Guardian
description: A collection of previously stored away posters will be displayed at a new exhibition to mark 25 years since the deadliest terrorist attack in US history
Author: David Smith
Headline: A collection of previously stored away posters will be displayed at a new exhibition to mark 25 years since the deadliest terrorist attack in US history
Content: An installation image from Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters.Photograph: Phil BuehlerView image in fullscreenAn installation image from Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters.Photograph: Phil BuehlerArt‘Please find daddy’: the haunting missing posters of September 11A collection of previously stored away posters will be displayed at a new exhibition to mark 25 years since the deadliest terrorist attack in US historyDavid Smithin WashingtonSat 5 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe saw the first one on September 11 itself. “Missing”, said a hastily designed poster on the window of a bar in Tribeca providing food and water to first responders. It was a plea for information about a person who had vanished in thedeadliest terrorist attack in US history.‘Led us down such a dark path’: documentary explores how 9/11 changed AmericaRead more“I was like, ‘Wow, this is going to be …’” recallsPhil Buehler, an artist and photographer who had watched the twin towers collapse from his office window. “But you knew that there would be very few survivors. You knew it then.”The missing posters kept coming in the days after 9/11, and Buehler kept photographing them. But having amassed more than 500 images, he put them away in a box on a top shelf because he could not bear to look at them.As the 25th anniversary of the atrocity neared, he decided to revisit them and will put a selection on public display for the first time this week. Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters, an installation atMost Holy Trinity – St Mary’s churchin Brooklyn, places 144 pictures across 24 translucent vellum panels, in vertical pairs reminiscent of the twin towers.The World Trade Center was always a favourite subject for Buehler. He had been photographing it since 1973, when he was 16. On September 11 2001, as an advisory board member for a tech startup, he had been invited toa conference at the Windows on the Worldrestaurant at the top of the north tower, but turned the offer down (a friend intended to go but was delayed).View image in fullscreenJason Jacobs. He called his wife, Jennifer, from his 97th-floor office to say a plane had hit the other tower and not to worry – his own building exploded moments later. Their daughter Zoe was just over a year old.Photograph: Phil Buehler“The guy that invited us died that day and I think my friend feels guilty about it,” he says quietly by phone, recalling the day on which nearly 3,000 people were killed by hijacked airliners inNew York, northern Virginia and Pennsylvania. “You realise how close–everybody had a story.”For the next two or three weeks, Buehler pedalled his bicycle through the eerie hush of New York City. Every night he updated a website, posting photographs and dispatches – an early form of what would soon be called blogging.He watched the spontaneous emergence of public shrines. Memorials bloomed in Union Square and Washington Square Park. On fences, subway entrances and storefronts,the missing posters multiplied, each a radical act of hope, though very few of those reported missing would ultimately be found alive.This was an era before cloud storage, smartphones and ubiquitously accessible digital photos. When families realised their relatives had not returned home, they frantically searched their living rooms for any tangible likeness.Some posters were designed by colleagues with desktop publishing software, cleanly formatted in neat typefaces. Others were raw, hurried cries for help: a snapshot Scotch-taped to a blank sheet of copy paper, bordered by frantic handwritten descriptions detailing physical marks that might identify an unconscious patient in a trauma ward.The posters listed height, weight, date of birth, company names, floor numbers and identifying traits: a butterfly tattoo on a lower back, surgical scars, wristwatches, the colour of a tie worn that morning. “They’re very personal,”Buehler says. “A lot of the pictures would be, say, a father holding their kids. One said, ‘Please find daddy.’ This was before digital phones, when everybody had pictures online, so a lot of them were done in copy shops.“You can just imagine somebody opening up their wedding album and ripping out the photo of a husband or wife and so you see them in a tuxedo. You see a lot of people in graduation gowns; it’s the pictures that we would have on our refrigerator or on the walls of our house that you’re proud of. I saw a lot of graduation photos, a lot of wedding photos, a lot of photos with kids, a lot of photos of men in suits and ties.”Yet as days turned into weeks, and rescue workers digging throughthe steaming pile at Ground Zerofound only twisted steel and ash, the meaning of the posters underwent a subtle and heartbreaking shift.View image in fullscreenManny Devalle. A seven-year FDNY veteran who responded on 9/11 just after finishing his overnight shift. Proud of his Puerto Rican heritage, he got Engine 5 to march in the Puerto Rican Day Parade.Photograph: Phil BuehlerBuehler explains:“When it was pretty clear there were no survivors, the posters started changing from ‘missing’ to almost ‘in memoriam’, but they didn’t say that. They went from explaining he has a tattoo of this on his arm or lower back and this is how tall and how much he weighs to being much more about what they did in life.“They morphed into ‘has three kids, I miss him’ and all the things they’re proud of: captain of the whatever or coach of the football team or whatever it was. Little memorials and they’re all different.”The posters also captured the democratic cross-section of the twin towers’ workforce. Within Buehler’s images, elite Wall Street investment bankers in tailored suits hang next to off-duty firefighters, paramedics and transit workers. Latino, Asian, Black and white faces appear side by side.“You saw the full range,” Buehler says. “You could tell just from looking at a guy in a suit, probably worked at one of the investment firms, and then right next to it would be somebody that works at Windows on the World as a server or waiter. A lot of Latino names. Mixed in there were firemen and women. A lot of service people. It was a big slice of America.”Eventually, having used about 20 rolls of film to catalogue more than 500 posters on hospitals, fire stations, random fences, roadside barricades andthe 69th Regiment Armoryon Lexington Avenue, Buehler had the film developed, picked up the contact prints and stopped.He could not face them. He packed the prints into a box, slipped in several bags containing samples of the dust he had gathered from the streets, added a rain-soaked poster he had salvaged, and shoved the container into the dark recesses of his studio for a quarter of a century.View image in fullscreenAn installation image from Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters.Photograph: Phil BuehlerWhen Buehler finally opened the box, he turned toSarah Celentano, a Brooklyn-based curator with whom he had previously collaborated on projects exploring public memory. The show is co-curated by Celentano and Olena Speranska, who was forced to flee her home in Ukraine after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.Celentano says: “I have a background as a medievalist and art historian and I often see connections between how we think and act today and how we’ve done this historically. That’s why I was so interested in thinking about these photos that Phil showed to me through historic traditions of devotion. They have such an incredible immediacy now, even 25 years later, that makes the person depicted present.”This tension between the physical image and the spiritual aura of the lost gave the exhibition its title.Celentano says:“Countenance can have two meanings. Both of them are very relevant in the case of what the show is doing. It can mean the human face, but it can also mean a sense of presence.“It’s something that is referring to the outer and inner aspects of a person simultaneously. What the show’s doing at the initial focus is on the faces of the 9/11 posters – people’s exterior humanity – but ultimately what that does is lead us to something that makes them present in a more profound way.”As the events of that day gradually fade from living memory to history, Celentano believes the exhibition provides a human bridge. “For somebody who wasn’t alive to remember or witness the September 11 attacks, the emphasis that these photographs put on humanity is the more important part of it.“They show what people did in the aftermath and how people dealt with or wrestled with their own grief and the way that they so spontaneously worked to memorialise them. It says a lot about how we function as a human society in that way. There’s a larger lesson to be learned.”For Celentano, the exhibition offers an antidote to the political cynicism of the present day.“It’s an invitation to empathise and to have compassion with people at a time when some frame empathy as weakness. I’m hoping this installation shows that empathy is actually quite a powerful thing and we should be looking for the humanity in all of us, not just the people who are in these posters but extending that beyond to one another.”View image in fullscreenJoe Hunter. Born in Brooklyn, he raced behind fire trucks on his bike as a kid and ran his own neighborhood ‘drill team’ at age 11 before joining FDNY Squad 288.Photograph: Phil BuehlerThat the work should find its home in Most Holy Trinity – St Mary’s church in Williamsburg is no accident. Founded in 1841, the majestic French Gothic Revival church is an active, multilingual parish that celebrates mass in English, Spanish and Polish. For Buehler, the church provided a spiritual antidote to the commercialism of the contemporary art world. “You don’t put grief on the white walls of a gallery,” he says.The church’s pastor,Rick Riccioli, a Franciscan friar originally from Montreal, immediately embraced the exhibition when Buehler approached him. The Franciscan order itself carries a 9/11 connection: Father Mychal Judge, the beloved FDNY chaplain who was the first certified fatality, was also a Franciscan.Friar Rick said in a statement: “Bringing these faces into this church is more than an art exhibition. It is an act of kinship, an act of remembrance, and, for us, an act of prayer. Twenty-five years later, we stand with those who were lost, with those who loved them, and with a city that still carries their memory.”Buehler is a creator of public memorials, producing installations such asEmpty Beds, honouring Ukrainian children abducted since Russia’s 2022 invasion, andWall of Tears, memorialising children killed in Gaza since October 2023, and In Lieu of Flowers, a sculptural presentation of the obituaries and lives of those who worked at the demolished Westinghouse Plant in Newark, New Jersey.Milestone anniversaries are an opportunity for reflection and taking stock. Looking back across the arc of 25 years, Buehler speaks with melancholy about the fleeting sense of common purpose that briefly united Americans in the autumn of 2001.“Post-9/11, America was one country – almost. I know there were groups that hated the Muslims at that time or blamed them, but it was pretty united. The red states, blue states didn’t exist. We still had some kind of working across the aisle. That’s gone.“When I was in Ukraine, it felt like they were all-for-one and for Ukraine beating Russia. As other people long for a different America, I longed more for how we suffered this tragedy, but the country felt what united us was more important than all those little things that divided us. That was an important moment and maybe the 25th anniversary will remind us of some of that.”Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters runs from 5-13 September at Most Holy Trinity – St Mary’s church, 138 Montrose Avenue, BrooklynExplore more on these topicsArtSeptember 11 2001New YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m amazed a human being could do so much’: Gloria Steinem celebrated by Margaret Atwood, Dua Lipa, Lynda Carter and more | Gloria Steinem | The Guardian
description: Authors, activists and admirers pay tribute to the feminist icon who died this week at the age of 92
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Authors, activists and admirers pay tribute to the feminist icon who died this week at the age of 92
Content: Gloria Steinem speaking at the Democratic national convention in Miami in 1972.Photograph: John Olson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGloria Steinem speaking at the Democratic national convention in Miami in 1972.Photograph: John Olson/Getty ImagesGloria Steinem‘I’m amazed a human being could do so much’: Gloria Steinem celebrated by Margaret Atwood, Dua Lipa, Lynda Carter and moreAuthors, activists and admirers pay tribute to the feminist icon who died this week at the age of 92Gloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotesMoira Donegan on how Gloria Steinem personified America’s feminist movementAs told toOwen Myers,Adrian HortonandBenjamin LeeSat 5 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 13.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘She pushed us all forward’Dua Lipa, musicianGloria was someone who pushed boundaries to their furthest extent. She fought for women all over the world, whether she knew them or not.Womenhave the rights we do today because of feminist icons like Gloria. She pushed us all forward and encouraged us to look beyond our own experience. It’s amazing to see how her work and legacy continue to be embraced by each new generation of feminists.‘Completely unapologetic’Sandra Bernhard, actor and comedianIn coming of age,Gloria Steinemwas my northern star: she gave me license to have unbridled confidence and audacity, first as a girl in high school and then as a fledgling performer. I never had to play down who I was: I didn’t have to. Gloria paved the way for me to put it all on the line – the first generation of women who could be funny and completely unapologetic. I owe so much to her.‘One of my models for standing your ground’Margaret Atwood, authorView image in fullscreenMargaret Atwood photographed for the Guardian in 2025.Photograph: Christopher Wahl/The GuardianI knew Gloria through her Ms magazine days – indeed, it was at a Ms party that I metDolly Parton, another terrific American star. Gloria was the epitome of second-wave feminism, and gave it a public face that nullified the bra-burning stereotypes that had been pasted on to it. Gloria was one of my models for standing your ground – gracefully if possible, but if not, not. She withstood a great many buckets of pig slop thrown her way. Reading the list of her accomplishments and of the movements in which she was active, I’m amazed that any human being could do so much. Wonder Woman was one of her heroes, and that’s what she was: a Wonder Woman.‘Impossible to imagine my life without her’Tavi Gevinson, author and actorI am one of countless people who can say that it’s impossible to imagine my life without the activism, vision, and courage of Gloria Steinem. There would have been noRookiewithout Ms magazine and its lineage. I am grateful beyond words for her example and encouragement.Founding editor of Ms magazine on Gloria Steinem: ‘The least egomaniacal person’Read more‘Cool, sexy and badass’Ronan Farrow, author and journalistGloria taught a generation how to live with a sense of purpose and justice. She found the good fights and fought them, even in unexpected corners; I discovered only after knowing her for years that she’d once intervened in a case involving my family, advocating for a child-welfare investigator who lost his job after finding a controversial allegation of abuse to be credible. But more than her great fights, Gloria was an example of how to be the best we can be. She was a riot. She was cool. She was sexy. She was a badass. She made no pretense of perfection, and reckoned with mistakes openly. Like a lot of people, I hoped to grow up to be Gloria. I still do.‘Invited everyone else to stand a little taller’Melinda French Gates, philanthropistGenerational change doesn’t happen by accident or fate – it takes leaders like Gloria Steinem, who work hand in hand with so many others to build a lasting movement. The decades of energy, brilliance and advocacy she devoted to women’s rights helped so many of us see that we belonged at the tables where decisions are made. Her dedication helped illuminate a simple truth: when women can stand in their power, they invite everyone else to stand a little taller, too. What a light she was for me and so many others. What a debt we owe her.‘She reimagined a more just world’Elaine Welteroth, author and Birthfund founderView image in fullscreenElaine Welteroth at the Social Impact Summit, Los Angeles, 2025.Photograph: Monica Schipper/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty ImagesLosing Gloria Steinem feels like losing a lighthouse in dark times. But her legacy will live on through the torches she lit inside women of every generation. I am humbled to consider myself one of millions of those torches, shining proudly in her honor. Gloria showed us what it means to use your voice, challenge the systems that diminish women, radically reimagine a more just world – and then have the courage to build it. Her life is a blueprint for the work still ahead of us.‘A very tall tree has fallen in our forest’Padma Lakshmi, TV host and authorGloria was very generous with her time and her energy, right up until the end. Every time I spoke to her, I heard about another event or trip or cause or organizing event. It’s been said many times and she’s spoken about it herself: she really loved getting people together.I want people to know that she had a wicked sense of humor. That she was always willing to listen. That she was a joy to be with and didn’t take herself very seriously, but took the world incredibly seriously. And in spite of all of the recent setbacks that we’ve had in America as it relates to women, she was hopeful. She was not deterred.I see her towering legacy as someone who really lit our way. Someone who told us that words matter – yes, she was such a tall figure in civic service and community organizing and in the women’s movement, but she was first and foremost a writer, and to me her words are what will outlive her for generations. She was intrepid. She made you feel motivated and fired up and made you feel powerful, too. She was not interested in just holding forth. She was interested in listening, as I think all great people are. She cast a long shadow, and I’ll miss her very, very much. It’s a big hole, not only in the world, but in my heart. A very tall tree has fallen in our forest.Gloria Steinem personified America’s feminist movement | Moira DoneganRead more‘Sex and the City wouldn’t exist without her’Candace Bushnell, authorSex and the City wouldn’t exist without Gloria Steinem. She gave me and so many other women the courage to question societal norms – and the patriarchy – around what women could do, be and, most of all, think.‘Called forth a radical redefinition of women and ageing’Margie Adam, musicianGloria Steinem made news when she turned 40 and a reporter remarked: “You don’t look 40!” She responded: “This is what 40 looks like.” I was 27 years old at the time. When I began to get this same comment when mentioning my age, I used Gloria’s exact words. By then her comment was part of the mantra women used to call forth a radical redefinition of women and aging that the on-going Women’s Liberation Movement continues to keep front and center. Just a few months ago I had a birthday and announced my age to a room full of people. Someone called out: “You don’t look 79!” To which I conjured Gloria and answered: “This is what 79 looks like.” Let us channel the force field that is Gloria Steinem.‘A model of empathy’Melissa Auf der Maur, musicianView image in fullscreenMelissa Auf der Maur photographed for the Guardian, 2026.Photograph: Bryan Derballa/The GuardianGloria Steinem has left us, but countless of her sayings are at hand for us to learn from: “We shall overcome” and “The truth will set you free, but first you will be pissed off” come to mind. But as I comb through her speeches, one from this year feels most urgent. “We only experience real empathy when we are flooded with oxytocin, and it only happens when we’re together,” she said while sitting in her living room, hosting a feminist salon in her 90s. The importance of coming together in person used to be a given, but not now in the age of digitized divide. May we gather in each other’s living rooms and activate empathy salons, united and empowered in honor of Gloria and all the women who have gathered before us.‘The most present person in the room’Sarah Ruhl, co-writer of The GloriasI had the honor of meeting Gloria Steinem when working on a film (The Glorias) about her extraordinary life. Gloria rushed into the meeting wearing her signature silver belt and black tunic. She apologized, with humility, for being late; she was coming from a meeting at the United Nations where she was speaking about the powerful connection between countries being peaceful and equal rights for women. I couldn’t believe she’d been apologetic about being late to a film meeting when she’d been busy addressing an international body about subjects of deep import. But that was Gloria: humble, charming, funny, insightful and concerned about everyone else.Every time I met with Gloria, she was the most present person in the room. When I say present, I do not mean the kind of charisma that demands attention for the self; I mean that she activated the entire room with the unique quality of her listening. I bonded with her over shared feminist values (which I’d inherited, in part, from her), but also over the act of writing. Many first associate the image of Gloria with her fist raised at a podium, speaking out and marching; what fascinated me as I dove into her history was how she managed to overcome a fear of public speaking because she had more latitude to speak freely at demonstrations than in print.First and foremost, she began as a writer. She came to speaking later, when the journalistic constraints of the 60s (pre-Ms magazine) barred her from writing about feminist concerns like abortion. This is one of her many enduring lessons: that great leaders are not born with every quality they need, but are created through incredible acts of bravery, shaped by their profound sense of mission. Thank God that we still have her writing and her example as a road map. We need her legacy now more than ever, and though we won’t have her robust and encouraging laughter in the room, we will always have her powerful words.‘She changed what we believed was possible’Judy Collins, musicianGloria Steinem didn’t just change the conversation, she changed what we believed was possible. She gave generations of women the language for their lives and the courage to claim them. And she reminds me of the spirit behindBread and Roses: that we fight not only for survival, but for dignity: for a life with both the bread we need and the roses we deserve.‘She was my Wonder Woman’Lynda Carter, actorGloria was bold, beautiful and feminine. She was my Wonder Woman.Explore more on these topicsGloria SteinemMargaret AtwoodDua LipaActivismFeminismWomenFictionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Brazilian documentary taught me the healing power of music | Ezra Collective | The Guardian
description: Favela Rising showed me how grassroots movements and community can change the lives of young people. Its ethos is baked into the youth charity I work for – and where two of Ezra Collective met
Author: Deborah Linton
Headline: Favela Rising showed me how grassroots movements and community can change the lives of young people. Its ethos is baked into the youth charity I work for – and where two of Ezra Collective met
Content: Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianMy cultural awakeningEzra CollectiveA Brazilian documentary taught me the healing power of musicFavela Rising showed me how a grassroots movement can change the lives of young people. Its ethos is baked into the youth charity I work for – and where two of Ezra Collective met‘Like painting with light’: photographer Temi Adegbayibi on capturing the energy of musicTamzyn Marchev; as told toDeborah LintonSat 5 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIgrew up in Great Yarmouth listening to classical music, learning piano and violin, playing in an orchestra and singing the Beatles in choir. Music was something that was arranged and formal, a privilege handed to me. At 18 I moved to London to study it at university. But outside my small town, I quickly realised that I didn’t have what it took to make it as a performer.There were, however, two course units that really resonated with me: music therapy and music in cultural industries. They weren’t about being a musician but about using music in the wider world. And so, as graduation approached, I determined that if I could build a career in organisations that helped people through music, that would be a valuable way to pass on the opportunities I’d been given to others.In 2004 I walked into my first day of a new job atKinetika Bloco– a summer school that used carnival music and dance to give south London kids a creative education – and found something culturally and musically totally different to anything I’d experienced.There were 150 teenagers learning drums, brass instruments and dance. It was chaotic, loud, scary and beautiful. For me, music had been instructive; here it was raw. Kids who’d never played the trumpet before were now part of a section and it felt joyful and free.The organisation was a couple of years old and took its name from Brazilianblocos– carnival-style street parties characterised by the same movement and sounds. Kinetika’s founder,Mat Fox, had visited them and been inspired by what it did for kids: they’d go to school in the morning, then spend the afternoon in this social space connecting and creating. A year after I joined, the filmFavela Risingcame out. It documented the true story of Anderson Sá, a drug trafficker turned social revolutionary who established the grassroots AfroReggae movement to draw young people away from crime and drugs in Rio’s slums. Mat suggested I’d like it.double quotation markThe kids in the film needed another place to belong. It made me realise this was what my job was – to show an alternativeI bought the DVD and sat down to watch it alone on the sofa. The kids on screen survived by selling drugs and guns, against a backdrop of massacres and extreme poverty. It hit hard but seeing how music became something that healed them and offered a path out was inspiring.As it is in London, these kids needed somewhere else, another place to belong to that would show them another way. It was while watching that I understoodthisis what Kinetika were really about – not a music project or an orchestra clocking up grades and performances, but a space to bring young people together and show them an alternative.Favela Rising became part of Kinetika’s ethos, and my own. AfroReggae led from the front. They came from the same community as the kids they were creating with. I wasn’t from south London, but I could inspire the young people who came through our doors so that they could lead their next generation.For years after, we showed the film at lunchtimes and in summer schools, as we created a space to grow local musicians.We grew from a summer school taking part in Notting Hill carnival to what we are today, running holiday programmes, workshops and after-school clubs for children and teens across London. We operate from the Southbank Centre and have created a leadership programme – the vast majority of our drum, brass and dance leaders were once young people in Bloco.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe perform across the country and we’ve taken kids to New Orleans and Cape Town. Thousands have passed through our doors, some of whom bring their kids now. Among Bloco’s alumnae are Ezra Collective’s Femi and Ife. They met here as teenagers; Femi did our leadership programme, working with kids with special needs. He always says he tries to recreate the spirit of Kinetika Bloco on stage. Our young people have performed with them, including Ezra’s 2025 performance with Jorja Smith at the Brits. Some years ago, we performed with AfroReggae too after they approached us, out of the blue, during a London visit. They had no idea about the inspiration we had taken from them and Favela Rising. I remember standing against the wall of that same school hall I first walked into, seeing them and 50 of our teenagers jumping with huge drums, thinking: this is quite incredible.At Kinetika Bloco, Favela Rising is still baked into our mindset. It has affected and inspired us. It encourages our young people and gives them perspective. It’s like Femi says: if you want to get a young person out of trouble, put a trumpet in their hands – then just watch what they do.Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.
