title: Colin from Accounts: a show so fearless and hilarious that I want to get a tattoo of it  | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s deliciously satirical, fizzes with electric chemistry – and it’s snortingly funny too. If you haven’t watched the worst named show on TV yet, do so. Right now!
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: It’s deliciously satirical, fizzes with electric chemistry – and it’s snortingly funny too. If you haven’t watched the worst named show on TV yet, do so. Right now!
Content: Co-parenting … Patrick Brammall as Gordon and Harriet Dyer as Ashley in Colin from Accounts season three.Photograph: John Platt/BBC/CBS StudiosView image in fullscreenCo-parenting … Patrick Brammall as Gordon and Harriet Dyer as Ashley in Colin from Accounts season three.Photograph: John Platt/BBC/CBS StudiosThe watcherTelevisionColin from Accounts: a show so fearless and hilarious that I want to get a tattoo of itIt’s deliciously satirical, fizzes with electric chemistry – and it’s snortingly funny too. If you haven’t watched the worst named show on TV yet, do so. Right now!Rhik SamadderSat 5 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSometimes the best things in life have the worst names. The Beatles. Smeg fridges. Nintendo Wii. But top of the tree isColin from Accounts(Monday 7 September, 10pm, BBC Two), a name so bland I almost slipped into medical unconsciousness upon hearing it. It’s worse than bland. There’s an aspect of comedy-tie zaniness to it, a “Look, we’re calling our possibly office-based sitcom the most boring thing we can think of!” tedium. One can imagine the lazy jokes, the stock characters. Within 15 minutes of watching it, I was genuinely toying with the idea of a CFA tattoo.How did this unpromising Australian import become my favourite? By being a showcase for fearless writing, electric chemistry and delicious comic timing. Written by real-life partnersPatrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer, it tracks the relationship of medical student Ashley and Gordon, a brewery owner and ball cancer survivor. The romance, like their writing, is allergic to schmaltz. Their meet-cute occurs in the street when Ashley flashes a boob at Gordon, causing him to crash his car and permanently disable a stray dog that they unwillingly adopt together. (That’s Colin. It’s not really about Colin.)If you haven’t watched the show before, you need to do that today. Right now. For Colinheads, this final series picks up three years after the cringey climax of the second, when a public declaration was badly handled. I’m impressed when shows do this – jump forward a few years between series. It shakes the snow globe, jumbling relationships and a world we’ve come to love, coating them in fresh unfamiliarity.View image in fullscreenZany … Justin Rosniak as Alistair and Genevieve Hegney as Chiara in Colin from Accounts season three.Photograph: Lisa Tomasetti/BBC/CBS StudiosThankfully, the characters are all present and incorrect. Ashley is now dating a pickleball player who works for an inner-city trout farm, and stinks. Her best friend Megan is a lesbian mumfluencer, having conceived using sperm donated from James, Ashley’s ex. Megan still has a frisson with Gordon’s colleague Chiara, the mother of three whose bisexuality she awakened. Chiara, meanwhile, is having an emotional time disclosing her recent ADHD diagnosis. “Who cares?” responds Gordon. “You’re in your 40s. It’s not like you’re in year 8 maths, distracting everybody.”In Colin from Accounts, no one escapes satire. Ashley’s deluded mother, Lynelle, is still standing by her man – a grotesque creep called Lee who lost his job following an online sex scandal. To defend his honour, Lynelle founded anti-feminist group WAWAM (Women Against Women Against Men). Now they’re married, the group has blossomed into a men’s rights advocacy and business platform. They counsel weedy losers to step into their male energy, mostly by yelling “I’m the man of the house!” This nearly made me wet myself. There’s a backlash on the horizon though, in the form of protest group WAWAWAMEN. You work it out.For all the brilliant ensemble clowning, it’s the love story that cements the show’s greatness. Brammall and Dyer are magnetic and tuned to each other, as the argumentative brewery boss and borderline-alcoholic graduate, now a practising GP. The first scene, which throws them together as doctor and patient in Ashley’s new surgery, sets up the question of the series: can these exes be just mates, and co-parent a dog? Given their fizzing banter, mutual attraction and the fact their every interaction could be subtitled with the word “yearning”, it seems as likely as a fruit bat and a chimpanzee co-parenting a banana.The show is definitely more romcom than sitcom (unless the sit stands for situationship). It makes me think about the criticism most levelled at romantic comedies: that they are fantasies, with nothing to say about the ongoing pressures of actual relationships. Here is one real enough to show us ambivalence and irritation between its lovers. It runs on messiness, breakups, age difference, money imbalances, sexual exploration and fertility panics. It does so with peppery, snortingly funny gags, and all without selling out the genre’s central article of faith – that love is real, and will out. I have snot-cried to this show.If the true test of the heart is embracing what annoys you, then Colin from Accounts is the best name for a show ever. I can’t conceive of a better one. I would be with this show if it were a worm. It’s classic and current, comforting as a quilt. I kinda wish it wasn’t back. Love hurts, but tattoos hurt more.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherColin from AccountsTV comedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tender Loving Care review – Mike Leigh’s tender and elusive study of love and mortality | Movies | The Guardian
description: Alice Bailey Johnson and Kate O’Flynn lead a tender, quietly heartbreaking drama about friendship, ageing parents and the sadness of lives moving inexorably on
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Alice Bailey Johnson and Kate O’Flynn lead a tender, quietly heartbreaking drama about friendship, ageing parents and the sadness of lives moving inexorably on
Content: Buoyant …  (from left) Kate O'Flynn, Marion Bailey  and Alice Bailey Johnson in  Tender Loving Care.Photograph: Courtesy TIFFView image in fullscreenBuoyant …  (from left) Kate O'Flynn, Marion Bailey  and Alice Bailey Johnson in  Tender Loving Care.Photograph: Courtesy TIFFMoviesReviewTender Loving Care review – Mike Leigh’s tender and elusive study of love and mortalityTelluride film festivalAlice Bailey Johnson and Kate O’Flynn lead a complicated, quietly heartbreaking drama about friendship, ageing parents and the sadness of lives moving inexorably onPeter BradshawFri 4 Sep 2026 21.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMike Leigh’s new film – perhaps his last – is a poignant, intergenerational drama of happy-sad acceptance that life goes on, until it doesn’t go on. And then you have to come to terms with the mortality of your elderly parents and by that same token, with the end that is waiting for you too. The decency and clarity of the film are a tonic. It is a movie with one of Leigh’s overtly positive and even sugary titles, like Life Is Sweet (1990) or Happy-Go-Lucky (2008), as distinct from his darker ones: Secrets & Lies (1996) or Hard Truths (2024). But his sweet titles are not simply satirical and intended to mean the opposite: it is more complicated and elusive, and even the contrast here between the two heroines’ private and professional lives isn’t straightforwardly a matter of irony.As so often, the dialogue has that unique Leigh cartoonish quality that isn’t caricature, and the characters often speak with an almost wartime chirpiness in a world of peckers kept up and noses kept clean. This is a perkiness that the thirtysomethings have unexpectedly inherited and modified from their old mum and dad, and Leigh leaves it to the audience to judge the consequent tone of the drama and the appropriate tone of their response.The setting is Ealing, west London, where, to paraphrase Larkin, people work all day and get half drunk at night, opening up the white wine that’s been in the fridge while worrying about themselves and their family. Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson) is a single woman and social worker who has started dating a fireman (no woke stuff about “firefighter”). She stays calm and polite in the face of aggressive behaviour from clients; her first scene is with an impassive old man in hospital who, asked for his address, recites only a number. He is perhaps a kind of choric spirit in the film, like the homeless man in Jack Rosenthal’s The Chain.Rosie, as caring in private as she is at work, has welcomed her best friend back into the spare room in her flat; this is Amy (Kate O’Flynn), a fellow social worker who cares specifically for vulnerable young people. She needs a place to stay as she has just split up with an odious boyfriend. The two women are deliriously happy to have each other’s company again: they drink, sing daft songs and tell goofy jokes together. Another type of movie would suggest that each woman is the love of the other’s life, and that they are in denial. Not this film. Rosie and Amy are just best pals and the tension and the unresolved issues lie elsewhere.In a way, Amy’s only other mates are her mum and dad, for which we have excellent and heartbreaking performances from Leigh stalwarts Marion Bailey and Paul Jesson, who was Turner’s elderly father in Mr Turner (2014). Rosie and Amy go round to see them together for cups of tea, and Amy’s mum unselfconsciously calls Rosie her “second daughter”. But there are problems. Amy can’t bring herself to confess to her parents that her relationship (from which they were hoping for grandchildren) is over, and her mum is uneasy about the way “Pops” zones out in the middle of conversation and seems forgetful. Like Amy and Rosie, the old couple love songs; they singDaisy BellandBoiled Beef and Carrotsin private and the simplicity and innocence of these moments is almost unbearable.As ever, the buoyant and exuberant dialogue passages show that the speaker is not a clever-clever person intent on impressing anyone, and for all the exaggeration, there is a realness in these moments. Bailey’s mum figure waxes lyrical about her husband and how wonderful it was, 50 years ago, to have met him: “He was one in a million … a needle in a haystack!” Of course, a needle in a haystack doesn’t exactly connote what she’s saying but the truth of it is plain enough, and if the audience laughs, it is with her, not at her.At work, Rosie and Amy are impeccably conscientious in the face of the most challenging people, though perhaps Amy is marginally the more successful of the two; we see her being able to connect with troubled teens. Rosie is as well-meaning, but often meets a blank wall. Leigh also shows us one moment when one woman appears to have a legitimate complaint against her; Rosie urges this woman, who has lost her children to the system and is now living in what are clearly squalid and chaotic conditions, to talk and open up – but the woman angrily replies that her words will just be held against her in court. She has a point; if she were under arrest, she would at least be warned that she had the right to remain silent. As for Amy’s mum, she is the caring friend and neighbour to a recently widowed woman painfully estranged from her son.Leigh shows us a world without cynicism, without malice, a world in which people do care, but in which they have a lot to care about. There is a lot of unhappiness here, an ocean of sadness which almost, but not quite, capsizes the boat – yet the mood, underscored by Gary Yershon’s music, is more ruminative than melancholy. The film’s structure is theatrically controlled, and the succession of scenes moves smoothly from Amy and Rosie’s lives at home and at work, to their parents’ lives and to their interaction with clients. There is no screenwriting-seminar character development or narrative arc here – except perhaps one which leads to a heart-wrenching moment in a bedroom from which the camera retreats sadly and tactfully on to the landing. We are not approaching a big monologue moment of explosive emotional catharsis. The storm, as so often with Leigh, rumbles towards us and then rumbles back over the horizon. And yet the sadness and the love stayed with me long after the closing credits.Tender Loving Care screened at theTelluride film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsMike LeighKate O'FlynnreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #259: What to watch this Oscars film season | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: A non-exhaustive list of the films to keep an eye out for this autumn
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: A non-exhaustive list of the films to keep an eye out for this autumn
Content: Book a season ticket at the cinema … clockwise from top left:  The Death of Robin Hood, Bad Apples, Digger, Just an Illusion.Composite: Warner Bros, Pulse Films,  Manuel Moutier, PAView image in fullscreenBook a season ticket at the cinema … clockwise from top left:  The Death of Robin Hood, Bad Apples, Digger, Just an Illusion.Composite: Warner Bros, Pulse Films,  Manuel Moutier, PAThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #259: What to watch this Oscars film seasonIn this week’s newsletter: A non-exhaustive list of the films to keep an eye out for this autumnDon’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGwilym MumfordSat 5 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe next three months or so is one of my favourite spells in the film calendar, as a load of Oscar hopefuls with big stars and auteurs attached come out of hiding. You can catch a decent movie at the cinema every week until Christmas – but you might want a guide to direct you to the right ones. This week’s Guide does exactly that.What’s more, it’s not exhaustive: there will be films landing from the autumn festivals that haven’t yet been given a release date and a host of big awards movies due in the UK in January (Danny Boyle’s Murdoch movie Ink, Robert Eggers’s Werewulf, Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut). But, this should keep you going until the days start getting longer again.4 Sept| The Death of Robin HoodGranted, we begin a little slowly. This reimagining of the final days of the outlaw (played in full, crusty, Logan-style makeup by Hugh Jackman) probably isn’t for everyone, with its ultraviolence and doomy mood, but some critics have chimed with its heady vibe. For more gritty middle-ages drama (that might also beRobin Hood-tinged), Paul Greengrass’s Andrew Garfield-starring The Uprising is due on 9 Oct.11 Sept| Just an IllusionA summer hit in France, this coming of age drama seems well timed for the turning of the leaves here. A wistful story of a 13-year-old boy’s first tentative steps into romance, while his parents’ own one is faltering, it has some great French acting talent at its core in the form ofLouis Garreland Call My Agent’s Camille Cottin. May well be in the best international film running at the Oscars.18 Sept| Bad ApplesThis is a last chance to catchSaoirse Ronanon our screens for a while before her schedule is swamped by Sam Mendes’s Beatles quadrilogy (she plays Linda McCartney). Here Ronan is the put-upon primary school teacher who resorts to desperate measures to subdue her class’s most disruptive student in Jonatan Etzler’s twisted little thriller.View image in fullscreenBack to the classics … Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus Features25 Sept| Sense and SensibilityNow we are starting to get some biggies. First up Blue Jean director Georgia Oakley’s take on S&S, a high-wire move given there’s a fondly remembered movie take on the same source material still in most people’s living memories. Daisy Edgar-Jones and George MacKay star in the first of two Austin adaptations this autumn: soon on Netflix is Dolly Alderton’s Pride and Prejudice series, starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden.2 Oct| DiggerThe single most intriguing film of the year, withTom Cruiseshunning acting hero-dom to star as an oil baron trying to undo his own potentially world-ending foul-up in Alejandro Iñárritu’s climate crisis satire. Iñárritu is the master of the mixed bag, Cruise hasn’t done anything like this in decades and the trailer looks, well, pretty odd. Could be a disaster, could be fantastic – either way it will be talked about.9 Oct| The Social ReckoningAnother maybe disaster/maybe classic: a sequel to one of the century’s most admired films, plagued by reports of reshoots and a widely disliked trailer. Social Network screenwriter Aaron Sorkin is directing this one, rather thanDavid Fincher– another red flag? Still, its subject is fascinating: the 2021 Facebook leak that revealed the company’s knowledge of the harmful effects its platforms were having on society. Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White and Jeremy Strong, as Mark Zuckerberg, star.16 Oct| WhalefallWhile this one is unlikely to trouble the prestige Oscar categories – though it might hoover up some sound/visual/technical nominations – it’s worth flagging here because, good grief what a terrifying premise: scuba diver gets swallowed by a sperm whale and has to find his way back out of it! Oh, and he only has 60 minutes of oxygen in his tank with which to do so. Claustrophobes: stay the hell away.View image in fullscreenMoody noir … Sandra Hüller in Fatherland.Photograph: Agata Grzybowska23 Oct| FatherlandAfter the brilliant pair of Ida and Cold War,Paweł Pawlikowskidelivers a third stylish, monochrome movie reflecting on postwar life east of the Berlin Wall. This one concerns the return to Berlin in 1949 of famed German author Thomas Mann (Hans Zischler), who is visiting from the US to accept literary awards in both west and east Berlin – a problem for both his CIA handlers and for his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller – who between this, Project Hail Mary and Digger, is having quite the 2026).30 Oct|PrimetimeRobert Pattinson is racking up quite the roster of ne’er-do-wells and losers in 2026: there was his snivelling, scheming suitor Antinous in the Odyssey; his brittle groom in The Drama; and his shapeshifting wannabe usurper in the forthcoming Dune 3. Joining that rogues gallery is his performance as Chris Hansen, the ethically murky host of notorious noughties TV series To Catch a Predator, in Primetime, one of the autumn’s most hotly tipped dramas.6 Nov| Wild Horse NineAfter filming The Banshees of Inisherin, on rainswept, beautiful Inishmore, Martin McDonagh decamps to the more exotic isle of Rapa Nui – AKA Easter Island – where, in his latest, two unscrupulous CIA men are holidaying just before the 1973 coup in Chile gets under way. Chris (John Malkovich) is nearing the end of his career and fancies writing a tell all memoir; Lee (Sam Rockwell) is tasked by the agency with keeping an eye on his loose-cannon mentor. Expect all manner of Oscar buzz for Malkovich.13 Nov| FjordCristian Mungiu (4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days) shook up Cannes with this spicy meatball of a movie about a devoutly Christian couple, who after moving from Romania to Norway, are accused of abusing their children by members of a community already suspicious of their evangelistic ways. Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve star in a film that sounds designed to inspire loud post-cinema debate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSettle in … clockwise from top left: Digger, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, Dune Part 3 and Fjord.Composite: Warner Bros/Netflix/Neon/20 Nov| A Talent for MurderA delicious-looking meta-murder mystery for late November nights.Helen Mirrenplays a reclusive Patricia Highsmith, hiding away in Switzerland at the end of her career, while Alden Ehrenreich is the lad sent by her publisher to convince her to write one final Tom Ripley novel. She will, but only if he helps her devise a suitably devilish plot – which offers director Anton Corbijn the chance to make a Ripley movie by stealth.27 Nov| The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff BoothLike Digger and The Social Reckoning, a big film with big questions around it: this Brad Pitt-starring Tarantino-penned (but not directed, with David Fincher instead in the chair) follow up to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood had to skip the autumn film festivals in order to squeeze in extensive reshoots. Could be in dog’s breakfast territory, but given the quality of the original, we’re still excited.View image in fullscreenLaugh it off … Anthony Boyle, Jay Lycurgo, Lola and Petticrew in I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning.Photograph: Chris Harris4 Dec| I See Buildings Fall Like LightningThis week you have a choice of hotly anticipated movies: there’s Behemoth!, Tony Gilroy’s tale of an itinerant, relationship-phobic concert cellist, starring Pedro Pascal; or this Clio Barnard drama about skint Birmingham twentysomethings, featuring some Great British talent (Anthony Boyle, Jay Lycurgo, Lola Petticrew). See both, but if you can only catch one, home bias dictates that we should probably back the Barnard: any film withan extended rendition of The Streets’ Don’t Mug Yourselfhas us sold.11 Dec| OnslaughtA lull, with most movies skipping town ahead of the impending arrival of two monster films next week (see below). One of the big festival films might drop into the schedules but for now your best bet is this genre-splicing horror thriller about an army sniper trying to protect her kid from genetically modified super soldiers. Cast looks fun: Adria Arjona, Dan Stevens, Eric Wareheim and Rebecca Hall all feature.18 Dec| Dune Part 3Quite why the final instalment of Denis Villeneuve’s space opus and Avengers: Doomsday are arriving in cinemas on the same weekend is beyond the ken of us non-movie execs. Neither film seems willing to budge, meaning that a showdown that has been given the Barbenheimerised moniker of “Dunesday” looks inevitable. We’re siding with Dune, likely to be gigantic, gorgeous and a little bit weird, if the source material of Frank Herbert’s Dune Messiah is anything to go by. title: The rise of south-east Asia’s girl bands: ‘The talent and popularity were always here’ | Culture | The Guardian
description: Girl bands from the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand are going global with their fusion of traditional and modern sounds
Author: Natasha May
Headline: Girl bands from the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand are going global with their fusion of traditional and modern sounds
Content: Filipina girl band BINI perform at Coachella, 2026.Photograph: Natt Lim/In Time MediaView image in fullscreenFilipina girl band BINI perform at Coachella, 2026.Photograph: Natt Lim/In Time MediaCultureThe rise of south-east Asia’s girl bands: ‘The talent and popularity were always here’Girl bands from the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand are going global with their fusion of traditional and modern soundsNatasha Mayin BangkokFri 4 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 14.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“We all know that music is a universal language,” says Maloi Ricalde from Filipina girl band BINI, which mixes tropical pop with traditional songs, English with Tagalog, and silver knee highs with pastel colours.“Incorporating Filipino language, Filipino culture, Filipino sound, into our music, it really gives identity and meaning to our music,” Ricalde tells the Guardian.‘People are exhausted by Blackpink and BTS’: the DIY Chinese bands redefining corporate ‘idol’ popRead moreMonths after becoming the first south-east Asian girl band to perform atCoachella, and now with a tour of Japan under its belt, the group is enjoying a surge in popularity.“Our next goal,” says BINI member Jhoanna Robles, “Is that we want Filipino culture, Filipino music to be part of a conversation naturally on a global stage.”BINI is not the only girl group from south-east Asia to recently gain wider traction, with other girl bands such as Indonesia’s no na, Thailand’s 4EVE, and Malaysia’s DOLLA taking to stages around the world, instigating viral dance challenges and racking up millions of views online.Industry experts say musical talent has always existed in the region, but the infrastructure is now backing it up after the huge popularity of K-pop showed that investment could push Asian artists into the mainstream.View image in fullscreenBINI performing at Coachella in April 2026.Photograph: Greg Noire/SuppliedThe music industry in the west largely ignored Asian music before the 2012 hitGangnam Style, which went viral in part thanks to its popularity in the Philippines and among its diaspora, says Piyapong Muenprasertdee, co-founder of music platform Fungjai.Many emerging artists and groups from the region are now gaining fans by blending modern and traditional elements, adds Piyapong.In Thailand indie acts as well asgirl bands such as BNK48are putting their own spin on local folk music Molam and Thai country music known as Luk Thung. In Vietnam and the Philippines, unique electronic dance music styles are becoming increasingly prominent in local club scenes.In Indonesia, girl band no na has mixed dangdut, a high-intensity genre with Indonesian, Malay, Arabic and Indian roots, with reggaeton and pop, including in their hitbilingual song Rollerblade, which has garnered 16m views.The group produces catchy, sometimes expletive-laden pop songs that feature traditional ceng-ceng cymbals, and gamelan, an ensemble from Java and Bali, which they perform in striking costumes and with occasional back-bending moves.“It’s been a consistent formula throughout our work process to find songs that have a global sound and add Indonesian elements as a cherry on top as our no na stamp,” the group tells the Guardian. “Because we’re a global girl group but still representing our country, we always try to find that balance without compromising too much of one or the other.”Thai girl group 4EVE reflects local elements like Bangkok’s bustling street culture in their music videos, while Malaysia’s DOLLA has released songs such asRaya Raya Rayacelebrating the end of Ramadan, which they perform in modest, but hot-pink kaftans.View image in fullscreenIndonesian girl band, no na.Photograph: kenchyro/SuppliedOne feature of Asian pop culture, says PR expert Bettina Miski, is the prominence of fandom and fanclubs, which have contributed to their popularity.“The relationship between the artists and the fans is a lot deeper,” says Miski, who runs a YouTube series called “THAI T”, which connects Asian artists with global audiences. “That devotion leads to spreading the word, a type of promotion that often goes beyond traditional marketing as it feels a lot more personal or intimate.”Girl bands in the region have special names for their fans, which provide support at concerts and online, including in posting dance challenges. BINI’s fans are called “Blooms”, for no na it’s “Orchids”, 4EVE’s “For Aye” (also meaning forever), and DOLLA’s “iDollas”.Therow over the Grammys’ new category for Asian popsuggests inclusivity in the industry still has a way to go. The move was criticised for potentially ringfencing Asian pop artists from contending in the top categories. It also explicitly mentioned only K-pop, J-pop, and C-pop despite the region’s diversity.Still, says Piyapong, south-east Asia is well positioned to be “the next powerhouse” in the global music landscape.“We just recently entered an era where borders or language matter less,” says Miski, “The talent and popularity were always here, the system just had to catch up.”Explore more on these topicsCultureMusic festivalsCoachellaThailandIndonesiaAsia PacificFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Bold, brilliant, thrilling’: leading authors on the novels every school should teach | Books | The Guardian
description: A new term, a new PM … time for a new English curriculum? We ask writers from Ben Okri to Samantha Harvey to pick books that will inspire a lifelong love of reading
Author: Kate Mosse
Headline: A new term, a new PM … time for a new English curriculum? We ask writers from Ben Okri to Samantha Harvey to pick books that will inspire a lifelong love of reading
Content: Composite: Getty/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Getty/Guardian DesignBooks‘Bold, brilliant, thrilling’: leading authors on the novels every school should teachA new term, a new PM … time for a new English curriculum? We ask writers from Ben Okri to Samantha Harvey to pick books that will inspire a lifelong love of readingKate MosseSat 5 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTShareFor the first time ever, we have a British prime minister who studied for an English degree. Not all of his 58 predecessors went to university, but those who did favoured subjects such as history and classics and, more recently, philosophy, politics and economics. Yet reading fiction is a fantastic preparation for life, for understanding people and the times through which we live. Novels encourage empathy, they help you to stand in other people’s shoes, to navigate complicated, sometimes conflicting emotions, they entertain and bring joy. The creative industries contribute some £145.8bn each year to the UK economy; it is our soft superpower.In other words, books matter. Reading matters.However, there has been a marked decline over recent years in the numbers of children reading for pleasure. It’s why the NationalLiteracyTrust designated 2026 the National Year of Reading. Already there has been a shift from a 20-year low in 2025 of 32.7% of eight-to-18-year-olds saying they enjoy reading in their free time up to 36.1%. It’s a start.We are also in a long-overdue moment of curriculum renewal for GCSE English, so when better to ask if what’s studied in school helps young people fall in love with reading – or possibly puts them off for life?SinceGCSEswere first introduced in 1986, we’ve seen the establishment of four main examination boards in England and Wales and surprising unanimity in the choice of books most schools choose to teach. In 2025, the educational charity End Sexism in Schools released a report – Manopolies – revealing that 76% of students study An Inspector Calls by JB Priestley for their modern text from a possible 21 modern texts (a play, wonderful as it is, that’s been on one board’s set text list for 39 years). Then a whopping 93% of students study either A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens or The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde by Robert Louis Stevenson for their 19th-century novel from nine possible texts (including Charlotte Brontë, Mary Shelley and Jane Austen). Only 5% of students in England and Wales study a female-authored text at GCSE.It’s true that there are diverse modern works by inspirational women on the lists of the four exam boards – Kit de Waal, Tanika Gupta, Jeanette Winterson, Malorie Blackman are all offered. The problem is that schools are disincentivised to change the texts they teach as this would involve costs and additional work. And no exam board wants to be the one to remove popular texts because that would bring commercial disadvantage and developmental costs. This is why it’s essential the Department for Education, as part of this review, mandates the regular changing of set-text lists and stipulates that students study works that reflect the gender balance and diversity of our society. Schools can’t do it on their own.Here, to get the conversation started, are suggestions of texts to inspire a passion for fiction in young readers. And, from me, a plea for the government to support teachers who want to better reflect the gender balance and diversity of their classrooms.This is the way to encourage a lifelong love of reading.Kate MosseNussaibah YounisThe Treesby Percival EverettView image in fullscreenWouldn’t it be refreshing to see a blisteringly funny novel on the syllabus? The Trees is a daring satire on racism, generational guilt and cultural complicity, inspired by the lynching of Emmett Till. Genre-bending and gloriously inventive, it finds morbid delight in the absurdities of American racial violence without ever trivialising its victims. With characters such as Dr Reverend Fondle, Junior Junior and Hot Mama Yeller, Everett exposes the grotesque stupidity of white supremacy through comedy that is as vicious as it is exhilarating. What better way to show teenagers that literature can be genuinely enjoyable, even laugh-out-loud funny, while remaining intellectually and morally serious.Frank Cottrell-BoyceStories of Your Life andOthersbyTed ChiangView image in fullscreenA great short story hits you like a left hook or an unexpected kiss – coming out of nowhere and leaving you gasping, what just happened? Which is the perfect state for learning, of course. Short stories work really well in the classroom because reading is best when it’s shared. I would, therefore, strongly suggest Ted Chiang’s astonishing science fiction collection Stories of Your Life and Others. Each story takes on a big idea – language, love, intelligence, the collateral damage to real estate that angels might cause when intervening in human affairs, that sort of thing. They go off in your head like bombs. The most famous is the title story, which was made into the movieArrival. Teenagers love ideas. They’re about to go into a world that their grownups are viewing as some kind of sci-fi nightmare. Here’s a bold, brilliant, thrilling set of thought experiments about how it could be OK after all. It’s a science fiction collection that opens with a story set in Old Testament Babylon. What else do you need to know?Patrice LawrenceRandomby Debbie Tucker GreenI recommend this play. For a Black working-class London family, it’s a normal weekday – until the teenage son is senselessly stabbed and killed.The work is performed by one actor, from the point of view of the sister. The dialogue is funny, tenderly painting the warm family relationships until that one moment destroys everything. Then follows grief, fury, helplessness and despair.Random is gripping and short. It’s a springboard for many different conversations, from topics such as the impact of race in the criminal justice system and the representation of working-class families, to the benefits and challenges of performing such an emotional piece in a stripped-back set.David MitchellThe Rest ofUs Just Live Hereby Patrick NessView image in fullscreenThis wise, chaotic, gentle, painful, funny, superb novel follows five teens trying to navigate the most difficult year of their lives, while the town’s cool indie kids are battling Stranger Things-sized perils in vignettes at the start of each chapter. It contains some of the truest (and helpful) lines about social anxiety I’ve ever read. For reluctant readers, The Rest of Us Just Live Here proves that great fiction is as compelling as a great video game; and unlike social media, it leaves you feeling nourished, smarter, and not wanting back the time you just spent on it. I was asked to provide one title only, but hey: class, now turn to that blast of medieval Tarantino, The Pardoner’s Tale. Chaucer, Patrick Ness and the language we’re using right now cohabit the same glorious entangled continuum. Compare and contrast Henry IV Part 2 Act 3 Scene 1, “Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown” with the lyrics to Stormzy’s song Crown. Art is made of art. It speaks across centuries. Now it’s your turn.Hollie McNishWild Geeseby Mary OliverView image in fullscreenAfter spending many evenings this spring testing my daughter on her GCSE English Literature quotes, I felt ready to vomit. Three set texts: Lord of the Flies, Macbeth and The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. Shared themes of blood, death, murder, violence, the evil of boys and men. Then, if you’re tired of revising prose, a little war poetry for a breather. Lovely. More death.In those two exam years, my daughter studied not one female prose writer, not one writer of colour, only four female characters in the entire trio of set texts (if you count Macbeth’s witches as individual characters, which is debatable, oh and a female pig, according to one teacher). Nearly 30 years ago, my experience was almost exactly the same.What a way to teach a love of literature; what a way to normalise only reading books by men about men, and only if violence is centre stage of the men’s worlds. English literature is an amazing opportunity to nurture a joy of reading, to open minds to other cultures and worlds and wonders. So why is every single text soaked in bloodshed? If I were to pick a text for young people to study, I’d suggestanything but more violence. Something loving, anything funny; just one book teenagers could smile at, laugh with even. Perhaps Ocean Vuong’s The Emperor of Sadness, a gorgeous story between a young man and an elderly woman. Or maybe on the poetry curriculum, Wild Geese by Mary Oliver. Something that has helped people the world over to feel more joy.Ben OkriAfrican Storieseditedby Ben OkriView image in fullscreenOne of the weaknesses of the literary education of this country is that students are not exposed early in life to the valuable literatures of non-European people, particularly Africans.This Everyman African Stories anthology brings together 36 classical African stories written in, or translated into, English. It tracks nearly 100 years and observes every aspect of life, from the domestic to the political, from the romantic to the existential.An average Briton could go through a whole lifetime of wide reading without ever reading any classic African text. These stories would not only provide entertaining and enlightening reading, they could serve as a gateway to discovering the rich literature of a much-overlooked continent.Kamila ShamsieSmall Things Like Theseby Claire KeeganView image in fullscreenIf you look at the most often assigned GCSE texts, the common denominator is a word count under 30,000. That factor knocks a great many wonderful books off the list, but it does also allow space for the brilliance of Claire Keegan. I’d choose Small Things Like These, a novel of remarkable depth within its brevity. “How does she do it?” is a question for any reader of the book – but there are plenty of other questions in it for students. The novel’s story within a story, its use of memory, the character of Bill Furlong, the internal and external landscapes, and the history of the Magdalene laundries are all rich ground for thought and discussion. No harm either in letting young readers recognise that what appears small and quiet is actually taut and fierce.Andrew McMillan100 Queer Poemsedited by Mary Jean Chan and Andrew McMillanView image in fullscreenThere has never been a more important time to ensure that our school libraries and our class curricula contain plenty of books by, about and for LGBTQ+ people. When Mary Jean Chan and I were co-editing 100 Queer Poems, it felt like making something that I needed to read when I was in secondary school. Anthologies are great to study because they allow for the necessity of not liking something. With 100 poets published by more than 45 different presses, a reader won’t enjoy all the different styles and schools of poetry on offer, but they might find some that strike a spark of recognition. There might be one poem that helps a student in developing their own individual language for articulating who they are, and who they might become, in the world.Kit de WaalFalloutby Eleanor AnstrutherView image in fullscreenSet in 1982, Fallout is a fictionalised account of theGreenham Common protestas seen through the eyes of a rebellious 15-year-old girl. Non-preachy, funny and sharp, it’s about family secrets, female empowerment and an important time in British history that we are in danger of forgetting.I’d also suggest Every Man for Himself by Beryl Bainbridge, which is as much about class as it is about the sinking of the Titanic. It’s a sort of whodunnit seen through the eyes of a young man who falls in love with an unobtainable young woman shortly before disaster strikes. It mixes fact with fiction, and the way it’s structured means you have to read it right to the end.Geoff DyerVoyage in the Darkby Jean RhysView image in fullscreenTwo things are of the utmost importance. To adhere to quality as the criterion of, well, of the utmost importance! And to give a sense of the evolving tradition of literature, rather than catering to a preference for the contemporary. The problem is that some things formerly deemed of high quality – crucial components of that tradition – now seem of dubious quality.The good news is that the reputations of plenty of female writers from the interwar period continue to soar. And many of the themes and concerns that preoccupy us now were being addressed by these writers almost a century ago. No one exemplifies this more than Jean Rhys, a writer of genius whose four novels, from 1928 and into the 1930s, were so far ahead of their time that they were doomed, like her heroines, to failure and obscurity. They also have the appealing virtue of extreme brevity, weighing in at about 150 pages apiece.If obliged to select just one of these, I would go for the third, Voyage in the Dark (1934), her devastating and funny account of 18-year-old Anna, who comes from the West Indies and finds herself alone and helpless in London. The perfect introduction to that sought after but mysterious ideal of a writer’s “voice”, it will leave new readers wanting to venture further into Rhys’s strangely defamiliarised world. Which means, in turn, that they will be drawn to her final masterpiece, Wide Sargasso Sea, and from there, inevitably, to Brontë’s Jane Eyre.Samantha HarveyMoon Tigerby Penelope LivelyView image in fullscreenMoon Tiger is a life story and a love story, the story of a woman called Claudia who, we learn on page one, is on her deathbed, ransacking her memories in order to give an account of herself. “Shake the tube and see what comes out,” she says. “Chronology irritates me. There is no chronology inside my head.” The story she tells is seductive, searching, confronting and compressed; scenes are played and differently replayed, truth is questioned, the idea of selfhood is dismantled.Although it’s the retrospection of an older woman, there’s something in this exploded, chaotic rendition of self that would have struck me hard in my teens – the self as a beautiful, dangerous, vulnerable mess. It’s about the harm we do and suffer, and about the possibility of happiness. The whole novel is hot to the touch. It pushes at what a novel can do. It’s experimental in the best, most necessary of ways and a perfect study of how narrative works. Nearly 40 years on, the writing is still fresh, gorgeous and daring. And, admittedly, quite sexy. English teachers up and down the country might be less enthusiastic about it being on the curriculum than I am.Benjamin MyersAddress UnknownbyKathrineKressmann TaylorView image in fullscreenThis epistolary novel is told via a series of letters between two business partners from 1932 to 1934 – Max is an art gallerist in the US while Martin has returned to their fatherland, where he is immediately energised by a bold new leader. But soon the hatred seeps in, and Martin asks his friend to cease communication lest he himself be mistakenly identified as a collaborator. Little more need be said about the plot, other than that it is a one-sitting/one‑lesson/one-hour read that challenges notions of friendship, loyalty, antisemitism and the sheer insidiousness of totalitarian regimes. Trump, Farage, Musk, Putin – all are reflected in Kressmann Taylor’s powerfully concise prose, perfectly constructed for the permanently distracted. Pair with Fred Uhlman’s equally economical 1932-set novelReunionfor a “compare and contrast” discussion -starter.Raymond AntrobusGlyphby Ali SmithView image in fullscreenFew contemporary novels manage to be this urgent and playful at once, which is exactly why it belongs in a classroom: it proves seriousness and playfulness aren’t opposites. At its centre are two estranged sisters, Petra and Patricia, grieving their mother and reckoning with childhood trauma. Smith threads their story through three wars: a horse blinded in the first world war; a flattened body found in the second; and the present-day war in Gaza. The novel asks what it means to watch history repeat itself while insisting it won’t. A ghost horse, conjured by the sisters as children, returns decades later to disturb the present, blurring memory, myth and reality in ways that reward close, repeated reading. Throughout, Smith’s inventive wordplay, puns, homophones – and the title, which mirrors its companion novelGliff–make language itself a subject, not just a vehicle. Students would leave Glyph asking what stories arefor, and whether imagination is escapism or the most soulful technology we have for facing a broken, divided society.

title: Novelist Sebastian Barry: ‘At 71, sex is somewhere between a memory and an ambition’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The author on dashed dreams of being the next Bob Dylan, cruel words from a revered poet and listening to his own snores
Author: Rosanna Greenstreet
Headline: The author on dashed dreams of being the next Bob Dylan, cruel words from a revered poet and listening to his own snores
Content: Sebastian Barry: ‘The greatest love of my life? My wife, Ali, who is a very complete person, unlike myself.’Photograph: Roberto Ricciuti/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSebastian Barry: ‘The greatest love of my life? My wife, Ali, who is a very complete person, unlike myself.’Photograph: Roberto Ricciuti/Getty ImagesThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewNovelist Sebastian Barry: ‘At 71, sex is somewhere between a memory and an ambition’Rosanna GreenstreetThe author on dashed dreams of being the next Bob Dylan, cruel words from a revered poet and listening to his own snoresSat 5 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in Dublin, Sebastian Barry, 71, published his first novel in 1982. In 2005 and 2008, A Long Long Way and The Secret Scripture were shortlisted for the Booker prize; three of his other books have been longlisted. Barry has twice won Costa book of the year and he was laureate for Irish fiction. Tomorrow he discusses his latest novel,The Newer World, atQueen’s Park book festivalin London. He is married with three children and lives in County Wicklow.When were you happiest?Purely and unconsciously, living on Greece’s Paros aged 25. Exhausted and happy, when our babies were small.What is your greatest fear?Running out of money or time.What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?Not listening, but I am training myself.Describe yourself in three wordsPeculiar, intense, awkward.Andrew O’Hagan: ‘The worst thing anyone’s said to me? That I was the spitting image of David Cameron’Read moreWhat makes you unhappy?Myself.What do you most dislike about your appearance?The grotesqueries of old age.If you could bring something extinct back to life, what would you choose?Selflessness in politicians.What is your most unappealing habit?Snoring. There’s an app now that lets you hear your own devastating din.What scares you about getting older?Getting even more old. But that’s a privilege, too.What did you want to be when you were growing up?I hoped to take over from Bob Dylan when he retired, but he never did.What is the worst thing anyone’ssaid to you?When I proudly walked into the Poetry Society in 1985 to do a reading and John Montague (whom I revered) said, “What are you doing here?”What do you owe your parents?Nearly impossible to answer in fewer than 80,000 words. Maybe a respect for writers and a reverence for actors.To whom would you most like to say sorry, and why?There was a vulnerable boy on one of our school tours and I wasn’t kind. I don’t just want to say sorry; I’d like to go back in time and be a decent friend.What or who is the greatest love of your life?I am happy to say my wife, Ali, who is a very complete person, unlike myself.What does love feel like?A responsibility, a test, a chasm, a mountain, a non-harming strike of joy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHave you ever said ‘I love you’and not meantit?Well, only in the sense that, unbeknownst to me, I didn’t.Which words or phrases do you most overuse?Radiant and mighty. Both good words.If you could edit your past, what would you changeTen thousand small edits, but I accept the general text. Can you edit out depressive episodes? Gross stupidities?How often do you have sex?At 71, this is somewhere between a memory and an ambition.Adele Parks: ‘If I could ​edit my pas​t, I’d be fitter younger – I​ would have been hotter’Read moreWhat single thing would improve the quality of your life?Full mental health.What do you consider your greatest achievement?I do make a very authentic moussaka.What keeps you awake at night?The usual things – am I a good person? How will I survive the next book tour?Would you rather have more sex, money or fame?Can we add humanity to that list? I’d rather have more of that.How would you like to be remembered?I dread to think. Foolish but fond?Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Q&ASebastian BarryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t like the term neurodivergence – it sounds like political correctness’: Werner Herzog on fans, fanaticism and baby foxes  | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Bavarian auteur talks directing Kate and Rooney Mara in Bucking Fastard and his popularity on Instagram
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: The Bavarian auteur talks directing Kate and Rooney Mara in Bucking Fastard and his popularity on Instagram
Content: ‘What I do is lively and creates some inner life’ … Werner Herzog with Rooney and Kate Mara.Photograph: Mario Cartelli/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘What I do is lively and creates some inner life’ … Werner Herzog with Rooney and Kate Mara.Photograph: Mario Cartelli/SOPA Images/ShutterstockMoviesInterview‘I don’t like the term neurodivergence – it sounds like political correctness’: Werner Herzog on fans, fanaticism and baby foxesPhilip Oltermannin VeniceThe Bavarian auteur talks directing Kate and Rooney Mara in Bucking Fastard and his popularity on InstagramSat 5 Sep 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn outsider visionaries such as Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo or Timothy Treadwell, renegade German directorWerner Herzoghas created some of cinema’s most memorable monomaniacs – characters singularly obsessed with finding mythical cities made of gold, with building opera houses in the middle of the rainforest, or with befriending wild grizzly bears.Bucking Fastard review – Herzog’s starry twins soap provokes a syncing feelingRead moreBut suggestions that they could be role models for the modern-day neurodiversity movement send this famously fearless film-maker running for the hills. “I don’t like the term neurodivergence and ADHD, or whatever – it sounds like political correctness, which scares me under the table,” Herzog said at theVenice film festival.The protagonist pair ofBucking Fastard, the new film that Herzog has brought to the Lido, slots right into his gallery of single-minded outsiders. Real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara play siblings Jean and Joan Holbrooke, who have separate bodies but speak in unison, dress the same and share the same preoccupations.View image in fullscreenOstracised … Kate and Rooney Mara as the Holbrookes in Bucking Fastard.Photograph: Stills - Courtesy of Gateway to Orkney LLCFirst they fall in love with their washed-up heart-throb neighbour (played by Orlando Bloom) and exact revenge when he marries another woman, then they embark on a quixotic quest to dig a tunnel connecting a cave in County Sligo to the Orkneys. Contemporary psychiatrists might detect behaviour consistent with autism or ADHD hyper-focus. Not Herzog.“I do not relate to all these trendy terms – I just can’t hear it, it dusts out of my ears,” said the Bavaria-born US-based director, speaking in the idiosyncratic, heavily accented English familiar to viewers of documentaries like My Favourite Fiend. “Neurodivergence sounds like there’s some sort of clinical aberration – these sisters are dead centre.”His first non-documentary feature in 17 years, Bucking Fastard revisits old Herzogian themes but also breaks with them. The film is loosely based on the lives of Freda and Greta Chaplin, an intensely mutually attached pair of twins from York whom the German director met in the 1980s and who coined the spoonerism of the title in a court hearing.Like the Chaplins, the Holbrookes are ostracised by their family and neighbours, but in the film they also show resilience and find allies and supporters. “What is certainly different [to my earlier films] is that the sisters are not just nice, they’re vengeful”, said Herzog. “They are arsonists, they destroy things.”View image in fullscreenHerzog (second left) directs Rooney and Kate Mara.Photograph: Stills - Courtesy of Gateway to Orkney LLCThe Werner Herzog ofsocial-media parodiesis bleakly preoccupied with the cruel chaos inherent in the natural world, telling stories ofsuicidal penguins, man-eating bears, and birds“who don’t sing but screech in pain”. Yet in Bucking Fastard, the sisters rescue a young fox who, contrary to the warnings of a gang of overzealous hunters, doesn’t infect them with rabies.“We had in mind to have a baby fox they would warm under their armpits, but we could not find one all over Ireland,” Herzog recalled. “There was an animal dealer who told me, ‘I can get you a little fox, but only under one condition: you must never ask how we got it.’” Herzog declined. “I’m not in this business. You want to dig up a den and bring me a little fox – I’m not into that.”At 83, could the radical doomsayer of European art-house cinema be discovering his sentimental side? “What I do is lively and creates some inner life, some excitement and some joy in the storytelling,” Herzog said. “I’m not a control freak.”His taste for pathos, however, remains irrepressible. Bucking Fastard features a sequence shot inside a large karst cave system near Postojna, Slovenia, which Herzog described in similarly reverential tones as the French subterranean landscape in 2010’sCave of Forgotten Dreams: “It is a landscape of the soul, a landscape of the imagination.”His old-fashioned way of looking at the world keeps winning him young admirers, he claimed. “A huge amount of audiences that contact me these days are 15, 16, maybe 17 years old,” he said.View image in fullscreenHerzog greets Rooney and Kate Mara on the red carpet at Venice.Photograph: Yara Nardi/ReutersLast year, he started his own Instagram account, where he has posted reels of himself barbecuing, doing DIY and unboxing packages. He said he did it at the behest of his youngest son, who told his father he shouldn’t be so isolated from his audience. Since he still doesn’t own a own mobile phone, however, he hasn’t been able to check out the content-creating competition.“I had a big retrospective at the Centre Pompidou in Paris in 2024, and the audience was all, all, all young people. The curators told me there was a Godard retrospective right before mine, and the people who came to that? They were all Godard’s age. They were all over 80.”Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalWerner HerzogFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content
