title: ‘It struck me as a minimalist tableau’: Henk Stam’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: The Dutch photographer was pleased to capture this suitably orange scene in some toilets in Rotterdam
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: The Dutch photographer was pleased to capture this suitably orange scene in some toilets in Rotterdam
Content: Portlantis Orange, 2025, shot on iPhone 14 Pro Max.Photograph: HJ StamView image in fullscreenPortlantis Orange, 2025, shot on iPhone 14 Pro Max.Photograph: HJ StamSmart shotPhotography‘It struck me as a minimalist tableau’: Henk Stam’s best phone pictureThe Dutch photographer was pleased to capture this suitably orange scene in some toilets in RotterdamGrace HollidaySat 5 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Imust admit I was very sceptical of phone photography at first,” Henk Stam says. Sixty years ago, he received his first camera for his 11th birthday. The advent of a newer technology initially stumped him. “My first portable phone, that we used to call ‘a brick’, had a terrible camera that took fuzzy pictures. But like everyone, I noticed the steady improvements,” he says.‘The photo we want to take is closer than we think’: Dominic Dähncke’s best phone pictureRead moreThis photo was taken in Portlantis, a visitors’ centre in the Port of Rotterdam that opened in spring 2025. Stam spent his working life in Canada but was born in the Netherlands and returned there on retirement. With a friend from his photo club, he went to visit Portlantis on a Monday, but found it closed. “As we were leaving, we noticed a large tour bus arriving filled with teenagers,” he says. “We simply joined the slipstream as they entered; no one batted an eyelid.”There was still construction work being done inside, and as Stam nipped to the toilet, he spotted this worker’s legs sticking out of a cubicle, toolbox at his side. “It struck me as a minimalist tableau. Here, the royal family are referred to as the House of Orange, national teams and fans wear orange, and we festoon our streets with orange flags during major events. But I found it odd one would colour the toilets orange.”Stam had left his camera with his friend, so grabbed this shot on his phone instead. He returned to Portlantis a few months later. “This time entering legitimately,” he says. “But nothing I captured then matched the uniqueness of this moment.”Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Robert Pattinson says he had ‘twice as much time’ after birth of first child | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Actor says of busy 2026 in which he has had several big roles: ‘Once you start spinning plates, it gets quite addictive’
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Actor says of busy 2026 in which he has had several big roles: ‘Once you start spinning plates, it gets quite addictive’
Content: ‘I just had a baby,’ Pattinson told a press conference at the Venice film festival, ‘so I had no desire to go out at night and suddenly had twice as much time.’Photograph: Fabio Frustaci/EPAView image in fullscreen‘I just had a baby,’ Pattinson told a press conference at the Venice film festival, ‘so I had no desire to go out at night and suddenly had twice as much time.’Photograph: Fabio Frustaci/EPAVenice film festivalRobert Pattinson says he had ‘twice as much time’ after birth of first childActor says of busy 2026 in which he has had several big roles: ‘Once you start spinning plates, it gets quite addictive’Philip Oltermannin VeniceSat 5 Sep 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobert Pattinson has talked about the “addictive” nature of working on several films simultaneously, having starred in several of this year’s most highly anticipated productions, despite recently becoming a father for the first time.“Once you get the momentum going, it’s strangely not that hard,” said Pattinson at theVenice film festival. “Once you start spinning plates, it gets quite addictive.”The London-born performer has drawn critical praise this year for his turn as Antinous, the primary antagonist in Christopher Nolan’sThe Odyssey, as well as playing a lead role in the dark romantic comedy The Drama and making his Dune debut in the third instalment of the franchise this December.View image in fullscreenPattinson in Primetime.Photograph: A24/APOn the Venice Lido, Pattinson was promoting Lance Oppenheim’s forthcoming arthouse thriller Primetime, which he joined as a producer before agreeing to star as the lead, and prepared while filming Lynne Ramsay’s Die My Love with Jennifer Lawrence.“I just had a baby,” the actor told a press conference on the Lido. “So I had no desire to go out at night, so suddenly I had twice as much time to do anything with, which was very helpful.”The 40-year-old actor had his first child with the English singer-songwriter and actor Suki Waterhouse in March 2024.‘He stole the show’: do Oscars beckon for Robert Pattinson, star of four of the year’s biggest films – and Batman?Read moreA “fever dream rather than a biopic”, Primetime sees Pattinson play Chris Hansen, the driven but ethically ambiguous host of To Catch a Predator, a mid-2000s US TV series that orchestrated elaborate sting operations to film adult men seeking to have sex with minors.“Obviously, I hope [Hansen] likes the movie,” Pattinson said, after Hansen saw the trailer and said he found the actor’s fictional portrayal “overly dramatic”.Pattinson said of Hansen: “There’s something electrifying about him. I would hope the amount of inspiration his character has given a lot of people for years is some kind of compliment.”Pattinson is due to reprise his role as the pointy-eared billionaire vigilante in The Batman II, which commenced filming in London in June and is due for release in early 2028.“I am definitely not doing simultaneous stuff during Batman,” the actor said. “It’s impossible.”Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalRobert PattinsonThe OdysseyThe DramaFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘Bizarrely, she suddenly realised she knew my daughter’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Don, 76, who works in TV and film, meets Claire, 63, a counselling charity manager
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Don, 76, who works in TV and film, meets Claire, 63, a counselling charity manager
Content:
Composite: Murdo MacLeodView image in fullscreenComposite: Murdo MacLeodBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘Bizarrely, she suddenly realised she knew my daughter’Don, 76, who works in TV and film, meets Claire, 63, a counselling charity managerSat 5 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenDon on ClaireWhat were you hoping for?To meet someone interesting. To be part of a cultural phenomenon called the Guardian Blind date. To have a pleasant lunch.Firstimpressions?Relaxed and friendly.What did you talk about?Family. Work. Alcohol. Catholicism. Buddhism … and other light topics!Most awkward moment?I didn’t feel any. Bizarrely though, Claire suddenly realised she knew one of my daughters, and her sister was a good friend of my mother a long time ago. Scotland is a small but beautiful nation.Good table manners?I have the worst table manners north of the border, so I couldn’t comment.Best thing about Claire?Very easy to have a conversation with. Freckly arms! A good human being.Would you introduce Claire to your friends?Yes, I have a disparate group of friends and most of them would like her company.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Claire in three wordsThoughtful, empathetic, compassionate.What do you think she made of you?Haven’t a clue. That’s for her to answer.Did you go on somewhere?We walked to the bus stop.And … did you kiss?In a European kind of way.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?That I had not had to drive to the railway station and so could have had a glass of cold white rioja.Marks out of 10?8.Would you meet again?Hopefully. Not sure we’ll run away to Gretna Green, but maybe see a film, or go for a walk or a meal.View image in fullscreenDon and Claire on their date.View image in fullscreenClaire on DonWhat were you hoping for?Good company and conversation.First impressions?Warm and friendly face.What did you talk about?His film script and past experiences as a producer and documentary-maker. My work as a counsellor. Meditation. Movies. Our kids and marriages. How bloody awful Trump is.Most awkward moment?Not really awkward for us, but the restaurant owner thought we were here for Dining across the divide, and when we said it was Blind date he was a bit thrown and very apologetic.Good table manners?No issue as far as I was concerned.Best thing about Don?Easy to talk with and asked interested questions.Would you introduce Don to your friends?Turns out he knows a fair few already.Describe Don in three wordsBon vivant, warm and interesting.What do you thinkhe made of you?That I am friendly, interesting and easy to talk with.Blind date: ‘I got the impression he liked me well enough, but who knows?’Read moreDid you go on somewhere?No, it was lunchtime so it was back to work for me.And … did you kiss?A continental farewell.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?An evening rather than lunch meet-up.Marks out of 10?8 – he was great company.Would you meet again?I need a spark and it wasn’t there for me. But numbers were exchanged –plenty more conversation to be had.Claire and Don ate atTapa,Edinburgh. Fancy a blind date? Emailblind.date@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsDatingBlind dateRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Deal or no deal? How to know if the retail price is right | Consumer rights | The Guardian
description: As the government prepares to crack down on ‘phoney bargains’ we ask experts about what exactly constitutes a genuine price reduction
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: As the government prepares to crack down on ‘phoney bargains’ we ask experts about what exactly constitutes a genuine price reduction
Content: Andy Burnham has promised to put an end to ‘phoney bargains’.Photograph: Laurence Berger/GettyView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has promised to put an end to ‘phoney bargains’.Photograph: Laurence Berger/GettyConsumer rightsDeal or no deal? How to know if the retail price is rightAs the government prepares to crack down on ‘phoney bargains’ we ask experts about what exactly constitutes a genuine price reductionDonna FergusonSat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen is a sale not a sale? Online and on the high street, some shops just always seem to be selling at a discount.Whether it’s the closing down sale that goes on for years, or the crossed-out original price that you can’t remember ever paying, some retailers try all kinds of ways to convince us we are getting a bargain.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, appears ready to act on this, and last month he pledged to put “an end to phoney bargains”, saying “people are sick and tired of rip-off discounts”.He said: “If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price.”This autumn a government consultation will look at whether fake claims that products were previously sold at higher prices, invented discounts and misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) should be added to thelist of practices bannedunder the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024.Ahead of that, we asked experts to explain what retailers can and cannot do when it comes to offering discounts. Be warned: it’s complicated, so ministers have a job on their hands.Deceptive pricingView image in fullscreenIf the CMA finds a retailer has misled customers it can impose a penalty and force it to issue refunds.Photograph: Jim Holden/AlamyThe good news is that the 2024 Act already prohibits “unfair commercial practices” by retailers, including misleading actions and omissions, so deceptive pricing tactics are already often illegal.Such practices are policed by regulators, including theCompetition and Markets Authority(CMA) and by Trading Standards.If the CMA finds a retailer has misled customers, it is able to issue a financial penalty of up to 10% of a company’s global turnover and force it to issue refunds, without going to court.But currently, to bring enforcement action about dodgy discounts, the CMA needs to meet certain legal thresholds – and that is not always easy.The regulator must go through an internal process to decide whether or not the retailer influenced the average consumer to take a decision other than the one they would otherwise have taken. That means demonstrating that a misleading price has affected a shopper’s choice about whether to buy something.This process can be time-consuming and costly, says Sue Davies, head of consumer rights policy at Which?, the consumer organisation. CMA investigations, for example, typically take three to six months, and can take even longer.So the government is keen to add egregious and false discount claims to the existing list of 32 practices that are banned under the act.That would ensure that deceptive pricing tactics would automatically be considered unfair in all circumstances – whether or not they had influenced anyone’s shopping choices.In theory, this would make it easier for the CMA and trading standards to protect consumers, and deter businesses from doing it in the first place.“It just makes it more straightforward for them to be able to pursue a case rather than having to go through more complicated legal arguments and provide a lot of evidence in order to make the case that something is misleading,” says Davies.‘Was £30, now £15’View image in fullscreenMost products offered in Black Friday deals are cheaper or the same price at other times of the year.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/AFP/GettyLate last year, research by Which? looked at 175 Black Friday offers from eight retailers and found that the vast majority of the products were cheaper than, or the same price as, at other times of the year.Davies says the consumer organisation has on numerous occasions “exposed businesses, including trusted household brands, ripping off customers with dodgy deals that aren’t what they seem”.In the past,government guidancestated that retailers should sell an item for at least 28 consecutive days at a higher price before they could use that figure as a reference price when discounting it. And it must have been offered at that price during the previous six months.Under the 2024 Act, “retailers are free to set their pricing, and it’s the intention behind that which really makes a difference”, says Hafsah Nawaz, a lawyer at A&O Shearman who specialises in competition law.She adds: “It’s not about telling retailers what prices to charge, but about ensuring that the way prices or discounts are presented doesn’t deceive shoppers.”As a result, some retailers will test the law and see what they can get away with, says Davies.“We’ve repeatedly found problems with misleading price practices across a whole range of different retailers, and it can be very difficult to get action taken against those [by regulators],” she adds. “And I think part of that is that there’s not enough clarity about what is illegal or not.”She thinks that putting specific pricing practices, such as the use of misleading RRPs, on a banned practices list “would send a much clearer message to businesses about what they have to do to comply”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut, she adds, “the wording is going to have to be thought out carefully… It’s not a simple thing to word it, because there will always be loopholes”.Good practiceView image in fullscreenExamples of bad practice include selling at the higher reference price for a shorter length of time than the discount price.Photograph: Tartezy/GettyTo help retailers better understand and stick to their obligations under consumer law, the Chartered Trading Standards Institute (CTSI) hasguidanceabout how to describe discounts. This guidance is not legally binding – but regulators, including the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) and the CMA, regularly refer to it when making decisions.According to the guidance, retailersmust not make “misleading or unfair” claimswhen comparing the new price of their products to a reference price, and the quoted saving must be “genuine”.The guidance does not set out any specific timings, but says it would be bad practice if a product was sold at the higher reference price for a shorter length of time (one month, say) than the discount price (two months, say). The guidance also says that the product should have been sold at the original price at the same store where it is being discounted.This prevents retailers selling their products at reference prices at, for example, only one outlet in the Outer Hebrides, says Geraint Lloyd-Taylor, a lawyer at Lewis Silkin who specialises in consumer regulation.“It’s not just about saying it’s on sale – it’s about basically making it available in the same way,” he says. “So if it’s on the retailer’s website as a discount, it should have been on their website at the higher price, too.”If a product has been getting steadily cheaper over several months, the shop should not quote an old, higher price as if it were the genuine, usual price. “You shouldn’t be talking about a price that was applied three prices ago,” says Lloyd-Taylor.Everything must go?View image in fullscreenThe government says it does not want to ban legitimate discounts or stop retailers from advertising previous prices.Photograph: Michael Cooper/GettyThe guidelines also state that a discount is unlikely to be a genuine discount if there is no evidence of “significant” sales having been made at the reference price.“If nobody really buys them, that’s an indication that the prices of those things are not genuine, so when they are discounted, the customer is not getting a good deal, says Lloyd-Taylor. “You’re just being fobbed off with a sort of ‘fake’ higher price.”Imagine a retailer sells a cushion for £20, then it raises the price to £30 a week before Black Friday, and then it puts the price back down to £20 in its Black Friday sales and claims it has been discounted by £10. In reality, few people will have paid £30 for that cushion throughout the year – but as long as a “significant” number paid that price in the preceding week, the discount may be deemed to be “genuine”.The situation becomes even more complicated if, during the week the product was on sale at the reference price of £30, it was part of another promotional offer, such as “3 for the price of 2”. In this situation, the £10 Black Friday discount may no longer be seen as “genuine”.Driving a hard bargainA government spokesperson told Guardian Money that existing rules to protect consumers from being misled or deceived “can be difficult to prove and uphold”.“That is why we are considering changing the law to crack down on these misleading pricing tactics … This is not about banning legitimate discounts or stopping retailers from advertising previous prices. It is about making it easier to tackle practices that mislead consumers.”A spokesperson for the CMA says it believes that “clear, accurate information about price discounts is vital for consumers and helps them shop around to make the best decision, particularly when household budgets are squeezed”.For its part, Which? says the government must implement these rules swiftly “to give consumers much-needed protection against sneaky pricing tactics, and hold businesses to account with tough enforcement, including fines, if they fall short”.Explore more on these topicsConsumer rightsAdvertisingRetail industryCompetition and Markets AuthorityConsumer affairsRegulatorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pungent and mealy’: the best (and worst) supermarket tuna, tasted and rated | Fish | The Guardian
description: From sustainable catch methods to the most pleasant texture and aroma, which tinned and jarred fish had our tester hooked and which left him reeling?
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: From sustainable catch methods to the most pleasant texture and aroma, which tinned and jarred fish had our tester hooked and which left him reeling?
Content: ‘Gruelling stuff’: the tuna was tested straight from the tin or jar, without seasoning, lemon, olive oil or mayonnaise.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.View image in fullscreen‘Gruelling stuff’: the tuna was tested straight from the tin or jar, without seasoning, lemon, olive oil or mayonnaise.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFishReview‘Pungent and mealy’: the best (and worst) supermarket tuna, tasted and ratedFrom sustainable catch methods to the most pleasant texture and aroma, which tinned and jarred fish had our tester hooked and which left him reeling?The best supermarket anchovies, tasted and ratedTom HuntSat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEaten straight from the tin, without seasoning, lemon, olive oil or mayonnaise, canned tuna is pretty gruelling stuff, not least because it’s pungent, mealy and hard to swallow. Testing tuna in this way demonstrates the overall poor quality of the product and why certain brands and species are revered for their superior texture and flavour. That said, a tuna mayo sandwich is one of my go-to lunches, so long as the fish is sustainably sourced (so as not to leave a bad taste in the mouth) and there’s enough pepper to balance out its flavour.Skipjack is a fast-growing species with a softer, flakier texture and fishier flavour than some others. Albacore tuna, meanwhile, is a larger, slower-growing fish, which makes it more sensitive to overfishing. Its flesh is much paler and more delicately flavoured, with large, meaty flakes.The Marine Conservation Society (MCS) is an independent registered environmental charity that uses scientific evidence to rate the sustainability of seafood. ItsGood Fish Guideuses a traffic-light system from green (best choice) to red (fish to avoid). Both skipjack and albacore have green-rated options available. However, fish sustainability is complicated and depends on the catch method, region and species.The Good Fish Guiderates pole and line as the best catch method, and recommends fish certified by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC). Hook and line is an umbrella term that includes less sustainable fishing methods such as longline fishing, which involves hundreds or thousands of baited hooks and is associated with much higher by-catch, including sharks, turtles and seabirds. However, hook and line combined with an MSC certification is a more sustainable choice because the catch method is specified.Purse seine fishingthat avoids using a fish aggregating device (FAD) to attract more fish, meanwhile, has a much lower by-catch than standard purse seine, which attracts and traps other marine life alongside the tuna. So look out for “pole and line” or “hooks and lines” on the label, in combination with an MSC certification; failing that, “FAD-free purse seine” means you’re making a slightly more sustainable choice.Seafood sustainability has been at the core of my campaign work for the past 15 years, and although there’s still alongway to go, it’s been a pleasure to see the industry take note of the public’s interest in it. This wasn’t the most enjoyable category to taste, but it was one of the most enjoyable to write.The best supermarket tuna in brine or waterBest overall:Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference albacore tuna steak in spring waterView image in fullscreen£2.55 for 160g at Sainsbury’s (£2.13/100g drained weight)★★★★☆A classic, pale albacore tuna. Well-formed large, flaky steaks. A sweet aroma and taste, with a mild and well-balanced flavour. Caught by pole and line in the north-east Atlantic or the Pacific Ocean, and MSC-certified.Best bargain:Co-op responsibly sourced tuna chunks in brineView image in fullscreen£2.70 for 3 x 145g at Co-op (88p/100g drained)★★★☆☆Skipjack steaks with a sweet aroma and taste and a firm texture, albeit with some more mushy pieces in the can. Caught by pole and line in the Pacific, which, as a more sustainable catch method, bumps this one up to this week’s best bargain.And the rest …Ocado tuna chunks in brineView image in fullscreen£4.20 for 4 x 145g at Ocado (£1.03/100g drained)★★★☆☆Skipjack with a saline, fishy aroma, quite a flaky texture, and noticeably sweet and pleasant flavour. Caught by FAD-free purse seine in the western central Pacific and MSC-certified.Waitrose No 1 albacore tuna in spring waterView image in fullscreen£4.25 for 220g at Waitrose (£2.83/100g drained)★★★☆☆Beautiful, hand-prepared, large pieces of jarred albacore steak with a pungent, slightly sulphurous aroma and a mealy texture. Sweet, fishy taste with a hint of bitterness. Caught by hook and line in the north-east and south-east Atlantic, and MSC-certified.Lidl Nixe tuna chunks in spring waterView image in fullscreen£2.49 for 4 x 145g at Lidl (61p/100g drained), in store only★★☆☆☆Large, flaky pieces of skipjack. Sweet at first, but with a slightly bitter aftertaste. Caught by purse seine in the eastern central Pacific or south-east Pacific. MSC-certified and very nearly my best bargain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. title: Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for kacang pool, or Malaysian bean stew  | Vegetables | The Guardian
description: A delicious and triumphant blend of Levantine and Malay cuisines
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: A delicious and triumphant blend of Levantine and Malay cuisines
Content: Meera Sodha’skacang pool, or Malaysian bean stew.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha’skacang pool, or Malaysian bean stew.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.Meera Sodha recipesVegetablesMeera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for kacang pool, or Malaysian bean stewA delicious and triumphant blend of Levantine and Malay cuisinesMeera SodhaSat 5 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 05.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is a dish with roots in ancient Egypt. There, it started life asful medames, the famous fava bean dish lightly seasoned with cumin, garlic and lemon. Then it was, reportedly, brought to Johor in Malaysia by Arab traders. It has since been adopted and adapted with a fierce sort of love, plus more spice and a tin of baked beans. I adore it. It’s a very delicious dinner and a triumphant blend of two cuisines.Kacang poolTraditionally, this dish is made with minced beef, but I’ve used soya mince. I ignore the packet instructions to rehydrate it before using, though.Prep10 minCook35 minServes430g unsalted butter3 tbsp rapeseed oil, plus extra for frying the eggs2 red onions, peeled and very finely chopped¾ tsp fine sea salt3 garlic cloves, peeled and minced1½cm x 1½cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely chopped1 tsp ground cumin1 tsp mild curry powder¾ tsp ground coriander¾ tsp ground fennel60g driedsoya mince– I likeClearspring1415g tin baked beans1400g tinborlotti beansin water, not drainedTo serve4 eggsButtered dinner rolls, or Greek-style flatbreads or baguette2 green finger chillies, finely sliced1 lime, quarteredPut the butter and oil in a wide frying pan or a medium-sized casserole pot for which you have a lid on a medium heat. When it’s hot, add three-quarters of the chopped onions and three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt, and cook, stirring, for 10 minutes, until soft, glossy and easily squashed with a wooden spoon. Add the garlic and ginger, cook for a further three or four minutes, until the garlic no longer smells raw, then add all the spices and the soya mince, stir to mix and cook for about three minutes more.Add both tins of beans, including the borlotti bean water, then half-fill one of the empty tins with water, and add half of that to the pan (so, a quarter of a tin’s worth). Stir, pop on the lid and leave to cook for about five minutes. Mash with a potato masher to a consistency you like – I like mine quite chunky – add more water, if need be, to loosen, then pop on the lid again and cook for another five minutes. Taste, add salt, if need be, then take off the heat and leave covered.Heat a tablespoon of oil in a wide, nonstick pan and, when it’s hot, crack in as many eggs as you can fit comfortably into the pan. Fry until the whites are set and the yolks are runny. Meanwhile, warm the bread.To serve, spoon a quarter of the bean mix into four lipped plates or wide bowls, top each serving with a fried egg, then sprinkle over a little green chilli and as much of the leftover chopped red onion as you like. Put a lime quarter on each plate, then dig in, serving the bread on the side for mopping.Explore more on these topicsVegetablesMeera Sodha recipesFoodMalaysian food and drinkBeans, pulses and legumesVegetarian food and drinkEggsHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: A £500 gift or a free toothbrush: is it worth switching bank accounts? | Banks and building societies | The Guardian
description: As the battle for current account customers takes a new twist we look at how tempting the offers really are
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: As the battle for current account customers takes a new twist we look at how tempting the offers really are
Content: Some of the bank switching deals come with a lot of strings attached.Photograph: Chris Rout/AlamyView image in fullscreenSome of the bank switching deals come with a lot of strings attached.Photograph: Chris Rout/AlamyBanks and building societiesA £500 gift or a free toothbrush: is it worth switching bank accounts?As the battle for current account customers takes a new twist we look at how tempting the offers really areRupert JonesSat 5 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFancy up to £500 of “free” cash – or how about a complimentary eco-friendly electric toothbrush? Many of Britain’s banks are offering sizeable “welcome bonuses” and other freebies in an attempt to convince people to switch to their current accounts.This week the battle was turned up a notch. Santander is offering £240, while NatWest is hoping to tempt high-earners to defect by dangling the carrot of £500.Several other banks are also offering cash bonuses, though digital bank Starling has taken a different tack. Eligible customers who open one of its personal current accounts before 11 October will be emailed a voucher code and instructions for how to claim a Suri Pro 2.0 electric toothbrush and UV clean-and-charge case “worth £105”. This “sustainable” toothbrush was awarded four out of five stars by the Guardian.View image in fullscreenThe Suri 2.0 toothbrush.Photograph: Courtesy of SuriAlternatively, the “free money” offered by many banks could provide a welcome boost during the cost of living crisis. But some of these deals come with quite a lot of strings attached.Take Santander’s new offer. You can now get £240 when you switch to its Everyday current account, which has no monthly fee. However, to be eligible, customers need to pay at least £1,500 into the account and set up at least two household direct debits, plus open and pay at least £200 into a Santander Regular Saver (which now pays a headline 8% interest), among other requirements.Meanwhile, HSBC is offering £220 when you switch. You must open the new account using its mobile banking app, set up at least two direct debits, pay in at least £2,000 and spend at least £500 on your HSBC debit card.HSBC’s First Direct brand is running its own offer, where you get £175 for switching to it. You have to set up at least two direct debits or standing orders, deposit £1,000-plus, make five or more debit card payments, and log on to digital banking.Nationwide is also offering £175, with not dissimilar requirements relating to funding and using the new account.The Co-operative Bank has a £200 offer, but it ends on Monday 7 September, so you will need to move fast. New customers switching to its standard current account, or Everyday Extra account (the latter carries a £12 monthly fee) can get £125 upfront, plus £25 a month for three months when they actively use the account.Again, there are requirements relating to how much you must pay in and how you use the account.View image in fullscreenA NatWest branch in Warrington, Cheshire. The bank is rewarding high earners.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAs of this week, NatWest is rewarding people who switch to its Premier Select or Premier Reward account (the latter has a £2 monthly fee) with a £500 “welcome bonus”. To be eligible, you must meet one of three criteria: at least £100,000 income (or £120,000 joint income) needs to be paid into your new account, or you have to hold at least £100,000 savings or investments with the bank, or have a mortgage of at least £500,000 with it. (There are other requirements, too.)The NatWest offer is very similar to one that HSBC has been running that also offers high earners a £500 welcome bonus if they switch to its Premier account.With these offers, to get the free cash or freebie, you usually have to fully switch an existing current account from another provider using the industry’scurrent account switch service(Cass).Rachel Springall, at the websiteMoneyfactscompare.co.uk, says Cass is quick and easy: “The service moves over any balance, and redirects standing orders and direct debits to the new account.”She says current account switching offers come and go throughout the year and can be pulled with not much notice, but adds that customers must not feel rushed. “There is no real ‘one-size-fits-all’ current account, as many are tailored for different needs.”If you sign up for a packaged current account – typically they offer various perks and add-ons in return for a monthly fee – you need to keep a close eye on it to make sure it is still good value; otherwise you can end up wasting your cash on the fee, says Springall.Explore more on these topicsBanks and building societiesConsumer affairsConsumer rightsBankingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kardashian curves: M&S launches £28 bodysuit with exaggerated hip padding | Fashion | The Guardian
description: The ‘hip boost’ aims to create hourglass silhouette, much like Kim Kardashian’s shapewear brand’s padded shorts
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: The ‘hip boost’ aims to create hourglass silhouette, much like Kim Kardashian’s shapewear brand’s padded shorts
Content: Body By M&S Body Sculpt Hip Boost All In One, Black, £28Photograph: M&SView image in fullscreenBody By M&S Body Sculpt Hip Boost All In One, Black, £28Photograph: M&SFashionKardashian curves: M&S launches £28 bodysuit with exaggerated hip paddingThe ‘hip boost’ aims to create hourglass silhouette, much like Kim Kardashian’s shapewear brand’s padded shortsChloe Mac DonnellSat 5 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor decades shapewear has been used to compress and cinch. But now there is a sub-genre emerging. Rather than shrinking a silhouette, it aims to add inches.This week M&S launched a bodysuit that features exaggerated padding at the hip allowing the wearer to create an hourglass shape, or at least the illusion of one.Similar to how bra inserts, AKA chicken fillets, are used to add extra volume to breasts,the £28 “hip boost”features pockets on each side of the suit that allow the wearer to add in enhancing pads.Charlotte Davies, the director of lingerie at the retailer, says the idea stemmed from customer interest in “solutions that offer subtle enhancement alongside everyday comfort and confidence”, with the trend being driven by the catwalks and celebrities. The hip booster’s predecessors at M&S includepadded bum shorts“to give the wearer a curvy, contoured look” and stick-on nipples for “a realistic raised profile beneath clothing”.Kim Kardashian’s shapewear brand, Skims, launched shorts with hip padding last year. Many users online claim such type of strategic padding can help minimise “hip dips” – a phrase used to describe the natural inward curves between the hipbone and thigh bone.The emergence of enhancing shapewear comes at a time when both the body and the idea of what a body can look like are increasingly scrutinised. From thewidespread use of GLP-1 drugstoa rise in cosmetic surgery procedures, bodies have never been more malleable.On the recent catwalks, designers have been playing with this idea of reconstruction too, coinciding witha return of ultra-thin models. At Schiaparelli, its creative director Daniel Roseberry used both visible and invisible padding to inflate hips and whittle waists. Meanwhile, Dior and Alaïa turned to panniers, rigid side hoop undergarments originally worn by women in the 17th and 18th century, to inspire modern-day dresses with hips similarly wide enough to force the wearer to turn sideways when passing through a door.“Weight-loss medications have changed many bodies dramatically, but they don’t automatically deliver conventional, ideal beauty, which in the current era is quite hard to achieve,” says Victoria Pitts-Taylor, a professor at Wesleyan University and the author of Surgery Junkies: Wellness and Pathology in Cosmetic Culture. “To be very thin in some areas of the body and thick in others often requires building and sculpting, which can happen in a dressing room with fabric or an operating room with scalpels.”This trompe d’oeil effect is also dominating the red carpet. Four years after Kim Kardashian wore a sauna suit to lose enough weight to squeeze into Marilyn Monroe’s dress, she and her hypercurves are back. At thebody-themed Met Gala in May, she emphasised her shape with a fibreglass breast plate. Meanwhile, her sisters Kylie and Kendall Jenner opted for moulded corsets with fake nipples and amplified hips. Tulip-like silhouettes have also been embraced by the singersRosalíaandTeyana Taylorand more are expected at theVenice film festivalthat has just got under way.Ali Bodley, a heritage specialist who curated the Shaping The Body exhibition at York Castle Museum, says everyone from the Tudors includingQueen Elizabeth Ito the Georgians and the Victorians played with their proportions. Long before Kardashian’s Skims empire, there were “bum shops” –stores specialising in padding.Susie Orbach describes the trend as “grotesque”. The psychotherapist, psychoanalyst and social critic says it puts women in a “position where they are constantly having to create a body”.Pitts-Taylor says the lives of celebrities in the 20th century were generally understood to be aspirational rather than attainable. However, “today consumer culture and social media put pressure on people in everyday walks of life to be image-minded”, she says. “The beauty ideal seems to promise belonging, being valued and successful, in a world in which actual, material equality is increasingly hard to achieve.”Orbach says there is no such thing as “an ideal body shape” explaining the parameters are always shifting. “There is always some type of body shape being promoted. But as soon as you get there, it is wrong.” Rather than “living and being allowed to have safety in our bodies”, she adds, “we are now always in a process of transformation.”Explore more on these topicsFashionMarks & SpencerKim KardashianRetail industryBody imagenewsShareReuse this content

title: What does Met’s U-turn on John Galliano augur for him, the gala and Anna Wintour? | John Galliano | The Guardian
description: NYC’s elite figures, led by Julie Menin, made Wintour blink, and the designer who in 2011 had gone on a drunken antisemitic rant, bowed out of industry’s biggest event
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: NYC’s elite figures, led by Julie Menin, made Wintour blink, and the designer who in 2011 had gone on a drunken antisemitic rant, bowed out of industry’s biggest event
Content: John Galliano and Anna Wintour attend a cocktail reception in London in 2021.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Galliano and Anna Wintour attend a cocktail reception in London in 2021.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty ImagesJohn GallianoWhat does Met’s U-turn on John Galliano augur for him, the gala and Anna Wintour?NYC’s elite figures, led by Julie Menin, made Wintour blink, and the designer who in 2011 had gone on a drunken antisemitic rant, bowed out of industry’s biggest eventEdward Helmorein New YorkSat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 08.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDidAnna Wintour, Vogue’s long-serving fashion titan and ringmaster of the annual Met Gala, meet her match in Julie Menin, the speaker of New York’s city council?The museum is the crown jewel of the wealthy neighborhood and some residents hold significant sway at the institution, financially and in terms of the art they plan to bequeath to it. So when it was announced late in July on a Friday afternoon that Galliano would be the focus of theMet Galanext year, it left many stunned.The designer, whose astonishing creativity as designer at Givenchy and later Dior in the 90s is not in question, had been videotaped in a Paris bar in 2011 abusing tourists in a drunken, antisemitic rant. “I love Hitler,”he slurred, and indicated their forebears should have been gassed.Galliano was dispatched to rehab, sought corrective instruction from Jewish leaders and picked up a conviction for making hateful remarks about Jews and Asians. He got sober, apologized and made amends. He visited Auschwitz and gingerly resumed his career, though not at the top of a Parisian design house.Wintour stood by him, using her power through job placements and a documentary, produced by Vogue parent Condé Nast, that placed equal attention on his creative life as on the scandal and its aftermath. Many of fashion’s powerful business executives were drafted in to attest to the designer’s restoration of spirit.Water under the bridge then? Not so fast. The extraordinary mess that has unfolded around the Met and New York’s social elite over the last 10 day – in which history, racism, global politics, clothes design and institutional and personal power intertwine – is going to take time to unpick.Wintour, according to friends, is sad that people show little forgiveness and acknowledges that she made a crucial misstep by announcing her gala 2027 pick without passing the idea through the Met’s 100-member board. But it was left to Galliano to decline Wintour’s invitation for a career-retrospective.“I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past,” he said, adding: “I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture.”Wintour, the longtime editor of Vogue and now chief content officer of corporate parent Condé Nast as well as a Met trustee, said in a notably brief statement that Galliano’s decision to step away from the celebration was “courageous” and “the right decision”.Opposing forces, their thinking crystalized ina letter of protestpublished by Menin, were by then in full revolt. Arne Glimcher, head of Pace Gallery, had informed the Met he was reconsidering gifting the museum 50 pieces of art. ⁠“I don’t think you have considered the cost of this action and its reverberations to come,” Glimcher wrote in an email to David Breslin, the Met curator in charge of the modern and contemporary art department.View image in fullscreenJulie Menin speaks during the Jewish Board’s spring benefit at Gotham Hall in June 2026 in New York City.Photograph: Sean Zanni/Patrick McMullan/Getty ImagesAlice Tisch, head of a powerful New York real estate family, sent a letter to Max Hollein, the Met director, calling the exhibit a “whitewash” of a “known” antisemite. Her letter, according to the Times, said the Galliano show “bespeaks a failure of governance as it seems you are unduly influenced and directed by a corporate donor and commercial enterprise, and mining it all for financial gain”.Menin, as the first Jewish speaker of the city council and a moderate Democrat who has emerged as a tempering counter to Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s progressivism, wrote to Wintour, Hollein and Andrew Bolton, curator of the Costume Institute, said that cultural institutions, and particularly those like the Met that receive funding from the city, “have a responsibility to demonstrate that hatred and bigotry carry consequences”.But none of this occurs in a vacuum. Upper East Side synagogues have been picketed by anti-Israel protesters, despite laws making it a crime to block entry to a house of worship. Last month, 63-year-old Larry Montes was hit with federal hate crime charges for violently disturbing a service at Central Synagogue, on Lexington Avenue near East 55th Street, 20 blocks from the Met.“This is not just about the antisemitism or protests outside synagogues, honoring Galliano while Jews are being attacked is just bad judgment. The Met was not obligated to become a participant in his rehabilitation campaign by throwing a celebrity gala in his honor,” says Gerard Filitti, senior council at The Lawfare Project.“The issue is not about separating the art from the artist,” Filitti said, and doubted that the exhibition’s planned “orientation gallery” would correct the issue. “The gala chose to make Galliano the centerpiece. So it was not conferring art and culture, it was conferring privilege,” he said.There are misgivings about the Met Gala, too. The business it brings to hotels is welcome but it ties up the neighborhood with street closures and limousines and, in recent years, attracts protests. The exhibition itself is rarely reviewed except as a costume party – fashion industry’s biggest night – and it’s a major promotions night for Wintour’s hand-picked guest list.Upper East Side society figures, who have largely been supplanted by celebrities at the gala itself, privately say they grew fed up with Wintour phoning to ask what they planned to wear.Fashion is often accused of existing in vacuum, but it’s also a popular one, even if fans can no longer afford the designs and the industry has been in recession for several years. The Devil Wears Prada 2, released this summer and with a main character inspired by Wintour (played by Meryl Streep), made $692m globally. The Costume Institute raised $42m at its most recent, and also controversial, Jeff and Lauren Bezos sponsored gala.But that sum, which is used to buy clothes for the collection, is a slender figure compared with the $125m donation made in 2021 by financier Oscar Tang and his wife, Agnes Hsu-Tang.The late cosmetics heir Leonard Lauder pledged in 2013 to give 78 cubist works to the museum, valued conservatively at $1bn, and plans have been announced to merge the Lauder’s Neue Galerie of 20th-century Austrian and German art with the Met in 2028. It’s unlikely that the ultra-rich of fashion, including LVMH’s Bernard Arnault, will donate to the Met – they have their own museums.Galliano is later this month set to release a collaboration with Zara, the Spanish clothing chain with revenues of nearly $30.1bn. If there are lines around the block, as expected, they will serve as proof that the furore around his now-cancelled retrospective means little to many ordinary fashion fans.An outpouring of personal support from prominent “creatives”, models, stylists, fellow designers and photographerson his Instagram pagesuggest the Met drama falls flat with some of them, too. The New York Times,which has led reporting deeply on the growing backlash,asked in two separate editorials last week if the Met was cancelling the fashionista and if it is Wintour, not Galliano, who should be shown the door, perhaps along with the party itself.“The exhibition should not have been canceled,” wroteRobin Givhan in the Times.“Instead, the Met Gala should have been canceled.” Bret Stephens, also in the Times, offered that it is, in principle, “best to separate judgments about an artist from judgments about the art”.Stephens noted the date of the gala coincided with Yom HaShoah or Holocaust Remembrance Day.“Whoops,” he wrote.“High fashion and good judgment rarely coincide.” It was not the museum’s job to act as a “contextualizer” and floated that “perhaps there’s another fashionista the Met could have canceled”.Others said the debaclewas “only possible because of Anna’s power”. A Vogue former colleague described their sense of schadenfreude: “Given that she’s spent the last 20 years purging everyone who was too old and too well paid it would be poetic if she got fired.”A standoff now exists between Wintour, 76, and Menin, 58. Officially, the exhibition “will not proceed as planned”. But Wintour, 76, via Vogue, said it has been “postponed”. Menin’s office points to a line in her statement that leaves the door ajar: “There are indeed more appropriate ways in which The Met could instead feature his work, including through a contextual exhibit or educational program.”But that leaves no room for a Galliano-themed gala and no room to prove the one axiomatic rule of fashion: that there’s no problem that can’t be solved with an outfit change. Two years after Galliano was arrested in Paris, he was photographed in New York in what appeared to some to be an Hasidic costume – a rounded large hat, short trousers and curled long sideburns.His publicistoffered a list of the clothes he selected that day– a Stephen Jones hat, Yohji Yamamoto trousers, Brooks Brothers shirt, Dolce & Gabbana vest. “In other words – fashionable,” she said. “The last thing on John’s mind would be to do anything that would offend the Jewish community.”Explore more on these topicsJohn GallianoMet GalaAnna WintourNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factories | Poland holidays | The Guardian
description: The imposing red-brick mills of its industrial past are a stunning example of urban regeneration in the former ‘city of a thousand chimneys’
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: The imposing red-brick mills of its industrial past are a stunning example of urban regeneration in the former ‘city of a thousand chimneys’
Content: The beautifully restored Manufaktura area has become a leisure and tourism hub.View image in fullscreenThe beautifully restored Manufaktura area has become a leisure and tourism hub.Poland holidaysA city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factoriesThe imposing red-brick mills of its industrial past are a stunning example of urban regeneration in the former ‘city of a thousand chimneys’Kevin RushbySat 5 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSometimes travel delivers a real shock. I’m moving along the boulevards in the Polish city of Łódź, enjoying the excellent cafes and warm sunshine, when I spot the vans. They are parked up on the verge, with racks of clothing and heavily laden tables behind. I can’t resist a Sunday morning market and walk towards a group of men huddled around a car that is covered in blankets. And then it happens. They turn – and I see they are weighing pistols in their hands. I recognise the lean profile of a German Luger, and then the bulkier Colt 45.There is a second of doubt. I hesitate. They replace the weapons on the display and walk away laughing. I approach. On the car roof is a row of dusty soldiers’ helmets. “We were repairing a pavement in the centre of town,” says the seller cheerfully, handing me a badge to inspect. “Imagine! For 80 years, all this stuff was just under our feet.”It’s a Wehrmacht shoulder badge from Kuban 1943, a last-ditch post-Stalingrad action on the Crimean peninsula. Who wore this, I wonder? A veteran of the Russian front who almost made it home? Nothing is clear, except that in Łódź, the past is never far away.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsI arrive the previous night, a little disoriented, whizzing past unlit buildings, huge brick structures like Victorian factories. “Are we in the city yet?” I ask.The taxi driver gives me a quizzical look. “Yes, this is Łódź.” I note the pronunciation, like “wudge”. I glimpse five-storey blocks, tree-lined streets, a tramline. “I could never live anywhere else,” he adds. A huge blue graffito is caught in the headlights, like a monstrous alien creature.“Why?” I ask, but we are already pulling up outside an immense red-brick building, my hotel, and he never answers my question. The reception area is huge, with a strange scalloped ceiling in red brick that hints at a previous incarnation as a factory.View image in fullscreenPaweł Pawlikowski’s Oscar for the film Ida on display at the Museum of Cinematography.This is my first visit to Łódź, a city about 75 miles (120km) south-west of Warsaw. My interest has been piqued by a list of notable people associated with the place. It features an astonishing number of Oscar-winning or nominated film directors connected to the city: Andrzej Wajda (The Promised Land), Roman Polanski (The Pianist), Paweł Pawlikowski (Ida), Agnieszka Holland (Europa Europa), Krzysztof Kieślowski (Three Colours trilogy) and Zbigniew Rybczyński (Tango).But under the bonnet there is a vast array of talent in acting, production and technical excellence. The city’s film school is responsible, of course, but Łódź itself features as a setting, too, notably in David Lynch’s Inland Empire and Wajda’s masterpiece The Promised Land.Łódź, I had decided, must be fascinating. Any visit starts with Piotrkowska Street, the longest shopping street in Europe at about 2½ miles. My guide, Anna, takes me through Plac Wolności (Freedom Square), where a dance festival is in progress, with hooded hip‑hoppers rubbing shoulders with troupes of line dancers and girls in colourfully embroidered traditional dress. This is a city where music and dance are never far away. We dodge down a side alley and emerge in a striking art installation – an entire street,Pasaż Róży(Rosa’s Passage), covered in mirrors by the artist Joanna Rajkowska. Back on the main pedestrianised route, the mix of ancient and modern continues: 19th‑century porticoed palaces adorned with colourful graffiti.I ask Anna how Łódź fared in the second world war. “It was not too badly damaged,” she says. “Both the Germans and the Russians wanted the industry intact.”There is no medieval heart, no ornate houses like in Wrocław or Kraków. What Łódź possesses is an impressive array of 19th-century factories, mostly textiles, built to show off their owners’ power, wealth and architectural aspirations. Now, this heritage has become a stunning example of urban regeneration.View image in fullscreenOFF Piotrkowska, where the old mills host a hive of small businesses.Photograph: Paweł AugustyniakWe turn intoOFF Piotrkowska, a complex of beautiful old textile mills reborn as a hive of small businesses. There are lots of vibrant restaurants and bars, but Anna wants to show me a shop that she likes:Pan Tu Nie Stał. “It was a saying in communist times: ‘You’re not in the queue.’ We said it to people trying to push in,” Anna says.This is the spot to pick up a T-shirt featuring Soviet combine harvesters or some Czas Pokaże (Time Will Tell) socks. The shop says a lot about the Polish attitude to communist times: none of the maudlinostalgieof East Germany; this nostalgia comes with healthy dashes of colour and humour.It did all start, however, with a disaster. The old mills had survived two world wars, but died in the economic collapse after communism ended in 1989. “Everything closed down,” says Anna. “We call that time thetransformacja. It was very hard.”We stroll into theManufakturaarea, once the site of a vast textile business started by a local scrap metal dealer, Izrael Poznański, in 1872, and now another beautifully restored collection of red-brick buildings housing restaurants, bars, shops and the fascinatingMuseum of the Factory. Next door is the palace that Poznański built, a neo-baroque monstrosity of bulging wealth, now thecity museum.double quotation markAndrzej Wajda needed to make only minor adjustments to start filming The Promised Land in the 1970s. The tired faces, the crashing looms – it was all very much like 1880After the Congress of Vienna in 1815, Łódź became part of the Russian empire, a melting pot of German, Jewish, Polish and Russian influences. In the 1870s, Poznański was one of a group of men who saw the potential of steam power. They imported looms from England and were soon amassing unimaginable wealth, constructing a city of handsome red-brick factories, the core of which still remains.The Museum of the Factory houses a collection of working looms that date back to the 1880s. Only four machines are ever turned on due to noise pollution laws – in the old days, one factory might have had hundreds. This was the city of the deaf, but the deafest of all were the bosses, oblivious to the terrible hardships of their workforce, from the founders through to their communist successors. When Wajda came to these mills in the early 1970s, planning The Promised Land, he needed to make only minor adjustments to start filming. The tired faces, the crashing looms, the heat and the dust – it was all very much like 1880.Is that your favourite film, I ask Anna? She shakes her head. “Cold Warby Pawlikowski,” she says. “I love that film.”View image in fullscreenThe Museum of the Factory has a collection of working looms dating to the 1880s.Photograph: PicasaThis 2018 masterpiece is the story of a tragic love affair conducted across the Iron Curtain in the years following the second world war. Based on the lives of Pawlikowski’s parents, it is dark and sensuous, full of great music and dance. Pawlikowski has used Łodż as a location.We move on to theMuseum of Cinematography, a tour de force that warrants some preparation (watch films by Polish directors). They have everything from early working equipment to props from the most recent Oscar triumphs. By the time I get to the end, I have only a few minutes to rush to theCentral Museum of Textiles.There I find a technician, Przemysław, about to start up a 1893 Greenwood loom. He’s a former policeman with a few tales to tell, but right now one question is bothering me. “Why did film-making succeed so brilliantly in this city of textiles?” I ask him.He taps the cast iron loom and chuckles. “I’ll show you.”With the flick of a switch, the loom begins to clank and turn. The noise is incredible. Przemysław is moving around, adjusting and calibrating, his face concentrated. I see the spools of thread begin to unwind, the shuttle dashing back and forth, the warp and weft rhythmically rising and falling. The different colours, each no more than a thin line, but magically coming together. And from the lip of the machine spills a beautiful multicoloured cloth.Przemysław looks at me and raises a questioning eyebrow. “Like weaving a story, right?”The trip was provided by thePolishTourism Organisation, withHoliday Extraslending travel support in car parking, insurance, airport transfers and hotelsExplore more on these topicsPoland holidaysCity breaksEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The unsettling rise of cat seducers: ‘My little companion was missing – and I was consumed with anger’ | Pets | The Guardian
description: Has your cat been gaining weight and staying out at night, only to arrive home reeking of marijuana? These are just some of the signs that a neighbour is trying to entice them away ...
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: Has your cat been gaining weight and staying out at night, only to arrive home reeking of marijuana? These are just some of the signs that a neighbour is trying to entice them away ...
Content: Held under false pretences … ‘cats have no concept of human boundaries’.Photograph: Cavan Images/Getty Images/Cavan Images RFView image in fullscreenHeld under false pretences … ‘cats have no concept of human boundaries’.Photograph: Cavan Images/Getty Images/Cavan Images RFPetsThe unsettling rise of cat seducers: ‘My little companion was missing – and I was consumed with anger’Has your cat been gaining weight and staying out at night, only to arrive home reeking of marijuana? These are just some of the signs that a neighbour is trying to entice them away ...Elle HuntSat 5 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Amy’s cat, Sid*, first started spending more time away from home, Amy* put it down to wanderlust. A former street cat, Sid had landed on his feet in her leafy London suburb, but still retained his free-roaming sociability. When Sid began disappearing for up to days at a time though, Amy worried. She put a tracker on his collar to find out where he was going. She didn’t expect to discover him a few doors up the road.Sidisroaming – but most of the time, for entire afternoons and even sometimes overnight, he is with Amy’s neighbour. “He is in her house, constantly, all the time,” she says. This is not a coincidence. Sid might not be getting six dinners, like his famous namesake inInga Moore’s 1990 children’s book, but the neighbour is certainly spoiling him, as she recently let slip to Amy’s partner. “She’s feeding him organic chicken!” Amy says indignantly.Amy does not blame Sid for being disloyal. “Cats are cats – they have no concept of human boundaries.” But her neighbour, she says, is overstepping by rewarding Sid’s visits despite frequent – and increasingly firm – requests to stop. “She’s literally enticing him away.”double quotation markTwo years ago her cat Scooby started coming home reeking of marijuana, well-nourished ‘but quite deranged’Cats have long been a source of neighbourly tensions, often stemming from their unwelcome flowerbed deposits or penchant for birdlife. These days, however, conflicts are just as likely to break out over their care and ownership. According to the steady stream of posts to local networking app Nextdoor and neighbourhood Facebook groups, people across the UK are feeding cats that don’t belong to them, accommodating them in their homes and allegedly making active efforts to lure them away from loving owners.The line might seem obvious: if you don’t pay the vet bills, it’s not your pet. Since the introduction of the Pet Abduction Act in 2024, there could even be a legal case. But therise of “rogue feeders”and cat seducers might not be as cut-and-dried as it seems, driven by broader changes in our relationships with pets and other people – and complicated, of course, by cats’ utter ungovernability.Amy and her partner have tried many tactics to stop their neighbour from indulging Sid, from buying him a collar that instructs strangers not to feed him, to telling her a white lie that he is permanently on medication. But: “She just does not listen. It’s outrageous.”View image in fullscreenPremium cat food is a powerful incentive.Photograph: Boy_Anupong/Getty ImagesSid’s second home makes it harder to give him medication when he really does need it, and otherwise care for him, says Amy. More than that, she misses his company. “It really upsets me: he is our cat, and we never, ever see him.” When the neighbour went away on holiday, Sid returned home. “It was like having a pet again – it was so nice.” The neighbour, meanwhile, has said she can’t get a cat of her own because she goes away too much.This points to a broader shift in our relationship with pets. According toCats Protection’s 2025 report, growth in ownership has been among younger, more affluent people, many of whom keep their cats indoors or restrict their access, via enclosed “catios”, for instance. That shift, along with collars being supplanted by microchips (legally required for cats since 2024), may be leading people to mistake much-loved pets for strays. Meanwhile, the number of stray cats is widely reported to haverisen in recent years; this is attributed to more people abandoning their pets due to rising costs, or failing to neuter them, leading to unwanted kittens. The Cats Protection report found that about 13% of the total UK cat population had been taken in from the street or somehow “acquired”, rather than bought or adopted from a UK agency.But the same financial pressures are also making people think twice before getting pets of their own. Cats Protection found more than 1.5m households wanted a cat but did not have one, with expense and unsuitable housing the key barriers. With cat ownershipestimated to costabout £1,000 a year, increasingly it seems people are opting to borrow someone else’s.When Alison Ward first moved to her central Norwich townhouse 18 years ago, she assumed the biggest threat to her four cats would be the busy roads. Instead, it has been people intent on “adopting them”, Ward says. “It’s gone off the scale. There’s not a week that goes by now without discovering that someone’s feeding one of them, or showing unnatural interest.”Mostly people are well-intentioned, at best “overeager”, says Ward. Her quartet of former street cats all roam, but are clearly cared for. They are now also Facebook famous from Ward’s regular posts, reminding people not to feed them or responding to concerned inquiries from “do-gooders”, she says. “People see a cat outside and assume it must be a stray. I have to check the group every day and say: ‘No, they’re owned!’”Concerned residents routinely give her cats unsuitable food (including once, memorably, steak) and take them to the local vet. The last time, Ward had to rush to collect her cat Monty lest she be charged for leaving him there overnight. Monty was in rude health – apart from an upset stomach caused by the journey. “Apparently, he’d vomited a load of fresh salmon that they’d fed him in the boot of the car.”More troubling is the trend of people taking Ward’s pets into their homes. Last year Monty would often disappear for days, returning distressed but “really well-fed – and actually groomed”, she says. Two years ago her other cat, Scooby, started coming home reeking of marijuana, again well-nourished “but quite deranged”. Ward tracked him to a house occupied by men in their 20s: “They said they thought he wastheircat.” They’d bought Scooby a basket, bowls, food and given him a fluorescent orange collar. (Her cats frequently come home with their collars removed.)View image in fullscreenThe bed is always softer on the other side of the fence.Photograph: Marcel ter Bekke/Getty ImagesSuch incidents used to be rare, and typically involved stereotypical “cat hoarders”, says Ward. Post-pandemic, cat seducers cut across all demographic categories. An unexpected number are men. “A lot seem to be single. I think they’re lonely, so they just go and ‘adopt’ a cat.” Many, she suspects, are renters, whose leases don’t allow them to have cats of their own. “It’s very easy to dip in and out of someone else’s pet: you haven’t got the responsibility, or the vet bills.”Ward has no issue with people enjoying her cats’ company, she says, but some interactions are hard to justify as well-intentioned or naive. Last summer, Ward told off a middle-aged man for persistently feeding Monty Twiglets in the park by her house. “He just said: ‘He enjoys them, he’s outdoors, you can’t stop me!’ I said, ‘Well, let’s hope he has diarrhoea on you.’” Earlier last year, Ward looked out of her bedroom window one night and saw a woman with two children, trying to coax Scooby into their car. “She said: ‘We’re just being friendly!’”When Ward’s four cats pass on, she plans to keep future pets indoors, which likely means she won’t get another older rescue cat. “It’s a bit against my ethos, but I can’t keep going through this.” For now, she has bought more custom-printed collars and keeps posting to Facebook. “We can’t do anything about it – trying to shame people is difficult if they know no shame.”The rise of rogue feeders is partly a technology-driven issue. Community Facebook groups and low-cost trackers have granted greater oversight of pets’ business – and with it the illusion of control. But someone else feeding your cat is more than just a nuisance: the stakes can be as great as losing the pet entirely.After moving house, Emily* noticed one of her cats gaining weight and staying out all night. When she tracked him to a neighbour’s, she asked them to stop feeding him: “They just ignored us.” Later, the cat was fatally struck by a car outside the neighbour’s house. “I’m sure this was because he would go wandering down the road for extra food. It was devastating.”Even if the cat seems content with its second home, the conflict over its care can be distressing for the owner. For the past year, Pauline* has been struggling with her neighbour’s persistent transgressions with her cat, Luka*. It began with texted pictures and updates about Luka’s visits. Pauline was initially encouraging – “trying to be neighbourly”, she says. But, over months, the neighbour’s fondness for Luka began to look suspiciously like efforts to coax her away – such as buying her a bed. “I was told she was being fed fresh salmon, and paté. It got to the point where I wasn’t seeing her.”When Luka was absent for an unprecedented six weeks, Pauline became more upset. “I was going through sleepless nights, constantly thinking about it. I even mentioned it at work – it was really affecting me. My little companion was missing.” Adding to her distress was the “sense of injustice”, she adds. “I was consumed with anger.”She tried “the negotiation route”, explaining cat behaviour and the importance of consistency, and politely asking her neighbour to stop encouraging Luka, but the woman persisted. “She said: ‘I’m not going to stop her from coming in if she wants to.’” Their interactions, conducted mostly over text, became increasingly fraught. Eventually the neighbour questioned Pauline’s care of Luka and suggested the cat had “chosen” a new owner. “She actually said that she wanted to keep her,” Pauline says, still disbelieving. “I was sobbing on the sofa, thinking: ‘Oh God, how am I going to pull this back?’” It took her days to compose a reply. She says the neighbour responded by accusing Pauline of harassment, “because just twice, in nine months, I’d asked her if she had Luka there –if”.Luka is lying on Pauline’s chest as she speaks, clearly content. Pauline has had her since she was a kitten – long before the neighbour moved to the area. Luka is sociable, and periodically “adopts” new owners, but it has never been a lasting issue, Pauline says. “When I notice her not coming home, I post on Facebook: ‘Please don’t feed her’ – because, obviously, that’s behavioural reinforcement – and she does eventually then come back.”View image in fullscreenGPS trackers are one way to keep track of an errant pet.Photograph: Richard Newstead/Getty ImagesHaving failed to change her neighbour’s behaviour, Pauline tried to divert her cat. She took steps to improve Luka’s home environment and routine, installed humane deterrents along her route to the neighbour’s, and kept her inside for four weeks in the hopes of resetting her territory. She also put a tracker on Luka’s collar, and set a motion-activated camera next to the window by which she comes and goes. In a desperate moment, she even reported the dispute to the police online, though she had no response. “I just thought I need to perhaps start logging the issue.”Pauline considered exploring the new law against pet abduction (“Honestly, it felt like that at the time”) but she did not want to risk further inflaming the situation. She also wondered whether it would apply: Luka was getting into her neighbour’s house through open windows. “I didn’t want to cause a neighbourly dispute – but I also wanted my cat back.”The Pet Abduction Act came into force in England, Wales and Northern Ireland two years ago, replacing the 1968 Theft Act, which treated pets like any other stolen property. It carries a maximum penalty of up to five years’ imprisonment and/or a significant fine, in recognition of the emotional investment in pets as family members. (They are still treated like chattel in the context of divorce or separation.)The cat-related offenceis definedas someone taking “a cat so as to remove it from the lawful control of any person”. That could include “causing or inducing the cat” to go with them; but the person charged may also argue that they had “reasonable excuse”.Between August 2024 and April 2026, the Crown Prosecution Service recorded 10 charged offences pertaining to dogs – and just one involving cats. Daniel Warren-Cummings, a central behaviour officer at Cats Protection, says the charity was advised by a legal expert that it was “nigh-on impossible” to draw the line, “bar somebody coming on to your property and stealing your cat”. The “messy grey area” is complicated by feline nature, he adds. They have a core territory, where they will most often eat and sleep, and a larger “home range” beyond that. That can stretch acres, but in built-up urban environments is more often curtailed.Likewise, Warren-Cummings attributes the rise in rogue feeding to increasing population density and more pets: “I think it is going to become more of a contentious issue.” But owners aren’t necessarily blameless, he adds. Cats can be enticed away from home, but often something is also driving them to leave. “Is there a reason why that cat is being so easily seduced?”View image in fullscreenMoggies that are bored at home may be seduced by strangers’ love and affection.Photograph: Guillermo Spelucin/Getty ImagesCommon explanations include the introduction of another pet or a baby, home renovations or tensions with another local feline. That’s not to blame owners for their wandering pets, Warren-Cummings adds, but often, they aren’t aware of environmental stressors, meaning efforts to keep their cats at home only worsen the problem. As for outside attractions, cats can be driven to seek out attention and play as much as a gourmet meal, he says. They might be dismissed as low-maintenance relative to dogs, “but if they’re left alone for long periods of time, boredom and frustration build up.”Instead of finger-pointing, Warren-Cummings would like to see greater focus on the animal’s welfare, from owners and “feeders” alike. “Go into conversations knowing that everyone here wants what’s best for the cat, even if it happens to be your cat.” Developing that relationship, and being transparent about the cat’s care, can be enough to reassure an overinvested neighbour, he says. If they have ulterior motives, or “their own stuff going on”, it can be trickier.The pet I’ll never forget: Karl, the tabby who went to college and learned to use a toiletRead moreEqually, owners can have unrealistic expectations of their pets, Warren-Cummings points out. “It’s sometimes a case of: ‘I have purchased you, therefore you must be in my home.’” If the cat is happy and healthy, he suggests, is it really a problem they have a home away from home? Anyone with genuine concerns about a cat’s welfare should contact their local rescue, rather than taking it into their own hands, he adds – but, as usual with these disputes, the path forward lies with “human behaviour change, not cat behaviour change”. And that, Warren-Cummings says, tends to be harder.Lately, Pauline and her neighbour seem to have reached an uneasy truce, and Luka has been spending more time at home, suggesting the paté tap has been shut off. “It could potentially start up again, so I’ve just got to arm myself emotionally for that,” Pauline says. She admits that the experience has left her overly attuned to Luka’s comings and goings, and “far more hypervigilant than I really want to be”. As for the cat, now curled up behind the television, Pauline says, “she’s completely oblivious”.*Some names have been changedDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
