title: Country diary: The wild, riotous sounds of otters in battle | Environment | The Guardian
description: Isle of Lismore, Argyll: They skim over the surface like stones, making such a hullabaloo you could hear them a mile away
Author: Cal Flyn
Headline: Isle of Lismore, Argyll: They skim over the surface like stones, making such a hullabaloo you could hear them a mile away
Content: Common otters. ‘And there, again – two small heads pop up, turn to one another, and seem to wrestle.’Photograph: Robin Chittenden/AlamyView image in fullscreenCommon otters. ‘And there, again – two small heads pop up, turn to one another, and seem to wrestle.’Photograph: Robin Chittenden/AlamyCountry diaryEnvironmentCountry diary: The wild, riotous sounds of otters in battleIsle of Lismore, Argyll:They skim over the surface like stones, making such a hullabaloo you could hear them a mile awayCal FlynSat 5 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhear them before I see them: a wailing, or something more like ululation. High-pitched, repeated vocalisations that are neither man nor cat, but somewhere in between. I throw open the cabin door, unsure what to look for, and for a moment see nothing new: only the rocky strand and the sweep of dark wrack high above the shoreline.The strange, warbling sound comes again.Ai-ai-ai-ai.Not quite screaming, not quite howling, not quite trilling, but all of those things at once.A flash of movement in the water, perhaps 50 metres out. A small, dark body leaps from the surf, followed smartly by another. My eyes struggle to understand what I’m looking at. Tiny figures catch a millisecond of clear air, then slice back through the surface, like dolphins or porpoises. But the silhouette is all wrong. And there, again – two small heads pop up, turn to one another, and seem to wrestle.View image in fullscreenDusk on the Isle of Lismore.Photograph: Cal FlynAi-ai-ai-ai. Are they playing? Fighting? Their forms are slick and dark. When one launches again from the water, I see it clearly: four limbs, and a long tail – two otters, locked in battle. Over a fish perhaps, or one of the crabs we were watching earlier from the rowing boat as we drifted on the breeze, hands trailing through saline, watching the tiny creatures on the seabed below like tourists from a cable car.They tussle and twist. Then one breaks free and makes a dash for the shoreline. The other shrieks and follows, both now skimming over the surface like stones.What drama! You would hear them a mile away. The otters disappear behind a boulder, and for a moment all is silent but for the wash of the waves.It has gone 8pm.The sun is lowering in the sky, ready for bed. The wind ruffles the heads of the trees on the island in the bay. A pair of little egrets pick their way through the shallows, pause to examine their surroundings, then move on, feet lifted high and deliberate. Then the voices come again.Ai-ai-ai-ai.The soap opera continues unseen.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentCountry diaryRural affairsAnimalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: my twice-daily baths are giving me a sinking feeling | Family | The Guardian
description: It’s raining in our hallway. Could my louche bathing regime be behind the showers?
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: It’s raining in our hallway. Could my louche bathing regime be behind the showers?
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: my twice-daily baths are giving me a sinking feelingIt’s raining in our hallway. Could my louche bathing regime be behind the showers?Tim DowlingSat 5 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAugust is the traditional time for something major to go wrong with my house. So I’m not surprised, as I’m getting dressed one morning, to hear the middle one shouting something about it raining in the hallway.“What?” I say, standing on the landing with a shirt half pulled over my head. “What do you mean?”“Look,” he says.I look down to see that water is indeed falling from the ceiling in a rain-like fashion, leaving a giant puddle on the floorboards near the front door. “That ain’t good,” I say.I go upstairs to the bathroom where, some minutes earlier, I had been reading in the bath. Beneath the big claw-foot tub is another puddle: evidently my bathwater emptied straight on to the floor, and then straight through the floor.double quotation markThe shower is upstairs, off the middle one’s bedroom, where I run the risk of striding past his Zoom meetings in a towel“Since when is that happening?” my wife says, coming out with a mop.“Since now, I guess,” I say.“I’ll call Alfie,” she says.It continues to drizzle for another 15 minutes, the hall ceiling darkened and bubbling in patches.“Ironically, we could use the rain,” I say. “Just not inside.”“Alfie can’t come until Thursday,” she says.My wife lays a “Do Not Use” sign in the bath. The shower is upstairs, off the middle one’s bedroom, where I run the risk of striding past his Zoom meetings in a towel. It’s not ideal.When we moved into the house, the big claw-foot tub was in the main bedroom, and I imagined late, louche mornings where I went straight from bed to bath. But in the end we gave that bedroom to the oldest one, and chose the attic room with the en suite shower instead. For years, I almost never had a bath.Alfie the plumber arrives on Thursday morning and confirms what I suspected: the plastic waste pipe beneath the bath has cracked at its bend, causing any discharged bath water to pour on to the floor.“I’ll have to order another one,” he says.“While you’re here,” I say, “the downstairs loo cold tap came off in my hand over the weekend.”“I’ll have a look,” he says.double quotation markI’ve become accustomed to louche mornings where I lie up to my neck in a giant bath. When I’m feeling extra louche, I bathe again in the afternoonWhen we reclaimed the main bedroom after the oldest one moved out, my wife decided the big bath had to go. We needed cupboards, she said, and there wasn’t enough space. At my insistence we had it moved to the bathroom, where it replaced a much smaller tub. Since then I’ve become accustomed to louche mornings where I lie up to my neck in a giant bath. Sometimes, when I’m feeling extra louche, I bathe again in the afternoon.We’re away on holiday when Alfie replaces the waste pipe. There is, however, another problem: after showing a picture of the installation to his dad (Mark the builder, who moved the claw-foot tub to the bathroom in the first place) they have both reached the conclusion that the bath is slowly sinking into the floor.The flooring – vinyl tiles over plywood – has been compressed by the heavy clawed feet. Under the weight of a full bath plus occupant – me, asleep with the lower edge of my paperback just dipping into the water – the bend in the waste pipe has been pressed against the floor, causing it to crack.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We might have to prop the bath up on a couple of small bits of wood until the floor can be changed,” Alfie writes.“Changed?” my wife says.“A new floor,” I say. “That’s how you know it’s August.”But Alfie can’t come that week, or the next. At the tail end of the month we are driving back home when he texts, postponing his arrival from Tuesday morning to Tuesday afternoon.“I can still have a bath though, right?” I say. “I really want a bath.”“I don’t know,” my wife says.Tim Dowling: my working holiday just isn’t workingRead more“I mean, whatever’s wrong with the floor, the new waste pipe is in,” I say. “Isn’t that how we left it?”“I can’t remember,” she says. “Text him.” I send a text on my wife’s phone, asking for permission to bathe.Alfie’s reply says: “I’d advise against it at the moment!!” I sigh dramatically.“A no, then?” my wife says.“He says his dad has a picture of the old pipe when it was installed,” I say, “and it was well clear of the floor.”“Oh well,” she says, “it’s just another two days.”I look out the passenger window as the baked fields roll by. “I’m having a bath as soon as we get home,” I say. “I don’t care.”Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sinn Féin traitors!’: how far-right rhetoric derailed party’s path to power in Ireland | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Party insider reveals how election campaign was blindsided by rise of anti-immigrant feeling in new book
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Party insider reveals how election campaign was blindsided by rise of anti-immigrant feeling in new book
Content: Sinn Féin’s leader, Mary Lou McDonald, was expected to become taoiseach at Leinster House.Photograph: Lorraine O’Sullivan/ReutersView image in fullscreenSinn Féin’s leader, Mary Lou McDonald, was expected to become taoiseach at Leinster House.Photograph: Lorraine O’Sullivan/ReutersIreland‘Sinn Féin traitors!’: how far-right rhetoric derailed party’s path to power in IrelandParty insider reveals how election campaign was blindsided by rise of anti-immigrant feeling in new bookRory CarrollIreland correspondentSat 5 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 05.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor Siobhán Fenton, the dream ofSinn Féinwinning power and leading a progressive leftwing government evaporated the day she was canvassing in Dublin and felt a cold, sharp sting on her neck.She was in the passageway of a block of flats in the inner city, knocking on doors, and looked around for the source. Fenton, a media adviser to the party leader,Mary Lou McDonald, felt another sting on her shoulder, then another on her forearm.They were coins, thrown from a balcony above, where a man’s voice was shouting. “Sinn Féin traitors!” he roared. “Mary Lou Mohammad!Irelandis full!”It was May 2024, and instead of steaming towards victory in local and European elections – widely deemed a foregone conclusion, to be followed by a historic triumph in a general election – the party was experiencing a backlash fuelled by anti-immigrant sentiment in what was usually a bastion of working-class support.The coins left Fenton with gashes and bruises that augured an electoral hammering.“By the time the party realised how bad things had gotten it was almost too late,” she said. “The far right had infiltrated lots of Sinn Féin strongholds and we hadn’t picked up on it.”In a rupture to the party’s reputation for secrecy and discipline, Fenton has written a rare insider’s account, titledOurselves Alone: Sinn Féin Behind Closed Doors.It lifts the lid on a debacle that ambushed the party on the path to power. Instead of winning a general election and turbo-charging the campaign for Irish unification by ratcheting up pressure for a referendum,the party stumbled and today remains in opposition.It is a cautionary tale for progressive movements across Europe and elsewhere that struggle to reconcile tolerance for immigrants and refugees with clamours for crackdowns on new arrivals.A surge in xenophobia among grassroots supporters had blind-sided and, for a time, paralysed party leaders, Fenton said in an interview. “There was a moment of genuine sheer panic and just not knowing what to do. We were struggling to adapt because it was a sense that things had started to spiral out of control.”View image in fullscreenSiobhán Fenton was media adviser to the party leader, Mary Lou McDonald.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianThe book, published this week, depicts a largely well-intentioned but hapless party, and is also an account from a member of an organisation that many perceive as secretive and still in thrall to former IRA leaders on both sides of the Irish border, a perception Fenton disputes.Fenton, 34, was an atypical “Shinner”, the informal name for party adherents. She came from a middle-class Belfast family that abhorred the violence of the Troubles and favoured constitutional nationalism, not flinty republicanism.Fenton briefly worked for the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP) before studying English literature at Oxford, researching gender-based violence at Cambridge and becoming a London-based journalist for the Independent before returning to Northern Ireland in 2016, where she freelanced for the BBC and other outlets,including the Guardian, and wrote a book on the Good Friday agreement.In early 2020, Sinn Féin offered Fenton a job in Dublin. The party was on a high. It had just won 24.5% of first preference votes in the Irish general election, overtaking Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael, two centrist parties that had alternated in power for a century.As successor toGerry Adams, McDonald, a Dubliner universally known as Mary Lou, offered a fresh alternative, especially to young voters who blamed the political establishment for a housing crisis.Sinn Féin had run too few candidates to capitalise on the breakthrough, so Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael mustered enough seats to form a coalition, leaving Sinn Féin in opposition. Analysts expected it to win power after the next election.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter Sinn Féin became the biggest party in Northern Ireland in 2022, which paved the way for Michelle O’Neill tobecome first ministerat Stormont, the onus was on the party’s southern branch to ensure McDonald became taoiseach at Leinster House. “Don’t fuck it up,” a Belfast colleague half-jokingly told Fenton.For three years, Fenton, having relocated to Dublin, experienced the giddy nervousness of a party soaring in the polls while the ruling coalition slumped. The republican mantra – “tiocfaidh ár lá”, our day will come – seemed apt.A section titled “the long fall” chronicles the unravelling amid missteps and a volatile public mood.McDonald appeared to blame police fora riot that rocked Dublinin November 2023, and alarmed middle-class property owners by suggesting average Dublin house prices should fall to €300,000. More damagingly, the party failed to navigate growing xenophobia, the result of a housing shortage, a cost of living crisis, an influx of migrants and refugees, and far-right activism on social media and the streets.“It was a blind spot,” said Fenton. Covid-19 restrictions and a focus on the parliamentary party withered grassroots networking, leaving leaders unaware of the extent to which conspiracy theories and hostility to Muslims had taken hold, she said.The party should have tried to combat racist narratives by peeling people away from smartphones and having “really difficult conversations”, said Fenton. “Go door to door, talk about community concerns but be very, very clear that scapegoating immigrants and refugees is the wrong response.”Instead of gains in the May 2024 local and European elections, the cascade of coins on to Fenton foretold haemorrhaging support, especially in working-class strongholds that branded McDonald a “traitor” for not seeking greater curbs on migration. Months later the party limped into a general election thatkept Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael in power.Fenton’s contract was not renewed and she returned to her native Belfast, where she now works as a writer and analyst. She is no longer a member of Sinn Féin.Immigration remains a fraught issue for a party squeezed between those wanting a harder line and those who favour solidarity, said Fenton. Leaders may be tempted to sidestep the issue until the next election, then take a stance, she said. “It will be dependent on what the political environment looks like then.”Explore more on these topicsIrelandSinn FéinNorthern IrelandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It cost me many friendships’: former Brazil military chief reveals inside struggle to stop Bolsonaro’s coup | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior describes 2022 meeting in new book as ex-leader’s son vies with Lula for presidency
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior describes 2022 meeting in new book as ex-leader’s son vies with Lula for presidency
Content: Brazil's former president Jair Bolsonaro stands outside his home in Brasília, where he is under house arrest, in September 2025.Photograph: Luis Nova/APView image in fullscreenBrazil's former president Jair Bolsonaro stands outside his home in Brasília, where he is under house arrest, in September 2025.Photograph: Luis Nova/APBrazil‘It cost me many friendships’: former Brazil military chief reveals inside struggle to stop Bolsonaro’s coupCarlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior describes 2022 meeting in new book as ex-leader’s son vies with Lula for presidencyTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroSat 5 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe far-right populistJair Bolsonarowas in his final days as Brazil’s president when, six weeks after losing the election and still refusing to recognise the result, he summoned the heads of the armed forces to a meeting.The defence minister, Gen Paulo Sérgio Nogueira de Oliveira, took out a document from a plastic folder and handed copies to the commanders of the navy, army and air force.It was a draft decree proposing to invalidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s election in October 2022 and keep Bolsonaro in power.“The draft coup decree – which some people still insist to this day never existed – was there, awaiting approval or rejection; consensus or a majority,” writes the then head of the air force, Lt Brig Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior, in a new book coming out this month.After learning that the document would prevent Lula from taking office, Baptista Júnior told the defence minister he refused even to receive it: “The air force will not take part in this.” He then stood up and left the room.View image in fullscreenCarlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior.Photograph: Personal archive, courtesy of Carlos de Almeida Baptista JúniorThe extensive investigation and trial thatconvicted Bolsonaroof attempting a coup concluded that the plot failed to move forward mainly because the heads of two of the three armed forces – Baptista Júnior and the army commander, Gen Marco Antônio Freire Gomes – refused to take part.The navy commander, Adm Almir Garnier Santos, was convicted, as was Nogueira. Both are serving their sentences at military facilities, while Bolsonarois under house arrest.Freire Gomes has kept a low profile, but Baptista Júnior, speaking to the Guardian by video call, said he had decided to write a book to help prevent history from repeating itself.In the book, the 65-year-old former fighter pilot gives a detailed, first-hand account of the various ways in which Bolsonaro tried to cling to power.Baptista Júnior said he was motivated by the fact that, despite the abundance of evidence presented during the former president’s trial, opinion polls still showed that about a third of the population did not believe there had been an attempted coup.“Keeping in power someone who lost an election is a coup d’état,” he said, speaking from his home in Brasília, where he was dressed in civilian clothes – having recently retired – and about to pick up his grandson from school.The book, the Portuguese title of which translates as I Said No! – An Anti-Coup Bulwark, is due to be published on 15 September, about two weeks before the first round of the presidential election, in whichLula will face one of Bolsonaro’s sons, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro.Some Bolsonaro supporters have accused Baptista Júnior of trying to influence the vote, although he makes clear that he will vote for neither Lula nor Flávio, and criticises both in the book. He said the timing of the book was simply the result of the writing and editing process.View image in fullscreenPresident Lula addressing supporters at a campaign rally in São Bernardo do Campo this month.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesDespite writing that he voted for the far-right populist in the 2018 and 2022 elections, and even recounting a lighthearted moment at a barbecue when he saw the first lady reprimand the president for drinking beer, Baptista Júnior is critical of Bolsonaro, a former army captain who spent 30 largely undistinguished years as a city councillor and then congressman before reaching the presidency.He describes his former boss as someone with “significant limitations in political, institutional and administrative experience” and an “almost total imperviousness to outside opinions or information that did not conform to the ‘truths’ he had already established as his own” – citing his refusal to accept facts such as the scientific evidence supporting Covid-19 vaccination.During the election, Bolsonaro became “entirely consumed by his own efforts to remain in office”, writes Baptista Júnior. After repeatedly casting doubt on the vote, the president ordered the armed forces to investigate the electronic voting system, but refused to accept their reports when they found no irregularities.“He may still not believe the election result even today. Whether that is a matter of character, personality or something pathological, I don’t know,” said Baptista Júnior.The book touches on, but does not go into detail about, one of the most shocking revelations from the coup investigation: a plan drawn up by army special forcesto kidnap or assassinate Lula, the newlyelected vice-presidentand a supreme court justice. Baptista Júnior writes that he was not summoned to those meetings and only learned about them through the press.He does, however, recount more than a dozen meetings in which Bolsonaro summoned the heads of the armed forces to discuss ways to remain in power. At one of them, he witnessed the army chief tell the president, after hearing a proposal for an institutional rupture: “If you do that, I’ll have to arrest you.”Baptista Júnior had already given that account in testimony, and during the trial both Freire Gomes and Bolsonaro denied it. But he stands by his account in the book, writing that it was not something anyone present would forget.Saying no to the coup cost the pilot “many friendships”, he said. Even some military personnel still call him a “traitor” or a “watermelon”, a slur for soldiers seen as green on the outside because of their uniforms, but communist red within.The attacks started soon after the air force chief refused to join the plot, when the army general Walter Souza Braga Netto, whom Baptista Júnior considered a friend, ordered other military officers to attack him on social media and “make his life and his family’s hell”. Braga Netto, Bolsonaro’s running mate, was also convicted over the attempted coup.Most of Baptista Júnior’s revelations in the book initially emerged in 2024, when he was summoned to testify to federal police and only then, more than a year after leaving office, revealed that he had witnessed an attempted coup.View image in fullscreenSupporters of Jair Bolsonaro face off with police Brasília in January 2023 in a demonstration calling for the overthrow of President Lula.Photograph: André Borges/EPAJuliano da Silva Cortinhas, who worked on the civilian side of the defence ministry between 2013 and 2016, before the Bolsonaro administration, said: “It’s positive that he [Baptista Júnior] and the army chief said no to the coup, but as a matter of duty they should have reported it to the police as soon as it happened.”Cortinhas, who heads a security research group at the University of Brasília, said the armed forces could not present themselves as the “saviours” of democracy because that would be like “tripping society up and then holding out a hand to help it back to its feet”.“It was the commanders who allowed active-duty officers to take part in politics,” he said, noting that the Bolsonaro administration had by far the largest number of military personnel serving in civilian posts since the end of the brutal 1964–85 military dictatorship.Brazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his wayRead moreCortinhas sees as positive the fact that high-ranking officers were convicted of an attempted coup for the first time, but noted that others involved in the plot escaped justice, and manywere not even identified.“The risk of a new coup is even greater today,” he said.The new factor, he said, was the US president, Donald Trump, who hassought to influence electionsacross Latin America in support of far-right candidates such as Flávio Bolsonaro. In 2022, when Joe Biden was in the White House, Bolsonaro’s vice-presidentacknowledgedthat attempting a coup would leave Brazil in a “difficult position before the international community”.Cortinhas said he feared that if Lula was re-elected and Trump refused to recognise the result, some members of Brazil’s military could feel emboldened. “Coup-supporting groups remain within the armed forces,” he said.Baptista Júnior confirmed that, although it was difficult to know how many, there remained active-duty military personnel who believed a coup d’état would be justified under certain circumstances.“That’s why eternal vigilance is the best path,” he said.Explore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime | Egypt | The Guardian
description: Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs
Content: Sarah Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and an event production company.View image in fullscreenSarah Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and an event production company.EgyptEgyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crimeSarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugsAFP in CairoSat 5 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 19.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.The verdict is subject to appeal.Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.Explore more on these topicsEgyptAfricaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s pique with UK could lead to favor to acolyte Milei over Falklands | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president suggests he might support his Argentinian ally’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: US president suggests he might support his Argentinian ally’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands
Content: The Falkland Islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, on 16 March 2026.Photograph: Ricardo Mazalán/APView image in fullscreenThe Falkland Islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, on 16 March 2026.Photograph: Ricardo Mazalán/APDonald TrumpAnalysisTrump’s pique with UK could lead to favor to acolyte Milei over FalklandsRobert Taitin WashingtonUS president suggests he might support his Argentinian ally’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islandsSat 5 Sep 2026 18.19 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 16.21 EDTShareDonald Trumphas long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” hedeclaredto an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House.It is unlikelyArgentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time.But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president.Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas.Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland IslandsRead moreThe centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory.Britain reclaimed it after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender.An uneasy peace has reigned in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their fewer than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British.This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over theFalkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now?Milei jumped onTrump’s commentthat he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control.Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’sdeep-rooted suspicions of Britainand its imperial past.The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked.And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf.In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday.“Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader: ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said: ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets.It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump.Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China.Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran.He has repeatedlythreatened to bombor “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping.The White House also announcedthe withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germanyafter the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict.Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally.Turbulence under TrumpBut Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side.Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did.Javier Milei: ‘winds of change’ support Argentina’s claim to Falkland IslandsRead moreThis time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him.But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of afamous speechin 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa.“The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.”In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced.He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor that may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses.Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes.But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpArgentinaFalkland IslandsTrump administrationUS foreign policyUS politicsAmericasanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Drone attack blamed on guerrillas kills at least three soldiers in Colombia | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Officials accuse National Liberation Army of launching strike followed by clash inside military compound
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Officials accuse National Liberation Army of launching strike followed by clash inside military compound
Content: Colombia’s minister of defence, Jorge Mora (centre), looking at the site of a guerrilla drone attack, at a military garrison in Ocaña, Colombia, on 5 September 2026.Photograph: Javier Cassela/Colombian ministry of defence/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenColombia’s minister of defence, Jorge Mora (centre), looking at the site of a guerrilla drone attack, at a military garrison in Ocaña, Colombia, on 5 September 2026.Photograph: Javier Cassela/Colombian ministry of defence/AFP/Getty ImagesColombiaDrone attack blamed on guerrillas kills at least three soldiers in ColombiaOfficials accuse National Liberation Army of launching strike followed by clash inside military compoundAssociated Press in BogotáSat 5 Sep 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn attack involving explosives dropped from drones followed by a clash inside a military compound in north-easternColombiahas killed at least three soldiers and wounded four, Colombia’s army said on Saturday.Local authorities blamed the attack – which took place late on Friday – on the rebel National Liberation Army (ELN).It targeted a military unit in the municipality of Ocaña, in the Norte de Santander department, which borders Venezuela. Two soldiers died at the site and a third after receiving medical attention, Colombia’s military said on X.Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, condemned the attack. “For every police officer or soldier murdered, we will bring the full weight and legitimate force of the state down upon the criminals,” he said.Much of ELN, an armed group active since 1964, is based in the Catatumbo region, which includes parts of the Norte de Santander and Cesar departments. ELN also harbours dissident factions of the now defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) that did not join the peace agreement a decade ago.Both groups are vying for control of the strategic region, which connects to the porous border with Venezuela and is one of Colombia’s primary coca-producing areas.In August, an explosion outside a police station in Cucuta injured 11 police officers and killed a police dog. Officials also blamed that attack on the ELN.Earlier this week, at least one civilian was killed and 11 other people were injured after a car bomb exploded outside a police station in north-eastern Colombia.Explore more on these topicsColombiaAmericasDrones (military)newsShareReuse this content
