He said the timing of the book was simply the result of the writing and editing process.View image in fullscreenPresident Lula addressing supporters at a campaign rally in São Bernardo do Campo this month.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesDespite writing that he voted for the far-right populist in the 2018 and 2022 elections, and even recounting a lighthearted moment at a barbecue when he saw the first lady reprimand the president for drinking beer, Baptista Júnior is critical of Bolsonaro, a former army captain who spent 30 largely undistinguished years as a city councillor and then congressman before reaching the presidency.He describes his former boss as someone with “significant limitations in political, institutional and administrative experience” and an “almost total imperviousness to outside opinions or information that did not conform to the ‘truths’ he had already established as his own” – citing his refusal to accept facts such as the scientific evidence supporting Covid-19 vaccination.During the election, Bolsonaro became “entirely consumed by his own efforts to remain in office”, writes Baptista Júnior. After repeatedly casting doubt on the vote, the president ordered the armed forces to investigate the electronic voting system, but refused to accept their reports when they found no irregularities.“He may still not believe the election result even today. Whether that is a matter of character, personality or something pathological, I don’t know,” said Baptista Júnior.The book touches on, but does not go into detail about, one of the most shocking revelations from the coup investigation: a plan drawn up by army special forcesto kidnap or assassinate Lula, the newlyelected vice-presidentand a supreme court justice. Baptista Júnior writes that he was not summoned to those meetings and only learned about them through the press.He does, however, recount more than a dozen meetings in which Bolsonaro summoned the heads of the armed forces to discuss ways to remain in power. At one of them, he witnessed the army chief tell the president, after hearing a proposal for an institutional rupture: “If you do that, I’ll have to arrest you.”Baptista Júnior had already given that account in testimony, and during the trial both Freire Gomes and Bolsonaro denied it. But he stands by his account in the book, writing that it was not something anyone present would forget.Saying no to the coup cost the pilot “many friendships”, he said. Even some military personnel still call him a “traitor” or a “watermelon”, a slur for soldiers seen as green on the outside because of their uniforms, but communist red within.The attacks started soon after the air force chief refused to join the plot, when the army general Walter Souza Braga Netto, whom Baptista Júnior considered a friend, ordered other military officers to attack him on social media and “make his life and his family’s hell”. Braga Netto, Bolsonaro’s running mate, was also convicted over the attempted coup.Most of Baptista Júnior’s revelations in the book initially emerged in 2024, when he was summoned to testify to federal police and only then, more than a year after leaving office, revealed that he had witnessed an attempted coup.View image in fullscreenSupporters of Jair Bolsonaro face off with police Brasília in January 2023 in a demonstration calling for the overthrow of President Lula.Photograph: André Borges/EPAJuliano da Silva Cortinhas, who worked on the civilian side of the defence ministry between 2013 and 2016, before the Bolsonaro administration, said: “It’s positive that he [Baptista Júnior] and the army chief said no to the coup, but as a matter of duty they should have reported it to the police as soon as it happened.”Cortinhas, who heads a security research group at the University of Brasília, said the armed forces could not present themselves as the “saviours” of democracy because that would be like “tripping society up and then holding out a hand to help it back to its feet”.“It was the commanders who allowed active-duty officers to take part in politics,” he said, noting that the Bolsonaro administration had by far the largest number of military personnel serving in civilian posts since the end of the brutal 1964–85 military dictatorship.Brazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his wayRead moreCortinhas sees as positive the fact that high-ranking officers were convicted of an attempted coup for the first time, but noted that others involved in the plot escaped justice, and manywere not even identified.“The risk of a new coup is even greater today,” he said.The new factor, he said, was the US president, Donald Trump, who hassought to influence electionsacross Latin America in support of far-right candidates such as Flávio Bolsonaro. In 2022, when Joe Biden was in the White House, Bolsonaro’s vice-presidentacknowledgedthat attempting a coup would leave Brazil in a “difficult position before the international community”.Cortinhas said he feared that if Lula was re-elected and Trump refused to recognise the result, some members of Brazil’s military could feel emboldened. “Coup-supporting groups remain within the armed forces,” he said.Baptista Júnior confirmed that, although it was difficult to know how many, there remained active-duty military personnel who believed a coup d’état would be justified under certain circumstances.“That’s why eternal vigilance is the best path,” he said.Explore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flash flood disaster | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation
Author: William Christou
Headline: Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation
Content: Rescuers in Nepal find two more people aliveNepal-Tibet flood disasterRescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flash flood disasterChinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operationWilliam ChristouSat 5 Sep 2026 07.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 14.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmergency responders have rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hitNepal.The Nepali military said on Saturday a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India,China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.Two Nepali workers wererescued from another tunnelin a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.Rescue of Nepal hydropower workers ‘triumph for humans and humanity’, tunnelling expert saysRead moreExperts have said the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapseon 26 August.Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalChinaTibetSouth and central AsiaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Possums in the roof, koalas in bed: study shows how animals resort to Australian homes after habitat loss | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Microbats and wombats among the most common species found in buildings, with some discovered in letter boxes or air conditioning systems
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: Microbats and wombats among the most common species found in buildings, with some discovered in letter boxes or air conditioning systems
Content: Sugar gliders under the sink. ‘[The caller] had reached under the sink for a dishwashing tablet and instead her hand landed on something furry,’ said a Wildlife Victoria spokesperson.Photograph: Wildlife VictoriaView image in fullscreenSugar gliders under the sink. ‘[The caller] had reached under the sink for a dishwashing tablet and instead her hand landed on something furry,’ said a Wildlife Victoria spokesperson.Photograph: Wildlife VictoriaAustralian climate and environmental reportingWildlifePossums in the roof, koalas in bed: study shows how animals resort to Australian homes after habitat lossMicrobats and wombats among the most common species found in buildings, with some discovered in letter boxes or air conditioning systemsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSupported byAbout this contentPetra StockSat 5 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 20.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePossums in the roof, bats in the curtains and ducks on the balcony: new research has revealed how native animals are making themselves at home in our houses.Death trap: what to do about the everyday items catching and killing Australian wildlifeRead moreResearchers have analysed a decade of wildlife rescue reports and found brushtail and ringtail possums make up half of all cases of animals in buildings, followed by microbats and bare-nosed wombats.The study inPeople and Natureincluded 2,400 cases of animals using buildings as habitat. Most were found in roof spaces, walls, garages and under the house, although some preferred more unusual locations such as letterboxes or air conditioning systems. About 10% were found in indoor rooms such as bedrooms and kitchens.Bethany Kiss, a University of Melbourne architect and the lead author of the study, said animals were seeking out buildings as substitute habitats as their natural homes and hollows disappeared.“We found native wildlife using almost every part of the house imaginable,” Kiss said. “People often think these are unusual incidents, but they’re actually very common.”View image in fullscreenFigure showing the top 14 building features used by wildlife and the top two species that used each feature. Interior roofs (1) represented the highest use, followed by garage/sheds (2), under the house (3), in or near roller doors (4), wall cavities (5), exterior roofs (6), heating, ventilation and cooling systems (7), balconies (8), general living spaces (9), mailboxes or hanging baskets (10), doors (11), outdoor living spaces (12), chimneys (13) and windows (14).Illustration: Kiss et al, People and NatureWildlife Victoria, which provided the data for the study, said one recent caller to its emergency response service discovered juvenile sugar gliders in her kitchen.“She had reached under the sink for a dishwashing tablet and instead her hand landed on something furry,” said Aleisha Hall, a spokesperson for the rescue organisation. Investigating further, they found two gliders curled up together in a small jar.When a volunteer was dispatched to collect the gliders, they found five more.View image in fullscreenWires reported a homeowner calling after a koala scampered down her hallway. By the time rescuers arrived, it was seated calmly on her bed.Photograph: WiresIn another recent case, an echidna found its way into a house and headed straight for the pantry. “The homeowner found him pulling items off the shelves, including a heavy food processor,” Hall said.Luckily, the homeowner was also a wildlife rescuer and was able to safely return it back outside.View image in fullscreenA little forest bat, one of the microbats of Melbourne.Photograph: Ericka TudhopeMicrobats often featured in calls to Wildlife Victoria’s hotline. Recently, while renovating, a homeowner found eight little forest bats roosting in a wall.Ericka Tudhope, a rehabilitation specialist from Microbats of Melbourne, said bats living in the roof was common and nothing to be concerned about – so long as people left them alone and didn’t touch them.“They make great housemates by keeping bug numbers down and rarely do any damage to the house. They don’t chew cables or wires,” she said.In New South Wales, the Wires rescue service said animals often sought shelter during cold or extreme weather.Last year a member of the public rang when a koala scampered down her hallway. By the time the rescue volunteer arrived, the animal was sitting calmly on her bed.While such cohabiting in Australian houses was mostly accidental, in the United Kingdom buildings were being intentionally designed for habitat, Kiss said, such as the requirement to include “swift nesting bricks” in new builds.“We’re in a biodiversity crisis and a housing crisis,” she said.While architecture often focused on ways to keep nature out, there were opportunities to design buildings that were better for both people and wildlife. That could includewildlife-friendly lightingand noise reduction measures, as well as habitat features, such as swallow shelves or possum boxes.“One of the things that I would really like to see in Australia, is that we think about embedding the ecologist in the design process like you would with, say, an engineer,” Kiss said.View image in fullscreenA common brushtail possum under a house in Brisbane.Photograph: Jaana DielenbergProf Sarah Bekessy, a co-author of the paper and Biodiversity Council lead councillor, said research consistently showed that people benefited from everyday interactions with wildlife.“Wildlife in our neighbourhoods can improve our mental wellbeing, strengthen people’s connection with nature and make cities healthier, more resilient places to live,” she said.Wildlife Victoria said it advocated for peaceful coexistence where possible, but anyone concerned about an animal in their home was encouraged to contact their local wildlife rescue.Explore more on these topicsWildlifeAustralian climate and environmental reportingAnimal welfareAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alarming AI ads are flooding social media in the lead-up to Victoria’s election. But who is behind them? | Victorian politics | The Guardian
description: A machete-wielding robber, a ‘tsunami of debt’ … campaigns echoing opposition talking points outspend major parties
Author: Benita Kolovos
Headline: A machete-wielding robber, a ‘tsunami of debt’ … campaigns echoing opposition talking points outspend major parties
Content: A screenshot from a Fix Victoria advertisement produced using artificial intelligence. The water symbolises Victoria's ‘tsunami of debt’ said to be endangering key services and childrenView image in fullscreenA screenshot from a Fix Victoria advertisement produced using artificial intelligence. The water symbolises Victoria's ‘tsunami of debt’ said to be endangering key services and childrenVictorian politicsAlarming AI ads are flooding social media in the lead-up to Victoria’s election. But who is behind them?A machete-wielding robber, a ‘tsunami of debt’ … campaigns echoing opposition talking points outspend major partiesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBenita KolovosandHenry BelotSat 5 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man clad in a balaclava and brandishing a machete terrorises a worker at a petrol station before firebombing the building on the way out.A woman gives birth on the side of the road, unable to reach a hospital due toambulance rampingand crater-like potholes, which also stop a fire truck in its tracks.Victorian prisoners to be sent out to repair roads under Labor’s pothole planRead moreA flood of water – emblematic of Victoria’s “tsunami of debt”,forecast to hit $199bnin the next four years – gushes from the steps of state parliament, towards a scared child.These are some of the AI-generated images being used as part of a social media advertising campaign attracting thousands of views less than 100 days out from the Victorian election.According to one expert, the ads, created by a group called Fix Victoria, cost up to $100,000 to publish in August, which is significantly more than most major parties and candidates spent.View image in fullscreenA screenshot from another Fix Victoria adAnother group, Better Victoria, is also spending big on short ads to pit Labor initiatives – such as the multibillion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop – against investment in roads, schools and hospitals.But who is behind these groups and are they affiliated with a political party?‘Issues-driven, not politics-driven’Fix Victoria is run by experienced political operatives who held senior positions at a conservative thinktank, the Institute of Public Affairs (IPA). It began plotting its ad campaign in May, when a group of like-minded people started recruiting paying members who could finance its operations and ads.Corporate filings show it was registered with Asic in early August by Deborah Henderson, who was until June the deputy executive director of the IPA. Its communications director is Andrew Hudgson, who held a similar role at the IPA until earlier this year. Its head of advocacy is Gideon Rozner, who spent six years at the IPA before working at an investment firm.Fix Victoria is a separate entity to the IPA and its staff say it is coincidence that three of them previously worked at the thinktank, which is a long-term critic of Labor governments.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIn November, Rozner told his social media followers that he was rejoining the Liberal party to support its new leader, Jess Wilson.“The best place for me is to stand with the thousands of Victorians who will get around Jess Wilson to defeat this disgusting Labor government and save the great state of Victoria,” Rozner posted on X.When asked by Guardian Australia whether he is still a member of the Liberal party, Rozner declines to answer but says: “I’ve been around for a long time – and my views and affiliations are well-known.”Rozner says Fix Victoria is an “issues-driven, not politics-driven” organisation that wants to “ensure our leaders know that everyday Victorians want a plan to get out of the mess we are currently in”.“Fix Victoria is focused on the three key issues dragging our state down, that being crime, corruption and debt,” Rozner says.These three issues happen to be key talking points of opposition parties.“Victoria’s tsunami of debt steals resources from policing so organised illegal tobacco criminals are making billions, recruiting vulnerable kids and making our streets unsafe,” one 30-second Fix Victoria ad says.Bar chart showing the top ten ad spend by political groups ahead of Victoria’s state election‘Campaign groups exploiting loopholes’A loophole in Victoria’s electoral laws means voters may never know who is ultimately funding these ads.Groups publishing political ads during campaigns don’t need to be registered as third-party campaigners unless they specifically promote or oppose a party or a candidate.The Centre for Public Integrity’s executive director, Catherine Williams, says Victoria’s laws are narrower in scope than their federal equivalent.“Unless an entity meets the definition of third-party campaigner, no disclosure obligations apply,” Williams says.During the federal election campaign, mandatory donation disclosures by one third-party campaign grouprevealed it had been bankrolled by the coal lobby. The group had been attacking Labor, Greens and independent candidates.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTransparency International Australia’s chief executive, Clancy Moore, says while Fix Victoria does not meet the legal threshold of a third-party campaign group, its ads are “clearly trying to influence voting”.Pauline Hanson courts wealthy donors with $2,000 ‘exclusive’ Melbourne lunch, but where are the receipts?Read more“It’s really important Victorians know who is behind these types of campaigns and what their political affiliations might be,” Moore says. “There is a long history of third-party and fake grassroots campaign groups exploiting loopholes in electoral laws to try to influence elections.”Rozner says Fix Victoria has “invested considerable resources to ensure strict compliance with all relevant laws, in particular the Victorian Electoral Act”.By avoiding reference to political parties or candidates, Fix Victoria’s financial backers are shielded from public view unless disclosed by the group itself.“We place a very high priority on protecting the security and privacy of our members and supporters,” Rozner says.View image in fullscreenAn advertising executive says Fix Victoria spent just under $100,000 on ads in AugustBetter Victoria was formed a month after Fix Victoria, with its first ads running on Facebook in early August. Its political content is endorsed by the group itself, rather than a office holder.Listings with Consumer Affairs Victoria show its secretary is Ronald Holzer, a lawyer based in the Melbourne suburb of Caulfied North. Holzer says he only has an administrative role with the group.He referred a series of questions from Guardian Australia to an unnamed spokesperson, who declined to say who was running the organisation.“Better Victoria has obtained independent legal advice regarding its activities,” the spokesperson said. “It is confident that its activities are fully compliant with Victoria’s electoral laws.”The spokesperson said the group had no relationship with any political party and was fully financed by donations from its members. Those donors will also remain hidden.“Our members include people from a range of backgrounds and professions, who have exercised their right to privacy,” the spokesperson said.‘They will have spent tens of thousands’An advertising executive, Ed Coper, who worked with Climate 200 and some teal candidates during the 2025 federal election, says the two groups are spending big.Coper’s agency, Populares, has tracked their spending using public data and says they spent more on Google and Meta ads than any other state election candidate or party in August.He says Fix Victoria spent just under $100,000 on ads, which was about a quarter of all the advertising spend related to the election. Better Victoria spent about $40,000.The two groups also outspent the Liberals, teal independents and One Nation on social media advertising, according to Populares.Then there’s the ad Fix Victoria ran in the middle of the AFL wildcard final between the Western Bulldogs and Collingwood on Channel Seven on 28 August.“They will have spent tens of thousands of dollars,” Coper says. “The actual content of their advertising is very, very similar to the way that a political operative will message during an election campaign.”Explore more on these topicsVictorian politicsVictoriaSocial mediaAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Putin begins talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on ending war with Ukraine | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Moscow and Kyiv vow not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during negotiations
Author: William Christou
Headline: Moscow and Kyiv vow not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during negotiations
Content: The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, welcomes Jared Kushner (left) and US envoy Steve Witkoff (second left) to the Kremlin.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/Kremlin/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Russian president, Vladimir Putin, welcomes Jared Kushner (left) and US envoy Steve Witkoff (second left) to the Kremlin.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/Kremlin/EPAUkrainePutin begins talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on ending war with UkraineMoscow and Kyiv vow not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during negotiationsWilliam Christouand agencySat 5 Sep 2026 18.13 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 10.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussian presidentVladimir Putinbegan talks with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the Kremlin on Saturday – aimed at ending more than four years of war in Ukraine, ahead of the pair’s first visit to Kyiv expected on Sunday.Both Russia andUkrainevowed not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during the negotiations, as Washington tries to revive US-led talks to end Europe’s worst conflict since the second world war.The visit came asDonald Trumpsuggested on Friday a new proposal to end the war, without providing any details on what his new plan might be. Trump made ending the war a priority early in his second term, but little has changed so far.Trump said his son-in-law Kushner and business ally Witkoff were bringing “a proposal to end the war”.“Dear colleagues, I warmly welcome you to Moscow. The situation is, of course, not simple,” Putin told the envoys in a grand Kremlin hall in footage aired by Russian TV. “But before we begin to address it, I would like to ask everyone to convey their best wishes and words of gratitude to US president Mr Trump.”The talks come as the grinding war, launched by Russia in 2022, saw increasing civilian deaths and attacks this summer. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine. The war has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.Russian strikes on Ukraine on Saturday killed at least seven people, including in the Kyiv suburbs, Ukrainian officials said.The Kremlin said it would not strike Kyiv from midnight on Saturday, while the Ukrainian president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he would halt strikes on Moscow “from now” until Monday.“The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight tonight not to strike Kyiv for three days,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said.Zelenskyy, who had offered a truce during the US visits, later said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow,” he said on social media.He said he had spoken to the US officials and that he expected them in Kyiv on Sunday.Europe would not be able to sustain war of attrition with Russia, defence officials sayRead moreLarge gaps remain between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the war. On Friday, the Kremlin said it was sticking by the position Putin set out two years earlier – that Ukraine should give up four regions claimed by Russia and not join Nato. That position is intolerable to Ukraine.As peace efforts floundered in recent months, with US attention turned to its war with Iran, the conflict has intensified.Ground troops have been locked in a grinding stalemate along the 775-mile (1,250km) frontline with little advances on either side. Both sides have intensified their aerial attacks in recent weeks, hitting increasingly distant targets.Ukraine has carried out long-range strikes on Russian military facilities,oil refineriesand e-commerce warehouses, to try to degrade Russia’s war effort and economy. Its strikes on Russian oil refineries have led to fuel shortages and rising prices at the pump.On Friday, a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), one of the agencies responsible for carrying out deep-strike operations in Russia. Zelenskyy has vowed to retaliate. Russia has also increased its attacks on Kyiv and other cities with waves of bombardments, stretching Ukraine’s air defence systems.Officials visiting Ukraine have largely done so by train, as Ukrainian airspace has been closed since 2022 due to the war.Russia had earlier struck Kyiv suburbs, reportedly killing two people in the Bucha district. Another attack on the Dnipro region killed five people and wounded five more at a factory, according to the local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha.He said those killed were employees working at the factory who were “doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives”. A 62-year-old man was injured and several homes and a building were damaged in another attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said.Russia also struck a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging the building and injuring a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl. Emergency services said they were repeatedly forced to withdraw because of the threat of more strikes.Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 drones overnight, including jet-powered UAVs. Ukrainian air defences disabled 128 of the drones, the air force said.Russia’s defence ministry said it had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.Explore more on these topicsUkraineJared KushnerUS foreign policyTrump administrationRussiaVladimir PutinUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Prince William to represent King Charles at funeral of Norway’s King Harald V | Monarchy | The Guardian
description: Duty falls by precedent to William to attend service of late monarch, alongside Princess Royal, who is godmother to new king Haakon VIII
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Duty falls by precedent to William to attend service of late monarch, alongside Princess Royal, who is godmother to new king Haakon VIII
Content: Members of Norway’s royal family including Queen Sonja (left), King Haakon VIII and Queen Mette-Marit (foreground) lay flowers in Oslo’s Palace Square on 31 August, three days after the death of King Harald.Photograph: Cornelius Poppe/EPAView image in fullscreenMembers of Norway’s royal family including Queen Sonja (left), King Haakon VIII and Queen Mette-Marit (foreground) lay flowers in Oslo’s Palace Square on 31 August, three days after the death of King Harald.Photograph: Cornelius Poppe/EPAMonarchyPrince William to represent King Charles at funeral of Norway’s King Harald VDuty falls by precedent to William to attend service of late monarch, alongside Princess Royal, who is godmother to new king Haakon VIIIPress AssociationSat 5 Sep 2026 18.11 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Prince of Wales is to represent his father at the funeral of King Harald V ofNorwaynext week, Buckingham Palace has announced.William, the heir to the throne, will be joined by his aunt the Princess Royal, who is attending in a private and personal capacity as godmother of the new king, Haakon VIII.Norway has seen an outpouring of grief for the much-loved late monarch, who died on 28 August at the age of 89.Harald has been hailed as an inclusive “people’s king” who modernised the Norwegian monarchy during his 35-year reign.View image in fullscreenKing Harald of Norway escorting Princess Catherine, then Duchess of Cambridge, to a dinner at the Royal Palace in Oslo in February 2018.Photograph: Ntb Scanpix/ReutersHis funeral will take place on 9 September at Oslo Cathedral, with mourners including his widow, Sonja, now the queen mother.In keeping with precedent that the sovereign does not attend funerals of other heads of state, the duty falls to William, a future king, to represent his father and pay his respects at the service.Charles paid a touching tribute to his “dear cousin” and “much-loved kinsman and friend” after the news of Harald’s death was announced.In a message of condolence, he praised Harald’s “unwavering dedication” and his “kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades”.The late Queen Elizabeth II and King Harald were second cousins. They shared the same great-grandparents, King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra.View image in fullscreenKing Harald V’s coffin is carried to Oslo’s Palace Chapel by members of the royal family including (at front) Haakon VIII and Queen Mette-Marit.Photograph: Ole Berg-Rusten/EPAIn April last year, William represented his father atthe funeral of Pope Francisin the Vatican.William and the now Princess of Wales carried out an official tour to Norway in 2018, dining with King Harald and Queen Sonja at the Royal Palace, where Harald described them as “family” and praised their support of the then Queen.The Norwegian sovereign processed into the banquet arm in arm with the pregnant Catherine, who was expecting Prince Louis and wearing a flowing Alexander McQueen gown, with the gesture mirrored by Sonja and William who walked behind them.William and Kate also spent time visiting the ski slopes with the then Crown Prince Haakon and Crown Princess Mette-Marit, now the King and Queen.Explore more on these topicsMonarchyNorwayPrince WilliamEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe would not be able to sustain war of attrition with Russia, defence officials say | Europe | The Guardian
description: Security experts fear Putin may be winning hybrid war with the west amid rise of pro-Kremlin, far-right parties
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Security experts fear Putin may be winning hybrid war with the west amid rise of pro-Kremlin, far-right parties
Content: Local people watch firefighters go to work after a Russian drone attack struck a residential building in Kyiv this week.Photograph: Francisco Seco/APView image in fullscreenLocal people watch firefighters go to work after a Russian drone attack struck a residential building in Kyiv this week.Photograph: Francisco Seco/APEuropeEurope would not be able to sustain war of attrition with Russia, defence officials saySecurity experts fear Putin may be winning hybrid war with the west amid rise of pro-Kremlin, far-right partiesPatrick Wintourin RomeSat 5 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDefence planners working with Nato fear that if war broke out withRussia, Europe could not currently sustain a prolonged war of attrition owing to a public lack of war readiness, a conference on the future of European military coordination heard this week.The pessimism reflects concern that Russia may be winning a so-called hybrid war withEurope, weakening the options available to Nato war planners in the event of military conflict.The surge in support for the populist forces in Europe’s main military states is also endangering proposals for a group of five European countries, including the UK, to take on a new coordination role as the US prepares to reduce its commitments to the conventional defence of Europe.Defence officials, speaking at a forum convened by the Munich Security Conference (MSC), the leading security foundation, said the European public may not have the appetite for a prolonged war, requiringNatoto focus its plans on a relatively quick conflict.One recent British cabinet member admitted the west had been “crap” at educating its public about the scale of the hybrid conflict with Russia. Another UK diplomat claimed successive British prime ministers had done nothing to explain the scale of the threat.They said this had left ministers locked in an unenviable task of persuading unprepared voters to cut welfare spending to fund defence. “The level of the debate has been at that of a kindergarten,” the UK diplomat admitted.View image in fullscreenRussia’s president, Vladimir Putin, takes part in a wreath laying ceremony in Moscow earlier this year.Photograph: Maxim Shipenkov/ReutersThe private criticism has been fuelled by the UK government’s inability to adopt a call in its 2025 strategic defence review to launch a national conversation on the scale of the security threat facing Europe and to build national resilience.A second diplomat said the collapse of the cold war dividing line with Russia had left Moscow free to exploit the anxieties of European publics on the left and the right. The remarks reveal a wider concern in senior European politicians that they may belosing the so-called hybrid war with Russia, and this may be reflected in rightwing populist surges next year in Poland, France and Italy.Most populist parties, including Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), are sympathetic to Russia and want an end to the Ukraine conflict.The MSC discussion – held under rules forbidding identification of the speaker – was given added urgency by the German government this week blaming Russia for anattempted drone attack on Leipzig airportlast month.One of the suspected culprits in the attack on 4 August, where an armed drone exploded, has been identified as aBelarusian citizen with a Russian passportwho appears to have entered Europe using an Italian tourist visa.The MSC, an independent but influential foundation, has been promoting the idea of the five main European military powers working much more closely: one means of bringing the UK, outside the EU, to the centre of European defence planning.Decisions in Washington on its troop deployments that could effectively leave Europe in charge of its own conventional defences are expected in the next few months. But the scale of hybrid war and the potential impact of next year’s elections, as well as the surge by the AfD inGermany, on plans for a stronger European defence coordination was described at the conference as “the elephant in the room”.Deadly escalation in Black Sea attacks prompts fears of even higher food pricesRead moreOne proposal is for the EU to publish a collective statement on the Russian threat that the populist forces would be challenged to accept or decline.The E5 group of European defence ministers already meet regularly, but they are at the early stages of agreeing of how to jointly procure capabilities such as integrated air and missile defence, deep precision strike and space-based early warning systems that are all currently provided mostly by the US.“Europe is stagnating at a time when the external threats were assuming a dimension which is really very serious. These are really huge and existential challenges requiring greater integration in defence,” said Wolfgang Ischinger, the chair of the MSC.He argued the E5 grouping offers a way of including all the European countries with substantial defence industrial capacity and may later be able to incorporateUkrainein the context of a truce since Kyiv now has the largest and strongest army in Europe.Advocates of the E5 insist it will neither duplicate nor underline Nato, but fears were expressed that the US would nevertheless block a stronger European pillar inside Nato. “The US are better at talking about burden shifting than power sharing,” said one diplomat.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionItaly is one of the E5 states most concerned about the impact of Russia’s hybrid warfare on its domestic politics as Giorgia Meloni’s rightwing administration – which has governed more moderately than many expected, and cultivated a pro-Ukraine image abroad – becomes its longest-running since the second world war.The Italian foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, warned Italy was suffering daily cyber-attacks, adding it was not immune from potential Russian interference in next year’s national elections, the first time an Italian politicians has warned the election may be manipulated.View image in fullscreenItaly’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, has warned of Russia meddling in his country’s elections next year.Photograph: Mohamed Hossam/EPA“There are many ways to wage hybrid warfare, it is not done using bombs, planes or tanks,” the minister said.Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, one of Meloni’s closest political allies, has said it was stupid not to recognise the level of Russian interference.He warned this summer at the Nato summit in Ankara: “We don’t have the antibodies and we’re penetrable: analyse bots and you’ll see it. The increase occurred thanks to social media.”His doubts have grown given Moscow’s ability to operate across so many domains, including social media, AI, cybersecurity, databases and critical infrastructure. On Tuesday, he said the Russian threat was growing all the time.Crosetto also said he recognises Russia is exploiting real problems such as low wages, and so attributing government unpopularity to Russian disinformation risks misidentifying a malaise afflicting western societies, including a general weariness with the cost of the war in Ukraine,In Italy, Roberto Vannacci, the leader of the far-right Futuro Nazionale who haschallenged the stability of Meloni’s coalition, is widely seen as the most probable carrier of the Russian message in the coming election, that could come as early as April.Speaking before the investigation into whether his party represents a revival of fascism, Vannacci gloried in the criticism. “Just discovered that I am a ‘Manchurian candidate’ sent by the Russian federation to complain about the unaffordable petrol prices in my country Italy,” he said. “Forgive me, but I still find it hard to accept the idea that dissent from Brussels’ orthodoxy is now, in practical terms, tantamount to disloyalty towards the west.”In an attempt to shift perceptions so Ukraine is seen not as a financial burden but rather as teaching Europe modern warfare, Crosetto has recruited theformer Ukraine defence minister Mykhailo Fedorovas his unpaid adviser for innovation. Ischinger praised the decision, describing Ukraine as possessing the best equipped and most modern army in Europe.In Ukraine, 200,000 drones are being built each month, with the goal of producing more than 7m by 2026. To support this growth, 500 small and medium-sized companies have sprung up, assembling drones even in small workshops, using mostly Chinese components.Explore more on these topicsEuropeRussiaUkraineDefence policyNatoGiorgia MeloniAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)newsShareReuse this content

title: Sweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since Brexit | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Scale of deportations made public for first time amid criticism of hardline approach to UK citizens
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Scale of deportations made public for first time amid criticism of hardline approach to UK citizens
Content: John Sellers, deported after living in Sweden since age 10, with his wife Caroline, who says people need to know how Brexit has ‘crushed families’.Photograph: John SellersView image in fullscreenJohn Sellers, deported after living in Sweden since age 10, with his wife Caroline, who says people need to know how Brexit has ‘crushed families’.Photograph: John SellersBrexitSweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since BrexitScale of deportations made public for first time amid criticism of hardline approach to UK citizensLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentSat 5 Sep 2026 05.16 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 05.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSweden has confirmed 458 British citizens have been deported or forcibly removed by police since Brexit.It is the first time the scale of the deportations of citizens who failed to secure residency in Sweden post-Brexit has been made public and comes amid mounting criticism of a cruel and hardline approach to Britons who had chosen to make the country their home beforeBrexit.Some have been told to go after more than 25 years in the country and even vulnerable elderly people with dementia have been affected. One man was deported even though he had lived in the country since he was 10 years old.Susanna Fonsell, a unit manager and legal expert at the Swedish Migration Agency, told Sverige Radio: “A rejected application does not necessarily result in deportation… and according to the agency statistics, the agency’s rejections of an application for resident status has been accomplished by a deportation decision in only approximately 400 cases,”she told Sweden Radio.The Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, confirmed to the Guardian that 458 British citizens had been deported since Brexit. “According to the agency’s statistics, the Swedish Migration Agency’s rejection of an application for residence status has been accompanied by a deportation decision in only 458 cases,” a spokesperson said.David Milstead, who heads up the 9,000-strong activist group Brits in Sweden, said it was important for Sweden to release full and transparent figures in relation to removals and deportations and their circumstances.“We need to understand exactly what the 458 represents. Does it capture people who gave up and left when they realised their withdrawal agreement application was unlikely to succeed? Does it include people who were refused withdrawal agreement status, subsequently obtained a permit under national law and were only later ordered to leave?“It certainly does not capture people who are currently managing to remain in Sweden on temporary permits, with little certainty about their long-term future.”He said the figures illustrated a “broader problem” in that the data was issued piecemeal and sometimes in an opaque manner. “We still do not have basic published figures showing how many people submitted a missed-deadline application and the fraction of these which succeeded,” he said.The last available data shows that there were 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency, which included family members joining British citizens after the deadline by 2024. Of those, just under 4,000 were rejected, a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3% and 4%, according to Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) analysis.Deportations are still happening. This week, the Swedish wife of a former business director from Cambridge told how her husband was detained in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a forced removal.She said they had been fighting to overturn the decision by the migration authorities for five yearsand felt that they had been “hunted”.Earlier this week, the Guardian revealed a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, who had lived in Sweden since he was 10,had been deported, separating him from his wife, Caroline, in Gothenburg, who said people needed to know how Brexit had “crushed families”.View image in fullscreenJoyce Thomas, 78, is facing removal from Sweden as a result of its hardline Brexit policy.Photograph: Felix AndlerAnother woman, 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, has been toldto remove herself from the country before next Wednesday. Friends are trying to get an injunction and have appealed to the European Commission for help.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf she fails to comply, not only will she face a forced deportation, but the court of appeal has told her she could face a “re-entry ban” and be “registered on a watchlist” preventing potential entry into a Schengen country, which includes Sweden “as long as the re-entry ban remains in effect”.The Swedish Migration Agency told the Guardian it had “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other member states. The Swedish Migration Agency has applied applicable law, and there has been an opportunity to appeal rejection decisions.”Late applications for post-Brexit residency are allowed under the Brexit withdrawal agreement, both in the EU and the UK, but applicants have to show “reasonable grounds” for missing the deadline.The FCDO has said that “in practice” late applicants in Sweden “are not likely to have their reasonable grounds accepted”.Earlier this week, Sweden’s migration minister, Johan Forssell,said his government had followed the rulesbut that it was willing to look into the matter. “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future,” he said.A spokesperson for the FCDO said: “We continue to raise this with the Swedish authorities and welcome their statement that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so.”Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for Sweden’s opposition Centre party, said the government needed to go much further. He pledged to bring in new laws if his party won power at the next general election to allow British to reapply for post-Brexit residence,saying “a touch of humanity” was needed.Explore more on these topicsBrexitSwedenEuropeEuropean UnionImmigration and asylumForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Every girl now wants to be a boxer’: excitement in Katie Taylor’s home town for her valedictory bout | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Irish boxer lauded for her tenacity and inspiration before her last fight in front of 80,000 people at Croke Park
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Irish boxer lauded for her tenacity and inspiration before her last fight in front of 80,000 people at Croke Park
Content: Katie Taylor greets a young fan Clodagh Keating, 10, during an open workout in Dublin on Wednesday.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAView image in fullscreenKatie Taylor greets a young fan Clodagh Keating, 10, during an open workout in Dublin on Wednesday.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAIreland‘Every girl now wants to be a boxer’: excitement in Katie Taylor’s home town for her valedictory boutIrish boxer lauded for her tenacity and inspiration before her last fight in front of 80,000 people at Croke ParkRory CarrollIreland correspondentSat 5 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 06.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenKatie Taylor steps into the ring on Saturday night to defend her titles and once again enthral Ireland, there will be a bittersweet tinge. After a singular career that pioneered women’s boxing, the super-lightweight champion and Olympic gold medallist is bowing out. She is 40 and it is to be her final bout.“The end of an era, isn’t it?” said Trevor McMahon, her brother-in-law and founder of a gym where she trains. “It’ll be an amazing night but it’ll also be a little bit sad. Everything she did, it might not ever be achieved again.”View image in fullscreenA billboard in Katie Taylor’s home town of Bray wishes her luck.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianThere is consolation in the manner of her farewell. Taylor will fight in front of an 80,000-strong roaring, pulsing crowd at Dublin’s Croke Park, the citadel of Irish sport, in a valedictory like no other.Before tickets went on sale in June, some worried that a boxing match might not fill such a vast stadium. The event sold out in 17 minutes.Westlifeand other musical acts have joined the bill, adding to the sense of extravaganza. The national broadcaster, RTÉ, will broadcast proceedings free to air, so every home and pub can tune in for Taylor’s showdown with Flora Pili, an unbeaten French champion.David Finnegan, 55, who was selling Taylor hats, flags and posters from a stall in her home town of Bray, County Wicklow, this week, said: “Business is tipping away. This is her farewell, everyone wants to be part of it.”Catherine Hill, 45, had a precious ticket and wanted a Taylor T-shirt for the occasion. “It’s going to be amazing for Katie, the whole country and all women,” she said. “Every young girl now wants to be a boxer or an athlete. It wasn’t like that before.”View image in fullscreenCatherine Hill and her son at a stall with Katie Taylor merchandise near the boxer’s family home in Bray.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianAnother customer, Denise, 71, bought flags for a pub in Kerry where she planned to watch the bout. “What I love about Katie is that she’s not full of herself. She’s down to earth and still meets up with her friends here. She’s so good with the children.”Even those with no interest in boxing have been swept up in excitement for an athlete who is adored for blazing a trail in female sports with talent, grit and humility.Encouraged and trained by her father, Pete, Taylor began sparring as a young girl at a gym so rudimentary it was nicknamed the Tin Can. Women and girls were banned from the ring in Ireland and the UK, so shedisguised herself as a boyand signed up to bouts as “K Taylor”.View image in fullscreenA mural of Katie Taylor at the site of her first gym.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianFather and daughter helped to persuade Irish authorities to lift the ban in 2001, when she was 15, and were instrumental in having women’s boxing added to the Olympic Games. Taylor won gold at London 2012 and went on toheadline Madison Square Gardenand win an epictrilogy with Amanda Serrano.View image in fullscreenTrevor McMahon, Katie Taylor’s brother-in-law and the founder of Liberty Boxing Gym.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianMcMahon, whose LibertyBoxinggym hosts Taylor during her return visits to Bray, said: “The talent was always there but it was more the dedication. She knew from the get-go what she was going to do. When she comes down to train in the club, the place is packed.”The last time Croke Park hosted a boxing match was in 1972, when Muhammad Ali fought Alvin Lewis. McMahon said Taylor’s farewell promised to be even more special.Pili, 29, has won all 12 of her professional fights and holds the IBO world super-lightweight title. She will be no pushover but McMahon said Taylor was determined to add another belt to her titles and go out on a high. “No matter how tough the fight is, Katie always seems to rise to the occasion. If she’s beaten, you’d have to carry her out of there in a box.”Laney O’Connell, 28, who lives on the estate where Taylor grew up, said she had inspired girls to be fit and active. “When you meet her, she’s completely normal. I don’t think she realises just how big she is,” she said. “And it’s great to see the country represented by a woman instead of a man, especially not McGregor,” she added, referencing the mixed martial artist Conor McGregor.Anne-Marie McHugh, 58, speaking below a supermarket’s Taylor mural, hoped that Bray’s most famous daughter will enjoy a restful post-boxing life. “It’s time for her to relax,” she said. “She’s earned it.”View image in fullscreenA mural of Katie Taylor overlooks Anne-Marie McHugh and her granddaughter in Bray, County Wicklow.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsIrelandKatie TaylorBoxingEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: US military says it struck three Iranian tankers after American warships came under missile attack | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Officials said US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided attacks before three Iranian tankers were struck by the US
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Officials said US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided attacks before three Iranian tankers were struck by the US
Content: A US Centcom image of a US military strike on an Iranian oil tanker off the in the Gulf of Oman on 5 September 2026.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA US Centcom image of a US military strike on an Iranian oil tanker off the in the Gulf of Oman on 5 September 2026.Photograph: US Central Command/AFP/Getty ImagesUS-Israel war on IranUS military says it struck three Iranian tankers after American warships came under missile attackOfficials said US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided attacks before three Iranian tankers were struck by the USMarina Dunbarand agenciesSat 5 Sep 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 17.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS militarysaid Saturday it struck three Iranian oil tankers after US navy warships came under missile attack, further escalating tensions in the region and warning it would “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet”.According to the military, a US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided “multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks” while patrolling the region. No US personnel were injured.Two of the Iranian oil carriers were “permanently disabled”, the Pentagon said, while a third tanker, which was unladen, was destroyed.Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US militaryRead moreThe US said the vessels were part of a shadow network that helped finance Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards and armed proxy groups operating across the region.“We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet,” the head of US Central Command, Adm Brad Cooper, said in thestatement.The announcement followed an earlier report from Iran that the US had attacked an Iranian tanker near Kharg Island in the Gulf. Tasnim, a semiofficial news outlet affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps,reportedthe strike happened on Saturday morning. It said the tanker’s crew survived and was being evacuated.The US said one tanker was struck off Kharg Island, while another was hit near Jask. The unladen tanker was struck in the Gulf of Oman. The US statement also shared what it described as video footage of the strikes.Iran’s state broadcaster said later Sunday that Iran targeted three oil tankers and three American vessels in response to the US strikes. This could not be immediately confirmed.The latest attacks came nearly a week after the US and Iran resumed strikes after about a month of relative calm in the on-again, off-again war that began with US and Israeli attacks in February. Attempts at negotiations have collapsed.One of the strikeshit a weddingin southern Iran on Tuesday, killing four people, including a child, and injuring dozens, according to Iranian officials.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe US vice-president, JD Vance, said “sometimes things happen” whenaskedon Thursday whether an US strike was responsible for killing people at the wedding celebration.The renewed strikes have also brought fresh scrutiny to a 28 February US attack in Minab thatstruck a school compoundand killed at least 156 people, most of them schoolchildren.A preliminaryUS militaryinquiry reportedly found that the attack resulted from a targeting error after outdated coordinates identified the school as part of a nearby Revolutionary Guards naval base. The Pentagon said at the time that it was investigating. A full report has not been made public.Associated Press contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranUS militaryUS foreign policyIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Civilians among at least 60 killed in Yemen as ground fighting escalates | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Houthi rebel offensive against government forces on west coast leads to some of deadliest clashes in years
Author: William Christou
Headline: Houthi rebel offensive against government forces on west coast leads to some of deadliest clashes in years
Content: Forces loyal to Yemen's Saudi-backed government ride along a road in the Hays district, south of Hodeidah, on Saturday.Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenForces loyal to Yemen's Saudi-backed government ride along a road in the Hays district, south of Hodeidah, on Saturday.Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty ImagesYemenCivilians among at least 60 killed in Yemen as ground fighting escalatesHouthi rebel offensive against government forces on west coast leads to some of deadliest clashes in yearsWilliam ChristouSat 5 Sep 2026 09.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClashes between Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel movement have killed more than 60 people, including civilians, as theHouthispushed forward with a military offensive on Yemen’s western coast.Twenty-six government troops and 31 Houthi fighters were killed during several hours of fighting in the country’s south-west on Saturday, medical and military sources told Agence France-Presse (AFP). A missile strike also killed six civilians and injured seven others travelling by bus in the city of Taiz.The killings were the latest in a series of bloody clashes in recent days as the Houthis continued an offensive in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah along the Red Sea coast. On Friday, 129 were killed in fighting between rebel and government forces, according to an AFP tally.Iran-aligned Houthis claim they attacked oil refinery in Saudi ArabiaRead moreThe fighting is some of the deadliest in years, after thecollapse in Julyof the 2022 ceasefire. The truce fell apart after an Iranian plane attempted to land in Houthi-controlled Sana’a, triggering attacks by the Yemeni government on the airport.The Houthis are trying to beat back governmental troops to capture strategic hills overlooking Bab al-Mandeb in order to advance towards port cities on the coast. So far, they have managed to capture areas in western Taiz.In Taiz, a government military officer said the “coming hours will be decisive” as the Houthis had taken positions near the city a day before. They added that reinforcements had been arriving from Aden to try to stem the Houthi advance.On Friday, government forces said that they had recaptured the al-Khazan and al-Makahna hills west of Taiz, two strategically important areas for controlling the region.The Houthis had previously controlled the port city of al-Makha overlooking Bab al-Mandeb, before being pushed out by government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition.The Bab al-Mandeb strait is a crucial maritime chokepoint for ships heading to the Suez canal. About 10% of global maritime trade passes through the strait.Saudi Arabiahas been using the strait to export oil for months after the start of the US-Iran war.If shipping is disrupted in Bab al-Mandeb, it will only further raise the cost of global goods, which has already rocketed as a result of the virtual closure of the strait of Hormuz since March 2026.If the Houthis manage to recapture the port city and take key areas along the Red Sea coast, it will help them control naval traffic in the Red Sea. In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, and they have repeatedlydisrupted trafficin solidarity with Gaza since the start of the war there in October 2023.Yemen has been embroiled in a civil war since 2014, when the Houthis and allied forces took the capital city of Sana’a and pushed the then government out of power. A Saudi-led coalition then began a military intervention to support the Yemeni government and fight the Houthis, a strategic ally of Iran.At least 150,000 people in Yemen have been killed in the fighting, and hundreds of thousands more have died from related causes such as hunger and diseases. About 4.5 million people have been displaced by the fighting and more than 18.2 million are in dire need of humanitarian assistance,according to the UN.Explore more on these topicsYemenSaudi ArabiaHouthisIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrike | Israel-Gaza war | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Guardian investigation reveals targeting of World Central Kitchen convoy was result of widely used military tactic
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Exclusive: Guardian investigation reveals targeting of World Central Kitchen convoy was result of widely used military tactic
Content: Top row, from left: Britons James Henderson, James Kirby and John Chapman were killed in the April 2024 Israeli strike on their aid convoy. The other victims were, bottom row, from left: Damian Sobol, Lalzawmi Frankcom, Jacob Flickinger and Saifeddin Abutaha.Composite: World Central Kitchen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTop row, from left: Britons James Henderson, James Kirby and John Chapman were killed in the April 2024 Israeli strike on their aid convoy. The other victims were, bottom row, from left: Damian Sobol, Lalzawmi Frankcom, Jacob Flickinger and Saifeddin Abutaha.Composite: World Central Kitchen/Getty ImagesIsrael-Gaza war‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrikeExclusive: Guardian investigation reveals targeting of World Central Kitchen convoy was result of widely used military tacticDeath on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted WCK aid workersMatan Cohen in Jerusalem, andJulian BorgerSat 5 Sep 2026 07.08 EDTFirst published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven aid workers killed in an airstrike in Gaza were marked as targets under an Israeli military practice of establishing guilt by association, a Guardian investigation shows.A top Israeli military prosecutor announced last month that he would not pursue criminal proceedings for the April 2024 incident in which drones fired missiles at three clearly marked World Central Kitchen (WCK) cars soon after they had escorted a food aid delivery toGaza. Three British humanitarian workers along with an Australian, a Palestinian, a Pole and a dual US-Canadian national were killed.The official Israel Defense Forces (IDF) version of events pointed to specific mistakes made by a handful of officers. The victims of the strike were also blamed for hiring armed guards to protect a food aid convoy and for allegedly “deviating” from their agreed route.Death on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted World Central Kitchen aid workersRead moreHowever, interviews with senior Israeli officers involved in the incident or familiar with the official Israel investigation suggest it glossed over the role played in the killings by a common IDF practice used to designate targets, which endangers aid workers and civilians in general, especially when combined with the army’s open-ended mission to end Hamas’s civil control in Gaza.More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military in the three years of the Gaza war. The army’sown internal datasuggests more than three-quarters of the dead have been civilians.The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, said the WCK workers became potential targets after they had a brief encounter, lasting just minutes, with armed guards assumed to be from Hamas (an assumption later shown to be groundless).He deemed them to have “mixed together” with alleged Hamas militants, where mixing together was defined as being “near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on”. Asked whether the presence of armed men made the entire convoy a target, Mendel replied: “Certainly.”He concluded: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.”View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the Israeli airstrike on the World Central Kitchen convoy in Gaza. Military prosecutors have ruled out criminal charges over the attack that claimed seven lives.Photograph: Ahmed Zakot/ReutersMendel was referring to a general policy ofhaflala, “incrimination”, which gives commanders in the field wide discretion on designating someone as a “terrorist”, including those “incriminated” by association. The manner in whichhaflalais to be applied in a given sector is often conveyed in a commander’s mission brief delivered verbally to other officers.He said his unit had been commended by the army hierarchy for its involvement in several strikes on what were deemed to be Hamas's attempted commandeering of aid. “They applauded us and were pleased with our action,” he said. The difference in the WCK incident was that foreign nationals were killed, he said. “That’s the whole difference. Not a substantive difference.”First location map and timelineWhen the WCK convoy was destroyed, it was nowhere near Israeli troops. Several Israeli officers familiar with the incident said the strikes were not ordered on the basis of an imminent threat to Israeli lives, but to fulfil the mission to thwart Hamas attempts to control aid deliveries.2nd location map and timelineAn IDF statement said the airstrikes were a result of an “erroneous assessment that Hamas military operatives were present in the vehicles, rather than from an intention to target the organisation’s personnel”.The statement added that “this assessment was compounded by serious failures to comply with applicable orders and procedures”. However, it said: “Following an in-depth examination of the findings and in light of the standards applicable under criminal law, it was determined that, despite the aforementioned failures, the circumstances of the incident did not give rise to a reasonable suspicion of a criminal offence warranting the opening of a criminal investigation.”The WCK said the Israeli decision not to pursue criminal proceedings was “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. “At the time of the lethal attacks, our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody,” the WCK said. “The IDF had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”Britain, Australia and Canada denouncedthe prosecutor’s decision as “shameful”, saying they would “continue to seek answers” on behalf of the slain aid workers. The UK opened an inquest in 2024 into the deaths of the three British team members: James Kirby, James Henderson and John Chapman.Saifeddin Abutaha, a Palestinian,Australian Zomi Frankcom, Damian Sobol, a Pole, and a dual Canadian-US citizen, Jacob Flickinger, were the other victims. The UK inquest was adjourned pending the outcome of the Israeli investigation.View image in fullscreenThe funeral in Bristol of James Kirby, 47, in May 2024.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesMendel, who is the only officer of such high rank to have been dismissed for his actions in the Gaza war, has been portrayed in army command briefings as a rogue operator. Questions have been raised about a political motive. Mendel is a settler who is reported to have been one of the 130 signatories of a 20 January 2024 letter to the IDF calling for the flow of aid to Gaza to be restricted.However, the way the Israeli army operates in Gaza – rules of engagement are made contingent on local circumstances and passed on, often verbally, down the chain of command – gives officers at Mendel’s level wide discretion in subjective judgments as to who is a “terrorist” and therefore a target.The IDF statement said its activity in the Gaza Strip was “regulated by a broad range of binding written orders and standing directives governing the use of force, the approval processes for strikes, strikes against sensitive sites, and other matters” and that these incorporated “the rules of the laws of armed conflict, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precautions in attack”.The statement said that “a person does not become a lawful target merely because they are in the vicinity of an armed individual, come into contact with them, or travel alongside them”.The IDF said: “Carrying a weapon may be a relevant factor in such an assessment, but is not sufficient on its own without meeting the definitions described above. In particular, and in the context of the incident in question, security personnel hired to protect a humanitarian convoy from looting do not become lawful targets merely because they are armed.”An IDF officer familiar with the WCK killings said that given the circumstances and the standing IDF procedures, the overwhelming majority of officers would have acted in the same way. “There were armed men next to them,” the officer said. “If you took qualified people and put them on the call, in 90% of cases this is what would have happened,” the officer said. “In my guess, 99% of the time the first bomb would have been dropped; 90% of the time the second; 80% of the time the third.”Reserve Brigadier General Oren Solomon, the battle manager of Gaza Division, said that a mistake had been made in determining that an armed man had entered one of the vehicles, but added that once that error had been committed, the incrimination procedure led inevitably to the three missile strikes.“If I incriminated this vehicle beforehand as Hamas – anyone who escapes from it and enters another vehicle: death comes,” Brig Gen Solomon said. “Together with him they will die. That meets the incrimination rules, no problem.”A senior officer involved in the initial Israeli military investigation into the WCK case, argued Mendel overstepped in interpreting the rules of incrimination.“You can’t incriminate 20 people if there’s one armed,” he said. The officer argued that the first strike could have been justified by the initial misidentification, even at the cost of civilian casualties, but not the subsequent missiles.“You struck someone you suspected, a vehicle you suspected had an armed man in it. The moment two people came out, nobody with a weapon, the second and third strikes are contrary to orders because you don’t know whom you’re striking,” he said.The other systemic factor that contributed to the deaths of the seven aid workers, and potentially countless more civilians, was one of the missions given to the army in Gaza by Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government: to destroy Hamas’s influence and control. That meant anyone deemed to be involved in – or assisting – the Hamas administration, including by distributing aid, could find themselves in the sights of an Israeli drone operator.“I remind you that part of our mission was to crush Hamas’s ability to govern,” Mendel said. “Part of the mission was to hit that [Hamas-controlled aid deliveries], and we hit it.”Interviews with IDF officers suggest there was a widespread belief in the ranks that Hamas had wrested control of the bulk of aid deliveries into Gaza. That assumption was unfounded, later analysis showed. It was a period of widespread hunger caused by an Israeli blockade, when food convoys were being mobbed by desperate civilians, criminal gangs and Hamas militia.The belief that Hamas hijacks were widespread meant that the appearance of armed men in proximity to the WCK vehicle in April 2024 fitted a “pattern of activity” that helped incriminate the whole convoy in the eyes of Mendel and his unit.The IDF officer familiar with the incident said it was common practice to designate any armed man in Gaza as Hamas or a “terrorist”, as Mendel did. The officer added: “How you define that it’s Hamas – he’s in proximity to weapons, and because he touches the trucks, and because he does all sorts of things that look as if he’s going to take over the trucks.”The role of the incrimination principle in the WCK killings shows how it has become a factor in the historically high proportion of civilians killed in the Gaza war. This sits alongside the routine acceptance of high “collateral damage” in the targeting of Hamas militants, the designation of large and shifting areas as free-fire zones, and the deliberate levelling of neighbourhoods to prevent the return of Palestinian communities.The common factor is that constraints on targeting were minimised in the interests of an open-ended mission. Since the start of the war in 2023, no Israeli soldier has been convicted of wrongful death or war crimes in Gaza operations.“I came to defeat Hamas,” Mendel said. “If such an event came before me again, I would do exactly the same thing.”He also dismissed the significance of the killings. “I think it’s an idiotic side event,” Mendel said. “It really isn’t a serious event.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
