title: Gaza refugee says sister-in-law ‘would be alive’ if Home Office had let her come to UK | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, says Home Office refused visa application despite Maryam having cancer
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, says Home Office refused visa application despite Maryam having cancer
Content: Tents sheltering displaced Palestinians amid the ruins of Gaza City. Maryam and her family were sleeping in tents while she had cancer without any medical facilities to treat her.Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/APView image in fullscreenTents sheltering displaced Palestinians amid the ruins of Gaza City. Maryam and her family were sleeping in tents while she had cancer without any medical facilities to treat her.Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/APImmigration and asylumGaza refugee says sister-in-law ‘would be alive’ if Home Office had let her come to UKAnwar, who lives in Glasgow, says Home Office refused visa application despite Maryam having cancerDiane TaylorSat 5 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man living in the UK has said he believes his sister-in-law who died from cancer in Gaza would still be alive today if theHome Officehad agreed to bring her and her family to Britain.Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, fled Gaza in 2020 and was granted refugee status in the UK in 2021. After the destruction of large areas of Gaza by Israeli forces following the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023, he applied to bring his brother Hassan, Hassan’s wife,Maryam, their two young children and other family members to the UK in October 2025. He said the Home Office rejected their application.The process required them to travel to a visa application centre (VAC) for biometric checks, but there was not, and still is not, a VAC inGaza. It is difficult for Palestinians to leave the territory to access a VAC elsewhere.In April this year the family asked the Home Office to waive this requirement and grant permission for “predetermination” of their application and “biometric excusal”.The Home Office is understood to have rejected this request, so the family launched a legal challenge. The Home Office agreed to reconsider its decision but issued a new refusal in July.Prior to the second Home Office refusal, and shortly after Maryam gave birth to Ismail, who is now seven months old, she was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, which had spread to her lungs. Doctors in Gaza said they did not have the facilities to treat her.The family provided the Home Office with medical evidence concerning Maryam’s condition, including cancer test results and medical referral reports. They also provided evidence of their living conditions in Gaza, which involved sleeping in tents and shortages of food, medicine and clean water.Anwar said the Home Office again refused the family’s request for predetermination and biometric excusal but that it accepted the evidence of Maryam’s cancer.In the Home Office’s letter refusing the visa application on 31 July, seen by the Guardian, officials stated: “Given the current situation in Gaza, reliable healthcare may not be accessible.”They accepted that Maryam was facing a significant risk of harm because she was in a conflict zone and could not travel to a VAC. Although the Home Office officials found the circumstances relating to travel to a VAC “somewhat compelling”, they concluded that owing to the difficulty in travelling to the VAC, it was “in the best interests of the children to stay with their parents and delay travel to the UK” for the time being.They concluded the family’s situation did not meet the threshold for “compelling circumstances” and said that pre-entry checks needed to be carried out because the family came from “a territory where terrorists operate”.In the legal challenge, the family’s lawyers stated: “It is difficult to understand what circumstances would ever qualify as compelling if the present circumstances do not.”Maryam died from cancer on 28 August.Gordon McKee, the Labour MP for Glasgow South, raised the family’s case with ministers in June. He warned about Maryam’s deteriorating health and the consequences of the collapse of reliable healthcare in Gaza.In his letter to Mike Tapp, then a Home Office minister, McKee said the case involved “exceptional humanitarian circumstances”. He asked Tapp to consider reviewing the case personally.Anwar said: “We believe Maryam’s case raises serious questions about how the UK government deals with Palestinian families in Gaza who are trying to reunite with their families in Britain, particularly when a family member becomes seriously ill while trapped in a conflict zone and unable to safely reach a VAC.“I believe that if the Home Office had agreed to bring Maryam and her family from Gaza to the UK when we first applied last October, Maryam would still be alive today.“Maryam is now gone, but her family remains in Gaza. We are now urgently asking the UK government to intervene to protect Maryam’s surviving family members and to find a way to bring them to safety and reunite them with their family in the UK.”Speaking from Gaza, Maryam’s husband, Hassan, said: “I am struggling to come to terms with losing my wife while I remain trapped in Gaza with our children, including our seven-month-old baby.“Throughout Maryam’s illness, we were trying to find a way for our family to overcome the biometric requirement and move forward with our applications. The Home Office accepted that Maryam had cancer and acknowledged the evidence, but decided that our circumstances were still not compelling enough to justify biometric deferral or predetermination.“Now I have lost my wife, and I am left trying to protect our children and find a way to get them out of Gaza and to safety.”Home Office sources said they did not routinely comment on individual cases.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeGazaPalestineRefugeesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Death on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted World Central Kitchen aid workers | Israel-Gaza war | The Guardian
description: The Israeli army had helped plan the delivery of food aid on 1 April 2024, but things went wrong from the beginning and ended in seven deaths
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: The Israeli army had helped plan the delivery of food aid on 1 April 2024, but things went wrong from the beginning and ended in seven deaths
Content: A hole in the roof of a WCK vehicle after the attack in April 2024.Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPAView image in fullscreenA hole in the roof of a WCK vehicle after the attack in April 2024.Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPAIsrael-Gaza warDeath on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted World Central Kitchen aid workersThe Israeli army had helped plan the delivery of food aid on 1 April 2024, but things went wrong from the beginning and ended in seven deathsExclusive: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrikeJulian Borgerand Matan Cohen in JerusalemFri 4 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 00.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the evening of 1 April 2024, a team of aid workers from World Central Kitchen (WCK) stood on Gaza’s Mediterranean shore overseeing the unloading of a barge full of desperately needed food on a makeshift jetty made of sand and rubble.The Gaza war had been raging for six months and Israel’s closure of land crossings had left the whole territory facing the threat of famine. WCK and local Palestinian contractors had constructed the jetty out of everything they could lay their hands on, including debris from the bombed house of one of the contractors, so that the pallets of humanitarian assistance could be delivered by boat from Cyprus.A consignment of 200 tonnes of rice, flour and other proteins had arrived two weeks earlier, the first sea shipment to dock in Gaza since 2007. This was the second shipment and it was even bigger, with enough food to prepare more than 1m meals, as well as a Ramadan gift of dates from the United Arab Emirates.‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrikeRead moreThe choreography of the delivery had been coordinated over several days with the Israeli army, and an officer was on the jetty to observe the proceedings. In the midst of a devastating bombing campaign after the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023, this humanitarian effort was supposed to be carried out under internationally agreed military protection.The shipment had been unloaded by 8.30pm but despite the lengthy planning, there was a delay in receiving final Israeli security clearance for the eight hired trucks and two WCK escort vehicles to leave the jetty. By the time the green light came from local Israeli commanders and the convoy began to move south, night had fallen.There was no initial overhead surveillance but two drones joined somewhere along the route to the first stop, a WCK welcome centre 6 miles to the south. Those drones were assigned to the Israel Defense Forces’ (IDF) Nahal brigade, which had not been fully briefed on the aid convoy’s itinerary.A special adviser assigned by the Australian government to assess the case (in the interests of justice for the Australian victim Lalzawmi Frankcom), found that “specific details about the pre-coordinated WCK aid mission had not been passed down from higher levels of Southern Command to the brigade and UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] operator”.Local guardsAt the WCK welcome centre, a few local men hired as guards were waiting, at least one of them armed. At a time of widespread hunger, many food convoys had been mobbed by desperate crowds as well as organised gangs, some of whom may have had been linked to Hamas, though Hamas never had the grip on food deliveries alleged by the Israeli authorities.Using local security for aid deliveries was not unknown in Gaza, but it was directly against WCK policy to use armed escorts. The WCK says it is unclear why the local team on that night agreed to accept armed guards. The official Israeli version of events suggests it was “due to the convoy’s delayed departure, during night-time hours,” and noted it “was not coordinated with IDF authorities”.The official Israeli version does not say how many armed men were waiting for the convoy (unofficial versions vary between two and four), but drone footage reportedly showed one of them climb on top of the cabin of one of the trucks and fire a shot in the air shortly afterwards, for reasons that remain unknown.The Nahal brigade officers and the drone operators assigned to them concluded it was a Hamas hijack, based in part on the false assumption that such hijackings were commonplace.“The troops also identified vehicles surrounding the trucks in a manner that, in their assessment and based on accumulated operational experience, corresponded to a scenario in which the Hamas terrorist organisation had taken control of the convoy,” the official account says.View image in fullscreenThree WCK vehicles were struck, each about two minutes apart.Photograph: Ahmed Zakot/ReutersThe Israeli military prosecutor’s version of events, published last month to justify his decision not to pursue criminal proceedings, does not mention the breakdown in communication between the army’s coordination and liaison administration, which handles humanitarian needs in the territory, and the Nahal brigade controlling that sector of the Gaza Strip.Furthermore, the prosecutor’s version says efforts by IDF personnel to contact WCK were unsuccessful. But according to WCK sources and the Australian report on events, contact was established that night with WCK headquarters in the US, which in turn got in touch with an employee in Gaza.According to the Australian report, the WCK worker on the ground told headquarters staff the guards only had “fake guns”. It remains unclear what the basis for that claim was, but the WCK assured the IDF that it had not lost contact with the convoy and it had not been hijacked.Arrival at destinationIt is unclear whether this exchange with WCK was relayed to the Nahal brigade before the strikes. But even if it was not, the fact that the convoy of eight food trucks continued on its journey and arrived at its intended destination, the WCK warehouse in Deir al-Balah, should have been ample proof that the aid had not been seized by Hamas.The military prosecutor’s summary acknowledges that the “convoy arrived at the designated warehouse and unloaded the aid” but does not address the seemingly straightforward conclusion that it had therefore not been diverted. The IDF has yet to release audio recordings of military communications that night.Route mapAfter the trucks entered the warehouse, the WCK workers and the local guards stayed outside by their own vehicles for about 10 minutes. That short period, observed by operators of Israeli drones, appears to have helped seal the aid workers’ fate. As far as the Nahal brigade’s chief of staff, reserve Col Nochi Mendel, was concerned, they were “mingling” with Hamas.Under the very loose procedures of “incrimination” that delegate much to the discretion of field commanders like Mendel, the WCK workers became unwitting targets as they celebrated the completion of a successful delivery of aid, because they were in the proximity to armed men.“There was incrimination. The incrimination was according to the rules,” Mendel said. “There were armed men there with certainty. With certainty, they [the aid workers] had mingled with armed Hamas men.”Attack mapOther IDF officers have confirmed to the Guardian that such a process of guilt by association is used widely to determine targets, though different field commanders use different standards in making decisions. The Israel military prosecutor, in making his assessment on criminal responsibility, did not address the practice of incrimination in targeting.Parting of waysAfter the brief pause outside the WCK warehouse in Deir al-Balah, the guards and the WCK workers went in separate directions. “The WCK vehicles departed together west towards the coast. Concurrently, the vehicle containing the locally contracted security personnel, including the previously identified gunmen, drove north,” the Australian report says. It also makes clear that the IDF was aware of this parting of the two groups.“One UAV tracked the locally contracted security vehicle heading north for approximately three minutes until it arrived at another warehouse where up to four gunmen were identified exiting the vehicle and entering the building,” the report says. “A decision was made to discontinue targeting them due to the time available before they entered the northern warehouse.”The military prosecutor’s version makes no mention of this drone or the fact that the suspected gunmen were seen driving off in a different direction and entering a separate building. It claims instead that “several individuals mistakenly … identified as armed persons” were observed getting into WCK vehicles.That is at odds with the Australian report and the accounts of Israeli officers familiar with the investigation. They said a bag was spotted by a drone operator being put in a WCK car, and that the operator mistook it for a gun, though sources briefed on the drone video said that later analysis showed no sign of a suspicious bag.Whether or not it was a gun was irrelevant as far as Mendel was concerned. He saw his task as carrying out the government policy of crushing Hamas governance in Gaza, which included stopping its seizure of aid deliveries.“If a Hamas operative takes over a truck and after that he sells it and that’s how he recruits more people, then what does it matter if he’s armed or not?” Mendel said.In its economical, dry prose, the Australian report describes what happened next as the WCK workers left the warehouse at about 11pm. “The WCK vehicles proceeded west to the coast. Due to the time delays encountered, rather than return to the WCK welcome centre as planned, a decision was made to return directly to the accommodation in Rafah,” the report says.“After turning south on to the coast road, the three WCK vehicles were struck in relatively quick succession, each strike being approximately two minutes apart. There were two survivors from the strike on the first (up-armoured) vehicle who quickly moved to the second vehicle, then two survivors from the second (up-armoured) vehicle who moved to the third vehicle. There were no survivors from the third (soft-skinned) vehicle. Over the four-minute period 23:09 – 23:13, the seven WCK workers were killed – likely one in the first vehicle, two in the second and four in the last.”The seven victims of the IDF drone strikes were from the UK, Australia, Poland,Palestineand the US. The Britons John Chapman, James Kirby and James Henderson were working as security consultants. Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha, a Palestinian driver and translator, was the youngest killed, at 25. Frankcom, Damian Soból, a Pole, and Jacob Flickinger, a US-Canadian dual citizen, were humanitarian workers for WCK.View image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha, Lalzawmi ‘Zomi’ Frankcom, Damian Soból, Jacob Flickinger, James Kirby, James Henderson, John Chapman.Composite: WCK via APThe military prosecutor claimed that in turning south towards Rafah, the WCK workers were “deviating from the route that the organisation had coordinated in advance with the IDF”, giving weight to the Nahal brigade’s mistaken impression that “Hamas operatives had taken control of the convoy”.Mendel also mentioned this “deviation” as a mitigating factor. However, the Australian report found that the fact that the WCK workers had changed their route only became known after they were killed, and “as such it did not play a factor” in the decision to open fire.The official Israeli version of events says Mendel and his brigade fire support commander ignored an order on the night of the airstrike from a superior officer to cease any attacks on humanitarian convoys, but Mendel has said the order is a fabrication.“It never happened, never existed,” Mendel said. “No operational directive reached the brigade to cease the strikes … We checked it a thousand times.”In explaining his own decision-making, Mendel stressed he was carrying out Israeli government policy by stopping Hamas taking control of food deliveries. He had been lauded by his superiors for ordering strikes on several earlier alleged Hamas attempts to hijack aid. In his mind, the events on the night of 1 April 2024 fitted the same pattern.“I didn’t plan to kill the aid workers,” Mendel said, but added: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.”Justifying this conclusion, he said: “They were mixed together with Hamas operatives …near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on.”In a written statement, WCK said: “It is extraordinary to learn now that some in the IDF considered our humanitarian work to be enemy activity based on the flimsiest evidence, or no evidence at all.“This undefined, unjustified and unlawful view is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. The IDF’s shifting excuses and explanations for these unlawful airstrikes are precisely why we continue to demand an independent investigation with the full release of the IDF’s evidence.”Explore more on these topicsIsrael-Gaza warGazaPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: London Paddington fire causes rail chaos as Heathrow trains cancelled | Public transport | The Guardian
description: Blaze causes electricity supply failure and disruption of services to airport and Reading
Author: Angus Thomson
Headline: Blaze causes electricity supply failure and disruption of services to airport and Reading
Content: Passengers in Paddington station, London after a fire near a train track in the area caused major disruption.Photograph: Mathilde Grandjean/PAView image in fullscreenPassengers in Paddington station, London after a fire near a train track in the area caused major disruption.Photograph: Mathilde Grandjean/PAPublic transportLondon Paddington fire causes rail chaos as Heathrow trains cancelledBlaze causes electricity supply failure and disruption of services to airport and ReadingAngus Thomsonand agencySat 5 Sep 2026 18.18 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 14.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of passengers were evacuated from a train, and services to Heathrow airport were cancelled, after a fire near tracks in theLondonPaddington area caused major disruptions to London’s rail network.The fire caused an electricity supply failure which left all lines between Paddington and the airport blocked, National Rail said on Saturday afternoon.Photographs on social media showed large plumes of smoke rising from the Paddington area.London fire brigade was called to the grass fire near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington, just after 4pm on Saturday, with six fire engines and 40 crew tackling the blaze.Fire crews were also called upon to help evacuate 380 passengers left stranded on an Elizabeth line train.The Elizabeth line was suspended between Paddington and Heathrow Terminals 4 and 5, and between Paddington and Reading, while the line to Abbey Wood also experienced severe delays.Passengers travelling to the airport were advised to use the Piccadilly line, although that line also experienced severe delays between Heathrow and Acton Town. There were minor delays along the rest of the line due to an earlier trespasser at Hammersmith,Transportfor London (TfL) said.Heathrow airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys.Great Western Railway (GWR) services to Reading were cancelled, and disruptions were expected until the end of Saturday.Explore more on these topicsPublic transportTransportLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mental health groups have ‘failed to acknowledge’ risk of violence, says Mind chief | Mental health | The Guardian
description: Sector has avoided issue because of stigma fears, expert warns ahead of closure of Nottingham attacks inquiry
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Sector has avoided issue because of stigma fears, expert warns ahead of closure of Nottingham attacks inquiry
Content: Ian Coates, Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, who were killed by Valdo Colocane. He was later diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.Composite: Nottinghamshire PoliceView image in fullscreenIan Coates, Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, who were killed by Valdo Colocane. He was later diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.Composite: Nottinghamshire PoliceMental healthMental health groups have ‘failed to acknowledge’ risk of violence, says Mind chiefSector has avoided issue because of stigma fears, expert warns ahead of closure of Nottingham attacks inquiryNeha GohilMidlands correspondentSat 5 Sep 2026 16.43 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMental health organisations have “failed to acknowledge” the risk of violence from a minority of people with severe mental illnesses, the chief executive of Mind has said ahead of the closure of the inquiry into the Nottingham attacks.Dr Sarah Hughes, who has led mental health charity Mind for four years and has worked in the sector for almost four decades, said charities had shied away from addressing the risk of violence due to the fact it had increased the stigma and harassment around people with mental health conditions.The inquiry into theNottinghamattacks is examining the events leading up to 13 June 2023, when 19-year-old students Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, and 65-year-old caretaker Ian Coates, were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, who was later diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.In 2024, Calocane was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order after admitting three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility and three counts of attempted murder.The public inquiry has heard evidence from various local authorities, including health professionals and police officers, as well as Calocane’s family, in order to assess the “events, acts and omissions” that led to the killings.The inquiry heard how Calocane had committed a string of violent incidents in the years before the attacks, repeatedly refused to take medication, and was sectioned four times in the space of two years. During her evidence, Calocane’s mother described the mental health system as “so broken”.View image in fullscreenDr Sarah Hughes, chief executive officer of Mind.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The GuardianSpeaking exclusively to the Guardian, Hughes said charities specialising in mental health had to become “more comfortable” with discussing the risk of violence that could exist from a minority of people with mental health illnesses.Hughes’s comments come after the charity Mind held a roundtable with experts in Westminster to discuss the role mental health services needed to play to keep the public and patients safe.“We, as a charity sector, have failed to acknowledge that violence does happen in some circumstances,” she said. “As a sector, [we] have held the narrative that the majority of people don’t commit violent crime. However, some do and the consequences are grave.”Hughes added: “My feeling is that we haven’t always been able to articulate the topic of violence and mental health well to the public and ultimately, we have softened the truth. Stigma and discrimination are incredibly harmful, however our efforts to reduce them have, at times, meant that some of the most difficult topics have been brushed under the carpet. That’s why it’s so important to bring together a wide range of experts and experiences to have an open and honest conversation.”NHS trust investigated for corporate manslaughter after Nottingham attacksRead moreEmma Webber, whose son Barnaby was killed by Calocane, said she welcomed the statement by Hughes. “I do feel like danger to others has been almost deliberately quietened down in the conversation in the past,” she said.Webber said there had not been enough acknowledgment from mental health organisations of the risk of violence.“It could be a really powerful voice for the charities to have that difficult conversation, and to not be fearful of saying about the risks of violence toward others, and that people that are mentally ill, like Calocane, can and do go on to kill.“Obviously the vast majority of people with mental health issues in this country are completely safe … but if somebody’s dangerous, they’re dangerous.“Had the risks in Calocane’s case been understood, then I genuinely believe we wouldn’t be having this conversation today.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCeleste Calocane giving evidence to the inquiry in May.Photograph: The Nottingham Inquiry/PASeena Fazel, a professor of forensic psychiatry at the University of Oxford who attended the event by Mind, said a minority of people with mental illnesses perpetrate violent acts and high-quality research on schizophrenia had “converged on the same picture”.“People with schizophrenia do have an elevated risk of violence compared with the general population, even after accounting for socioeconomic factors, but the absolute risk is small. Only a minority will commit a serious violent act,” he said.“That risk increases when other factors are present, particularly drug or alcohol problems, a history of violence, or having been a victim of violence themselves. The important point is that treatments we already have, and which are widely available, can bring that risk down.”Hughes, who said she had experienced violence when she was a mental health practitioner from people experiencing psychosis, said many in the sector feared that addressing such issues could increase stigma and discrimination, and that could lead to dangerous health outcomes.“We are incredibly frightened of deepening that stigma and discrimination because we know how dangerous it can be,” she said. “This could risk going back to a more restrictive approach. My view is that’s not the answer, but stigma creates a pathway to that as being the only solution to this problem.”Hughes said this meant the sector had “shied away” from difficult conversations around violence. “The public, I think, are more ready [and] we’ve got to get our act together,” she said. “Even within Mind there was a reluctance internally and we had to really talk it though.”Hughes said the UK government’s upcoming mental health strategy must improve support and treatment for those with severe mental illnesses, as well as address matters of public safety.This includes ensuring an adequate number of beds in hospitals, assertive outreach, and accountability and communication with services.“I hope that by us having these conversations openly we can both make sure that the people we’re advocating for know that we’re doing this safely with their consent, but equally, the public and families and victims know that we recognise that we have to come together to solve this problem,” Hughes said.“Crucially, there is a role for Mind – and the sector as a whole – to show that patient and public safety are not mutually exclusive. Both are possible if we want to change our mental health system so people can get the right care before or after reaching crisis point,” she added.Explore more on these topicsMental healthCharitiesEnglandHealthNottinghamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Black-clad protesters in balaclavas block road at port of Dover in Kent | Kent | The Guardian
description: Port authorities say access roads ‘free flowing’ again after large group forces road closures in both directions
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Port authorities say access roads ‘free flowing’ again after large group forces road closures in both directions
Content: Balaclava-wearing protesters blocking a road in Dover on Saturday.Photograph: SWNSView image in fullscreenBalaclava-wearing protesters blocking a road in Dover on Saturday.Photograph: SWNSKentBlack-clad protesters in balaclavas block road at port of Dover in KentPort authorities say access roads ‘free flowing’ again after large group forces road closures in both directionsDonna Ferguson,Priya Bharadiaand agenciesSat 5 Sep 2026 15.57 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 04.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDozens of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road at the port of Dover inKent, forcing closures in both directions on Saturday morning.Kent police said they were were in attendance and engaging with the protest, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. No arrests were made during the incident. Responsibility for the demonstration appears to have been claimed by an anti-immigration group with links to the far right.The behaviour of the participants and the travel disruption they have caused has been condemned by the government. Traffic in and out of the port on the A20 was stopped, causing delays of up to 30 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways.Videos shared online showed a large number ofmasked people in black marching on the road in a large group as lorries waited in traffic next to police cars.By lunchtime, the protesters had dispersed and access roads to the port were “free flowing”, according to the Port of Dover. Ferry operators pledged to put those who had been delayed by the disruption on to the next available sailings.View image in fullscreenMasked people on the road in Dover.Photograph: Ay_audits/YouTubeThe number of people involved was not immediately clear. One livestreamer estimated he was marching with hundreds of people but police did not give an official estimate.Social media videos showed demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20 and chanting “stop the boats”and “England till I die.”A group called Patriot Platform, which styles itself as having “a fierce love for our homeland”, claimed responsibility for the blockade.The far-right activistTommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, reposted videos of the blockade, highlighting a live stream of the protest that directed viewers towards Patriot Platform.In his post, Robinson encouraged more to join, saying: “Get there to support them.”In another post, he wrote: “Simultaneously at different locations across Dover patriots have mobilised to close down the port. There are 3 plus locations that patriots have shut down so far with many more planned to be closed. People wanted action I’m guessing there are 100,000s of men willing to fill their shoes.”Map including DoverThe founder of Patriot Platform, Danny Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, wrote on social media “live Dover somethings [sic] happening” and posted a live stream.In a video posted on 2 September, he told his followers he was meeting with “a huge group [of] top, proper patriots” to prepare for a message he was planning to send to the government.“Very, very soon, we are going to send a message that will make sure they understand that we will not go down without a fight. We will not allow our nation to be plagued in the way that it is.“And when you see it and when you feel it, I guarantee the whole thing will change for the better. Because once the message is sent once, imagine the sheer numbers that will be sent on the second, the third, the fourth message.”In further comments, he said: “From the hills of Scotland to the fields of Wales to the streets of Northern Ireland and to the towns and cities of England, we are building something that’s never been built before.“And when you’re part of it and you see what’s about to go down, you will understand … we’re about to show you what can be done when men and women of this country, who have the blood that runs through them like their grandfathers, get off their asses and do something about it.”View image in fullscreenBalaclava-wearing protesters gather earlier on Saturday.Photograph: Ay_audits/YouTubeOn Saturday morning, the Port of Dover confirmed in a statement that the disruption was affecting “all routes” in and out, as well as around the town.Nathan Ditchburn, who was on his way to work when he saw the group arrive at about 6.45am, told KentOnline: “I would say there are around 300 men, maybe more. Nobody will speak; they just handed me a piece of paper to look at. They have blocked off every entrance and exit of the Dover port area.”One woman, who asked to remain anonymous, said: “I was at Dover port this morning, trying to get on a ferry to France. In the end we left and returned home – it wasn’t worth our while, we were only going to Lille for the day.“But the headlines calling it a ‘protest’ suggest something very different to what took place – which looked like a highly organised event.“Masked teenagers in black clothes were coordinated by walkie-talkie and I directly witnessed an older man, not in black, on an electric bike – coordinating in plain sight and being applauded by the masked teenagers as he gave them the thumbs up for their ‘good work’.“The guy on the bike then went to the nearest police stop, [he was] obviously monitoring and reporting police activity.“There were no banners and no slogans, just pure intimidation. It was a demonstration only in the sense that they wanted to demonstrate their power and to intimidate.”Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, criticised what he described as “idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption”. In a post on Facebook, he said: “Parkrun cancelled and port access disrupted. I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption.“I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossings are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess. Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.”Chris Vinson, the leader of the Conservative group on Dover district council, said the protest appeared to be “illegal migration-related”, but said the demonstrators did not appear to have placards or banners.“I’m not aware that there’s been any violence, although clearly, having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating, especially when it’s not clear why they’re there, and the police weren’t aware and so haven’t been able to warn people in advance and make sure that they are made to feel safe.”A Home Office spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused.“We appreciate the frustration of those who have been impacted today. Access to the port is now restored and traffic is flowing. Those travelling to the port are advised to allow for extra travel time and to follow guidance from providers.”The shipping company DFDS and P&O Ferries said they would offer customers whose journeys were disrupted access to the next available departure.Explore more on these topicsKentTransportProtestTommy RobinsonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage brushes aside Reform controversies in closing conference speech – UK politics as it happened | Politics | The Guardian
description: ‘Sometimes we will get things wrong and get a bit of a kicking for it,’ party leader tells gathering in Birmingham
Author: Taz Ali
Headline: ‘Sometimes we will get things wrong and get a bit of a kicking for it,’ party leader tells gathering in Birmingham
Content: 11.43 EDT'Sometimes we will get things wrong,' says Farage in conference closing speechReform UK leader Nigel Farage has downplayedthe controversies that overshadowed his party’s conference yesterday.“Much of mainstream media today says theReform UKconference was subdued,” he told audience members in his closing remarks. “Are you subdued?”He continued:double quotation markI tell you what we learned yesterday and today. There will be times in this journey when there are good days, and times when there are difficult days.More often than not, things will be put upon us that are unfair. But sometimes we will make mistakes, sometimes we will get things wrong and get a bit of a kicking for it.But what this conference has shown is whatever you throw at the leadership, whatever you throw at the people’s army, we immediately pick ourselves up, dust ourselves down and start all over again.”Nigel Farage delivering his closing speech at the Reform UK conference in Birmingham.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAShareUpdated at11.46 EDT

title: ‘I wasn’t even listening,’ Farage says of donations scandal meeting  | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Reform UK leader maintains innocence in overseas funding controversy on last day of party conference
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Reform UK leader maintains innocence in overseas funding controversy on last day of party conference
Content: Farage’s party had been hoping to move the focus to policy announcements as Reform’s conference closed in Birmingham on Saturday.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFarage’s party had been hoping to move the focus to policy announcements as Reform’s conference closed in Birmingham on Saturday.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianNigel Farage‘I wasn’t even listening,’ Farage says of donations scandal meetingReform UK leader maintains innocence in overseas funding controversy on last day of party conferenceBen QuinnandPeter WalkerSat 5 Sep 2026 12.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage has claimed that he “wasn’t even listening” during a meeting at the centre of a controversy about whether his party considered evading the law on accepting donations from overseas.TheReform UKleader also claimed he knew donation law “better than anybody” during interviews as he sought to salvage the final day of his party conference from the fallout that has already cost him two of his closest aides.The two-year trail of financial controversy dogging Reform and FarageRead moreFarage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes andReform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigationappearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.The undercover reporters from a group called Verbatim posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party when it was published in national newspapers.The Reform leader himself remains under pressure over a separate clip in which he was heard saying “it’s all above board” after one of the reporters who was posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy US backer told Farage he had been in discussions with Jukes and Orr for some time.“I’ll be the registered donor,” the son says. “But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that’s done and all those conversations are had the money is available.”In an interview on Saturday, Farage told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that “of course” he knew it was illegal for foreign firms to donate to UK parties, adding he was told the money was being given via a UK family office.When challenged by Kuenssberg that while in Farage’s presence, one of the undercover reporters had said they “run an American family office”, the Reform leader said: “I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton byelection. I turn up. I frankly wasn’t even listening.”He added: “I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore. The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have come from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.”Farage’s party had been hoping to move the focus to policy announcements, including on tax cuts, as Reform’s conference closed in Birmingham on Saturday.View image in fullscreenReform MP Robert Jenrick addresses the conferencePhotograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianIts Treasury spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, gave a keynote speech in which he pledged to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 within the first 100 days if the party were to take office. The threshold has been set at £12,570 since 2021 and is due to remain there until 2031.But in interviews given earlier in the day to trail the policy, he also found himself forced to deflect from the donations controversy. “That’s been dealt with,” he told GB News. “The two individuals concerned have gone, and we’re here today moving forward. The language that they used was clearly inappropriate, that was very disappointing.”In an interview with Times Radio he said Orr and Jukes had been “permanently suspended”, appearing to differ from the latest party line that they had “stepped down pending outcome of an investigation”, indicating a possible way back.Farage meanwhile accused “the establishment” of trying to derail Reform UK, when challenged by ITV’s Robert Peston on thestring of allegations related to his and the party’s finances.“And it will go on. You come back and see me in six months, there’ll be five more investigations. It won’t end. This won’t end,” he said.Farage said he had some “thoughtful” moments over the summer, claiming his family had been asking him to “walk away” from politics amid pressure on them and him.Despite Reform’s efforts to insulate Farage, the Met police are now assessing evidence after a complaint that the Reform leader, as well as Orr and Jukes,may have broken political funding laws. They all deny wrongdoing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe final day of the conference also coincided with an appeal by West Midlands police for a woman, who was among climate activists who were removed from the hall on Friday as they heckled Farage’s speech, to come forward after footage emerged over her allegedly being assaulted.The police initially responded on X to a clip that appeared to show audience members pulling her hair and grabbing her head as she was carried out of the conference hall. West Midlands police later said in a statement that they were aware of a video circulating from the Reform UK conference showing an incident with a protester, and had asked the woman to come forward.The activist group Climate Resistance, which claimed responsibility for the protest during Farage’s speech , said the protester was considering whether to speak to police.View image in fullscreenA heckler is carried out during Nigel Farage’s keynote speech on the second day of Reform UK Annual Conference at NEC in Birmingham, Britain, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPANadine Dorries, a former Conservative MP who has joined Reform, said sensitivities were “heightened” in the aftermath of the killing of the Reform spokesperson Ann Widdecombe in July.“They tried to completely derail the speech. It was an organised sting again,” she said in an interview with LBC when asked about the incident.Also speaking on Saturday was Suella Braverman, the party’s education spokesperson who, like Jenrick, is another defector from the Conservatives.Her speech announced a planned cut of 20% to the number of student loans given, with funds only granted to university courses that can demonstrate good economic returns, with exceptions for some courses “of strategic or cultural importance”.View image in fullscreenThe Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, closed the conference with some final comments.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianFarage ended the conference with closing comments to the main hall, where sections of seating were unoccupied and the mood was more subdued than earlier in the event, by telling the Reform faithful that “there would be good days and bad days”.“Sometimes we will get things wrong and get a bit of a kicking, but what this conference has shown is that whatever you throw at the leadership, whatever you throw at you, the people’s army, we immediately stop, pick ourselves up and start all over again,” he said.Get in touchContact Guardian Politics about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. title: Falling ceiling debris at Kennedy Center may mire debate over renovations | Washington DC | The Guardian
description: Preservationists worry board may seize on incident ‘to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down’
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Preservationists worry board may seize on incident ‘to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down’
Content: The Kennedy Center in Washington DC on 27 August.Photograph: Pablo Martínez Monsiváis/APView image in fullscreenThe Kennedy Center in Washington DC on 27 August.Photograph: Pablo Martínez Monsiváis/APWashington DCFalling ceiling debris at Kennedy Center may mire debate over renovationsPreservationists worry board may seize on incident ‘to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down’Edward HelmoreSat 5 Sep 2026 19.21 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 19.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFalling debris from a ceiling in the grand foyer of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts may have complicated a battle over renovations of theWashington DCarts center that could result in the building being demolished.A portion of the ceiling collapsed on Friday evening after heavy rain swept through the area, prompting officials to temporarily close the Edward Durell Stone-designed building. No one was injured by the debris.Kennedy Center officialsposted onlineon Saturday that the incident showed renovations to the building were urgently needed – an argument that Donald Trump has made in concert with a broader second-term agenda to reshape Washington.“Another warning we can’t ignore,” the Kennedy Center said in the post. “A section of the Grand Foyer ceiling collapsed after this week’s storms. Thankfully no one was hurt. Decades of deferred maintenance made this inevitable.”View image in fullscreenThe grand foyer at the Kennedy Center in Washington DC on 27 August.Photograph: Pablo Martínez Monsiváis/APRoma Daravi, the center’s vice-president for public relations, said in a statement that the collapse was “another example of the urgent need to close for renovation and revitalization, as our Chairman President Trump has championed”.Alongside the White House ballroom, a proposed triumphal arch, fitful renovations to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool and a remodeled golf course on the banks of the Potomac, the Kennedy Center has become a significant project for the president.The Trump-aligned board has proposed adding Trump’s name to the building’s facade and to close the center for two years as it undergoes $250m in renovations.Last month, a federal judge expressed doubts about the Kennedy Center’s stated intention to return Trump’s name to the building after a district court blocked the renovations and said Trump’s name had been added to the center illegally and ordered it to be removed.The board voted earlier this month to inscribe “The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J Trump” on the facade by 8 September.If a fund for the renovations reaches $100m, another inscription would be added, reading: “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” Congress has approved $257m for the project, and theTrump administrationwants to raise an additional $500m through private donations.Administration attorneys have argued that without Trump’s name on the building it would struggle to raise money for renovations.Without the Trump-backed funding, they argue, the building “will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years”.Last week a sculpture titled Blue by American post-minimalist Joel Shapiro was taken down. The Kennedy Center offered no reason for its removal, but said in a statement “we are honored to have been stewards” of the work.Friday’s debris shower may strengthen the center’s position that the building needs a complete overhaul. Grace Terpstra of Keep the KC, a group fighting the center’s closure, told the Associated Press that the board may seize on the incident “to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down, that it’s going to fall on everybody”.“I think they’ll try to make it into a bigger thing and show that they’ve found a lot of other things,” said Terpstra.Explore more on these topicsWashington DCArts and humanitiesTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican | US news | The Guardian
description: Latest data from Gallup, showing 49% leaning Democrat and 39% Republican, marks sharp reversal from 2024
Author: Roque Planas
Headline: Latest data from Gallup, showing 49% leaning Democrat and 39% Republican, marks sharp reversal from 2024
Content: A polling station in North Carolina on 3 March.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersView image in fullscreenA polling station in North Carolina on 3 March.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersUS newsMore voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves RepublicanLatest data from Gallup, showing 49% leaning Democrat and 39% Republican, marks sharp reversal from 2024Roque PlanasSat 5 Sep 2026 17.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves Republican, according to thelatest quarterly data published by Gallup.Some 49% of voters surveyed leaned Democrat, including independent voters asked to pick one party or the other. Only 39% of respondents leaned Republican.That 10-point spread marks a sharp reversal from the four-point advantage that Republicans held over Democrats in the fourth quarter of 2024, when voters sent Donald Trump back to the White House and Republicans swept both houses of Congress. Democrats are seeing their most sizable advantage since 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president,according to the New York Times.The data offers the latest evidence that Trump’s second term has proved unpopular with voters, driving a potential backlash.Trump’s approvalrating stood at 52%at the time of his second inauguration in January of 2025, according to an average of polls published by the New York Times.But his popularity dwindled immediately, as he cleaved the federal workforce, imposed price-inflating tariffs, passed a profligate spending bill and launched a rudderless war with Iran. Some 58% of voters now disapprove of his performance, with only 38% approving, according to the Times.Democrats are hoping to take advantage of Trump’s tanking popularity. Liberals are likely to retake the US House of Representatives in midterm elections this November. The party is much less certain to retake the US Senate, though polling is giving Democratsreasonstofeel optimistic.A growing share of American voters have not identified with either party in recent years. Back in 2002, roughly a third of voterssurveyed by Gallupidentified as either Republican, Democrat or independent. By last year, 45% of respondents called themselves independents, with only 27% identifying as either Democrat or Republican.Explore more on these topicsUS newsDemocratsRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Robin Morgan, child star who became feminist, poet and editor, dies aged 85 | US news | The Guardian
description: Leading second-wave feminist co-founded Women’s Media Center with Jane Fonda and Gloria Steinem
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Leading second-wave feminist co-founded Women’s Media Center with Jane Fonda and Gloria Steinem
Content: Robin Morgan at the Milford readers and writers festival in Milford, Pennsylvania, on 16 September 2017.Photograph: Zuma Press Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenRobin Morgan at the Milford readers and writers festival in Milford, Pennsylvania, on 16 September 2017.Photograph: Zuma Press Inc/AlamyUS newsRobin Morgan, child star who became feminist, poet and editor, dies aged 85Leading second-wave feminist co-founded Women’s Media Center with Jane Fonda and Gloria SteinemAssociated PressSat 5 Sep 2026 14.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobin Morgan, a child star of the 1940s and 50s who grew up to become an all-American radical as a poet, essayist, editor and second-wave feminist, has died. She was 85.Morgan’s death was confirmed Saturday by the Women’s Media Center, an organization she co-founded with Jane Fonda and the celebrated author and activistGloria Steinem, who died Wednesday.During the 1960s and 70s, Morgan embodied and inspired historic changes in how women lived and thought. As she was happy to point out, the one-time “ideal American girl” and adored “little Robin Morgan” was a rule breaker and justice seeker with a notable list of achievements, along with a prison record and an FBI file.Julie Burton, president of the Women’s Media Center, called Morgan “one of the architects of the contemporary women’s movement”, hailing her writing and “global leadership for justice and equality”. The statement didn’t specify the location, date or cause of Morgan’s death.Morgan was at the center of some of the defining moments of what came to be called second-wave feminism, expanding upon the achievements of the suffragists a half-century earlier. In 1968, she was among the organizers of the first protest against the Miss America pageant, joining fellow activists in tossing their bras (soon mythologized as burning) into a “freedom trash can”. The 1970 essay anthology she edited, Sisterhood Is Powerful, is considered one of the essential texts of the modern women’s movement.Robin Morgan, age 75, on voting for a female presidentGuardianHer legacy was one of deeds, words and images. Morgan is widely credited with coining the term “herstory”, the feminist reworking of “history”, and popularizing the clenched fist/female symbol icon of the liberation movement. Her poem Monster, with such lines as “I want a women’s revolution like a lover/I lust for it” was quoted at feminist rallies and beyond. Her poem Arraignment helped capture the movement’s embrace of the late Sylvia Plath and condemnation of her husband, poet Ted Hughes, whom Morgan and others blamed for Plath’s suicide in 1963. Morgan’s rhyming couplet “I accuse/Ted Hughes” inspired the title for Sonic Youth’s song J’Accuse Ted Hughes.Labeled an “anarchist housewife” in one government report, Morgan confronted the establishment, left and right. In 1970, she and fellow protesters were arrested and jailed after occupying the offices of the avant garde Grove Press, whose owner, Barney Rosset, was fighting employees’ efforts to unionize. In the widely reprinted 1970 essay Goodbye to All That, she called out activists and libertines from Abbie Hoffman and Hugh Hefner to Dave Dellinger and the music group the Fugs.View image in fullscreenMorgan, then the editor-in-chief of Ms, celebrates the magazine’s spring comeback in her New York office on 28 February 1990.Photograph: Susan Ragan/APIn her personal life, Morgan had male and female lovers and was married for more than 20 years to the gay poet Kenneth Pitchford, with whom she had a son, the musician, activist and record company executive Blake Morgan. She once described her marriage as a “two-member commune” and was so resistant to labels that she remembered being “straight-baited” by feminists who thought she should be a lesbian and chastised by conservatives who assumed she was a lesbian.In her 2001 memoir Saturday’s Child, she expressed joy and amazement at how her life had turned out and how she was able to retain “a threadbare, somewhat surreal sense of humor”.“Put that in your apple pie and smoke it,” she wrote.Besides Saturday’s Child, she completed more than 20 books, including The Word of a Woman: Feminists Dispatches and the poetry collections Monster and Dark Matter. She followed Sisterhood Is Powerful with Sisterhood Is Global (1984) and Sisterhood Is Forever (2002), featuring such contributors as Steinem, Simone de Beauvoir and Eve Ensler. For several years, she was editor-in-chief of Ms magazine.In 1984, she was a founder of an early feminist thinktank, the Sisterhood Is Global Institute. In 2005, she, Steinem and Fonda launched the Women’s Media Center, which has a mission to support “the visibility, viability and decision-making power of women and girls in media”.View image in fullscreenMorgan at age five, in New York on 8 August 1947.Photograph: Robert Kradin/APMore recently, she hosted a syndicated radio show and remained active despite being diagnosed with Parkinson’s, which inspired several poems and a TEDWomen talk in 2015.In a different era, she might have been just another forgotten child star. Born in 1941 in Lake Worth, Florida, and raised in New York, she never saw her father while growing up and was told – falsely – by her mother that he was dead. Her mother also shaved a year off her age, claiming she was born in 1942, to make her early public career seem even more impressive.She would meet some of the era’s biggest stars, from Abbott and Costello to Sal Mineo, and was popular enough to inspire such commercial tie-ins as Robin Morgan dolls. Magazines described her as “unspoiled” and “courteous” and “the ideal girl-next-door”, immune from “violent outbursts of antagonism against established society”.As she recalled in Saturday’s Child, producer Dan Ehrenreich squeezed her shoulder so hard that Morgan could feel his fingernails. He turned her microphone away and eventually placed his hand over her mouth.“I realized that I loved and respected that child who fought back in what was the first political act I recall ever daring to make,” Morgan wrote.Explore more on these topicsUS newsActivismWomennewsShareReuse this content

title: Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash | Technology | The Guardian
description: Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech
Content: A Flock Safety camera mounted on a pole beneath a solar panel in Waltham, Massachusetts, on 24 August 2026.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Flock Safety camera mounted on a pole beneath a solar panel in Waltham, Massachusetts, on 24 August 2026.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersTechnologyAnalysisCut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlashThor BensonPoliticians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the techSat 5 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTShareGrowing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly75%of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas.Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans per month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who haveusedthem to stalk ex-lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequentlyutilizedby US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).Data and polling from theWashington Postshow that social media posts about Flock have increased since July, and about 46% of Americans oppose ALPRs being used in their community – up 13 points from the previous year.Vigilantes are posting videos of themselves destroyingthe cameras to digital applause. According to privacy and surveillance experts, hatred of Flock cameras has become bipartisan.“In my 20-plus years at the ACLU, I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology like this,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’ – keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.”Both liberal and conservative politicians are pushing back against Flock cameras. Greg Abbott, Texas’s Republican governor,blockedstate agencies from procuring Flock products. On the other side of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator, ispromisingto introduce legislation to restrict the use of Flock cameras. Republican senator Josh Hawley haslaunchedan investigation into potential Flock privacy abuses, and Democratic congressman Ro Khanna iscosponsoringa bill with Republican congressman Thomas Massie to prevent federal funds from being used to purchase Flock cameras.Municipal leaders of all political stripes aredropping contracts with Flock, though sometimes theyreplace the license plate readerswith another brand of camera and continue the surveillance. We reached out to Flock Safety for a statement and did not receive a response before publishing.Surveillance hasn’t always been a unifying topic in US politics. Debates over the Foreign IntelligenceSurveillanceAct (Fisa), the Patriot Act and other surveillance issues have often been divisive. This appears to be an unusual case where politicians are getting on the same side of a hot-button issue.“Privacy, to some extent, is bipartisan,” said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “When you put up these cameras, they last longer than the current administration. You might trust the people in power now who put them up – but are you going to trust the next people who get access to that equipment?”Americans havebeenshowing up at town hall meetings by the dozen over the past six months or so, and there have been numerous protests to show opposition to Flock surveillance cameras around the country. More than 100 jurisdictions have canceled their contracts so far, according to data from the non-profit Institute for Justice. An organization called DeFlock, founded in 2024, hopes to increase the numbers by compiling a map of the cameras’ locations.While ALPRs aren’t new, Flock, founded in 2017, has made them far more prevalent than they used to be. The company’s software allows disparate law enforcement agencies to share data with one another, meaning a license plate scan by a police department in one state could easily and quickly be used in another.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Flock represents tech companies in bed with governments, doing the exact stuff people have become distrustful of and resentful about for the past few decades. It feels like it’s finally hit the boiling-over point,” said Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law and computer science at Boston University.Hartzog predicts the actions against Flock Safety will continue at the state and local level amid this growing popular outrage. He expects people are going to stay angry about the issue, and politicians will have to respond.“The pushback we’re seeing against Flock cameras is one of the most vivid illustrations I can think of that surveillance is not inevitable – that these tools aren’t inevitable,” Hartzog says. “It’s up to all of us to stop them.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologySurveillanceDemocratsRepublicansUS politicsDatacenters – USPrivacyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial ends in dramatic deadlock – what comes next? | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: District attorney must decide whether to retry case after jury’s failure to reach verdict despite hours of deliberation
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: District attorney must decide whether to retry case after jury’s failure to reach verdict despite hours of deliberation
Content: Defendant Lindsay Clancy and attorney Kevin Reddington listen to the judge declare a mistrial, in Plymouth, U.S., September 4, 2026.Photograph: Greg Derr/ReutersView image in fullscreenDefendant Lindsay Clancy and attorney Kevin Reddington listen to the judge declare a mistrial, in Plymouth, U.S., September 4, 2026.Photograph: Greg Derr/ReutersMassachusettsAnalysisLindsay Clancy murder trial ends in dramatic deadlock – what comes next?Edward HelmoreDistrict attorney must decide whether to retry case after jury’s failure to reach verdict despite hours of deliberationSat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTShareLindsay Clancy, prosecutors, defense lawyers, the judge and millions watching on are back where they started after her five-week trial over the murder of her three children ended in a mistrial.America’s saddest case has ceased for the moment, but the legal wrangling is not over, and a second trial could now be on the horizon, prolonging and repeating an agonizing spectacle that has gripped America and the world.The trial lurched to its conclusion on Friday as jurors inMassachusettsfailed to come to a unanimous verdict. A lone male juror holdout appeared to be preventing a conclusion to the case.That meant the trial ended as it had begun: with no legal certainty about what was in Clancy’s mind when on 24 January 2023 she killed five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson, and eight-month-old Callan, and later cut her wrists and jumped from a bedroom window, sustaining injuries that paralyzed her.Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, did not deny the killings but pleaded not guilty to the murders. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington blamed postpartum psychosis coupled with overmedication. Prosecutors said she knew what she was doing.The jury deliberated for six days and over 30 hours, coming back three times in total in a deadlock. The jury foreperson said in a note to the judge on Thursday that a single juror had expressed reasonable doubt but would “not follow the law”.The mistrial finally came after a nail-biting delay when the judge allowed Clancy’s defense to petition the Massachusetts supreme court to replace the outlying juror with an alternate. Massachusetts justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt took the matter under advisement and soon after issued a decision not to intervene in the proceedings, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial.Reddington stared at the ground and let out a sigh as the judge made the ruling. At the back of the courtroom, largely occupied by supporters, people could be seen wiping away tears.And now it starts again.Reddington said he would file a motion for a directed finding of not guilty within days – a ruling that Sullivan could make on grounds that the prosecution failed to present enough evidence to prove the case. A status hearing is set for 29 September when a new trail date could be set.“This whole case has been unbelievable,” said victims’ rights attorney and survivor advocate Shari Karney. “Eleven jurors believed that Lindsay Clancy did not have criminal intent to commit this crime, understood the consequences of her act, and could not conform her conduct to the law.”The decision to try Clancy again rests with Plymouth county district attorney Tim Cruz, a prosecutor since 1985 who has served as district attorney for more than 20 years. Before Cruz’s most recent re-election, in 2022, he took aim at progressive district attorneys, saying they have been causing “anarchy and chaos” across the US. “I am against getting rid of life without parole for first-degree homicide people,” said in a debate. “I am against having a list of cases that will not be prosecuted because it does not work.”Outside court on Thursday, Reddington said he was ready to retry the case. “Bring it on,” he told reporters. But he did not rule out the possibility of a plea deal. “We’ll see what Mr Cruz wants to do, and then we’ll talk about our options,” he said. For now, Clancy returns to Tewksbury hospital, where she has been held since the killings.According to Karney, the complexity of the Massachusetts law on proving “criminal responsibility” – or what in other states would rest on the defense showing the defendant was insane – is a double standard. “It’s very complicated,” she says.Part of the difficulty jurors may have had is that mental health issues are not as a transparent as physical issues, and under criminal law there is a bias against them, she says.Karney said: “Clancy was basically having a mental health stroke, and mental health is the stepsister of the healthcare system. It’s not right. But because we cant see it, that doesn’t mean it doesn’t exist. And the medical healthcare system doesn’t want to recognize and pay for mental healthcare apart from giving out drugs to make them go away.”During the trial, jurors heard from mental health experts who clashed over Clancy’s medical records. But it was her mother and step mother who may have provided the most powerful testimony when they testified about the steps Clancy had taken to seek help.Paula Musgrove, Clancy’s mother, testified that she often stayed with her daughter in the months leading up to the killings because Clancy was afraid of sleeping alone, was increasingly paranoid and believed the medications she was taking “were destroying her mind”.Susan Clancy, Lindsay Clancy’s former mother-in-law, said she was “begging for help” and “was struggling – we were all concerned”.Forensic psychiatrist Phillip Resnick, for the defense, testified near the end of the trial testimony that that Clancy was “frankly psychotic” the day of the killings, and supported her claim that she heard a voice that ordered her to kill the children and herself.Resnick said he believed Clancy had experienced “command hallucinations … almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings”.Avram Mack, a forensic psychiatrist, said he did not believe Clancy was showing signs of psychosis but suffered from a major depressive episode and retained the ability to know right from wrong. “There was the ability to act normally,” he testified.In theory, prosecutors and defense attorneys could agree on voluntary manslaughter, a lesser charge. “The problem with a jail sentence for this woman is that she’s paraplegic,” said Karney. “How would you incarcerate a woman in a wheelchair with tremendous mental health problems in a woman’s prison, and ensure her safety?”One takeaway from the Lindsay Clancy trial, says Karney, is the job of getting inside the head of a woman suffering postpartum psychosis is a tough task and that diagnosis and treatment is woefully insufficient.“Telehealth is good for a sprained ankle or a cold, but not for postpartum depression or psychosis. And then you prescribe more psychotropic drugs via telehealth appointment? It’s crazy and it’s not responsible,” she said.Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Francisco Cerundolo roars back from brink to stun home hope Taylor Fritz at US Open | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Francisco Cerundolo beat No 9 seed Taylor Fritz 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4 after the US player had three break points in the final set for a chance to serve for the match
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Francisco Cerundolo beat No 9 seed Taylor Fritz 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4 after the US player had three break points in the final set for a chance to serve for the match
Content: Francisco Cerundolo overcame the odds to make his way into the next round at Flushing Meadows.Photograph: Brian Hirschfeld/EPAView image in fullscreenFrancisco Cerundolo overcame the odds to make his way into the next round at Flushing Meadows.Photograph: Brian Hirschfeld/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Francisco Cerundolo roars back from brink to stun home hope Taylor Fritz at US OpenArgentinian beats No 9 seed 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4Fritz had three break points for chance to serve for matchTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsSat 5 Sep 2026 17.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs his last, desperate backhand soared far past the baseline inside Arthur Ashe Stadium, Taylor Fritz instantly held his face in his hands, unable to hide the agony of squandering such a great opportunity.For much of his afternoon, Fritz was cruising. He had established two sets to love lead against Francisco Cerundolo before breaking serve in the opening game of the third. One unfocused service game was enough to shift the momentum and once Fritz had lost control, he spent another two hours failing to retrieve it. His US Open ended with an excruciating 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4 third-round defeat by a courageous Cerundolo.US Open tennis: Gauff and Swiatek go through; Cobolli, Fritz and Keys tumble out – liveRead moreAny early loss at a home grand slam is incredibly difficult to accept, but Fritz’s timing was fatal. Having been ranked as high as No 4 last year, he is the most successful American male player of his generation. In 2024, Fritz became the first American man to reach the US Open singles final since Andy Roddick in 2006, a breakthrough run sandwiched between two quarter-final losses to Novak Djokovic in 2023 and 2025. The 28-year-old is a tremendously committed and diligent competitor who, despite his own athletic shortcomings, has eked so much out of his game. There has always been a far superior tennis player, usually an all-time great, standing before him and the major titles.This year’s US Open, however, presents a completely different challenge for most of the men’s field. Jannik Sinner, the world No 1 and four-time grand slam champion, is absent due to injury and the now 39-year-old Novak Djokovic wasdramatically defeated in the first round. Carlos Alcaraz, the seven-time grand slam champion and defending champion, is competing his first tournament back from a four month injury layoff.View image in fullscreenTaylor Fritz later said of his defeat: ‘I don’t really want to talk to anybody … I don’t know how I let that happen today.’Photograph: Brian Hirschfeld/EPAIn the absence of an obvious favourite in obvious grand slam-winning form, this tournament is such a great opportunity for any player with aspirations of winning a grand slam title. Fritz, who was high up on the list of names hoping to take advantage, was understandably disgusted with the way he let this opportunity slip. In the deciding set he had three break points for a 5-3 lead and the chance to serve for the match.“I don’t even know what to say,” he said. “I don’t really want to talk to anybody, see anybody. I kind of just need to get out for a couple days and then just get back to work. I don’t know how I let that happen today.”At the beginning of the day, seven American men remained in the singles draw: Ben Shelton, Fritz, Frances Tiafoe, Learner Tien, Tommy Paul, Alex Michelsen and Michael Zheng. In the bottom half of the draw, where the fourth-round berths were decided on Friday, there is an American man in each of the four matches. Fritz’s defeat is a warning to any of his compatriots with hopes of becoming the first American man since Roddick at the 2003 US Open to win a grand slam title. More opportunity means more pressure. The coming week will reveal so much about the character of every player in the men’s draw.Saturday proved a challenging day for American players as a whole. Two days after Madison Keys completed one of the more dramatic comeback victories of her career, saving five match points en route to her tight three-set win over Anna Bondar, she suffered one of her worst ever collapses.
