A sloppy early pass from Jaydee Canvot inside the first minute that almost handed Palacios an opportunity betrayed the nerves of a Palace defence that had the Chelsea loanee, Axel Disasi, in the centre of the back three also favoured by Sage’s predecessor.View image in fullscreenCésar Palacios scored his first goal for Fulham to put them back in front before half-time.Photograph: Tony O Brien/ReutersFulham took the lead when Adam Wharton failed to clear a cross from Oscar Bobb and it fell straight into the path of King, whose shot took a big deflection to deceive Dean Henderson. It was typical of Sage’s luck in his first month at the helm that a superb apparent Palace equaliser less than two minutes later was chalked off. Daichi Kamada had strayed millimetres offside before volleying in a brilliant cross with the outside of his boot from Yéremy Pino.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe visitors could have found themselves 2-0 down when Henderson saved a Timothy Castagne shot from close range, but Mitchell beat Bernd Leno at his near post to equalise against the run of play after being set up by Eddie Nketiah. Palace’s joy was short-lived, however. Chris Richards – being watched by his USA manager Mauricio Pochettino – was fooled by King’s clever dummy and the England Under-21 midfielder accepted the invitation to burst into the box. His cross would have been diverted into his own net by Canvot had it not been for an excellent save from Henderson, but even that only left Palacios with the opportunity, which he accepted, to put the ball into the empty net.Yet Palace’s fortunes suddenly changed for the better when they scored a comical second equaliser. Mitchell’s initial effort was cleared by Gonzalo García as the striker charged back into the area, but the Palace defender volleyed hopefully towards goal as he fell, and García somehow managed to miss the ball altogether as it trickled over the line.Fulham seemed to shrink after conceding and Palace sensed an opportunity. The comeback was completed when Chilwell volleyed in after Anan Khalaili’s effort had been blocked, and Fulham were forced to accept their fate once more after their own substitute left-back, Ryan Sessegnon, found the sidenetting in injury time.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueFulhamCrystal Palacematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Own goal and inspired debut from keeper Akane Okuma earn Villa point at Chelsea | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Veerle Burman turned the ball into her own net to secure Aston Villa a WSL season-opening 1-1 draw at Chelsea, who took the lead through Lauren James but were thereafter frustrated by Villa’s new goalkeeper
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Veerle Burman turned the ball into her own net to secure Aston Villa a WSL season-opening 1-1 draw at Chelsea, who took the lead through Lauren James but were thereafter frustrated by Villa’s new goalkeeper
Content: Akane Okuma produced nine saves to keep Aston Villa in the game in their season opener at Chelsea.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenAkane Okuma produced nine saves to keep Aston Villa in the game in their season opener at Chelsea.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersWomen's Super LeagueOwn goal and inspired debut from keeper Akane Okuma earn Villa point at ChelseaSuzanne Wrackat Stamford BridgeSat 5 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 12.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Veerle Buurman own goal punished a profligate Chelsea at Stamford Bridge, securing a point for Aston Villa in a frustrating start to the hosts’ push to win back the WSL title.How Villa came away with a point having conceded 65% possession and having amassed just seven shots to Chelsea’s 34 and five touches in the opposition box to the home team’s 57 is somewhat inexplicable.Alexia Putellas begins WSL ride as London City outclass Manchester UnitedRead moreChelsea were creative and Lauren James was at her free-flowing best, but they could not convert their many chances, and the new Villa goalkeeper Akane Okuma’s monumental performance was a big part of that.“If you analyse the performance today and the statistics of the game you can say that’s crazy we couldn’t win the game,” said the Chelsea manager, Sonia Bompastor. “You need to make sure you kill the game because when you are only one-nil up, you are always exposed. That’s what happened today and I think at the end of the game we are all frustrated because it’s not a good result.”View image in fullscreenAlmost every Villa outfield player joined the celebrations for their equaliser.Photograph: Katie Chan/Action Plus/ShutterstockChelsea’s summer has been one of change after a somewhat transitional season that broke a run of six consecutive WSL titles, and spirits have been high about their potential. However, they have a problem up front: with the new signing Melvine Malard, whocame off the bench and scored twoin their Champions League qualifier home leg against Real Sociedad, out with an injury, and Mayra Ramírez yet to make her return from a long lay-off, Aggie Beever-Jones failed to make the most of the opportunity to lead the line.“In football, some of these things are also about mentality and mindset when it comes to being ruthless, being critical in the box,” said Bompastor. “The best teams don’t need to have many opportunities. So, that’s something we need to work on and find solutions for.”Ushering in a new era in front of 7,900 fans at Stamford Bridge, where they will play all their WSL home games for the first time, Chelsea’s aggressive and relentless pressing in the opening half-hour caused all sorts of problems for Natalia Arroyo’s team, forcing error after error.View image in fullscreenLauren James gave an early sign of what she is capable of with a finish that left the Villa keeper helpless.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersIt was no surprise when that physical effort yielded results. In the 11th minute when pressure caused confusion between Okuma and the target of her pass out from the back, the loose ball was worked to James who glided into the box, shifting her weight as she went, before lashing the ball into the roof of the net. It was a statement goal from a statement player.This was always going to be a tough opening game for Villa, who had lost all 12 of their previous WSL games against Chelsea and were startingfive of their eight summer signings,. They only began to look a little more comfortable and structured as the home team’s pressure eased off towards the end of the first half.“We just need to go through that and understand that when you’re in the middle of the jungle or whatever, at some point, you arrive at a point where there’s no more trees and I think that’s what we do at the end of the first half,” said Arroyo. “We get the energy back in the changing room and we talk about how to avoid these moments.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChelsea’s profligacy in front of goal was the big frustration for Bompastor, and Villa were clinging on for large swathes of the game with Okuma, signed from the Japanese champions INAC Kobe Leonessa, key to keeping the margin to one goal.View image in fullscreenNoelle Maritz’s (centre) shot led to Veerle Buurman’s own goal.Photograph: Katie Chan/Action Plus/ShutterstockAt no stage had it felt like the visiting team would be able to take something from the game. They were patient, but Chelsea were the masters of their own downfall, and in the 79th minute the ground was silenced when they failed to clear Lynn Wilms’ cross, Noelle Maritz swiped it goalwards from eight yards out, and Hannah Hampton’s block sent the ball bouncing off Buurman and over the line.The home side pushed hard for the winner but Okuma was equal to every attempt. “We gave her some nice tests this week trying to know where she was at, if she was nervous, if she had any doubt and in which ways we could help her,” said Arroyo. “She’s still settling in here, she’s still trying to learn the language to be able to communicate with all the players, but we were surprised to see that she was safe in some of the actions, she read the game really well.”On the final whistle the Japanese goalkeeper was enveloped in the hugs of her teammates as the players in blue digested how they had ended up with only a point from such a dominant performance.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueChelsea WomenAston Villa WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Audrey Werro fends off Femke Broeders-Bol’s charge in Diamond League final 800m | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Audrey Werro did just enough to hold off Femke Broeders-Bol in the Diamond League 800m in Brusssels
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Audrey Werro did just enough to hold off Femke Broeders-Bol in the Diamond League 800m in Brusssels
Content: Audrey Werro (right) holds on in the home straight as Femke Broeders-Bol closes on her in the final strides.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAView image in fullscreenAudrey Werro (right) holds on in the home straight as Femke Broeders-Bol closes on her in the final strides.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAAthleticsAudrey Werro fends off Femke Broeders-Bol’s charge in Diamond League final 800mSwiss athlete wins by 0.06sec in meeting-record 1:54.75Georgia Hunter Bell wilts to fourth in final lap of 1500mSean Ingleat the Stade Roi BaudouinSat 5 Sep 2026 17.04 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 17.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the last 30 metres of a boisterous and compelling women’s 800m Diamond League final, Femke Broeders-Bol slipped out of Audrey Werro’s slipstream and surged towards glory. “I thought I had it,” the Dutch star admitted afterwards. “I’ve never been so close.”But as Broeders-Bol and Keely Hodgkinson have found repeatedly this season, the towering Werro is a mightily difficult athlete to knock off her perch. The Swiss athlete gritted her teeth, found a little more, and took the spoils once again.Ingebrigtsen sorry for calling 1500m rivals ‘losers’ but maintains Hocker ‘acted cowardly’Read more“I felt her coming,” admitted Werro. “And I really enjoyed this battle because it pushes me to always work and not to really get in my comfort zone. I just keep in mind that one day I will get beaten. But now I just enjoy the first place.”Broeders-Bol at least had the comfort of knowing that she had got closer than ever before – just 0.05sec behind Werro’s winning time of 1min 54.75. And when asked afterwards what made her Swiss opponent so good, she smiled.“You should ask her because I would like to know,” she said. “But I think first of all she’s very strong in her mind. I think she’s a real fighter. She really goes for it with no fear and just all in. But I think just her last 200m is phenomenal. I think I could learn something from it but I think it’s her mind combined with her physical. She’s still so young, but so extremely fast.”The good news for track and field fans is that Werro and Broeders-Bol will race one more time this season, at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest next week, with a $150,000 (£111,000) first prize on the line. Hodgkinson’s coach, Trevor Painter, confirmed to the Guardian that she has recovered from a minor niggle and will be lining up too.Elsewhere there was a surprise as Britain’s Georgia Hunter Bell could only finish fourth in the women’s 1500m. After the Polish athlete Klaudia Kazimierska charged to victory in a personal-best 3:54.05, Hunter Bell admitted that she had felt tired going into the race.“I was definitely tired,” she said “The past few days have been struggling to find the adrenaline to kick in, because I’ve had to tap into that so much this year. Three major championships, three golds, a bunch of Diamond League wins, British champs, like all this stuff. So you hit this point in the season, and it is hard to keep up that intensity.”Amy Hunt capped a fine weekend by coming second in the women’s 100m in 11.06, ahead of the 2023 world champion Sha’Carri Richardson in third. It was a decent time on a cool night, but there was no stopping the Jamaican Tina Clayton, whose lightning start had the race won in the opening 30 metres before she floated home in 10.93.However Hunt wasn’t too disappointed, having also finished third inFriday night’s 200m. And while this was her 43rd race of the season – including 13 indoors, 15 over 100m, 11 over 200m and four relays – Hunt believes she still has something left for next week’s Ultimate Championships.“I’m super-happy with that,” she said. “My aim for this weekend was to come away with a podium finish, so to come away with two, and to also be the only athlete to actually attempt a double at this championship, I can be incredibly proud of that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It maybe wasn’t a weekend for running quick times,” she added. “But it was a weekend for really going head to head, and I find that’s always one of my strengths – my ability to stay calm and have no fear and take on the best in the world.”View image in fullscreenKenny Bednarek (centre) finishes well clear of the field in 19.62, equalling the world lead time this year.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAElsewhere there were plenty of fast times despite the conditions. The event started with Marileidy Paulinho running a meeting record of 48.64 in the women’s 400m to beat Henriette Jager, while the American Kenny Bednarek equalled the fastest 200m time in the world this year to win at a canter in 19.62.“I’m definitely happy with this result,” said Bednarek, who will also run in Budapest next week. “To get the win under these cold conditions and a bit of sickness … I can’t ask for more. Next week, if I execute well, I can drop a massive PB.”Explore more on these topicsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

Headline: The main supporting bout to Katie Taylor’s pre-retirement fight ended abruptly, with Dave Allen bemused while his stricken opponent received oxygen
Content: A seemingly innocuous punch to the back of Thomas Carty’s head was suddenly followed by him falling through the ropes.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersView image in fullscreenA seemingly innocuous punch to the back of Thomas Carty’s head was suddenly followed by him falling through the ropes.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersBoxingBoxer Thomas Carty falls out of ring after 92 seconds in bizarre no-contestBout on Katie Taylor’s final undercard ends abruptlyDave Allen baffled as opponent receives oxygen ringsidePress AssociationSat 5 Sep 2026 16.49 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDave Allen’s heavyweight clash with Thomas Carty at Croke Park ended in a bizarre no-contest after the Irish favourite fell out of the ring in the first round.The chief support forKatie Taylor’s final fightbefore her retirement was over after just one minute and 22 seconds with Carty – seeking the biggest win of his 12-bout career – unable to continue.Allen caught Carty on the back of the head with a clubbing right hand and the Dublin southpaw tumbled through the ropes as much through momentum as the shot itself and on to the floor, where he lay on his back.View image in fullscreenThomas Carty leaves the arena after his fight was abandoned.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAAfter receiving medical attention – including oxygen for several minutes – Carty then walked back to the changing room and the fight was abandoned.Allen, a 34-year-old journeyman from Doncaster, looked as bemused as the 80,000 crowd at the way the fight had ended.Explore more on these topicsBoxingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lewis Hamilton urges Ferrari to put full weight behind F1 title challenge | Ferrari | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton said Ferrari needs to stay hungry for success and back his F1 title push, warning that light at the end of the tunnel was ‘getting dimmer’
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton said Ferrari needs to stay hungry for success and back his F1 title push, warning that light at the end of the tunnel was ‘getting dimmer’
Content: Lewis Hamilton was mystified by his car’s lack of pace during Q2 qualifying at the Monza track.Photograph: Anna Szilagy/Pool EPA/APView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton was mystified by his car’s lack of pace during Q2 qualifying at the Monza track.Photograph: Anna Szilagy/Pool EPA/APFerrariLewis Hamilton urges Ferrari to put full weight behind F1 title challengeLight at end of tunnel is ‘getting dimmer’Team needs to show hunger and ‘passion’Giles Richardsat MonzaSat 5 Sep 2026 14.56 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 16.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton has suggested it is time his Ferrari team put their full weight behind his efforts to challenge for the Formula One world championship if he is to have a shot at the title, and warned his chances were diminishing with every race.Hamilton trails Kimi Antonelli, the championship leader, by 59 points with 11 races to come. Having qualified in fifth for the Italian Grand Prix, one place behind hisFerrariteammate Charles Leclerc, who is 87 points off the lead, Hamilton was asked if it was time Ferrari gave him priority as their best chance for the title.Pierre Gasly takes shock pole for F1 Italian GP as Alpine stun big gunsRead more“Yeah, there’s light at the end of the tunnel, but it’s getting dimmer the further we get through,” he said. “The team is doing an amazing job in bringing upgrades and pushing us forward, I always want to make sure that I acknowledge them and recognise them for that.“I want them to continue to push and I want them to stay hungry and keep that passion on fire. But also at the track we need to come correct and act. We need to make sure we get the results we need.”Hamilton had very nearly been eliminated during Q2 in qualifying, struggling for pace and questioning Ferrari’s decision-making in trying to give both drivers a chance of a tow at a high-speed circuit where it is vital for a quick lap.“I don’t really fully understand why we were lacking so much pace in Q2, because we should have had pace like we did in the first one, but everyone just advanced forward, so I don’t know if that’s tyre pressure. I’m not quite sure, I need to look into that.“I think at the end, the team was solely focused on trying to get an equal tow for each driver and we just stumbled.“We were supposed to do a push, cool, cool, push [sequence of laps]. But because everyone was waiting and Charles didn’t want to go out first, we had to wait, wait, wait, and then we only got one push. It made it pretty challenging for us.”Quick GuideItalian F1 GP qualifying resultsShow1Pierre Gasly🇫🇷Alpine1:21.8762George Russell🇬🇧Mercedes1:21.846†3Oscar Piastri🇦🇺McLaren1:21.9664Charles Leclerc🇲🇨Ferrari1:22.0045Lewis Hamilton🇬🇧Ferrari1:22.0116Max Verstappen🇳🇱Red Bull1:22.070*7Kimi Antonelli🇮🇹Mercedes1:22.0938Franco Colapinto🇦🇷Alpine1:22.2209Lando Norris🇬🇧McLaren1:22.25610Arvid Lindblad🇬🇧Racing Bulls1:22.286Q2 eliminations11Gabriel Bortoleto🇧🇷Audi1:22.51712Oliver Bearman🇬🇧Haas1:22.75613Nico Hülkenberg🇩🇪Audi1:22.779*14Liam Lawson🇫🇷Red Bull1:22.82115Carlos Sainz🇪🇸Williams1:23.45316Esteban Ocon🇫🇷Haas1:23.454Q1 eliminations17Yuki Tsunoda🇯🇵Racing Bulls1:23.755*18Alexander Albon🇹🇭Williams1:24.35619Valtteri Bottas🇫🇮Cadillac1:24.36420Sergio Pérez🇲🇽Cadillac1:24.59521Fernando Alonso🇪🇸Aston Martin1:25.15022Lance Stroll🇨🇦Aston Martin1:25.22† Piastri given a three-place grid penalty for impeding Lawson. *Antonelli, Lawson and Albon all relegated to the back of the grid for taking new power unit elementsWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Alpine’s Pierre Gaslytook a remarkable pole positionfor the race, with Mercedes’ George Russell, who is equal with Hamilton on points – 59 behind Antonelli – in second place. With the Mercedes looking formidable in race pace and Antonelli starting from 20th after an engine-change grid penalty, Russell is in a strong position to make points back, and Hamilton emphasised this was a potentially crucial moment for Ferrari.“We’re at a point in the year where 59 points is a huge deficit to recover from, especially when Mercedes continue to be the leaders in speed,” he said. “So yeah, we do have to work as a team.”Leclerc and Hamilton will start from third and fourth respectively on Sunday after McLaren’s Oscar Piastri was given a three-place grid penalty.Explore more on these topicsFerrariLewis HamiltonFormula OneFormula One 2026Motor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ingebrigtsen sorry for calling 1500m rivals ‘losers’ but maintains Hocker ‘acted cowardly’ | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen has issued a part-apology for calling his rivals ‘losers’ and a ‘bunch of cowards’ after a spicy men’s 1500m Diamond League final on Friday
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Jakob Ingebrigtsen has issued a part-apology for calling his rivals ‘losers’ and a ‘bunch of cowards’ after a spicy men’s 1500m Diamond League final on Friday
Content: Jakob Ingebrigtsen (right) was unhappy with how most of his fellow competitors approached Friday’s 1500m, in which he finished fourth.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAView image in fullscreenJakob Ingebrigtsen (right) was unhappy with how most of his fellow competitors approached Friday’s 1500m, in which he finished fourth.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAAthleticsIngebrigtsen sorry for calling 1500m rivals ‘losers’ but maintains Hocker ‘acted cowardly’Fiery Diamond League comments partially walked backOn Hocker: ‘Cole and I talked it through after the race’Sean Ingleat the Stade Roi BaudouinSat 5 Sep 2026 15.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe double Olympic champion Jakob Ingebrigtsen has issued a part-apology for calling his rivals “losers” and a “bunch of cowards” after aspicy men’s 1500m Diamond League finalon Friday.However, Ingebrigtsen has continued to maintain that he was still right to accuse the Olympic 1500m champion Cole Hocker of cowardice – because he asked for a strong pace and swapped in his own pacemaker only to then hide behind others in the race.Audrey Werro fends off Femke Broeders-Bol’s charge in Diamond League final 800mRead moreIn a statement issued on Saturday, Ingebrigtsen, who finished fourth behind Australia’s Cameron Myers in a tight finish in 3min 30.52sec, said: “I shouldn’t have called anyone losers. I apologise for that. It was beneath me, regardless of the adrenaline and emotions. But I stand by what I said about Cole and his team acting cowardly.“They told the other athletes and the organisers that they were targeting a specific pace and were bringing in their own pacemaker to set that pace, but then they did something completely different.“When you promise the crowd a fast race, you have a responsibility to follow through – at least in my view. This isn’t about me losing. I wasn’t good enough. It’s about taking responsibility for the commitments you’ve made to the meeting organisers, the crowd and your competitors.”Ingebrigtsen, who returned to racing in August after 11 months out after an achilles sheath injury, ended up following the pacemakers himself after no one else went with them.But despite running a season’s best time, he was bluntly honest about his “shitty, terrible and extremely disappointing” run afterwards – before criticising his fellow racers.On Saturday Ingebrigtsen insisted that he had talked to Hocker afterwards and the matter was settled. However the row flared up again when Hocker’s agent Ray Flynn accused Ingebrigtsen of whining.“Jakob now appears as a whiny runner who blames others,” Flynn wrote in an email to the Norwegian newspaper Dagbladet. “It is embarrassing to see a great champion complain and blame other runners when he doesn’t win. It is completely disrespectful to his competitors, who now regularly beat him in the 1500 metres.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever Ingebrigtsen said that his broader comments were good for the sport as he returned fire on Flynn.“Cole and I talked it through after the race,” the Norwegian added. “As far as we’re concerned, the matter is settled, so I don’t really understand why his agent is getting involved in all of this now. If you’re not allowed to show a bit of passion after a race, you should find a sport that doesn’t want an audience.”The pair could renew acquaintances next week at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest, when Ingebrigtsen is down to run the 1500m and 5,000m. However, according to Dagbladet, the Norwegian is now likely just to focus on the 5,000m.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Ruiz Jr’s comeback bid in tatters after sobering defeat to Damian Knyba | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Former unified heavyweight champion dropped and comprehensively outpointed in Newark as hopes of another title run suffer potentially terminal blow
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Former unified heavyweight champion dropped and comprehensively outpointed in Newark as hopes of another title run suffer potentially terminal blow
Content: Damian Knyba lands a punch on Andy Ruiz Jr during their heavyweight bout at the Prudential Center in Newark on Friday night.Photograph: Ed Mulholland/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDamian Knyba lands a punch on Andy Ruiz Jr during their heavyweight bout at the Prudential Center in Newark on Friday night.Photograph: Ed Mulholland/Getty ImagesBoxingAndy Ruiz Jr’s comeback bid in tatters after sobering defeat to Damian KnybaKnyba wins unanimous decision after dropping RuizFormer champion struggles badly after 762-day layoffRuiz, 36, insists another title run remains possibleBryan Armen Grahamat the Prudential CenterSat 5 Sep 2026 04.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 05.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Ruiz Jr’s comeback bid was left in tatters on Friday night after the former unified heavyweight champion was knocked down and picked apart in a sobering unanimous-decision defeat to Damian Knyba in Newark, New Jersey.Knyba won by scores of 117-110 and 114-113 twice, handing Ruiz the third defeat of his professional career and dealing a devastating blow to his hopes of becoming a two-time champion in boxing’s prestige division. The baffling pair of 114-113 cards flattered Ruiz considerably and bore little relation to the mostly one-way traffic that unfolded. (The Guardian had it 117-110.)“This feeling is so amazing,” the New Jersey-based Pole said afterwards through a translator. “Not many people in the world can feel what I’m feeling right now.”Ruiz (35-3-1, 22 KOs), who turns 37 next week and was returning from a 762-day layoff, cut a lamentable figure for most of the night, his once-blurring combinations carrying little of their old snap, his head almost stationary as the 30-year-old Knyba’s jab found it time and again. By the end of 12 dispiriting rounds at the home of the NHL’s New Jersey Devils, he looked less like a contender launching one final climb toward the summit than a shot fighter badly compromised by inactivity and injury.Seven years ago, Ruiz authoredone of the greatest upsets in boxing historyat Madison Square Garden, climbing off the canvas to knock down the undefeated Anthony Joshua four times before stopping him in the seventh round and becoming the first fighter of Mexican descent to win a world heavyweight title. Barely six months later, the fairy tale was over. After months of partying and an abbreviated training camp, Ruiz arrived for the rematch 15lb heavier andsurrendered the titles back to Joshuain a listless points defeat in Saudi Arabia, ending his unlikely reign after just 190 days.View image in fullscreenAndy Ruiz Jr is knocked down by Damian Knyba during the seventh round of their heavyweight bout at the Prudential Center in Newark on Friday night.Photograph: Ed Mulholland/Getty ImagesFor Ruiz, who had fought only three times in more than six years, Friday was meant to mark the beginning of one last run at a title suddenly within reach with 39-year-oldOleksandr Usykpreparing to exit the stage. Instead, Ruiz spent most of the night plodding after the 6ft 7in Knyba, unable to access the hand speed or footwork required to overcome the enormous physical disparity. There was little power behind his punches and even less of the explosive drive through his legs that once gave them such menace, perhaps a consequence of his surgically repaired right knee.For six rounds it was a dour display. Knyba established the pattern early with a long, pawing left jab while moving backward, content to concede ground without allowing Ruiz into punching range. Whenever Ruiz did close the distance, the Pole swallowed him up inside his 86in reach and waited for referee David Franciosi to separate them. Ruiz trudged forward with almost no head movement, struggling to negotiate the 12in difference in reach while eating one jab after another.The fight suddenly caught fire toward the end of the seventh when Knyba detonated a sharp one-two that badly wobbled Ruiz. A follow-up flurry sent him crashing to the canvas in a heap, where he stayed until the count of eight before hauling himself upright. By the time the bell sounded moments later, Ruiz had absorbed even more punishment and appeared out on his feet.“I thought the fight was over,” Knyba said. “I didn’t want to make the same mistake thatAnthony Joshuamade where he just came onto him. I wanted to stay disciplined, keep my distance and just keep doing what I was doing.”View image in fullscreenDamian Knyba lands a punch on Andy Ruiz Jr during their heavyweight bout at the Prudential Center in Newark on Friday night.Photograph: Ed Mulholland/Getty ImagesRuiz emerged for the eighth with his face bruised and reddened, but for a moment the old instincts returned as he pounded Knyba with thudding shots to the head and body during his best offensive sequence of the night. The revival proved short-lived. Even as a crowd squarely in his corner urged him forward with chants of “Si se puede!” into the championship rounds, Knyba re-established the distance behind his jab and found Ruiz had little left to offer. By the 12th, the Pole was peppering his visibly depleted foe with unanswered jabs as the final bell approached.“It was just him holding every time I tried to come in,” Ruiz said. “He’d hold me really tight and I couldn’t let my combinations go. But he played a good game plan. I’d love to run it back and do things a lot different.”Before Friday, another run at the title was more than wishful thinking. With the unbeaten Usykhaving vacated his remaining titlesin June, the heavyweight championship has splintered among Murat Gassiev (the WBA beltholder), Agit Kabayel (WBC), Filip Hrgović (IBF) and Daniel Dubois (WBO), offering any number of potential pathways back to the top for a fighter with Ruiz’s name recognition. Even a rubber match with Joshua, once seemingly fanciful, appeared in play after the Englishman’s anticipated November showdown with Fury.Knyba (18-1, 11 KOs), whose lone professional defeat came against Kabayel in January, was deliberately chosen as a meaningful test rather than a soft re-entry for the first outing of Ruiz’s three-fight deal with MatchroomBoxing. Eddie Hearn had said beforehand that if Ruiz truly intended to win another world championship, he needed to beat opponents of this level. Instead, against a foe who had never previously gone beyond eight rounds, Ruiz looked ordinary, hittable and alarmingly short of ideas. Still, he refused to concede that the defeat had ended his hopes of another title shot.“Of course I [believe], man,” Ruiz said. “It was just a long layoff and it was a great opponent. I didn’t want to take an easy fight. That’s why I took Damian. He’s a big guy, but we’ve got to take risks.”Explore more on these topicsBoxingAnthony JoshuaUS sportsOleksandr UsykShareReuse this content

title: Williams sisters’ US Open return ends in heartbreak with third-set tie-break defeat | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: American duo Serena and Venus crash out of women’s doubles in first round with 6-3, 6-7(6), 7-6(7) loss to Maya Joint and Chan Hao-ching
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: American duo Serena and Venus crash out of women’s doubles in first round with 6-3, 6-7(6), 7-6(7) loss to Maya Joint and Chan Hao-ching
Content: Williams sisters Serena and Venus embrace after defeat to Maya Joint and Hao-Ching Chan in a women’s doubles first round match at the US Open.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWilliams sisters Serena and Venus embrace after defeat to Maya Joint and Hao-Ching Chan in a women’s doubles first round match at the US Open.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesUS Open Tennis 2026Williams sisters’ US Open return ends in heartbreak with third-set tie-break defeatAmerican duo lose 6-3, 6-7(6), 7-6(7) to Maya Joint and Chan Hao-chingSerena and Venus crash out of women’s doubles in first roundTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsSat 5 Sep 2026 00.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the end, after so much toil and admirable fight, defeat came swiftly for one of the greatest doubles teams to ever share a tennis court. Upon theirreturn to prime time in New York, Venus and Serena Williams fought desperately to overturn the various deficits they found themselves in over three hours inside a thunderous Arthur Ashe Stadium.They came close. The Williams sisters had clawed their way back into the match after trailing a 1-4 in their final set against Chan Hao-ching and Maya Joint, and they established a 5-0 lead in the third set tie-break. Just as they appeared to be on the verge of victory, they were brushed aside, losing 6-3, 6-7 (6), 7-6 (7) in the first round of the US Open.‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka halts US Open match due to cannabis smellRead moreThis was one of the few times in recent tennis history where a player’s doubles appearance seemed far more important than their singles contributions. While the 44-year-old Serena had opted out of taking a singles wildcard for the US Open aftersuffering a knee injuryduring her singles comeback at Wimbledon in July against Joint, the 46-year-oldVenus lost in the singles first roundhere to Sofia Kenin, her15th consecutive singles loss. No matter, from the moment it became clear that the Williams sisters were aiming to compete alongside each other in doubles again, this was the match that people wanted to see.Before this summer, when the Williams sisters finallyrejoined forcesat the Cincinnati Open,losing in a tight first round battle, the last time Venus and Serena had competed together was here in 2022, supposedly Serena’s final tournament. Serena had been extremely impressive in hermixed doubles appearance alongside Carlos Alcarazthis year, who she had even outperformed for a large part of her matches. Here, perhaps under the additional pressure alongside her sister, the four years of rust was still visible on Serena’s game as she struggled badly throughout the match.View image in fullscreenSerena Williams serves alongside sister Venus during a women’s doubles first round match at the 2026 US Open.Photograph: Kena Betancur/AFP/Getty ImagesA week after cracking 120mph aces on pressure points, Serena had so many troubles with her serve that, by the final set, she had been reduced to simply rolling in her first serve and she similarly struggled to land any returns. Venus, meanwhile, was often the best player on the court, but the pair paid for her failure to put away key volleys deep in the match.Regardless, the Williams sisters fought desperately for three hours, produced numerous moments of brilliance and nearly defeated the 14th seed team in the draw. They were eventually outplayed by a solid pairing in Joint, a top 30 doubles player, and the former world No 5 and Wimbledon finalist Chan. The Australian-Taiwanese pair were at times overwhelmed by the increasingly intense crowd inside Arthur Ashe Stadium and their indefatigable opponents. But in the decisive moments deep in the final set tie-break they handled business as they should, absorbing the Williams sisters’ first strike while tidying up around the net.Serena has repeatedly stressed that, in stark contrast to the rest of her career when she expected herself to win every tournament she entered, this comeback is not about winning. She is back solely to enjoy herself and to show her daughters, Olympia and Adira, the world she used to inhabit. She will not be competing again for long. Despite the fact that Serena has compiled a 1-4 record in singles and women’s doubles since her return, it has been enjoyable to again see her legendary service motion, feel her competitive spirit and hear her roar. She also has clearly enjoyed the feeling of being back in the arena.View image in fullscreenWilliams sisters Serena and Venus shake hands with Maya Joint and Hao-Ching Chan after their women’s doubles match at the 2026 US Open.Photograph: Kena Betancur/AFP/Getty ImagesThe big question for both players, though, is when this will finally end. From the moment Serena announced her return, retiring hand-in-hand at the US Open seemed like the perfect ending to their story. But neither player gave any indication that this might be their last appearance as they discreetly departed the court and later declined to conduct a post-match press conference.It has now been over three decades since Venus and Serena started their careers, Venus in 1994 and Serena in 1995. Venus made her iconic breakthrough run to the US Open final at the age of 17 in 1997, losing to Martina Hingis. Serena won her first grand slam title here at 17 in 1999, beating Hingis. The following year, Venus followed her little sister by winning her first US Open singles title. Then in 2001 at the US Open they became the first pair of siblings in history to face each other in a grand slam final.All those years later, here they are. Still out there on Arthur Ashe Stadium, still fighting till the death, still trying hard to overcome yet painfully coming up short. Although they did not leave the court with a victory, they did offer a full, passionate crowd of 23,000 spectators a reminder of their unending passion and love for the sport that has defined their lives for so long.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Serena WilliamsVenus WilliamsUS Open tennisTennisUS sportsAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models
Content: With every increase in the power of AI, there is a potential increase in risk. Illustration: Just_Super/Getty ImagesA spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced modelsByRobert BoothUK technology editorSat 5 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePicture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium.These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence.Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAIclaimedthe technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI – artificial general intelligence – with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra.That claim came as the company prepared for a potential $850bn (£630bn) stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.The tasks it claims Astra can automate include designing circuit boards, filling out tax returns, building video games, financial modelling, engineering design and helping assemble legal documents. The threat to some white-collar jobs is implicit.View image in fullscreenOpenAI launched its latest AI model this week, GPT-6 Astra.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockYet, the AGI claim coincides with rising fears about AI risks among safety experts and political leaders, whose nerves have been jangled by the increasing power and impenetrability of AI models this summer and a spate of serious safety accidents viewed by some as possible final warning shots.“We’re heading through the rapids and we’re really hoping there isn’t some kind of drop in front of us and we don’t really know,” said Trager. “We’re plausibly close to crossing the line to what’s called recursive self-improvement, where [AI] systems improve themselves. That kind of recursivity is actually the definition of an explosion.”The latest worry came on Friday, just hours after Astra’s launch, with reports that a swarm of AI agents had repurposed a German website as a message board to share tactics to cheat on tasks,according to Reuters. OpenAI said it was reviewing the matter but would not characterise it as a hack.Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn dealRead moreThere is a sense of an awakening among politicians. On Thursday, the US senator Bernie Sanders cited this summer’s alarming breakout of a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents whichhacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store, when he called for “an immediate pause on advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence”.He said countries around the world must “work together to prevent this nightmare scenario”, which he defined as “an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control”.View image in fullscreenA swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockConcerns currently focus on AIs mounting cyber-attacks that could cripple real-world social and economic infrastructure, but future concerns include their ability to create biohazards and control military hardware.Across the Atlantic, a cross-party group of UK parliamentarians has called for AI “kill switches” to be required by law to prevent disastrous loss of control, citing “a recent spree of rogue AI incidents”.Darren Jones, an MP and former chief secretary to Keir Starmer, is also urgently attempting to set up a body to help legislators grapple with the technology. “AI is developing at such a pace that neither government nor parliament can keep up,” he warned. And next week a bill will be proposed by the Labour MP Alex Sobel toprohibit superintelligent AIdevelopment in the UK.The increasing anxiety comes amid a torrent of new AI models. Already this year, 67 have been released by the leading US companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, and their Chinese rivals Moonshot, Z.ai and Qwen,according to one count.With every increase in power, there is a potential increase in risk. OpenAI’s rivalAnthropic, which is targeting a $2tn stock exchange listing, this week admitted its own AIs were “not perfectly aligned” with human values and said there had been a “failure of operational security” in July hacks by its own model, Claude. It said the incidents had “stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defences is even higher than we previously believed”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe ability to monitor what AI models are thinking as they advance is another growing source of safety fears.Illustration: Yuichiro Chino/Getty ImagesAI’s double edge – opportunity and risk – was on show when OpenAI launched Astra on Thursday. Itsmarketing videofocused not on the risks but on the breezy convenience that AI could offer to a certain kind of customer. It showed an upmarket San Francisco woman simultaneously booking a tennis court and designing a presentation for her high-end rainwear collection; a thirtysomething man being helped to build his dream space invaders game and order a takeaway; a law firm executive being helped to draft some contracts.Yet only weeks ago, this was a model whose training had to be partly paused because of safety concerns after the Hugging Face incident. An independent safety researcher drafted in to investigate, Ajeya Cotra,said it was“more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover”.Astra also has whatOpenAIcalls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability – the first time it has given a model such a label. It means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”. The company’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, insisted the model was properly aligned not to do that, but added that “as these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder”.The ability to monitor what AI models are “thinking” as they advance is another growing source of safety fears. This week it was reported that OpenAI had been training Astra to reason not only in natural language, but in a more opaque manner that is faster and more efficient – and can make models’ chains of reasoning harder to follow. It means a model’s internal calculations may not always be written out as directly readable words – as if it was thinking in its head, rather than showing its working. Some experts fear this could help AIs covertly conspire against their human overseers.OpenAI confirmed Astra “shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models” and Pachocki said “as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging”.View image in fullscreenOpenAI’s Sam Altman: ‘We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time.’Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersThe company played down the development, but the increase in opaque reasoning sparked concern from AI safety researchers. Ryan Greenblatt, the chief scientist at Redwood Research, a nonprofit examining AI safety and security, called it “extremely concerning”. Gary Marcus, an influential AI sceptic, compared it to kicking away an already “rickety scaffolding before we have something better”.OpenAI’s chief executive,Sam Altman, said this week he felt conflicted about the advances of AI models. He admitted OpenAI’s security had “failed” in the Hugging Face incident and called it “a legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure”.“We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us,” he said in a tweet. “We know it is much more discordant for other people.”His rationale for releasing OpenAI’s most powerful model so soon after a safety crisis appears to be that the world needs to see how AIs perform in the real world to understand where AI is heading. He said: “An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.”And yet he can see the risks. On Tuesday he addressed the G20 ministerial summit in North Carolina in the US and told politicians that “some things are going to go very wrong with cybersecurity unless people act quite urgently”.He added: “There will be other challenges in the next five years. People talk about biosecurity and the things we are going to face there. There will be bigger ones yet to come.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingOpenAIAnthropicBernie SandersSam AltmanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash | Technology | The Guardian
description: Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech
Content: A Flock Safety camera mounted on a pole beneath a solar panel in Waltham, Massachusetts, on 24 August 2026.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Flock Safety camera mounted on a pole beneath a solar panel in Waltham, Massachusetts, on 24 August 2026.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersTechnologyAnalysisCut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlashThor BensonPoliticians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the techSat 5 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTShareGrowing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly75%of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas.Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans per month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who haveusedthem to stalk ex-lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequentlyutilizedby US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).Data and polling from theWashington Postshow that social media posts about Flock have increased since July, and about 46% of Americans oppose ALPRs being used in their community – up 13 points from the previous year.Vigilantes are posting videos of themselves destroyingthe cameras to digital applause. According to privacy and surveillance experts, hatred of Flock cameras has become bipartisan.“In my 20-plus years at the ACLU, I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology like this,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’ – keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.”Both liberal and conservative politicians are pushing back against Flock cameras. Greg Abbott, Texas’s Republican governor,blockedstate agencies from procuring Flock products. On the other side of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator, ispromisingto introduce legislation to restrict the use of Flock cameras. Republican senator Josh Hawley haslaunchedan investigation into potential Flock privacy abuses, and Democratic congressman Ro Khanna iscosponsoringa bill with Republican congressman Thomas Massie to prevent federal funds from being used to purchase Flock cameras.Municipal leaders of all political stripes aredropping contracts with Flock, though sometimes theyreplace the license plate readerswith another brand of camera and continue the surveillance. We reached out to Flock Safety for a statement and did not receive a response before publishing.Surveillance hasn’t always been a unifying topic in US politics. Debates over the Foreign IntelligenceSurveillanceAct (Fisa), the Patriot Act and other surveillance issues have often been divisive. This appears to be an unusual case where politicians are getting on the same side of a hot-button issue.“Privacy, to some extent, is bipartisan,” said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “When you put up these cameras, they last longer than the current administration. You might trust the people in power now who put them up – but are you going to trust the next people who get access to that equipment?”Americans havebeenshowing up at town hall meetings by the dozen over the past six months or so, and there have been numerous protests to show opposition to Flock surveillance cameras around the country. More than 100 jurisdictions have canceled their contracts so far, according to data from the non-profit Institute for Justice. An organization called DeFlock, founded in 2024, hopes to increase the numbers by compiling a map of the cameras’ locations.While ALPRs aren’t new, Flock, founded in 2017, has made them far more prevalent than they used to be. The company’s software allows disparate law enforcement agencies to share data with one another, meaning a license plate scan by a police department in one state could easily and quickly be used in another.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Flock represents tech companies in bed with governments, doing the exact stuff people have become distrustful of and resentful about for the past few decades. It feels like it’s finally hit the boiling-over point,” said Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law and computer science at Boston University.Hartzog predicts the actions against Flock Safety will continue at the state and local level amid this growing popular outrage. He expects people are going to stay angry about the issue, and politicians will have to respond.“The pushback we’re seeing against Flock cameras is one of the most vivid illustrations I can think of that surveillance is not inevitable – that these tools aren’t inevitable,” Hartzog says. “It’s up to all of us to stop them.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologySurveillanceDemocratsRepublicansUS politicsDatacenters – USPrivacyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Alarming AI ads are flooding social media in the lead-up to Victoria’s election. But who is behind them? | Victorian politics | The Guardian
description: A machete-wielding robber, a ‘tsunami of debt’ … campaigns echoing opposition talking points outspend major parties
Author: Benita Kolovos
Headline: A machete-wielding robber, a ‘tsunami of debt’ … campaigns echoing opposition talking points outspend major parties
Content: A screenshot from a Fix Victoria advertisement produced using artificial intelligence. The water symbolises Victoria's ‘tsunami of debt’ said to be endangering key services and childrenView image in fullscreenA screenshot from a Fix Victoria advertisement produced using artificial intelligence. The water symbolises Victoria's ‘tsunami of debt’ said to be endangering key services and childrenVictorian politicsAlarming AI ads are flooding social media in the lead-up to Victoria’s election. But who is behind them?A machete-wielding robber, a ‘tsunami of debt’ … campaigns echoing opposition talking points outspend major partiesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBenita KolovosandHenry BelotSat 5 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man clad in a balaclava and brandishing a machete terrorises a worker at a petrol station before firebombing the building on the way out.A woman gives birth on the side of the road, unable to reach a hospital due toambulance rampingand crater-like potholes, which also stop a fire truck in its tracks.Victorian prisoners to be sent out to repair roads under Labor’s pothole planRead moreA flood of water – emblematic of Victoria’s “tsunami of debt”,forecast to hit $199bnin the next four years – gushes from the steps of state parliament, towards a scared child.These are some of the AI-generated images being used as part of a social media advertising campaign attracting thousands of views less than 100 days out from the Victorian election.According to one expert, the ads, created by a group called Fix Victoria, cost up to $100,000 to publish in August, which is significantly more than most major parties and candidates spent.View image in fullscreenA screenshot from another Fix Victoria adAnother group, Better Victoria, is also spending big on short ads to pit Labor initiatives – such as the multibillion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop – against investment in roads, schools and hospitals.But who is behind these groups and are they affiliated with a political party?‘Issues-driven, not politics-driven’Fix Victoria is run by experienced political operatives who held senior positions at a conservative thinktank, the Institute of Public Affairs (IPA). It began plotting its ad campaign in May, when a group of like-minded people started recruiting paying members who could finance its operations and ads.Corporate filings show it was registered with Asic in early August by Deborah Henderson, who was until June the deputy executive director of the IPA. Its communications director is Andrew Hudgson, who held a similar role at the IPA until earlier this year. Its head of advocacy is Gideon Rozner, who spent six years at the IPA before working at an investment firm.Fix Victoria is a separate entity to the IPA and its staff say it is coincidence that three of them previously worked at the thinktank, which is a long-term critic of Labor governments.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIn November, Rozner told his social media followers that he was rejoining the Liberal party to support its new leader, Jess Wilson.“The best place for me is to stand with the thousands of Victorians who will get around Jess Wilson to defeat this disgusting Labor government and save the great state of Victoria,” Rozner posted on X.When asked by Guardian Australia whether he is still a member of the Liberal party, Rozner declines to answer but says: “I’ve been around for a long time – and my views and affiliations are well-known.”Rozner says Fix Victoria is an “issues-driven, not politics-driven” organisation that wants to “ensure our leaders know that everyday Victorians want a plan to get out of the mess we are currently in”.“Fix Victoria is focused on the three key issues dragging our state down, that being crime, corruption and debt,” Rozner says.These three issues happen to be key talking points of opposition parties.“Victoria’s tsunami of debt steals resources from policing so organised illegal tobacco criminals are making billions, recruiting vulnerable kids and making our streets unsafe,” one 30-second Fix Victoria ad says.Bar chart showing the top ten ad spend by political groups ahead of Victoria’s state election‘Campaign groups exploiting loopholes’A loophole in Victoria’s electoral laws means voters may never know who is ultimately funding these ads.Groups publishing political ads during campaigns don’t need to be registered as third-party campaigners unless they specifically promote or oppose a party or a candidate.The Centre for Public Integrity’s executive director, Catherine Williams, says Victoria’s laws are narrower in scope than their federal equivalent.“Unless an entity meets the definition of third-party campaigner, no disclosure obligations apply,” Williams says.During the federal election campaign, mandatory donation disclosures by one third-party campaign grouprevealed it had been bankrolled by the coal lobby. The group had been attacking Labor, Greens and independent candidates.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTransparency International Australia’s chief executive, Clancy Moore, says while Fix Victoria does not meet the legal threshold of a third-party campaign group, its ads are “clearly trying to influence voting”.Pauline Hanson courts wealthy donors with $2,000 ‘exclusive’ Melbourne lunch, but where are the receipts?Read more“It’s really important Victorians know who is behind these types of campaigns and what their political affiliations might be,” Moore says. “There is a long history of third-party and fake grassroots campaign groups exploiting loopholes in electoral laws to try to influence elections.”Rozner says Fix Victoria has “invested considerable resources to ensure strict compliance with all relevant laws, in particular the Victorian Electoral Act”.By avoiding reference to political parties or candidates, Fix Victoria’s financial backers are shielded from public view unless disclosed by the group itself.“We place a very high priority on protecting the security and privacy of our members and supporters,” Rozner says.View image in fullscreenAn advertising executive says Fix Victoria spent just under $100,000 on ads in AugustBetter Victoria was formed a month after Fix Victoria, with its first ads running on Facebook in early August. Its political content is endorsed by the group itself, rather than a office holder.Listings with Consumer Affairs Victoria show its secretary is Ronald Holzer, a lawyer based in the Melbourne suburb of Caulfied North. Holzer says he only has an administrative role with the group.He referred a series of questions from Guardian Australia to an unnamed spokesperson, who declined to say who was running the organisation.“Better Victoria has obtained independent legal advice regarding its activities,” the spokesperson said. “It is confident that its activities are fully compliant with Victoria’s electoral laws.”The spokesperson said the group had no relationship with any political party and was fully financed by donations from its members. Those donors will also remain hidden.“Our members include people from a range of backgrounds and professions, who have exercised their right to privacy,” the spokesperson said.‘They will have spent tens of thousands’An advertising executive, Ed Coper, who worked with Climate 200 and some teal candidates during the 2025 federal election, says the two groups are spending big.Coper’s agency, Populares, has tracked their spending using public data and says they spent more on Google and Meta ads than any other state election candidate or party in August.He says Fix Victoria spent just under $100,000 on ads, which was about a quarter of all the advertising spend related to the election. Better Victoria spent about $40,000.The two groups also outspent the Liberals, teal independents and One Nation on social media advertising, according to Populares.Then there’s the ad Fix Victoria ran in the middle of the AFL wildcard final between the Western Bulldogs and Collingwood on Channel Seven on 28 August.“They will have spent tens of thousands of dollars,” Coper says. “The actual content of their advertising is very, very similar to the way that a political operative will message during an election campaign.”Explore more on these topicsVictorian politicsVictoriaSocial mediaAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Food delivery riders call on platforms to open up AI ‘black box’ they say has cut pay | Gig economy | The Guardian
description: Workers who blame algorithms for lowering their earnings are getting help from academics to find out how the system works
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Workers who blame algorithms for lowering their earnings are getting help from academics to find out how the system works
Content: Delivery riders (from left) Graeme Frances, Bijyan, Xabier Villares and Michael Angus in central Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDelivery riders (from left) Graeme Frances, Bijyan, Xabier Villares and Michael Angus in central Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianGig economyFood delivery riders call on platforms to open up AI ‘black box’ they say has cut payWorkers who blame algorithms for lowering their earnings are getting help from academics to find out how the system worksJoanna PartridgeSat 5 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 02.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGig economy workers are urging delivery platforms to open up the “black box” of computer-driven algorithms that determine the jobs they are offered and how much they are paid, blaming increased use of AI for lowering wages.A group of food delivery riders inEdinburghsay their rates of pay have fallen and their working conditions have deteriorated at the same time as Deliveroo, Uber Eats and Just Eat, the three dominant gig economy platforms in the UK and Ireland, have increased their use of automation.“I am making half the money I was making four years ago, for the same amount of hours. It makes no sense,” said David, a food delivery rider in Edinburgh for the past seven years who did not want to share his surname.View image in fullscreenDeliveroo rider Xabier Villares.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOn a weekday afternoon in the Scottish capital, David and other food delivery riders are sharing their experiences of worsening pay and conditions before they go their separate ways to carry food and groceries to customers’ doorsteps during the dinnertime rush.Standing next to their bikes and insulated food delivery bags in central Edinburgh’s Bristo Square, many have cycled the city streets for several years and tracked a gradual decline in the amount they are paid, even though they continue to deliver similar numbers of orders.The group has come together through the Workers’ Observatory, a charity founded by gig economy workers alongside academics at St Andrews and Edinburgh universities. Its aim is to help riders research the parts of their working experience that are mostly concealed by the companies that operate delivery platforms, to help them to challenge their working conditions.David’s experience is echoed by Xabier Villares, who has been riding for eight years and is now the observatory’s lead organiser. “There has been a dramatic change in the last three years,” he said. “I used to work four or five days a week, especially evenings and some lunchtimes, and was able to pay my rent and bills and make a decent living with that. But that’s not an option any more.”The observatory, which has justgained research fundingfor the next decade, has previously carried out experiments to monitor the variable levels of pay offered to different workers by algorithms, a system known as “dynamic pricing” that purports to match real-time supply and demand.Trades unions arecampaigning to banthe practice, saying it leaves workers uncertain about their earnings.The introduction of a dynamic pricing algorithm in 2023 resulted in Uber drivers earning “substantially less” an hour, according to research fromthe University of OxfordandNew York’s Columbia business school.This week drivers from the UK, the Netherlands and other countrieslaunched a landmark class action against the ride-hailing appclaiming they live in “constant fear” of the “soulless” algorithm it uses to set pay and allocate jobs.The legal case lodged in Amsterdam, which could run into billions of dollars, alleges the AI-powered system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings based on what each driver is willing to take.Uberdenies adjusting trip prices based on an individual driver’s behaviour and has put discrepancies down to other features of its system such as GPS.Cailean Gallagher, director of the observatory and a lecturer at St Andrews university business school, said “there is so much infrastructure of knowledge and data that’s concealed” by the platforms, leaving gig economy riders “working in the dark”.View image in fullscreenCailean Gallagher, director of the Workers’ Observatory.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianHe added: “What we are trying to do with the observatory is to get on the ground floor in terms of understanding how the whole apparatus works.”In one Workers’ Observatory test, a group of riders in Dunfermline, Fife, logged on to a delivery platform at the same time, with some rejecting job offers below a certain rate. This boosted the rate for some workers in the short term, while others were penalised – with one deactivated from the platform shortly afterwards, although it was unclear why – in a way that Gallagher says “seemed very arbitrary”. The major delivery platforms insist riders are not deactivated for rejecting job offers.Dylan* has notched up more than five years riding forDeliverooin Scotland. Since mid-2023, he has kept meticulous records tracking his monthly income, number of orders delivered and what the average pay per order is.The number of orders Dylan delivers each hour has remained constant between 3.6 and 3.8 for the past three years. However, his records highlight how the average fee paid for each order has steadily declined over that period, from £3.67 in 2023, to £3.63 in 2024, £3.51 in 2025 and to £3.42 in the first half of 2026.“I like to keep a close eye on everything, normally just to make paying my taxes easier,” he said. “I started noticing a couple of years ago there was actually a big drop-off in my earnings. If you are doing the same amount of work, that equates to getting paid quite a lot less for the same work.”Dylan blames the algorithm for constantly undercutting rates, along with the introduction of what Deliveroo calls “stacked orders”, where riders can accept two or three orders from restaurants located close to each other, but not receive the level of fees they would get for delivering these separately. “Some of the offers they give you view you as a clown,” he said.View image in fullscreenRider Graeme Frances was unable to log on to work with a black eye due to the app’s facial recognition system.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianRider Graeme Frances believes the delivery platforms “rely on [the work] being opaque”. He said: “You don’t know what is in the black box of how they work out what to pay to whom.”Deliveroo has named its algorithm Frank andhas previously described it as “super smart”and able to decide “which rider to offer which order”. The company, which wastaken over by its US rival DoorDashin 2025, said Frank was “made up of machine-learning technology, which predicts the timings of every order”, allowing food to be delivered “in the most efficient and reliable way”.Frances also blames increased use of AI by the platforms for more log-on difficulties. After ending up with a black eye following an accident outside work in August 2025, the facial recognition technology did not allow him to log-on to the Deliveroo app, preventing him from working. He was unable to get help from human support staff.Deliveroo acknowledged Frances failed the facial recognition checks multiple times, stopping him from working, which it said was due to a blurry picture.Frances says he requested a manual review of his facial recognition check and was not aware he had passed this until the next time he logged in, leading him to believe he could not work until his injury had healed. Deliveroo says Frances would have been able to work after the manual review.Deliveroo, Uber Eats and Just Eat all say their riders earn more than the national living wage while they are on an order, but this does not include time waiting for job offers.A Deliveroo spokesperson said: “Riders are guaranteed to earn a minimum hourly fee while on an order, which … rose by 3.8% this year – an above inflation increase.“The vast majority of riders are satisfied working with us, and we continue to partner with the GMB Union to raise the bar on security and wellbeing standards. Information on our algorithm and fees are set out on our rider website.“We have a dedicated team in place to support riders, and any significant decision over a rider account is not automated, but reviewed by our team.”An Uber spokesperson said: “Our matching tools follow a process that balances a number of different factors, such as time and distance, to provide the best possible experience for everyone using the app.”A Just Eat spokesperson said: “As a delivery platform we use technology, overseen by a human team, to match deliveries with available couriers.”* Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsGig economyAI (artificial intelligence)DeliverooUberWorkers' rightsEdinburghScotlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The US attorney general is fretting about a ‘pandemic’ of gender transitions in schools | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Todd Blanche’s remarks are part of a totally-not-invented moral panic that stretches the limits of the imagination
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Todd Blanche’s remarks are part of a totally-not-invented moral panic that stretches the limits of the imagination
Content: ‘Our intrepid attorney general, Todd Blanche, is on the case.’Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Our intrepid attorney general, Todd Blanche, is on the case.’Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersOpinionTodd BlancheThe US attorney general is fretting about a ‘pandemic’ of gender transitions in schoolsArwa MahdawiTodd Blanche’s remarks are part of a totally-not-invented moral panic that stretches the limits of the imaginationSat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 17.32 EDTShareBeing a public school teacher in the US these days is tough. You’ve got topayfor a lot of your own supplies, deal with smartphone-addicted children and perform gender-affirming surgeries on your lunch break.Luckily our intrepid attorney general, Todd Blanche, is on the case. Blanche appeared on Fox News this week todecrya “pandemic” of gender transitions in schools across the US. “There’s not a parent in America, no matter where you live, that would want their school to change and call their child by a different name and not expect to be told about that. We partnered with the Department of Education recently to combat this very trend and, really, pandemic that’s happening in some school districts around the country,” Blanche said. He seemed more concerned with name changes than with surgery, but the president himself has suggested on severaloccasionsthat schools are furtively doing surgery on children. During a campaign speech in 2024, for example, Donald Trumpsaid: “Can you imagine … your son leaves the house and you say: ‘Jimmy, I love you so much. Go have a good day in school,’ and your son comes back with a brutal operation? Can you even imagine this?”No, I can’t even imagine this. The public schools near me can’t affordair conditioning, so I’m not sure where they are getting all these operating theaters and surgeons from.Still, don’t let my lack of imagination stop you from getting outraged over this totally-not-invented moral panic, which is consuming valuable government resources. Blanche’s Fox News interview came shortly after the justice departmentfiledwhat itdescribedas a “first-of-its-kind lawsuit” against a Kansas school district, aimed at stopping itfrom“facilitating secret ‘gender transitions’ for children at school without their parents’ knowledge or consent”. The district, which denies wrongdoing, risks losing almost $70m in federal funds if it is found to have violated federal law.While this all sounds terribly dramatic, the substance of the Kansas public school lawsuit is actually rather mundane. It seems what is riling the Trump administration up are some extremely reasonable internal school guidelines, never adopted asformal policy, whichstate, according to the justice department complaint, that if a transgender student doesn’t want their parents notified about their preferred names and pronouns “that request will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis”.There’s certainly a sensible conversation to be had about whether teachers should inform parents if their child wishes to be known by a different name. And Blanche might actually want to ask the vice-president to weigh in on that matter, considering JD Vance has changed his own namemultiple times. But let’s not pretend that Blanche and Fox News are interested in sensible conversations. One suspects they just want to whip viewers up into a frenzy about trans people, a favourite boogeyman, in order to distract from the fact that the Trump administration is pillaging the country for personal gain.Let’s also not pretend that the attorney general, who wasconfirmedlast month, is in his job because he is deeply invested in the wellbeing of America’s young people. Blanche was Trump’s personalcriminal defense lawyerbefore he was brought into the White House; he eventually became attorney general following the ousting of Pam Bondi. He is a Trump loyalist who oncesaidhe’d tell the president: “Thank you very much. I love you, sir” if Trump nominated someone else for the job. He’s got his job, I’d wager, because he’s made it clear he’ll protect the president and advance Trump’s agenda. Indeed, one of the very first things that Blanche’s justice department did after he was confirmed as attorney general was to issue an opinion stating that the president’s “executive privilege” can extend to advisers whodon’t work for his administration. Which makes it harder for Democrats to investigate Trump in the future.But maybe I’m being uncharitable here. Maybe the attorney general isn’t just interested in advancing his own career by finding ways to give Trump carte blanche to do whatever he likes. Maybe he really does care about vulnerable young people. In which case, may I suggest he focus some of his attention on revisiting theJeffrey Epsteinfiles? I’m sure that I don’t need to remind you that theonly personin jail right now because of their connection to the late sex offender is Ghislaine Maxwell. An awful lot of powerful people seem to have successfully dodged any accountability.One would think an unpunished international pedophilia ring might worry Blanche more than schoolkids experimenting with their names in Kansas. However, Blancheseemsa littleresistantto taking the investigation much further – possibly because Trump is named in the Epstein files thousands oftimes. The attorney general also made sure to stress on Fox News earlier this yearthat“it isn’t a crime to party with Mr Epstein”.Still, it doesn’t matter how much Blanche tries to distract us with culture wars – he can’t escape the ghost of Epstein.
