This week, the outgoing congressman Thomas Massie, a staunch Trump critic, noted that millions of Epstein files have yet to be publicly disclosed andurgedthe Department of Justice to launch an immediate investigation into 14 named Epstein associates, including the billionaire Leon Black. “Perhaps hearing these names will shame the Department of Justice into delivering justice,”he said. One would hope so. But it’s hard to shame the shameless.Trailblazing feminist Gloria Steinem dies aged 92“Steinem, unlike some of her contemporaries, never recanted or modified her many causes, which included civil rights, violence against women, and the struggle for equality,” Yvonne Roberts writes in the Guardianobituary. “She continued to argue that every economics course ought to start not with production but with reproduction, and an understanding of the patriarchal instinct to restrict a woman’s right to contraception and abortion.”Eighty-nine percent of Americans believe there’s ‘widespread corruption’ within US governmentThat’s according to a newGallup poll, which found perceptions of corruption are at their highest level in 20 years. Gosh, I wonder why.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTennessee is about to execute its first woman since 1819Christa Pike isdueto be executed at the end of the month for a murder she committed with two others when she was 18. Pikesufferedchild sexual abuse, neglect and violent rape growing up; according to one psychologist she “experienced more severe adverse events than 99% of the US population”. Her case raises troubling questions, Austin Saratwritesin the Guardian: “For women as well as men, capital punishment offers no solution to the problems that give rise to the most serious crimes.”Israel ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’Anyone paying attention could seethis wasalways the plan.Health department accused of using fake AI studies to justify teen pregnancy cutsThe US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)canceled53 teen pregnancy prevention grants earlier this year and wants to direct millions in funding to organizations that emphasize “body literacy” and abstinence instead. This is despite (or perhaps because of) studies that have shown abstinence-only approachesincreaserates of teen pregnancy. There’s now a lawsuit over this, and the HHS has defended its decision with references todubiousstudies. In anopiniongranting a preliminary injunction, the judge said: “On the topic of body literacy, the notices (remarkably) reference public health studies that appear either not to exist or not to support the propositions for which they are cited – a hallmark of AI-generated citations.” This is on-brand for the HHS secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, whose team released a report on children’s health last yearfull of fake citations. It’s almost as if the man is dangerously unqualified for his job.JD Vance is OK with his work leading to the ‘end times’“While I wouldn’t be shocked if we are living in the end times, what I’m trying to focus on is doing as much of God’s work as possible right now,” the vice-presidentsaidduring apodcastinterview with Bryce Crawford, a young Christian evangelist. Vance added: “And if that leads to the end times, OK.”Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsTodd BlancheOpinionGenderTrump administrationDonald TrumpJeffrey EpsteinUS politicsKansascommentShareReuse this content

title: CTE in football players is a health crisis. It’s time for us to stop watching | NFL | The Guardian
description: A new study offers more evidence that America’s biggest sport produces life-altering head trauma. The NFL will never turn itself off, so it’s on fans to do so
Author: Nathan Kalman-Lamb
Headline: A new study offers more evidence that America’s biggest sport produces life-altering head trauma. The NFL will never turn itself off, so it’s on fans to do so
Content: A new NFL season begins on Wednesday.Photograph: John Amis/APView image in fullscreenA new NFL season begins on Wednesday.Photograph: John Amis/APNFLCTE in football players is a health crisis. It’s time for us to stop watchingNathan Kalman-LambandDerek SilvaA new study offers more evidence that America’s biggest sport produces life-altering head trauma. The NFL will never turn itself off, so it’s on fans to do soSat 5 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 10.59 EDTShareAs a newNFLseason begins this Wednesday, the danger of America’s most-watched sport has never been more clear.A new and widely circulatedstudypublished in theBritish Medical Journalexamined the donated brains of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 and compared them with the overall number of players who died during that period. Of the 235 donated brains in that period, 215 had evidence of the degenerative brain condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). That group of 215 comprised 24.5% of the former players who died during that periodin total. Given the finding, the study’s authors estimate that the prevalence of CTE among players who died in that period was at minimum 24.5% to a maximum of 97.7%, with the actual rate likely somewhere in between.At least one in four former NFL players in study suffered from degenerative brain disease CTERead moreThe implication of that finding cannot be overstated: it suggests that CTE is a disease that may affect a substantial share of those who spend their careers in the NFL. The players taking the field this season are being exposed to the same fundamental risk: the repeated blows to the head that have been linked to the disease. When we watch players deliver and receive those devastating if also thrilling hits, when we watch the lines collideon every play, we are watching the repetitive head trauma that puts players at risk of developing CTE. We are watching lives being permanently altered in ways that will in the end result in heartbreak.And yet, as recently as Friday, theWall Street Journalpublished an op-ed by former senator Ben Sasse that makes the titular claim “America needs its boys to play football.” That sentiment isn’t just a vestige of should-be-antiquated gender politics – it is better understood as tantamount to child endangerment.Because, perhaps the most disconcerting statistic is one that we already know: every2.6 years of participationin football doubles the chances of developing CTE, in large part because a typical high school or college football season can deliver between600 and 1,000 subconcussive blows to a single athlete, and that these blows heavily predict later-lifeclinical depression, apathy, executive dysfunction and cognitive impairment. We also know that participation in football increases the chances of developing Parkinson’s disease by 61% compared with athletes in other organized sports (and that risk is 2.93 times greater for those who play football at the college/pro level compared with youth/high school).When you put these figures in the context of the reality that in many parts of the United States, children are enrolled in tackle football as early as5years old, it becomes clear that this is a potential public health crisis.The statistics only tell part of the story. In our 2024 bookThe End of College Football: On The Human Cost of an All-American Game,we talked to former big-time college football players – a level lower than the NFL, meaning fewer total head impacts than those at the pinnacle of the game – about how their lives had been affected by head injury in the sport. These players understood that their lives were at stake. One told us frankly: “I feel like there’s a good chance that I will have CTE. Especially if I kept playing, it’ll probably be guaranteed. But I won’t find out until I die, which isn’t comforting at all.”Another explained, “The scariest part about that for me is I don’t know the price that I paid in terms of cognitive ability, in terms of how many concussions did I play through, how many times did I have a concussion and didn’t report it?”A third player told us that his career had bequeathed him a “panic disorder related to probably all the sub-concussive blows”.One player said that after enduring 10 concussions, “I could barely do school. … I would forget what I was talking about mid-sentence. I’d be forgetting everything that happened like 10 minutes ago. I would just completely zone out sometimes. It was like I was halfway there. I couldn’t really control it.”Still a different player told us, “I played with guys in the NFL that took their own lives and then were diagnosed with CTE when they did the autopsy, so you think about that, like, ‘Boy, I hit my head against that guy’s head, so what’s going on with me if that was obviously was going on with him?’”No one wants to see football players die for this sport. But they are. In 2025 alone,nine former NFL playersunder the age of 48 died. Seven of those deaths were a result of suicide, underscoring the fears surrounding the long-term neurological and psychiatric consequences of repeated head trauma.The tragedy of death by football is thus happening whether we realize it or not. Far too much evidence now exists that the sport systematically produces life-altering head trauma for us to continue with business as usual when we know that football is morally unsustainable.The NFL will of course never turn itself off. So, starting this season, it’s up to us as fans to do that. There are too many lives at stake.Nathan Kalman-Lamb is Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of New Brunswick. Derek Silva is Associate Professor of Sociology and Criminology at King’s University College at Western University.In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123, or emailjo@samaritans.orgorjo@samaritans.ie. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsNFLConcussion in sportUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: When Dad asked me to edit his novel, I wanted to say no – but ran directly towards the lion’s den | Anna Spargo-Ryan | The Guardian
description: My father doesn’t ask for help from just anyone. And yet he asked for mine. He believed in me
Author: Anna Spargo-Ryan
Headline: My father doesn’t ask for help from just anyone. And yet he asked for mine. He believed in me
Content: ‘My dad was asking me to teach him something new, and I realised he wasn’t perfect at everything first go; he was perfect at persevering.’Photograph: Lesia Larionova/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘My dad was asking me to teach him something new, and I realised he wasn’t perfect at everything first go; he was perfect at persevering.’Photograph: Lesia Larionova/AlamyOpinionFather's DayWhen Dad asked me to edit his novel, I wanted to say no – but ran directly towards the lion’s denAnna Spargo-RyanMy father doesn’t ask for help from just anyone. And yet he asked for mine. He believed in meSat 5 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.52 EDTShareMy dad and I believe in many of the same things: cheesecake; the Geelong football club; my mum. And that we should immediately be experts at anything. First try. No practice. No revision.He taught me this in kindergarten. Every day he pushed me to be brilliant. We played spelling games in the car and did maths workbooks for fun. Before I started school I had “published” a library of my own books, complete with copyright information. I had become – and I’m assuming this is true of most Guardian writers – a precocious kid who irritated everyone around her by being boisterously, aggressively right about everything all of the time. Just like my dad. (Obviously I’ve grown a lot since then.)The kindness of strangers: After losing my wife and son, I ate alone one Father’s Day – and another diner paid my billRead moreSo when he asked, at age 77, if I would edit the novel he’d been working on, I responded with what I’ll generously call abject terror. I knew, from teaching hundreds of later-life would-be writers, that there would be feedback. Good Lord, would there. And I also knew, from a lifetime of being explicitly told, that we always got things right the first time. No exceptions.I wanted to say no. I wanted to tell him, Dad, our relationship is too precious to me. “I’m not sure I have time,” I said, because I am the worst daughter on Earth. But, after my life had flashed before my eyes, I took a beat. The truth is: his outrageous self-belief is well founded. Most people are worse than him at most things. My dad doesn’t ask for help from just anyone. And yet, he had asked for mine.He didn’t just believe in cake and footy and my mum. He believed in me.So I did a 180. I ran directly towards the lion’s den. “Sure,” I said, impaling myself on the sword of my dad’s validation, “I would love to edit your novel.”He sent me the manuscript and I sent him some ground rules: everything was open to suggestion; he wasn’t allowed to yell at me; critiquing his work wasn’t the same as critiquing who he is as a person (writers know this is a lie). He agreed. I opened his document with fear in all four chambers of my heart and started reading.View image in fullscreenAnna Spargo-Ryan and her father, David RyanI had a lot of feedback. He had written a gorgeous story about young men and football and friendship, but like most new writers, his dialogue clanged. His characters’ actions didn’t ring true. He told too much and showed too little. Nervously, I added comments. At first they were like, “Hi Dad, I love you so much!!!!!! I would maybe consider removing this word ONLY IF YOU WANT TO! Shall we get a coffee?” I sent him a chapter at a time, waiting for him to call and tell me I was out of the will and also a live shark was on its way to kill me.But he didn’t. Mum sent secret photos of him bent over his laptop, writing and rewriting.Around page 260, I noticed something. Inside this story about vulnerable young men was a vulnerable older man. As his characters trained and competed to be better than before, so did he. With his 80th birthday in the near distance, my dad was asking me to teach him something new, and I realised he wasn’t perfect at everything first go; he was perfect at persevering. When I was little and frustrated at not being the best, he didn’t show me I didn’t have to try. He wasn’t teaching me I could get things right the first time but that I should never stop believing I might.The tables turned. “This doesn’t make sense,” I wrote. “She would never do this.” I began to lean on what I knew about him. “You know how the wind comes through Norwood Oval and it brings the pie smell? Show me that.” I had a shorthand for everything. A common anecdote. A memory we shared.Familyfolklore, in-jokes, people we’ve known. “WHY is this character behaving like Simon from the fruit shop???” Sometimes I just called him and made him explain himself, rationalise his choices, workshop a problem until it was solved.Dad made revisions. The harder I challenged, the better he wrote. Each chapter he returned was an improvement on the last, with people and scenes and conversations busting out of the pages. Not on his first go, or even second go, but on his ninth and 10th goes. “Thank you,” he said, over and over. “This is so helpful.”The more honest I was, the more he appreciated it. He did not yell at me. He did not think I loved him less.When Dad published his book this year, we did apodcastabout father-daughter editing. He spoke about how much it meant to him that I said yes. I ordered my copy the minute it went live, and when it arrived, I shelved it alongside my own books. Our little library – not of getting it right first time, but of learning to believe you might.Anna Spargo-Ryan is the author of A Kind of Magic, The Gulf and The Paper House, and a winner of the Horne prize. David Ryan is the author of The Medal and The Butterfly’s Daughter.Due to an inadvertent editorial omission, David Ryan’s books were not listed on this page at time of publication. This has now been corrected.Explore more on these topicsFather's DayOpinionParents and parentingFamilyAustralian bookscommentShareReuse this content

title: An algorithm off switch isn’t enough. A digital duty of care must hold tech bros accountable for addictive designs | Zoe Daniel | The Guardian
description: As AI advances minute by minute and governments grapple with new developments they don’t know how to manage, holding big tech accountable becomes even more urgent
Author: Zoe Daniel
Headline: As AI advances minute by minute and governments grapple with new developments they don’t know how to manage, holding big tech accountable becomes even more urgent
Content: It is already proven that addictive design features in the digital media platforms can erode attention and productivity, writes Zoe Daniel.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreenIt is already proven that addictive design features in the digital media platforms can erode attention and productivity, writes Zoe Daniel.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersOpinionSocial mediaAn algorithm off switch isn’t enough. A digital duty of care must hold tech bros accountable for addictive designsZoe DanielAs AI advances minute by minute and governments grapple with new developments they don’t know how to manage, holding big tech accountable becomes even more urgentSat 5 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.12 EDTShareAdigital duty of care is about a lot more than opting out of “the algorithm”. And after the simplistic andat best patchyexercise of the under-16s social media ban, we shouldn’t let the government get away with another populist policy that looks good on the surface but doesn’t get to the core of the problem.A digital duty of care must hold the tech bros accountable for the safety of the spaces that they have created.Like the social media age ban – and indeed the government’s paltry efforts on gambling advertising – an algorithm opt-out maintains the onus on the consumer and is only one piece of the framework needed to manage the fact “the algorithm” is currently controlling the world.Tech giants are trying to obliterate privacy. Australia has a rare chance to take back part of their power | Lizzie O’SheaRead moreThere’s a lot to be said for theChanel Contos-driven “Fix our feeds” campaign, which has drawn much-needed attention to the effect of “the algorithm” – particularly when it comes to online misogyny and sexual violence, normalisation of pornography and strangulation during sex.“It is too easy for big tech to design schemes that appear as structural reform but actually suit them just fine,” the sexual consent advocatesaid in a speechto the National Press Club in Canberra on Thursday.She’s right. The issue is that giving users control over their exposure to “the algorithm” alone won’t be enough to create real accountability – particularly if the user has to opt out.“The algorithm” is a suite of systems which, in part, profile users and then leverage our personal habits to keep us scrolling. This embeds the potential for considerable societal harm, which we are now seeing unfold in real time.Addictive design features are eroding attention spans and productivity; mental health issues are increasing; divisive and outrageous content is amplified over consensus; and social isolation is increasing statistically across all age groups.The key to beginning to retake our “information sovereignty” – to keeping some level of say in what’s happening in the digital realm – is applying a mandatory and enforceable duty of care on big tech.This is becoming ever more urgent as AI advances minute by minute and governments grapple with new developments that they don’t know how to manage. It’s big tech v community – and we know who wins there, with smart glasses the latest iteration of a complex debate that is also an opportunity.An effective update of ourwoefully out-of-date privacy laws, together with the implementation of a legislated and enforceable digital duty of care, would be a powerful step forward.In 2024 I tabled aprivate members’ digital duty of care billin federal parliament, modelled on the best of UK and EU legislation. As I said in my introductory speech for the bill, the core aim has to be to make the platforms make their spaces safe for us, for our kids and for our communities.A duty of care is not only just, but essential. It is appropriately broad in scope to ensure that all of the systems, processes and elements of a digital service are captured, including “dark patterns” and addictive design features.The bill included the strongest-possible default privacy settings and the ability for users to both reset and “switch off” the algorithm.Enabling this was targeted particularly at young people with eating disorders and mental health issues, problem gamblers and others.But the bill went much further than that. It required detailed evidence of risk assessment and mitigation by the platforms; transparency and access for independent researchers to get “under the hood” and understand the algorithm; and penalties of up to 10% of global turnover for non-compliance.In other words, it had teeth for enforcement.And this is far less about the content itself than it is about the systems that drive it. The old game of removing content via whack-a-mole is pointless.A well-executed duty of care would protect everyone, whether they opt out or not, by holding the platforms to account for the design of their systems and the resultant risk to emotional wellbeing, political and social cohesion and addictive design features.It could also include misinformation and disinformation. This would risk the usual culture war debate about free speech, while we blithely accept the changes to our culture and society that are being freely imposed by Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and others.What we should be worried about is the sovereignty of the information landscape and the fact that we’re being controlled by the systems – not the other way around.Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and former independent member for GoldsteinExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionSocial media banDigital mediaSocial media bansAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: The pressure on Burnham to appease the right is huge. But now is the time to step out of Reform’s shadow | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: A scandal-besieged Reform still has a loyal base that won’t budge. That should free up the PM to deliver some home truths, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: A scandal-besieged Reform still has a loyal base that won’t budge. That should free up the PM to deliver some home truths, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Attenders at the second day of the Reform UK conference in Birmingham, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenAttenders at the second day of the Reform UK conference in Birmingham, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionAndy BurnhamThe pressure on Burnham to appease the right is huge. But now is the time to step out of Reform’s shadowAndy BeckettA scandal-besieged Reform still has a loyal base that won’t budge. That should free up the PM to deliver some home truthsSat 5 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 11.42 EDTShareDespite the bright start to Andy Burnham’s premiership, and Reform UK’s sudden disarray, a shadow still hangs over British centre-left politics. Labour has a smallpoll lead, a cautious air of confidence and a leader who seems energised rather than overwhelmed by trying to solve the country’s problems. Meanwhile, Reform is having a terrible 2026: mired in deepening funding scandals, losing winnable byelections and, thanks to the drama and novelty of Burnham’s leadership coup and new government, no longer the freshest story around.Yet Reform UK’s support has either held up or fallen only slightly in most polls since Burnham entered Downing Street. Even in the Makerfield byelection, where he beat it more decisively than expected, Reform’s vote share and total supportactually rose. Nigel Farage may have spent the year uncharacteristically avoiding journalists, or in his prickly rather than jolly public mode, but the overwhelming majority of Reform supporters, almost a quarter of the electorate, remain faithful. “Power is within our grasp!” insisted Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesman, at its party conference in Birmingham on Friday, and they applauded with determined gusto.Meanwhile, their preoccupations continue to shape politics and how the media processes it. Immigration, crime, the benefits system, “wokeness”,net zero policies: all are constantly presented as out of control and contributing to national decline. From our overcrowded prisons to our almost exhausted North Sea oil- and gasfields, what are widely considered to be the most politically realistic options for the government are generally what most Reform voters would like to happen. The likelihood that permanent crime crackdowns and further large-scale fossil-fuel drilling – which the government looksincreasingly likely to approve– will bedisastrous for a country with an ever more obvious climate crisis and unprecedentedlylarge prison population, by historical and European standards, does not disturb this deep-rooted rightwing consensus. The pressure on Burnham to go along with it as prime minister will be never-ending.Yet the risks of governing under Reform’s shadow, while less discussed, are much larger. So far, Labour’s fragile poll recovery has mainly been built by taking support back from the Greens and Lib Dems, as the dip in their poll ratings since a Burnham premiership became likely has demonstrated. This change would almost certainly be undone if Burnham decided to follow a Reform-defined agenda. Keir Starmer’s abrupt announcement that he will leave parliament is the ultimate result of him making exactly that mistake in Downing Street – and has given the Greens’ leader, Zack Polanski, a chance to reverse the momentum shift from his party to Labour bystanding as a byelection candidate.Meanwhile, with Reform, Restore and the Tories all competing to be the most rightwing, and this country’s many reactionary media outlets doing the same, many right-leaning voters are even more convinced than usual that noLabourgovernment is acceptable. So the appeasement of conservative Britain, designed by Morgan McSweeney and carried out by Starmer, not always with conviction, was never likely to win many converts for long. In a deeply divided country, the days of Labour premiers attracting and holding on to large numbers of rightwing voters, as Tony Blair, Harold Wilson and Clement Attlee once did, are gone, at least for now.As a politician unusually keen by modern standards on cross-party collaboration and broad coalitions, Burnham could waste much of what may not be a long premiership trying to build bridges with the right. But there are some early signs he may pursue a more streetwise strategy. His debut contributions as prime minister in parliament this week mixed consensual catchphrases such as “problem-solving over point-scoring”, which made the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, sound rigidly confrontational in response, with sweeping attacks on areas where the right is vulnerable. Austerity, Brexit, privatisation and the centralisation of power in London have dwindling electoral support and even less credibility, however loudly the Tories and Reform defend some or all of them, because for decades these old-fashioned rightwing remedies have clearly failed to revive the country.“Far from ‘taking back control’, the combination of those policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain,”said Burnham, deftly turning a key promise of populism back against the rightwing populists. He knows that while Margaret Thatcher is still revered by Farage and Badenoch, the sometimes brutal economic changes that she and her Conservative successors drove through are not popular with all Tory and Reform voters. They may never switch to supporting Labour, but could support parts of Burnham’s programme, such as stronger public control over “the essentials of life” currently provided at excessive cost by toxic Thatcherite creations such as Thames Water.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAndy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations | George MonbiotRead moreThe approval, tacit or otherwise, of usually hostile voters on a specific issue can provide useful political cover for a government – especially an unpopular one, which Burnham’s is likely to be, however he performs, given the number of parties arrayed against him in our fragmented political landscape. He may well need that cover if his government is going to restructure the economy even half as ambitiously as he promises. The shareholders, financiers, lawyers and corporate executives who have done extremely well out of privatisation are not going to give up their gains and privileges without a fight.A temporary coalition of leftwing and rightwing voters may be the only way to overcome them. The economy is not democratic – much to the disappointment of generations of radical leftists – but in a democracy, powerful interests can be curbed or even defeated if they are challenged by a premier acting with broad public consent, as Attlee and Franklin D Roosevelt once did against some of the 20th century’s most entrenched economic elites.Yet if Burnham is to govern with anything like those legendary reformers’ effectiveness, then in other policy areas his government is going to have to stand up to Reform supporters. New research about them by King’s College London and UK in a Changing Europe shows that, despite this summer being the UK’s hottest ever, almost two-thirds “want to scrap the 2050 net zero target”. Meanwhile, anew Ipsos pollshows that immigration remains the number one public issue, particularly for Reform and Tory voters, despite the fact that immigration israpidly falling.Sooner or later, Burnham is going to have to use his celebrated communications skills to tell Britons some home truths, whether rightwing voters want to hear them or not. Otherwise, Reform’s shadow will chill his government for good.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourReform UKImmigration and asylumPrisons and probationClimate crisiscommentShareReuse this content

title: Booyakasha! Ali G is back – but even he can’t match the absurdity of modern Britain | Jason Okundaye | The Guardian
description: Sacha Baron Cohen’s character once exposed the contradictions of an emerging multicultural nation. But nearly 30 years on Britain has changed – and so has the joke, says assistant Opinion editor Jason Okundaye
Author: Jason Okundaye
Headline: Sacha Baron Cohen’s character once exposed the contradictions of an emerging multicultural nation. But nearly 30 years on Britain has changed – and so has the joke, says assistant Opinion editor Jason Okundaye
Content: A still from the forthcoming film Ali G: Who Iz I?.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosView image in fullscreenA still from the forthcoming film Ali G: Who Iz I?.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosOpinionSacha Baron CohenBooyakasha! Ali G is back – but even he can’t match the absurdity of modern BritainJason OkundayeSacha Baron Cohen’s character once exposed the contradictions of an emerging multicultural nation. But nearly 30 years on Britain has changed – and so has the jokeSat 5 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 07.04 EDTShareAnd so the nostalgia machine grinds on, dragging another pop culture corpse back into the light: yes, it’s the return of Ali G. Respeck.Sacha Baron Cohen’s skull-cap-wearing, “rudebwoy” wankster is staging a comeback with Ali G: Who Iz I?. The new film, premiering next month, is amockumentarythat sees the character starting a family with long-term companion Julie (thinking his approach to fatherhood will be “absent”) and embracing TikTok, all while donning new fake dreads and a rastacap.It’s taken little time for this revival to enter Britain’s terminal “ARE U OFFENDED, SNOWFLAKE?” culture-war cycle. The Telegraph’s chief film critic, Robbie Collin, wrote that Ali G would save us fromcomedy’s offence police: “We need a good dose of this sort of puerile needling more than ever.” And now there is apressure campaignasking cinemas not to screen Baron Cohen’s “racist caricature”, which has accruedmore than 46,000 signatures.The old hits never die. Yet I think this reboot, however tedious, prompts some worthwhile reflection about the changing state of Britain. Since Ali G’s debut in 1998, there has been disagreement over who the joke is on. Erstwhile defenders viewed the character’s absurdity as a reflection of society’s soft bigotry, a satire of white liberal elites’ prejudices.Ali G’s initial premise was interviews with unsuspecting public figures while posturing as a low-educated wannabe, and lobbing inane questions that reliably wrongfooted the interviewee. With a few exceptions, these interviewees were white, from Noam Chomsky to Newt Gingrich to Donald Trump (who walked out). The socialist MP Tony Benn, victim of such a set-up on the 11 O’Clock Show,admitted in 2000that “at no stage during our talk did I suspect for a second that it was other than a genuine programme”. The idea then was that you were laughing at the gullibility of the liberal middle classes.View image in fullscreenSacha Baron Cohen in Ali G Indahouse (2002).Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyBut some viewed this interpretation as apologia for something sinister. Black British comedians in particular viewed Ali G as a straight-upracist caricature. Comedian Felix Dexter was candid: “I feel that a lot of the humour is laughing at black street culture and it is being celebrated because it allows the liberal middle classes to laugh at that culture in a safe context where they can retain their sense of political correctness.”I think the most interesting intervention worth revisiting is that of the sociologist Paul Gilroy, who saw the comedy as a reflection of multicultural Britain’s coming-of-age.Writing in 2002, after the premiere of the film Ali G Indahouse, Gilroy posited that the character provided “a satirical Rorschach blot in which even the most neurotic scrutineers of the national psyche can discover their fears and hopes”.That interpretation fit with Gilroy’s theory of cultural hybridity: Ali G’s incoherence as a “shapeshifting” white English man performing a pastiche of Black urban street culture embodied the cultural mongrelisation that had been shaping Britain under New Labour. Ali G represented a cartoonish version of the very real destabilising of racial categories that was happening at the time. Some were optimistic about cultural diversity, while others were anxious. In particular the influence of nascent “yardie” culture, American hip-hop and conspicuous consumption was sometimes viewed as a social contagion impeding British youth.The salient question for me, then, is less whether it’s OK to find Ali G funny, or if it’s offensive, but rather what the character’s function and purpose is in 2026. His particular cultural bricolage is now being thrown into a far more charged political environment.Cultural boundaries remain porous, but the political boundaries around national belonging have hardened. Ali G emerged from a politics fascinated by cultural change and mixing, and returns to a politics dominated by a more severe policing of who gets to be British. The anxiety Ali G once represented is now a far more antagonistic struggle; just take a look at the ubiquitous“yookay”meme, the idea that multiculturalism has socially corrupted the UK.The mediums through which we absorb culture have also changed. Ali G’s racial politics were originally mediated through television: editing, scheduling and official channels for regulation meant that, however controversial, Baron Cohen and his collaborators could control its message. Online, that control disappears. You can easily imagine an Ali G scene now being clipped and shared as an anecdote of Britain’s decline.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd so Ali G arrives from the analogue world into one that is far more racialised, online and politically volatile. But the character has become obsolete because it is no longer transgressive: the cultural mix that once made Ali G ludicrous is now mundane. The seemingly exotic language Ali G parodies has for a long time now been understood asMulticultural London English.There is also the problem of Baron Cohen himself. His original approach had an incredibly effective comedy mechanism, using interviews to make powerful establishment figures reveal themselves. But Baron Cohen is no longer the outsider performing the outsider role, he is now a very famous 54-year-old multimillionaire attempting a last-gasp revival. Will anyone be duped, and what exactly could he reveal now anyway?It’s easy to dismiss the furore around Ali G’s return as political correctness. But it’s not that Britain has become too sensitive for the joke, it may be that the joke simply doesn’t work any more. And so what returns with Ali G is little more than the same old stereotype in a new costume, detached from the time in which it meant something more.Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the GuardianDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsSacha Baron CohenOpinionComedy filmsRaceComedycommentShareReuse this content

title: Losing a parent is a bewildering, lonely experience. Here are the things I wish I had known before | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: There’ll be exhaustion, love tinged with occasional rage, even moments of black humour. But my mum would want me to tell you: don’t be afraid, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: There’ll be exhaustion, love tinged with occasional rage, even moments of black humour. But my mum would want me to tell you: don’t be afraid, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Illustration: R Fresson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: R Fresson/The GuardianOpinionBereavementLosing a parent is a bewildering, lonely experience. Here are the things I wish I had known beforeGaby HinsliffThere’ll be exhaustion, love tinged with occasional rage, even moments of black humour. But my mum would want me to tell you: don’t be afraidSat 5 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 12.22 EDTShareMy mother’s house looks exactly as she left it.Two novels sit by the armchair, their pages neatly marked for book group. Pinned to the noticeboard is a shopping list in only slightly shaky writing, with “FRUIT!” in urgent capitals, and “make soup” underlined. The sole outward signs of something missing are her cats twining needily around me – loneliness having finally overcome their innate horror of visitors – and the one thing I can’t bear to look at, which is the empty hospital bed marooned bleakly in the sitting room. Delivered by social services when it was deemed she could no longer manage stairs, it is now stripped bare, awaiting collection. Another family will be needing it.This is not my childhood home – my parents moved here only a few years ago – but it’s the one, I suppose, where childhood formally ended. Washing up at her kitchen sink a fortnight ago, looking out at the same scarlet fuchsia I remember blazing in the garden when my father died, it struck me for the first time that soon I would no longer be anyone’s daughter. What I didn’t know then was that the loss of both parents would feel less like the end of a relationship and more like its transition to a new stage, of finally being able to see them clearly as people in their own right.I thought I’d nailed that years ago, but of course I was wrong. When news spread of her diagnosis – an aggressively fast-moving cancer, erupting from nowhere to overwhelm her in six weeks – my mother’s friends descended in hordes, bringing soup and cake and clove-scented sweet peas from their gardens. But they also brought stories I hadn’t heard before. Though my father was the outwardly gregarious one and my mother more self-effacing, evidently she was the one who watched and listened and caught what others missed. I already knew that for a while she’d channelled that into volunteering as a Samaritan – her way of dealing with the suicide of a close family friend – and training as a Relate counsellor. I was vaguely aware, too, that in retirement she’d founded local hillwalking groups, a social club for widows – and who knows what else. But stupidly, I hadn’t realised what the things we took for granted – “there goes Mum, on one of her missions again” – meant to others. She had been the author of small kindnesses remembered for decades.double quotation markHave a baby and the world falls over itself to offer advice. But losing a parent remains a private, bewildering, lonely affairWhy wait for a funeral, one of her friends argued, to say nice things? There was talk of a pre-party, a wake Mum could actually join in, abandoned when it became clear she was already too tired. But the urge to invent new rituals makes sense. With modern medicine rendering heart attacks and strokes more survivable, death increasingly announces itself to elderly people not suddenly overnight but slowly, and with plentiful warning. The creeping degenerative diseases of old age allow more time to say goodbye, or make amends if necessary. But they also force us all to look death squarely in the face, and that takes no little courage.Fiercely independent at 84, my mother dreaded going into a home. So when she was given less than three months to live, my sister and I promised to nurse her at home, despite having no real plan for managing that alongside jobs and teenage children, beyond somehow basically winging it. Have a baby and the world falls over itself to offer advice. But losing a parent remains a private, bewildering, lonely affair. Here, then, are a few things I wish I’d known at the beginning of summer, in case – like that empty bed – another family can use them.That care for the dying will trigger the instant muscle memory of caring for small children, if you had them: the same broken nights, same constant vigilance, same exhaustion after a day in which you can’t name a single thing you actually did, and the same unmistakable feeling of love tinged with occasional rage. Then as now we wouldn’t have coped without understanding employers, good friends and neighbours, an army of often overworked NHS and care staff, and things my sister learned from training as a midwife. (For the love of your lower back, get a professional to show you how to move a bedbound patient safely.)That there are moments of unspeakably black humour to be found even in dying, if you’re that kind of family.That there are times when your role is to argue with their doctors, and times for shutting up and listening, and you may never be wholly certain which is which.That if an old person in beady possession of all their marbles goes seemingly mad overnight, test for an underlying infection causing delirium. Antibiotics work miracles.That you should keep the bad photographs, because afterwards they’re the ones you invariably want to look at: anything where the kids were scowling, the haircuts sorely regrettable, the beach day rained off. It’s the life actually lived, not the one curated for Instagram, that you miss.That death can trigger an overwhelming urge to put one’s house in order in ways that make sense to the dying, but absolutely nobody else. (My mother had to be dissuaded from getting the sitting room repainted; a friend’s father insisted on alphabetising his CDs.) Within reason, don’t fight it. Like the manic nesting phase of late pregnancy, it’s all part of the process.That if you find old letters, you should read them only when feeling resilient. Your parents had lives before you existed and secrets they may not have shared.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat death itself is different for everyone, but that even the most peaceful kind looked to me like a form of work. The best way I can describe it is like a reverse childbirth: you can comfort the person going through it, but you cannot be in it with them.That it wasn’t nearly as frightening as that may sound.That grief doesn’t always wait for death. Dementia meant I lost my father in some ways years before he died, and a wise friend said that nursing my mother might feel, in retrospect, like starting to work through bereavement in advance. She wasn’t wrong.That adrenaline may power you through initially, and kindness may undo you.And lastly, what I think my mother would have wanted me to say: that if this is something you have yet to face, don’t be afraid. But if you’re already there and struggling, then you are nowhere near as alone as you think.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBereavementOpinionDeath and dyingFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t like the term neurodivergence – it sounds like political correctness’: Werner Herzog on fans, fanaticism and baby foxes  | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Bavarian auteur talks directing Kate and Rooney Mara in Bucking Fastard and his popularity on Instagram
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: The Bavarian auteur talks directing Kate and Rooney Mara in Bucking Fastard and his popularity on Instagram
Content: ‘What I do is lively and creates some inner life’ … Werner Herzog with Rooney and Kate Mara.Photograph: Mario Cartelli/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘What I do is lively and creates some inner life’ … Werner Herzog with Rooney and Kate Mara.Photograph: Mario Cartelli/SOPA Images/ShutterstockMoviesInterview‘I don’t like the term neurodivergence – it sounds like political correctness’: Werner Herzog on fans, fanaticism and baby foxesPhilip Oltermannin VeniceThe Bavarian auteur talks directing Kate and Rooney Mara in Bucking Fastard and his popularity on InstagramSat 5 Sep 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn outsider visionaries such as Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo or Timothy Treadwell, renegade German directorWerner Herzoghas created some of cinema’s most memorable monomaniacs – characters singularly obsessed with finding mythical cities made of gold, with building opera houses in the middle of the rainforest, or with befriending wild grizzly bears.Bucking Fastard review – Herzog’s starry twins soap provokes a syncing feelingRead moreBut suggestions that they could be role models for the modern-day neurodiversity movement send this famously fearless film-maker running for the hills. “I don’t like the term neurodivergence and ADHD, or whatever – it sounds like political correctness, which scares me under the table,” Herzog said at theVenice film festival.The protagonist pair ofBucking Fastard, the new film that Herzog has brought to the Lido, slots right into his gallery of single-minded outsiders. Real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara play siblings Jean and Joan Holbrooke, who have separate bodies but speak in unison, dress the same and share the same preoccupations.View image in fullscreenOstracised … Kate and Rooney Mara as the Holbrookes in Bucking Fastard.Photograph: Stills - Courtesy of Gateway to Orkney LLCFirst they fall in love with their washed-up heart-throb neighbour (played by Orlando Bloom) and exact revenge when he marries another woman, then they embark on a quixotic quest to dig a tunnel connecting a cave in County Sligo to the Orkneys. Contemporary psychiatrists might detect behaviour consistent with autism or ADHD hyper-focus. Not Herzog.“I do not relate to all these trendy terms – I just can’t hear it, it dusts out of my ears,” said the Bavaria-born US-based director, speaking in the idiosyncratic, heavily accented English familiar to viewers of documentaries like My Favourite Fiend. “Neurodivergence sounds like there’s some sort of clinical aberration – these sisters are dead centre.”His first non-documentary feature in 17 years, Bucking Fastard revisits old Herzogian themes but also breaks with them. The film is loosely based on the lives of Freda and Greta Chaplin, an intensely mutually attached pair of twins from York whom the German director met in the 1980s and who coined the spoonerism of the title in a court hearing.Like the Chaplins, the Holbrookes are ostracised by their family and neighbours, but in the film they also show resilience and find allies and supporters. “What is certainly different [to my earlier films] is that the sisters are not just nice, they’re vengeful”, said Herzog. “They are arsonists, they destroy things.”View image in fullscreenHerzog (second left) directs Rooney and Kate Mara.Photograph: Stills - Courtesy of Gateway to Orkney LLCThe Werner Herzog ofsocial-media parodiesis bleakly preoccupied with the cruel chaos inherent in the natural world, telling stories ofsuicidal penguins, man-eating bears, and birds“who don’t sing but screech in pain”. Yet in Bucking Fastard, the sisters rescue a young fox who, contrary to the warnings of a gang of overzealous hunters, doesn’t infect them with rabies.“We had in mind to have a baby fox they would warm under their armpits, but we could not find one all over Ireland,” Herzog recalled. “There was an animal dealer who told me, ‘I can get you a little fox, but only under one condition: you must never ask how we got it.’” Herzog declined. “I’m not in this business. You want to dig up a den and bring me a little fox – I’m not into that.”At 83, could the radical doomsayer of European art-house cinema be discovering his sentimental side? “What I do is lively and creates some inner life, some excitement and some joy in the storytelling,” Herzog said. “I’m not a control freak.”His taste for pathos, however, remains irrepressible. Bucking Fastard features a sequence shot inside a large karst cave system near Postojna, Slovenia, which Herzog described in similarly reverential tones as the French subterranean landscape in 2010’sCave of Forgotten Dreams: “It is a landscape of the soul, a landscape of the imagination.”His old-fashioned way of looking at the world keeps winning him young admirers, he claimed. “A huge amount of audiences that contact me these days are 15, 16, maybe 17 years old,” he said.View image in fullscreenHerzog greets Rooney and Kate Mara on the red carpet at Venice.Photograph: Yara Nardi/ReutersLast year, he started his own Instagram account, where he has posted reels of himself barbecuing, doing DIY and unboxing packages. He said he did it at the behest of his youngest son, who told his father he shouldn’t be so isolated from his audience. Since he still doesn’t own a own mobile phone, however, he hasn’t been able to check out the content-creating competition.“I had a big retrospective at the Centre Pompidou in Paris in 2024, and the audience was all, all, all young people. The curators told me there was a Godard retrospective right before mine, and the people who came to that? They were all Godard’s age. They were all over 80.”Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalWerner HerzogFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tender Loving Care review – Mike Leigh’s tender and elusive study of love and mortality | Movies | The Guardian
description: Alice Bailey Johnson and Kate O’Flynn lead a tender, quietly heartbreaking drama about friendship, ageing parents and the sadness of lives moving inexorably on
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Alice Bailey Johnson and Kate O’Flynn lead a tender, quietly heartbreaking drama about friendship, ageing parents and the sadness of lives moving inexorably on
Content: Buoyant …  (from left) Kate O'Flynn, Marion Bailey  and Alice Bailey Johnson in  Tender Loving Care.Photograph: Courtesy TIFFView image in fullscreenBuoyant …  (from left) Kate O'Flynn, Marion Bailey  and Alice Bailey Johnson in  Tender Loving Care.Photograph: Courtesy TIFFMoviesReviewTender Loving Care review – Mike Leigh’s tender and elusive study of love and mortalityTelluride film festivalAlice Bailey Johnson and Kate O’Flynn lead a complicated, quietly heartbreaking drama about friendship, ageing parents and the sadness of lives moving inexorably onPeter BradshawFri 4 Sep 2026 21.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMike Leigh’s new film – perhaps his last – is a poignant, intergenerational drama of happy-sad acceptance that life goes on, until it doesn’t go on. And then you have to come to terms with the mortality of your elderly parents and by that same token, with the end that is waiting for you too. The decency and clarity of the film are a tonic. It is a movie with one of Leigh’s overtly positive and even sugary titles, like Life Is Sweet (1990) or Happy-Go-Lucky (2008), as distinct from his darker ones: Secrets & Lies (1996) or Hard Truths (2024). But his sweet titles are not simply satirical and intended to mean the opposite: it is more complicated and elusive, and even the contrast here between the two heroines’ private and professional lives isn’t straightforwardly a matter of irony.As so often, the dialogue has that unique Leigh cartoonish quality that isn’t caricature, and the characters often speak with an almost wartime chirpiness in a world of peckers kept up and noses kept clean. This is a perkiness that the thirtysomethings have unexpectedly inherited and modified from their old mum and dad, and Leigh leaves it to the audience to judge the consequent tone of the drama and the appropriate tone of their response.The setting is Ealing, west London, where, to paraphrase Larkin, people work all day and get half drunk at night, opening up the white wine that’s been in the fridge while worrying about themselves and their family. Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson) is a single woman and social worker who has started dating a fireman (no woke stuff about “firefighter”). She stays calm and polite in the face of aggressive behaviour from clients; her first scene is with an impassive old man in hospital who, asked for his address, recites only a number. He is perhaps a kind of choric spirit in the film, like the homeless man in Jack Rosenthal’s The Chain.Rosie, as caring in private as she is at work, has welcomed her best friend back into the spare room in her flat; this is Amy (Kate O’Flynn), a fellow social worker who cares specifically for vulnerable young people. She needs a place to stay as she has just split up with an odious boyfriend. The two women are deliriously happy to have each other’s company again: they drink, sing daft songs and tell goofy jokes together. Another type of movie would suggest that each woman is the love of the other’s life, and that they are in denial. Not this film. Rosie and Amy are just best pals and the tension and the unresolved issues lie elsewhere.In a way, Amy’s only other mates are her mum and dad, for which we have excellent and heartbreaking performances from Leigh stalwarts Marion Bailey and Paul Jesson, who was Turner’s elderly father in Mr Turner (2014). Rosie and Amy go round to see them together for cups of tea, and Amy’s mum unselfconsciously calls Rosie her “second daughter”. But there are problems. Amy can’t bring herself to confess to her parents that her relationship (from which they were hoping for grandchildren) is over, and her mum is uneasy about the way “Pops” zones out in the middle of conversation and seems forgetful. Like Amy and Rosie, the old couple love songs; they singDaisy BellandBoiled Beef and Carrotsin private and the simplicity and innocence of these moments is almost unbearable.As ever, the buoyant and exuberant dialogue passages show that the speaker is not a clever-clever person intent on impressing anyone, and for all the exaggeration, there is a realness in these moments. Bailey’s mum figure waxes lyrical about her husband and how wonderful it was, 50 years ago, to have met him: “He was one in a million … a needle in a haystack!” Of course, a needle in a haystack doesn’t exactly connote what she’s saying but the truth of it is plain enough, and if the audience laughs, it is with her, not at her.At work, Rosie and Amy are impeccably conscientious in the face of the most challenging people, though perhaps Amy is marginally the more successful of the two; we see her being able to connect with troubled teens. Rosie is as well-meaning, but often meets a blank wall. Leigh also shows us one moment when one woman appears to have a legitimate complaint against her; Rosie urges this woman, who has lost her children to the system and is now living in what are clearly squalid and chaotic conditions, to talk and open up – but the woman angrily replies that her words will just be held against her in court. She has a point; if she were under arrest, she would at least be warned that she had the right to remain silent. As for Amy’s mum, she is the caring friend and neighbour to a recently widowed woman painfully estranged from her son.Leigh shows us a world without cynicism, without malice, a world in which people do care, but in which they have a lot to care about. There is a lot of unhappiness here, an ocean of sadness which almost, but not quite, capsizes the boat – yet the mood, underscored by Gary Yershon’s music, is more ruminative than melancholy. The film’s structure is theatrically controlled, and the succession of scenes moves smoothly from Amy and Rosie’s lives at home and at work, to their parents’ lives and to their interaction with clients. There is no screenwriting-seminar character development or narrative arc here – except perhaps one which leads to a heart-wrenching moment in a bedroom from which the camera retreats sadly and tactfully on to the landing. We are not approaching a big monologue moment of explosive emotional catharsis. The storm, as so often with Leigh, rumbles towards us and then rumbles back over the horizon. And yet the sadness and the love stayed with me long after the closing credits.Tender Loving Care screened at theTelluride film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsMike LeighKate O'FlynnreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Jay-Z 30 tour review – the sheer profusion of nailed-on classics is dizzying | Jay-Z | The Guardian
description:
Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, London
Even though Beyoncé rumours prove unfounded, there are plenty of guests, from Idris Elba to Lauryn Hill – but this show doesn’t need cameos to lift it
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, LondonEven though Beyoncé rumours prove unfounded, there are plenty of guests, from Idris Elba to Lauryn Hill – but this show doesn’t need cameos to lift it
Content: ‘Sheer star power and genuine charisma mean you seldom tear your eyes from him’ … Jay-Z performs at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.Photograph: Roc NationView image in fullscreen‘Sheer star power and genuine charisma mean you seldom tear your eyes from him’ … Jay-Z performs at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.Photograph: Roc NationJay-ZReviewJay-Z 30 tour review – the sheer profusion of nailed-on classics is dizzyingTottenham Hotspur Stadium, LondonEven though Beyoncé rumours prove unfounded, there are plenty of guests, from Idris Elba to Lauryn Hill – but this show doesn’t need cameos to lift itAlexis PetridisSat 5 Sep 2026 07.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJay-Z’s first solo tour in nine years bills itself as a celebration: it marks the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt. But it feels less concerned with nostalgic reverie than a show of strength in the present day. Hip-hop is a genre predicated on constant forward motion, in which careers tend to burn brightly, then dim as the music moves on. Jay-Z may not be the only fiftysomething rapper out on a career retrospective tour in 2026, but he is, unequivocally, the only one who’s capable of doing it at this level: packing out the biggest stadiums in the world nearly a decade after helast released an album, his standing impressively undiminished by a retreat into semi-retirement.Moreover, he’s doing it in considerable style. The show’s musical approach can clearly trace its origins back to 2001, the year Jay-Z solved the problem of how on earth a rapper was supposed to appear on MTV Unplugged by eschewing hip-hop’s standard DJ-and-backing-tapes approach and employing a live band: the Roots were apparently astonished to be asked, but the end result was pretty jaw-dropping. Back in May, his first solo gig in five years essentially recreated it – he headlined the Roots’ annual Picnic festival with Questlove and co in tow once more – but the Jay-Z 30 tour supersizes it, featuring not just a 10-piece band, but an 18-piece string section. The resulting sound can, very occasionally, feel a littlede trop– the squealing metal guitar solo appended to Can I Live definitely seems surplus to requirements – but for the most part, it works extraordinarily well, amping up the cinematic sweep ofEmpire State of Mindand the lush 70s-soul inflections of Izzo (H.O.V.A), adding a thunderous heft to Public Service Announcement and 99 Problems. It also serves to underline Jay-Z’s technical skill: a lesser rapper would be swallowed up by the density of the sound, but the precision of his delivery consistently cuts through.View image in fullscreenThe tour marks the 30th anniversary of the release of Jay-Z’s debut album, Reasonable Doubt.Photograph: Roc NationThere’s a sense in which the actual staging feels quite risky. At the rear there’s a vast LED screen that usually shows the footage you might expect – grainy video of 90s New York, black and white images of the city’s Black residents, aerial shots of the Marcy projects from whence Shawn Carter came, Jay-Z at various stages of his career – and sometimes doesn’t: at one point, presumably as explanation of where the rapper’s extravagant dreadlocks went, we’re treated to the sight ofBeyoncé, clippers in hand, giving her husband a No 1 crop, a surprisingly thrifty approach to hairdressing for a couple worth an estimated $2.8bn (£2.1bn). His band and orchestra are clustered in the shadows beneath the screen, leaving a vast expanse of bare stage, which Jay-Z occupies more or less alone for most of the show. An audience of 50,000 people watching a solitary black-clad figure for two hours is theoretically a big ask, but there’s something strangely magnetic about the sight of him prowling the stage, a combination of sheer star power and genuine charisma that means you seldom tear your eyes from him.The persistent rumour is that he’s going to be joined onstage by his wife – it’s her 45th birthday. He isn’t, although Mrs Carter gets a spotlight shone on her in the VIP box, a chorus of Happy Birthday and a firework display in her honour. Still, you don’t want for guests. The opening monologue is performed by Idris Elba and Jay-Z graciously cedes centre stage for the UK rapper Giggs to perform Talkin’ the Hardest, while Lauryn Hill andWyclef Jeanmake an appearance towards the end of the set to perform a brace of Fugees classics to a roar of astonishment from the crowd: Fu-Gee-la and Ready or Not sound fantastic, and that Jay-Z can get Hill to actually turn up onstage when she’s supposed to feels like an achievement in itself.But in truth, the show doesn’t really need guest appearances to lift it. The sheer profusion of nailed-on classics in Jay-Z’s back catalogue, and the intensity with which they’re performed, are more than enough: at one point, he rattles off No Church in the Wild, 99 Problems, Girls, Girls, Girls, ’03 Bonnie & Clyde, Excuse Me Miss and I Just Wanna Love U in such close proximity it feels faintly dizzying. Underneath his baseball cap,Jay-Zallows himself a rare grin. “We got a million of those,” he says: a slight exaggeration, but, under the circumstances, one you can forgive him.Explore more on these topicsJay-ZRapHip-hopBeyoncéIdris ElbaLauryn HillWyclef Jeanlive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The rise of south-east Asia’s girl bands: ‘The talent and popularity were always here’ | Culture | The Guardian
description: Girl bands from the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand are going global with their fusion of traditional and modern sounds
Author: Natasha May
Headline: Girl bands from the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand are going global with their fusion of traditional and modern sounds
Content: Filipina girl band BINI perform at Coachella, 2026.Photograph: Natt Lim/In Time MediaView image in fullscreenFilipina girl band BINI perform at Coachella, 2026.Photograph: Natt Lim/In Time MediaCultureThe rise of south-east Asia’s girl bands: ‘The talent and popularity were always here’Girl bands from the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand are going global with their fusion of traditional and modern soundsNatasha Mayin BangkokFri 4 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 14.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“We all know that music is a universal language,” says Maloi Ricalde from Filipina girl band BINI, which mixes tropical pop with traditional songs, English with Tagalog, and silver knee highs with pastel colours.“Incorporating Filipino language, Filipino culture, Filipino sound, into our music, it really gives identity and meaning to our music,” Ricalde tells the Guardian.‘People are exhausted by Blackpink and BTS’: the DIY Chinese bands redefining corporate ‘idol’ popRead moreMonths after becoming the first south-east Asian girl band to perform atCoachella, and now with a tour of Japan under its belt, the group is enjoying a surge in popularity.“Our next goal,” says BINI member Jhoanna Robles, “Is that we want Filipino culture, Filipino music to be part of a conversation naturally on a global stage.”BINI is not the only girl group from south-east Asia to recently gain wider traction, with other girl bands such as Indonesia’s no na, Thailand’s 4EVE, and Malaysia’s DOLLA taking to stages around the world, instigating viral dance challenges and racking up millions of views online.Industry experts say musical talent has always existed in the region, but the infrastructure is now backing it up after the huge popularity of K-pop showed that investment could push Asian artists into the mainstream.View image in fullscreenBINI performing at Coachella in April 2026.Photograph: Greg Noire/SuppliedThe music industry in the west largely ignored Asian music before the 2012 hitGangnam Style, which went viral in part thanks to its popularity in the Philippines and among its diaspora, says Piyapong Muenprasertdee, co-founder of music platform Fungjai.Many emerging artists and groups from the region are now gaining fans by blending modern and traditional elements, adds Piyapong.In Thailand indie acts as well asgirl bands such as BNK48are putting their own spin on local folk music Molam and Thai country music known as Luk Thung. In Vietnam and the Philippines, unique electronic dance music styles are becoming increasingly prominent in local club scenes.In Indonesia, girl band no na has mixed dangdut, a high-intensity genre with Indonesian, Malay, Arabic and Indian roots, with reggaeton and pop, including in their hitbilingual song Rollerblade, which has garnered 16m views.The group produces catchy, sometimes expletive-laden pop songs that feature traditional ceng-ceng cymbals, and gamelan, an ensemble from Java and Bali, which they perform in striking costumes and with occasional back-bending moves.“It’s been a consistent formula throughout our work process to find songs that have a global sound and add Indonesian elements as a cherry on top as our no na stamp,” the group tells the Guardian. “Because we’re a global girl group but still representing our country, we always try to find that balance without compromising too much of one or the other.”Thai girl group 4EVE reflects local elements like Bangkok’s bustling street culture in their music videos, while Malaysia’s DOLLA has released songs such asRaya Raya Rayacelebrating the end of Ramadan, which they perform in modest, but hot-pink kaftans.View image in fullscreenIndonesian girl band, no na.Photograph: kenchyro/SuppliedOne feature of Asian pop culture, says PR expert Bettina Miski, is the prominence of fandom and fanclubs, which have contributed to their popularity.“The relationship between the artists and the fans is a lot deeper,” says Miski, who runs a YouTube series called “THAI T”, which connects Asian artists with global audiences. “That devotion leads to spreading the word, a type of promotion that often goes beyond traditional marketing as it feels a lot more personal or intimate.”Girl bands in the region have special names for their fans, which provide support at concerts and online, including in posting dance challenges. BINI’s fans are called “Blooms”, for no na it’s “Orchids”, 4EVE’s “For Aye” (also meaning forever), and DOLLA’s “iDollas”.Therow over the Grammys’ new category for Asian popsuggests inclusivity in the industry still has a way to go. The move was criticised for potentially ringfencing Asian pop artists from contending in the top categories. It also explicitly mentioned only K-pop, J-pop, and C-pop despite the region’s diversity.Still, says Piyapong, south-east Asia is well positioned to be “the next powerhouse” in the global music landscape.“We just recently entered an era where borders or language matter less,” says Miski, “The talent and popularity were always here, the system just had to catch up.”Explore more on these topicsCultureMusic festivalsCoachellaThailandIndonesiaAsia PacificFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How Gloria Steinem’s lifechanging stay in India shaped her approach to feminism | Gloria Steinem | The Guardian
description: The activist said her two years studying and travelling in country ‘made me who I am’
Author: Penelope MacRae
Headline: The activist said her two years studying and travelling in country ‘made me who I am’
Content: Gloria Steinem adopted the sari as everyday dress during her time in India.Photograph: Gloria's FoundationView image in fullscreenGloria Steinem adopted the sari as everyday dress during her time in India.Photograph: Gloria's FoundationGloria SteinemHow Gloria Steinem’s lifechanging stay in India shaped her approach to feminismThe activist said her two years studying and travelling in country ‘made me who I am’‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotesGloria Steinem: A life in picturesPenelope MacRaein DelhiFri 4 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 20.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenGloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.Steinem,who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem at home. She said: ‘If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them. I believe I learned that in India.’Photograph: Gloria’s FoundationSteinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.Gloria Steinem: A life in picturesRead moreShe met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem and Dorothy Pitman Hughes attending the Ms. Foundation for Women Gloria awards in 2014.Photograph: Scott Roth/Invision/APBut the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.Explore more on these topicsGloria SteinemFeminismActivismIndiaWomenCivil rights movementfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Bold, brilliant, thrilling’: leading authors on the novels every school should teach | Books | The Guardian
description: A new term, a new PM … time for a new English curriculum? We ask writers from Ben Okri to Samantha Harvey to pick books that will inspire a lifelong love of reading
Author: Kate Mosse
Headline: A new term, a new PM … time for a new English curriculum? We ask writers from Ben Okri to Samantha Harvey to pick books that will inspire a lifelong love of reading
Content: Composite: Getty/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Getty/Guardian DesignBooks‘Bold, brilliant, thrilling’: leading authors on the novels every school should teachA new term, a new PM … time for a new English curriculum? We ask writers from Ben Okri to Samantha Harvey to pick books that will inspire a lifelong love of readingKate MosseSat 5 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTShareFor the first time ever, we have a British prime minister who studied for an English degree. Not all of his 58 predecessors went to university, but those who did favoured subjects such as history and classics and, more recently, philosophy, politics and economics. Yet reading fiction is a fantastic preparation for life, for understanding people and the times through which we live.
