Novels encourage empathy, they help you to stand in other people’s shoes, to navigate complicated, sometimes conflicting emotions, they entertain and bring joy. The creative industries contribute some £145.8bn each year to the UK economy; it is our soft superpower.In other words, books matter. Reading matters.However, there has been a marked decline over recent years in the numbers of children reading for pleasure. It’s why the NationalLiteracyTrust designated 2026 the National Year of Reading. Already there has been a shift from a 20-year low in 2025 of 32.7% of eight-to-18-year-olds saying they enjoy reading in their free time up to 36.1%. It’s a start.We are also in a long-overdue moment of curriculum renewal for GCSE English, so when better to ask if what’s studied in school helps young people fall in love with reading – or possibly puts them off for life?SinceGCSEswere first introduced in 1986, we’ve seen the establishment of four main examination boards in England and Wales and surprising unanimity in the choice of books most schools choose to teach. In 2025, the educational charity End Sexism in Schools released a report – Manopolies – revealing that 76% of students study An Inspector Calls by JB Priestley for their modern text from a possible 21 modern texts (a play, wonderful as it is, that’s been on one board’s set text list for 39 years). Then a whopping 93% of students study either A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens or The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde by Robert Louis Stevenson for their 19th-century novel from nine possible texts (including Charlotte Brontë, Mary Shelley and Jane Austen). Only 5% of students in England and Wales study a female-authored text at GCSE.It’s true that there are diverse modern works by inspirational women on the lists of the four exam boards – Kit de Waal, Tanika Gupta, Jeanette Winterson, Malorie Blackman are all offered. The problem is that schools are disincentivised to change the texts they teach as this would involve costs and additional work. And no exam board wants to be the one to remove popular texts because that would bring commercial disadvantage and developmental costs. This is why it’s essential the Department for Education, as part of this review, mandates the regular changing of set-text lists and stipulates that students study works that reflect the gender balance and diversity of our society. Schools can’t do it on their own.Here, to get the conversation started, are suggestions of texts to inspire a passion for fiction in young readers. And, from me, a plea for the government to support teachers who want to better reflect the gender balance and diversity of their classrooms.This is the way to encourage a lifelong love of reading.Kate MosseNussaibah YounisThe Treesby Percival EverettView image in fullscreenWouldn’t it be refreshing to see a blisteringly funny novel on the syllabus? The Trees is a daring satire on racism, generational guilt and cultural complicity, inspired by the lynching of Emmett Till. Genre-bending and gloriously inventive, it finds morbid delight in the absurdities of American racial violence without ever trivialising its victims. With characters such as Dr Reverend Fondle, Junior Junior and Hot Mama Yeller, Everett exposes the grotesque stupidity of white supremacy through comedy that is as vicious as it is exhilarating. What better way to show teenagers that literature can be genuinely enjoyable, even laugh-out-loud funny, while remaining intellectually and morally serious.Frank Cottrell-BoyceStories of Your Life andOthersbyTed ChiangView image in fullscreenA great short story hits you like a left hook or an unexpected kiss – coming out of nowhere and leaving you gasping, what just happened? Which is the perfect state for learning, of course. Short stories work really well in the classroom because reading is best when it’s shared. I would, therefore, strongly suggest Ted Chiang’s astonishing science fiction collection Stories of Your Life and Others. Each story takes on a big idea – language, love, intelligence, the collateral damage to real estate that angels might cause when intervening in human affairs, that sort of thing. They go off in your head like bombs. The most famous is the title story, which was made into the movieArrival. Teenagers love ideas. They’re about to go into a world that their grownups are viewing as some kind of sci-fi nightmare. Here’s a bold, brilliant, thrilling set of thought experiments about how it could be OK after all. It’s a science fiction collection that opens with a story set in Old Testament Babylon. What else do you need to know?Patrice LawrenceRandomby Debbie Tucker GreenI recommend this play. For a Black working-class London family, it’s a normal weekday – until the teenage son is senselessly stabbed and killed.The work is performed by one actor, from the point of view of the sister. The dialogue is funny, tenderly painting the warm family relationships until that one moment destroys everything. Then follows grief, fury, helplessness and despair.Random is gripping and short. It’s a springboard for many different conversations, from topics such as the impact of race in the criminal justice system and the representation of working-class families, to the benefits and challenges of performing such an emotional piece in a stripped-back set.David MitchellThe Rest ofUs Just Live Hereby Patrick NessView image in fullscreenThis wise, chaotic, gentle, painful, funny, superb novel follows five teens trying to navigate the most difficult year of their lives, while the town’s cool indie kids are battling Stranger Things-sized perils in vignettes at the start of each chapter. It contains some of the truest (and helpful) lines about social anxiety I’ve ever read. For reluctant readers, The Rest of Us Just Live Here proves that great fiction is as compelling as a great video game; and unlike social media, it leaves you feeling nourished, smarter, and not wanting back the time you just spent on it. I was asked to provide one title only, but hey: class, now turn to that blast of medieval Tarantino, The Pardoner’s Tale. Chaucer, Patrick Ness and the language we’re using right now cohabit the same glorious entangled continuum. Compare and contrast Henry IV Part 2 Act 3 Scene 1, “Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown” with the lyrics to Stormzy’s song Crown. Art is made of art. It speaks across centuries. Now it’s your turn.Hollie McNishWild Geeseby Mary OliverView image in fullscreenAfter spending many evenings this spring testing my daughter on her GCSE English Literature quotes, I felt ready to vomit. Three set texts: Lord of the Flies, Macbeth and The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. Shared themes of blood, death, murder, violence, the evil of boys and men. Then, if you’re tired of revising prose, a little war poetry for a breather. Lovely. More death.In those two exam years, my daughter studied not one female prose writer, not one writer of colour, only four female characters in the entire trio of set texts (if you count Macbeth’s witches as individual characters, which is debatable, oh and a female pig, according to one teacher). Nearly 30 years ago, my experience was almost exactly the same.What a way to teach a love of literature; what a way to normalise only reading books by men about men, and only if violence is centre stage of the men’s worlds. English literature is an amazing opportunity to nurture a joy of reading, to open minds to other cultures and worlds and wonders. So why is every single text soaked in bloodshed? If I were to pick a text for young people to study, I’d suggestanything but more violence. Something loving, anything funny; just one book teenagers could smile at, laugh with even. Perhaps Ocean Vuong’s The Emperor of Sadness, a gorgeous story between a young man and an elderly woman. Or maybe on the poetry curriculum, Wild Geese by Mary Oliver. Something that has helped people the world over to feel more joy.Ben OkriAfrican Storieseditedby Ben OkriView image in fullscreenOne of the weaknesses of the literary education of this country is that students are not exposed early in life to the valuable literatures of non-European people, particularly Africans.This Everyman African Stories anthology brings together 36 classical African stories written in, or translated into, English. It tracks nearly 100 years and observes every aspect of life, from the domestic to the political, from the romantic to the existential.An average Briton could go through a whole lifetime of wide reading without ever reading any classic African text. These stories would not only provide entertaining and enlightening reading, they could serve as a gateway to discovering the rich literature of a much-overlooked continent.Kamila ShamsieSmall Things Like Theseby Claire KeeganView image in fullscreenIf you look at the most often assigned GCSE texts, the common denominator is a word count under 30,000. That factor knocks a great many wonderful books off the list, but it does also allow space for the brilliance of Claire Keegan. I’d choose Small Things Like These, a novel of remarkable depth within its brevity. “How does she do it?” is a question for any reader of the book – but there are plenty of other questions in it for students. The novel’s story within a story, its use of memory, the character of Bill Furlong, the internal and external landscapes, and the history of the Magdalene laundries are all rich ground for thought and discussion. No harm either in letting young readers recognise that what appears small and quiet is actually taut and fierce.Andrew McMillan100 Queer Poemsedited by Mary Jean Chan and Andrew McMillanView image in fullscreenThere has never been a more important time to ensure that our school libraries and our class curricula contain plenty of books by, about and for LGBTQ+ people. When Mary Jean Chan and I were co-editing 100 Queer Poems, it felt like making something that I needed to read when I was in secondary school. Anthologies are great to study because they allow for the necessity of not liking something. With 100 poets published by more than 45 different presses, a reader won’t enjoy all the different styles and schools of poetry on offer, but they might find some that strike a spark of recognition. There might be one poem that helps a student in developing their own individual language for articulating who they are, and who they might become, in the world.Kit de WaalFalloutby Eleanor AnstrutherView image in fullscreenSet in 1982, Fallout is a fictionalised account of theGreenham Common protestas seen through the eyes of a rebellious 15-year-old girl. Non-preachy, funny and sharp, it’s about family secrets, female empowerment and an important time in British history that we are in danger of forgetting.I’d also suggest Every Man for Himself by Beryl Bainbridge, which is as much about class as it is about the sinking of the Titanic. It’s a sort of whodunnit seen through the eyes of a young man who falls in love with an unobtainable young woman shortly before disaster strikes. It mixes fact with fiction, and the way it’s structured means you have to read it right to the end.Geoff DyerVoyage in the Darkby Jean RhysView image in fullscreenTwo things are of the utmost importance. To adhere to quality as the criterion of, well, of the utmost importance! And to give a sense of the evolving tradition of literature, rather than catering to a preference for the contemporary. The problem is that some things formerly deemed of high quality – crucial components of that tradition – now seem of dubious quality.The good news is that the reputations of plenty of female writers from the interwar period continue to soar. And many of the themes and concerns that preoccupy us now were being addressed by these writers almost a century ago. No one exemplifies this more than Jean Rhys, a writer of genius whose four novels, from 1928 and into the 1930s, were so far ahead of their time that they were doomed, like her heroines, to failure and obscurity. They also have the appealing virtue of extreme brevity, weighing in at about 150 pages apiece.If obliged to select just one of these, I would go for the third, Voyage in the Dark (1934), her devastating and funny account of 18-year-old Anna, who comes from the West Indies and finds herself alone and helpless in London. The perfect introduction to that sought after but mysterious ideal of a writer’s “voice”, it will leave new readers wanting to venture further into Rhys’s strangely defamiliarised world. Which means, in turn, that they will be drawn to her final masterpiece, Wide Sargasso Sea, and from there, inevitably, to Brontë’s Jane Eyre.Samantha HarveyMoon Tigerby Penelope LivelyView image in fullscreenMoon Tiger is a life story and a love story, the story of a woman called Claudia who, we learn on page one, is on her deathbed, ransacking her memories in order to give an account of herself. “Shake the tube and see what comes out,” she says. “Chronology irritates me. There is no chronology inside my head.” The story she tells is seductive, searching, confronting and compressed; scenes are played and differently replayed, truth is questioned, the idea of selfhood is dismantled.Although it’s the retrospection of an older woman, there’s something in this exploded, chaotic rendition of self that would have struck me hard in my teens – the self as a beautiful, dangerous, vulnerable mess. It’s about the harm we do and suffer, and about the possibility of happiness. The whole novel is hot to the touch. It pushes at what a novel can do. It’s experimental in the best, most necessary of ways and a perfect study of how narrative works. Nearly 40 years on, the writing is still fresh, gorgeous and daring. And, admittedly, quite sexy. English teachers up and down the country might be less enthusiastic about it being on the curriculum than I am.Benjamin MyersAddress UnknownbyKathrineKressmann TaylorView image in fullscreenThis epistolary novel is told via a series of letters between two business partners from 1932 to 1934 – Max is an art gallerist in the US while Martin has returned to their fatherland, where he is immediately energised by a bold new leader. But soon the hatred seeps in, and Martin asks his friend to cease communication lest he himself be mistakenly identified as a collaborator. Little more need be said about the plot, other than that it is a one-sitting/one‑lesson/one-hour read that challenges notions of friendship, loyalty, antisemitism and the sheer insidiousness of totalitarian regimes. Trump, Farage, Musk, Putin – all are reflected in Kressmann Taylor’s powerfully concise prose, perfectly constructed for the permanently distracted. Pair with Fred Uhlman’s equally economical 1932-set novelReunionfor a “compare and contrast” discussion -starter.Raymond AntrobusGlyphby Ali SmithView image in fullscreenFew contemporary novels manage to be this urgent and playful at once, which is exactly why it belongs in a classroom: it proves seriousness and playfulness aren’t opposites. At its centre are two estranged sisters, Petra and Patricia, grieving their mother and reckoning with childhood trauma. Smith threads their story through three wars: a horse blinded in the first world war; a flattened body found in the second; and the present-day war in Gaza. The novel asks what it means to watch history repeat itself while insisting it won’t. A ghost horse, conjured by the sisters as children, returns decades later to disturb the present, blurring memory, myth and reality in ways that reward close, repeated reading. Throughout, Smith’s inventive wordplay, puns, homophones – and the title, which mirrors its companion novelGliff–make language itself a subject, not just a vehicle. Students would leave Glyph asking what stories arefor, and whether imagination is escapism or the most soulful technology we have for facing a broken, divided society.

title: ‘Please find daddy’: the haunting missing posters of September 11 | Art | The Guardian
description: A collection of previously stored away posters will be displayed at a new exhibition to mark 25 years since the deadliest terrorist attack in US history
Author: David Smith
Headline: A collection of previously stored away posters will be displayed at a new exhibition to mark 25 years since the deadliest terrorist attack in US history
Content: An installation image from Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters.Photograph: Phil BuehlerView image in fullscreenAn installation image from Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters.Photograph: Phil BuehlerArt‘Please find daddy’: the haunting missing posters of September 11A collection of previously stored away posters will be displayed at a new exhibition to mark 25 years since the deadliest terrorist attack in US historyDavid Smithin WashingtonSat 5 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe saw the first one on September 11 itself. “Missing”, said a hastily designed poster on the window of a bar in Tribeca providing food and water to first responders. It was a plea for information about a person who had vanished in thedeadliest terrorist attack in US history.‘Led us down such a dark path’: documentary explores how 9/11 changed AmericaRead more“I was like, ‘Wow, this is going to be …’” recallsPhil Buehler, an artist and photographer who had watched the twin towers collapse from his office window. “But you knew that there would be very few survivors. You knew it then.”The missing posters kept coming in the days after 9/11, and Buehler kept photographing them. But having amassed more than 500 images, he put them away in a box on a top shelf because he could not bear to look at them.As the 25th anniversary of the atrocity neared, he decided to revisit them and will put a selection on public display for the first time this week. Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters, an installation atMost Holy Trinity – St Mary’s churchin Brooklyn, places 144 pictures across 24 translucent vellum panels, in vertical pairs reminiscent of the twin towers.The World Trade Center was always a favourite subject for Buehler. He had been photographing it since 1973, when he was 16. On September 11 2001, as an advisory board member for a tech startup, he had been invited toa conference at the Windows on the Worldrestaurant at the top of the north tower, but turned the offer down (a friend intended to go but was delayed).View image in fullscreenJason Jacobs. He called his wife, Jennifer, from his 97th-floor office to say a plane had hit the other tower and not to worry – his own building exploded moments later. Their daughter Zoe was just over a year old.Photograph: Phil Buehler“The guy that invited us died that day and I think my friend feels guilty about it,” he says quietly by phone, recalling the day on which nearly 3,000 people were killed by hijacked airliners inNew York, northern Virginia and Pennsylvania. “You realise how close–everybody had a story.”For the next two or three weeks, Buehler pedalled his bicycle through the eerie hush of New York City. Every night he updated a website, posting photographs and dispatches – an early form of what would soon be called blogging.He watched the spontaneous emergence of public shrines. Memorials bloomed in Union Square and Washington Square Park. On fences, subway entrances and storefronts,the missing posters multiplied, each a radical act of hope, though very few of those reported missing would ultimately be found alive.This was an era before cloud storage, smartphones and ubiquitously accessible digital photos. When families realised their relatives had not returned home, they frantically searched their living rooms for any tangible likeness.Some posters were designed by colleagues with desktop publishing software, cleanly formatted in neat typefaces. Others were raw, hurried cries for help: a snapshot Scotch-taped to a blank sheet of copy paper, bordered by frantic handwritten descriptions detailing physical marks that might identify an unconscious patient in a trauma ward.The posters listed height, weight, date of birth, company names, floor numbers and identifying traits: a butterfly tattoo on a lower back, surgical scars, wristwatches, the colour of a tie worn that morning. “They’re very personal,”Buehler says. “A lot of the pictures would be, say, a father holding their kids. One said, ‘Please find daddy.’ This was before digital phones, when everybody had pictures online, so a lot of them were done in copy shops.“You can just imagine somebody opening up their wedding album and ripping out the photo of a husband or wife and so you see them in a tuxedo. You see a lot of people in graduation gowns; it’s the pictures that we would have on our refrigerator or on the walls of our house that you’re proud of. I saw a lot of graduation photos, a lot of wedding photos, a lot of photos with kids, a lot of photos of men in suits and ties.”Yet as days turned into weeks, and rescue workers digging throughthe steaming pile at Ground Zerofound only twisted steel and ash, the meaning of the posters underwent a subtle and heartbreaking shift.View image in fullscreenManny Devalle. A seven-year FDNY veteran who responded on 9/11 just after finishing his overnight shift. Proud of his Puerto Rican heritage, he got Engine 5 to march in the Puerto Rican Day Parade.Photograph: Phil BuehlerBuehler explains:“When it was pretty clear there were no survivors, the posters started changing from ‘missing’ to almost ‘in memoriam’, but they didn’t say that. They went from explaining he has a tattoo of this on his arm or lower back and this is how tall and how much he weighs to being much more about what they did in life.“They morphed into ‘has three kids, I miss him’ and all the things they’re proud of: captain of the whatever or coach of the football team or whatever it was. Little memorials and they’re all different.”The posters also captured the democratic cross-section of the twin towers’ workforce. Within Buehler’s images, elite Wall Street investment bankers in tailored suits hang next to off-duty firefighters, paramedics and transit workers. Latino, Asian, Black and white faces appear side by side.“You saw the full range,” Buehler says. “You could tell just from looking at a guy in a suit, probably worked at one of the investment firms, and then right next to it would be somebody that works at Windows on the World as a server or waiter. A lot of Latino names. Mixed in there were firemen and women. A lot of service people. It was a big slice of America.”Eventually, having used about 20 rolls of film to catalogue more than 500 posters on hospitals, fire stations, random fences, roadside barricades andthe 69th Regiment Armoryon Lexington Avenue, Buehler had the film developed, picked up the contact prints and stopped.He could not face them. He packed the prints into a box, slipped in several bags containing samples of the dust he had gathered from the streets, added a rain-soaked poster he had salvaged, and shoved the container into the dark recesses of his studio for a quarter of a century.View image in fullscreenAn installation image from Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters.Photograph: Phil BuehlerWhen Buehler finally opened the box, he turned toSarah Celentano, a Brooklyn-based curator with whom he had previously collaborated on projects exploring public memory. The show is co-curated by Celentano and Olena Speranska, who was forced to flee her home in Ukraine after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.Celentano says: “I have a background as a medievalist and art historian and I often see connections between how we think and act today and how we’ve done this historically. That’s why I was so interested in thinking about these photos that Phil showed to me through historic traditions of devotion. They have such an incredible immediacy now, even 25 years later, that makes the person depicted present.”This tension between the physical image and the spiritual aura of the lost gave the exhibition its title.Celentano says:“Countenance can have two meanings. Both of them are very relevant in the case of what the show is doing. It can mean the human face, but it can also mean a sense of presence.“It’s something that is referring to the outer and inner aspects of a person simultaneously. What the show’s doing at the initial focus is on the faces of the 9/11 posters – people’s exterior humanity – but ultimately what that does is lead us to something that makes them present in a more profound way.”As the events of that day gradually fade from living memory to history, Celentano believes the exhibition provides a human bridge. “For somebody who wasn’t alive to remember or witness the September 11 attacks, the emphasis that these photographs put on humanity is the more important part of it.“They show what people did in the aftermath and how people dealt with or wrestled with their own grief and the way that they so spontaneously worked to memorialise them. It says a lot about how we function as a human society in that way. There’s a larger lesson to be learned.”For Celentano, the exhibition offers an antidote to the political cynicism of the present day.“It’s an invitation to empathise and to have compassion with people at a time when some frame empathy as weakness. I’m hoping this installation shows that empathy is actually quite a powerful thing and we should be looking for the humanity in all of us, not just the people who are in these posters but extending that beyond to one another.”View image in fullscreenJoe Hunter. Born in Brooklyn, he raced behind fire trucks on his bike as a kid and ran his own neighborhood ‘drill team’ at age 11 before joining FDNY Squad 288.Photograph: Phil BuehlerThat the work should find its home in Most Holy Trinity – St Mary’s church in Williamsburg is no accident. Founded in 1841, the majestic French Gothic Revival church is an active, multilingual parish that celebrates mass in English, Spanish and Polish. For Buehler, the church provided a spiritual antidote to the commercialism of the contemporary art world. “You don’t put grief on the white walls of a gallery,” he says.The church’s pastor,Rick Riccioli, a Franciscan friar originally from Montreal, immediately embraced the exhibition when Buehler approached him. The Franciscan order itself carries a 9/11 connection: Father Mychal Judge, the beloved FDNY chaplain who was the first certified fatality, was also a Franciscan.Friar Rick said in a statement: “Bringing these faces into this church is more than an art exhibition. It is an act of kinship, an act of remembrance, and, for us, an act of prayer. Twenty-five years later, we stand with those who were lost, with those who loved them, and with a city that still carries their memory.”Buehler is a creator of public memorials, producing installations such asEmpty Beds, honouring Ukrainian children abducted since Russia’s 2022 invasion, andWall of Tears, memorialising children killed in Gaza since October 2023, and In Lieu of Flowers, a sculptural presentation of the obituaries and lives of those who worked at the demolished Westinghouse Plant in Newark, New Jersey.Milestone anniversaries are an opportunity for reflection and taking stock. Looking back across the arc of 25 years, Buehler speaks with melancholy about the fleeting sense of common purpose that briefly united Americans in the autumn of 2001.“Post-9/11, America was one country – almost. I know there were groups that hated the Muslims at that time or blamed them, but it was pretty united. The red states, blue states didn’t exist. We still had some kind of working across the aisle. That’s gone.“When I was in Ukraine, it felt like they were all-for-one and for Ukraine beating Russia. As other people long for a different America, I longed more for how we suffered this tragedy, but the country felt what united us was more important than all those little things that divided us. That was an important moment and maybe the 25th anniversary will remind us of some of that.”Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters runs from 5-13 September at Most Holy Trinity – St Mary’s church, 138 Montrose Avenue, BrooklynExplore more on these topicsArtSeptember 11 2001New YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Nish Kumar to the Bayeux tapestry: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Our premier political comedian heads out on tour, while the 70-metre-long woven story of 1066 arrows its way to Britain for the first time
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Our premier political comedian heads out on tour, while the 70-metre-long woven story of 1066 arrows its way to Britain for the first time
Content: Nice work … Nish Kumar.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNice work … Nish Kumar.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockGoing out, staying inCultureFrom Nish Kumar to the Bayeux tapestry: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadOur premier political comedian heads out on tour, while the 70-metre-long woven story of 1066 arrows its way to Britain for the first timeSat 5 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaView image in fullscreenFree love … Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass.Photograph: Sony Pictures/Everett/ShutterstockGail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex PassOut nowWidely popularised by an episode of Friends in which Ross makes an ass of himself with Isabella Rossellini, the notion of the “celebrity sex pass” completes some sort of cultural loop here as another Friends star, Jennifer Aniston, comes full circle to play a version of herself, the subject of Tom’s (Michael Cassidy) get-out-of-jail lust freebie. A romcom from David Wain (Wet Hot American Summer).The IncomerOut nowThis British comedy follows a pair of isolated siblings, Isla (Gayle Rankin) and Sandy (Grant O’Rourke), whose parents disappeared 30 years ago. Having fended for themselves ever since, they aren’t eager to welcome Daniel (Domhnall Gleeson), who has been given the task of relocating them from their remote Scottish island home.Super NatureOut nowFilmed on Super 8mm film via cameras sent to 40 collaborators across 25 countries and five continents, this nature documentary is the brainchild of director Ed Sayers, and edits together footage of all creatures great (including rhinos) and small (snails).Late FameOut nowWillem Dafoe and Greta Lee star in Kent Jones’s adaptation of a posthumously published novella by Austrian modernist author Arthur Schnitzler. Dafoe plays a post office worker and former poet living in downtown Manhattan who is flattered by the attention of a group of wealthy young writers who apparently want to revive his career.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenLucky star … Hilary Duff.Photograph: Lauren DunnHilary Duff6to 15 September; tour starts DublinAfter breaking a decade-long musical hiatus with February’s Top 5 album, Luck … Or Something, the artist formerly known as Lizzie McGuire keeps up the momentum with this arena tour. Probably best to save your voice for 2003 teen-angst classic So Yesterday.Michael CraggMelanie MartinezThe O2, London,11 September; touring to 12 SeptemberWith the follow-up to March’s alt-pop opus Hades apparently due by the end of the year, the gloriously OTT New York curio brings her head-spinning show to the UK. Expect elaborate set pieces, skin-singeing flames and theatrical, dark-hued anthems.MCTête-à-Tête: The Opera festivalThe Cockpit, London,8to 20 SeptemberIt may be annual, but this showcase by the Cornwall-based new opera powerhouse is always one of a kind. This year’s crop of novelties features Orpheus and Mary, Queen of Scots, folk horror, morris dancing and Old Norse: a typically colourful retort to anyone who thinks that opera is dead.Flora WillsonEmma RawiczLondon,5 September;Manchester,9 September;Gateshead,10 SeptemberThe whirlwind evolution of UK sax original Emma Rawicz since her 2022 debut album at 19 now finds her leading her own exciting orchestra, working with A-list players, and gigging all over Europe. She brings the big band to Ronnie Scott’s (5 September), then follows that up with shows with her fusion-angled Inkyra quintet.John FordhamGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenMonika Sosnowska’s Ghosts.Photograph: Courtesy of Monika Sosnowska/Gisela Capitain Gallery, CologneMonika SosnowskaSouth London Gallery, London,10 Septemberto 22 NovemberUltra-minimal installation and half-tonne hanging sculptures all about architecture and its impact on everyday life by this Polish artist, who uses a whole raft of industrial materials to look at the legacies of modernism and communism.The Bayeux TapestryThe British Museum, London,10 Septemberto 11 JulyThe world-famous Bayeux tapestry is finally making its long-awaited journey back to England for the most hyped, hotly anticipated and sure-to-sell-out blockbuster exhibition in a decade.A Mughal SongbookThe Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge,8 Septemberto 7 MarchA fascinating, colourful, melodious look at the ornate pages of the Plowden songbook, a rare manuscript of songs from the Mughal empire, which ruled most of the Indian subcontinent from 1526 to 1857.Tschabalala SelfTrafalgar Square’s fourth plinth, London,from10 SeptemberWe’ve had a big thumb, a giant ship in a bottle and a huge dollop of cream; now the fourth plinth is going to be home to something more traditional for public sculpture: an enormous human figure, striding positively forwards in a blue dress, by American artist Tschabalala Self.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenPite size … Scottish Ballet in Emergence.Photograph: Andy RossScottish Ballet: EmergenceTheatre Royal, Glasgow,10 to 12 September; touring to 3 OctoberA visually arresting ballet by Crystal Pite is the main draw here. Pite’s Emergence, from 2009, uses the impact of the corps de ballet en masse to great effect. There’s also a premiere from Julia Cheng, award-winning choreographer of Cabaret and Fiddler on the Roof.Lyndsey WinshipNish Kumar9 September to 27 November; tour starts BelfastImpassioned but never pious, righteous but never smug, Kumar’s ability to temper strident takes with goofy likability means he’s fast becoming our premier progressive political comedian. New show Angry Humour from a Really Nice Guy sees the 41-year-old mine laughs from the threat of autocracy and the ageing process.Rachel AroestiBloodsport: After Helen of TroyTheatre Royal Stratford East, London, to 10 OctoberBrilliant new(ish) playwright Ava Pickett (1536) imagines what might have happened when Helen returned home from Troy, after a war fought in her name. Starring Michelle Dockery and Laura Aikman.Miriam GillinsonTartuffe (Remixed)Marylebone theatre, London,to 24 OctoberMark Rylance stars alongside an ensemble of Intermission Youth graduates in Darren Raymond’s modern take on Molière’s classic comedy – which sees, in this case, a Nigerian-Jamaican family’s wedding plans blown apart by the arrival of a mysterious guest.MGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenLicensed to chill … Maxine Peake and Brendan Cowell in Last Seen.Photograph: Ben King/Apple TVLast SeenApple TV,9 SeptemberIn what is quite the career gear change, Colin from Accounts star Patrick Brammall sloughs off his warm and fuzzy romcom associations to lead this chilling drama with Maxine Peake about a police dispatcher convinced he’s answered a call from his daughter, abducted a decade earlier.The PaperSky One & Now,10 September, 9pmSeason one of this feelgood and impeccably performed US Office-universe comedy saw ambitious editor Ned (Domhnall Gleeson again) take the Toledo Truth Teller from depressing clickbait factory to award-winning bastion of actual journalism. Now he’s searching for a showstopping scoop to cement his reputation.Britain’s Forgotten GirlsBBC Two & iPlayer,9 September, 9pmAlessia Camoirano Bruges’s 2022 film about the Italian mafia’s recruitment of young teenagers via social media was nominated for an Emmy; now the documentarian turns her attention to the vulnerable children abused and trafficked by drug-dealing gangs in the UK, and asks why the authorities have done so little to help.The Drop: A Snowfall SagaDisney+, 9 SeptemberThis spin-off from the critically acclaimed Damson Idris series Snowfall shifts focus from LA’s 1980s crack epidemic to the following decade’s west coast hip-hop scene. Gail Bean’s Wanda is now clean and ready to capitalise on rap’s thrilling rise – something that requires a savvy navigation of street politics and nerves of steel.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenBehind the mask … Halloween: The Game.Photograph: IllFonicHalloween: The GamePC, PS5, Xbox; out8 SeptemberPlay as a hapless teenager or take on the role of masked psychopath Michael Myers in this multiplayer gorefest set during the original film’s timeline. It looks like an absolute scream.ValheimPC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox; out9 SeptemberThe acclaimed Viking-inspired survival adventure is finally getting a full release after several years in “early access”. Survive in a hostile purgatory with up to nine pals as you conquer beasts, gather resources and, of course, build pretty houses.Keith StuartStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenSerge overkill … Kasabian.Photograph: Neil BedfordKasabian – Act IIIOut nowFlamboyant rock wizard Serge Pizzorno and his band of merry men are back with their ninth album. Co-produced by Mark Ralph (Years & Years, Clean Bandit), Act III mixes bright pop moments (Superpowers) with more noodly new wave songs such as the festival-ready Great Pretender.Natalie Imbruglia – AlgorithmOut nowPop’s other Ramsay Street resident turned singer returns with this seventh album. The follow-up to 2021’s Firebird tackles Imbruglia’s ADHD and OCD diagnoses, and features the peppy soft-rock of single Upside Down, plus the Robyn-esque electropop bop, Just Drive.Mykki Blanco – Cafe ParadisoOut nowInspired by a life lived in transit, and influenced by New York, Paris and Tangier (where the American rapper and performance artist is now based), Cafe Paradiso is billed as a record for “artsy kids”. They should find a lot to love in the scuzzy art-rock of Butt Sex.Adéla – PrimaOut nowWith the Bangerz-esque current single Ain’t in LA all over TikTok, the Slovak alt-pop experimentalist releases her long-awaited debut album. As you’d imagine for someone who auditioned to be in girl band Katseye, pop runs through Adéla’s veins, as shown on the bratty KGB and Red Bottoms’ sultry midtempo catharsis.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreenWhat Music Looks LikePodcastWriter Paul Weedon explores how artful design can enhance music, speaking to artists such as Adam Smith on his immersive stage visuals for the Chemical Brothers and Laura LiPuma on her 1980s work with Prince.InCinematicYouTubeVideo essayist InCinematic presents fascinating and often niche takes on the efficacy of different creative techniques in cinema. A recent highlight explores Leslie Nielsen’s deadpan delivery in Airplane! and the experimentalism of The Lion King.Hamza: African Birds of PreyBBC iPlayerWildlife cameraman Hamza Yassin takes his infectious enthusiasm for nature to Kenya in this beautiful film where he goes in search of some of Africa’s most threatened birds of prey, such as the crowned eagle.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Gary Lineker makes Z-listers do silly things for his new show  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Joey Essex and John Bercow are unlikely team mates in The Box. Plus, the inside story of Saturday Night Live. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Joey Essex and John Bercow are unlikely team mates in The Box. Plus, the inside story of Saturday Night Live. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Games master … The Box on ITV1.Photograph: Two Four/ITVView image in fullscreenGames master … The Box on ITV1.Photograph: Two Four/ITVTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Gary Lineker makes Z-listers do silly things for his new showJoey Essex and John Bercow are unlikely team mates in The Box. Plus, the inside story of Saturday Night Live. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Ali Catterall,Jack SealeandSimon WardellSat 5 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Box8.15pm, ITV1Gary Lineker’s latest gig involves chuckling from a tower as Z-listers stumble around a disused car park to find tokens. Graeme Souness, Shakira Khan and JB Gill are among the celebrities playing mundane games – egg-and-spoon races, rock-paper-scissors – with minor twists. The fun is in the team bonding: Joey Essex asking John Bercow if he’s feeling reem is surprisingly pleasing.Phil HarrisonCelebrating Disney at the Proms: The Music of Menken5.30pm, BBC TwoBe Our Guest! Friend Like Me! Part of Your World! It’s a night of Disney bangers at the Royal Albert Hall, as an ode to the man behind the music, Alan Menken. The BBC Philharmonic Orchestra will be joined by special guests and the National Youth Music Theatre to create the magic.Hollie RichardsonAlan Carr’s Celebrity Picture Slam6.20pm, BBC OneGareth Malone may be able to spot a bum note at 50 paces, but can he spot the answers in Carr’s picture puzzles? The choirmaster pairs up with Steph McGovern to battle Will Best and Fleur East, plus standup Ellie Taylor and Derry Girls’ Jamie-Lee O’Donnell – all vying to bank £10,000 for their chosen charities.Ali CatterallCasualty: 40th Anniversary8pm, BBC OneThis hardy medical drama has surprisingly polemical roots, beginning its long life as a defence of the NHS in the face of Thatcherism. It ruffles fewer feathers in middle age but, even so, this birthday special is a furious affair as a firebombing in Holby means a frantic, eventually devastating night in A&E.PHBeck9pm, BBC FourA church burns, artily, in a dark wood – the veteran Swedish sleuthing series is back. As the fiery death of a rock musician turned pastor disturbs a web of guilt and hidden loyalties, Alex (Jennie Silfverhjelm) conceals a personal link to the congregation that could banjax the investigation.Jack SealeLorne9pm, Sky DocumentariesLorne Michaels is revered in US TV circles for creating Saturday Night Live in 1975. The producer is also fairly elusive – a fact this entertaining documentary is happy to lean into. Fortunately, there are plenty of big hitters to tell his story – Conan O’Brien, Tina Fey, Chris Rock and Andy Samberg are among those testifying to his brilliance.PHFilm choiceThe Mandalorian and Grogu, out now, Disney+View image in fullscreenDream team … The Mandalorian and Grogu on Disney+.Photograph: Nicola Goode/Lucasfilm/Disney/APWith one of the best Star Wars series going feature-length, its biggest draw, “Baby Yoda”, rightly shares top billing with Pedro Pascal’s perma-helmeted bounty hunter. Otherwise, it’s business as usual for the grumpy Mando and his cute, Force-friendly ward as they get involved in a spot of Hutt family politics. Hired by the New Republic to track down a warlord still sympathetic to the old empire, they must deal with Jabba the Hutt’s siblings, who want the return of their abducted nephew Rotta (Jeremy Allen White) in exchange for information. Featuring a bizarre cameo from Martin Scorsese as a multi-limbed food truck cook, Jon Favreau’s sci-fi adventure is a light, lithe addition to the canon.Simon WardellMayday, out now, Apple TVRyan Reynolds is always an easy watch, with his relatable (for a film star) charm and unforced gift for comedy. Both are leaned on heavily in John Francis Daley and Jonathan Goldstein’s cold war actioner, set in 1987. Reynolds plays fighter pilot Troy “Assassin” Kelly, whose spy plane is downed over the Soviet Union. Wounded and alone in a Siberian forest, he meets Nikolai (Kenneth Branagh), a Top Gun fan of Misery-like proportions but also, handily, a very disaffected KGB covert ops agent. Trains, planes and military automobiles all feature in an undemanding buddy caper.SWLive sportPremier League Football: Newcastle v Bournemouth, 11am, TNT Sports 1Hull v Aston Villa is at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event.Women’s Super League Football: Chelsea v Aston Villa, 12.25pm, BBC OneBrighton v Arsenal is on Sun at 11.30am on Sky Sports Main Event.Snooker: British Open, 12.45pm, Channel 5The opening semi-final.Super League Rugby: Wakefield v Warrington, 2.45pm, BBC TwoAt the DIY Kitchens Stadium.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factories | Poland holidays | The Guardian
description: The imposing red-brick mills of its industrial past are a stunning example of urban regeneration in the former ‘city of a thousand chimneys’
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: The imposing red-brick mills of its industrial past are a stunning example of urban regeneration in the former ‘city of a thousand chimneys’
Content: The beautifully restored Manufaktura area has become a leisure and tourism hub.View image in fullscreenThe beautifully restored Manufaktura area has become a leisure and tourism hub.Poland holidaysA city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factoriesThe imposing red-brick mills of its industrial past are a stunning example of urban regeneration in the former ‘city of a thousand chimneys’Kevin RushbySat 5 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSometimes travel delivers a real shock. I’m moving along the boulevards in the Polish city of Łódź, enjoying the excellent cafes and warm sunshine, when I spot the vans. They are parked up on the verge, with racks of clothing and heavily laden tables behind. I can’t resist a Sunday morning market and walk towards a group of men huddled around a car that is covered in blankets. And then it happens. They turn – and I see they are weighing pistols in their hands. I recognise the lean profile of a German Luger, and then the bulkier Colt 45.There is a second of doubt. I hesitate. They replace the weapons on the display and walk away laughing. I approach. On the car roof is a row of dusty soldiers’ helmets. “We were repairing a pavement in the centre of town,” says the seller cheerfully, handing me a badge to inspect. “Imagine! For 80 years, all this stuff was just under our feet.”It’s a Wehrmacht shoulder badge from Kuban 1943, a last-ditch post-Stalingrad action on the Crimean peninsula. Who wore this, I wonder? A veteran of the Russian front who almost made it home? Nothing is clear, except that in Łódź, the past is never far away.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsI arrive the previous night, a little disoriented, whizzing past unlit buildings, huge brick structures like Victorian factories. “Are we in the city yet?” I ask.The taxi driver gives me a quizzical look. “Yes, this is Łódź.” I note the pronunciation, like “wudge”. I glimpse five-storey blocks, tree-lined streets, a tramline. “I could never live anywhere else,” he adds. A huge blue graffito is caught in the headlights, like a monstrous alien creature.“Why?” I ask, but we are already pulling up outside an immense red-brick building, my hotel, and he never answers my question. The reception area is huge, with a strange scalloped ceiling in red brick that hints at a previous incarnation as a factory.View image in fullscreenPaweł Pawlikowski’s Oscar for the film Ida on display at the Museum of Cinematography.This is my first visit to Łódź, a city about 75 miles (120km) south-west of Warsaw. My interest has been piqued by a list of notable people associated with the place. It features an astonishing number of Oscar-winning or nominated film directors connected to the city: Andrzej Wajda (The Promised Land), Roman Polanski (The Pianist), Paweł Pawlikowski (Ida), Agnieszka Holland (Europa Europa), Krzysztof Kieślowski (Three Colours trilogy) and Zbigniew Rybczyński (Tango).But under the bonnet there is a vast array of talent in acting, production and technical excellence. The city’s film school is responsible, of course, but Łódź itself features as a setting, too, notably in David Lynch’s Inland Empire and Wajda’s masterpiece The Promised Land.Łódź, I had decided, must be fascinating. Any visit starts with Piotrkowska Street, the longest shopping street in Europe at about 2½ miles. My guide, Anna, takes me through Plac Wolności (Freedom Square), where a dance festival is in progress, with hooded hip‑hoppers rubbing shoulders with troupes of line dancers and girls in colourfully embroidered traditional dress. This is a city where music and dance are never far away. We dodge down a side alley and emerge in a striking art installation – an entire street,Pasaż Róży(Rosa’s Passage), covered in mirrors by the artist Joanna Rajkowska. Back on the main pedestrianised route, the mix of ancient and modern continues: 19th‑century porticoed palaces adorned with colourful graffiti.I ask Anna how Łódź fared in the second world war. “It was not too badly damaged,” she says. “Both the Germans and the Russians wanted the industry intact.”There is no medieval heart, no ornate houses like in Wrocław or Kraków. What Łódź possesses is an impressive array of 19th-century factories, mostly textiles, built to show off their owners’ power, wealth and architectural aspirations. Now, this heritage has become a stunning example of urban regeneration.View image in fullscreenOFF Piotrkowska, where the old mills host a hive of small businesses.Photograph: Paweł AugustyniakWe turn intoOFF Piotrkowska, a complex of beautiful old textile mills reborn as a hive of small businesses. There are lots of vibrant restaurants and bars, but Anna wants to show me a shop that she likes:Pan Tu Nie Stał. “It was a saying in communist times: ‘You’re not in the queue.’ We said it to people trying to push in,” Anna says.This is the spot to pick up a T-shirt featuring Soviet combine harvesters or some Czas Pokaże (Time Will Tell) socks. The shop says a lot about the Polish attitude to communist times: none of the maudlinostalgieof East Germany; this nostalgia comes with healthy dashes of colour and humour.It did all start, however, with a disaster. The old mills had survived two world wars, but died in the economic collapse after communism ended in 1989. “Everything closed down,” says Anna. “We call that time thetransformacja. It was very hard.”We stroll into theManufakturaarea, once the site of a vast textile business started by a local scrap metal dealer, Izrael Poznański, in 1872, and now another beautifully restored collection of red-brick buildings housing restaurants, bars, shops and the fascinatingMuseum of the Factory. Next door is the palace that Poznański built, a neo-baroque monstrosity of bulging wealth, now thecity museum.double quotation markAndrzej Wajda needed to make only minor adjustments to start filming The Promised Land in the 1970s. The tired faces, the crashing looms – it was all very much like 1880After the Congress of Vienna in 1815, Łódź became part of the Russian empire, a melting pot of German, Jewish, Polish and Russian influences. In the 1870s, Poznański was one of a group of men who saw the potential of steam power. They imported looms from England and were soon amassing unimaginable wealth, constructing a city of handsome red-brick factories, the core of which still remains.The Museum of the Factory houses a collection of working looms that date back to the 1880s. Only four machines are ever turned on due to noise pollution laws – in the old days, one factory might have had hundreds. This was the city of the deaf, but the deafest of all were the bosses, oblivious to the terrible hardships of their workforce, from the founders through to their communist successors. When Wajda came to these mills in the early 1970s, planning The Promised Land, he needed to make only minor adjustments to start filming. The tired faces, the crashing looms, the heat and the dust – it was all very much like 1880.Is that your favourite film, I ask Anna? She shakes her head. “Cold Warby Pawlikowski,” she says. “I love that film.”View image in fullscreenThe Museum of the Factory has a collection of working looms dating to the 1880s.Photograph: PicasaThis 2018 masterpiece is the story of a tragic love affair conducted across the Iron Curtain in the years following the second world war. Based on the lives of Pawlikowski’s parents, it is dark and sensuous, full of great music and dance. Pawlikowski has used Łodż as a location.We move on to theMuseum of Cinematography, a tour de force that warrants some preparation (watch films by Polish directors). They have everything from early working equipment to props from the most recent Oscar triumphs. By the time I get to the end, I have only a few minutes to rush to theCentral Museum of Textiles.There I find a technician, Przemysław, about to start up a 1893 Greenwood loom. He’s a former policeman with a few tales to tell, but right now one question is bothering me. “Why did film-making succeed so brilliantly in this city of textiles?” I ask him.He taps the cast iron loom and chuckles. “I’ll show you.”With the flick of a switch, the loom begins to clank and turn. The noise is incredible. Przemysław is moving around, adjusting and calibrating, his face concentrated. I see the spools of thread begin to unwind, the shuttle dashing back and forth, the warp and weft rhythmically rising and falling. The different colours, each no more than a thin line, but magically coming together. And from the lip of the machine spills a beautiful multicoloured cloth.Przemysław looks at me and raises a questioning eyebrow. “Like weaving a story, right?”The trip was provided by thePolishTourism Organisation, withHoliday Extraslending travel support in car parking, insurance, airport transfers and hotelsExplore more on these topicsPoland holidaysCity breaksEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pungent and mealy’: the best (and worst) supermarket tuna, tasted and rated | Fish | The Guardian
description: From sustainable catch methods to the most pleasant texture and aroma, which tinned and jarred fish had our tester hooked and which left him reeling?
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: From sustainable catch methods to the most pleasant texture and aroma, which tinned and jarred fish had our tester hooked and which left him reeling?
Content: ‘Gruelling stuff’: the tuna was tested straight from the tin or jar, without seasoning, lemon, olive oil or mayonnaise.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFishReview‘Pungent and mealy’: the best (and worst) supermarket tuna, tasted and ratedFrom sustainable catch methods to the most pleasant texture and aroma, which tinned and jarred fish had our tester hooked and which left him reeling?The best supermarket anchovies, tasted and ratedTom HuntSat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEaten straight from the tin, without seasoning, lemon, olive oil or mayonnaise, canned tuna is pretty gruelling stuff, not least because it’s pungent, mealy and hard to swallow. Testing tuna in this way demonstrates the overall poor quality of the product and why certain brands and species are revered for their superior texture and flavour. That said, a tuna mayo sandwich is one of my go-to lunches, so long as the fish is sustainably sourced (so as not to leave a bad taste in the mouth) and there’s enough pepper to balance out its flavour.Skipjack is a fast-growing species with a softer, flakier texture and fishier flavour than some others. Albacore tuna, meanwhile, is a larger, slower-growing fish, which makes it more sensitive to overfishing. Its flesh is much paler and more delicately flavoured, with large, meaty flakes.The Marine Conservation Society (MCS) is an independent registered environmental charity that uses scientific evidence to rate the sustainability of seafood. ItsGood Fish Guideuses a traffic-light system from green (best choice) to red (fish to avoid). Both skipjack and albacore have green-rated options available. However, fish sustainability is complicated and depends on the catch method, region and species.The Good Fish Guiderates pole and line as the best catch method, and recommends fish certified by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC). Hook and line is an umbrella term that includes less sustainable fishing methods such as longline fishing, which involves hundreds or thousands of baited hooks and is associated with much higher by-catch, including sharks, turtles and seabirds. However, hook and line combined with an MSC certification is a more sustainable choice because the catch method is specified.Purse seine fishingthat avoids using a fish aggregating device (FAD) to attract more fish, meanwhile, has a much lower by-catch than standard purse seine, which attracts and traps other marine life alongside the tuna. So look out for “pole and line” or “hooks and lines” on the label, in combination with an MSC certification; failing that, “FAD-free purse seine” means you’re making a slightly more sustainable choice.Seafood sustainability has been at the core of my campaign work for the past 15 years, and although there’s still alongway to go, it’s been a pleasure to see the industry take note of the public’s interest in it. This wasn’t the most enjoyable category to taste, but it was one of the most enjoyable to write.The best supermarket tuna in brine or waterBest overall:Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference albacore tuna steak in spring waterView image in fullscreen£2.55 for 160g at Sainsbury’s (£2.13/100g drained weight)★★★★☆A classic, pale albacore tuna. Well-formed large, flaky steaks. A sweet aroma and taste, with a mild and well-balanced flavour. Caught by pole and line in the north-east Atlantic or the Pacific Ocean, and MSC-certified.Best bargain:Co-op responsibly sourced tuna chunks in brineView image in fullscreen£2.70 for 3 x 145g at Co-op (88p/100g drained)★★★☆☆Skipjack steaks with a sweet aroma and taste and a firm texture, albeit with some more mushy pieces in the can. Caught by pole and line in the Pacific, which, as a more sustainable catch method, bumps this one up to this week’s best bargain.And the rest …Ocado tuna chunks in brineView image in fullscreen£4.20 for 4 x 145g at Ocado (£1.03/100g drained)★★★☆☆Skipjack with a saline, fishy aroma, quite a flaky texture, and noticeably sweet and pleasant flavour. Caught by FAD-free purse seine in the western central Pacific and MSC-certified.Waitrose No 1 albacore tuna in spring waterView image in fullscreen£4.25 for 220g at Waitrose (£2.83/100g drained)★★★☆☆Beautiful, hand-prepared, large pieces of jarred albacore steak with a pungent, slightly sulphurous aroma and a mealy texture. Sweet, fishy taste with a hint of bitterness. Caught by hook and line in the north-east and south-east Atlantic, and MSC-certified.Lidl Nixe tuna chunks in spring waterView image in fullscreen£2.49 for 4 x 145g at Lidl (61p/100g drained), in store only★★☆☆☆Large, flaky pieces of skipjack. title: Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for kacang pool, or Malaysian bean stew  | Vegetables | The Guardian
description: A delicious and triumphant blend of Levantine and Malay cuisines
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: A delicious and triumphant blend of Levantine and Malay cuisines
Content: Meera Sodha’skacang pool, or Malaysian bean stew.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha’skacang pool, or Malaysian bean stew.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.Meera Sodha recipesVegetablesMeera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for kacang pool, or Malaysian bean stewA delicious and triumphant blend of Levantine and Malay cuisinesMeera SodhaSat 5 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 05.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is a dish with roots in ancient Egypt. There, it started life asful medames, the famous fava bean dish lightly seasoned with cumin, garlic and lemon. Then it was, reportedly, brought to Johor in Malaysia by Arab traders. It has since been adopted and adapted with a fierce sort of love, plus more spice and a tin of baked beans. I adore it. It’s a very delicious dinner and a triumphant blend of two cuisines.Kacang poolTraditionally, this dish is made with minced beef, but I’ve used soya mince. I ignore the packet instructions to rehydrate it before using, though.Prep10 minCook35 minServes430g unsalted butter3 tbsp rapeseed oil, plus extra for frying the eggs2 red onions, peeled and very finely chopped¾ tsp fine sea salt3 garlic cloves, peeled and minced1½cm x 1½cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely chopped1 tsp ground cumin1 tsp mild curry powder¾ tsp ground coriander¾ tsp ground fennel60g driedsoya mince– I likeClearspring1415g tin baked beans1400g tinborlotti beansin water, not drainedTo serve4 eggsButtered dinner rolls, or Greek-style flatbreads or baguette2 green finger chillies, finely sliced1 lime, quarteredPut the butter and oil in a wide frying pan or a medium-sized casserole pot for which you have a lid on a medium heat. When it’s hot, add three-quarters of the chopped onions and three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt, and cook, stirring, for 10 minutes, until soft, glossy and easily squashed with a wooden spoon. Add the garlic and ginger, cook for a further three or four minutes, until the garlic no longer smells raw, then add all the spices and the soya mince, stir to mix and cook for about three minutes more.Add both tins of beans, including the borlotti bean water, then half-fill one of the empty tins with water, and add half of that to the pan (so, a quarter of a tin’s worth). Stir, pop on the lid and leave to cook for about five minutes. Mash with a potato masher to a consistency you like – I like mine quite chunky – add more water, if need be, to loosen, then pop on the lid again and cook for another five minutes. Taste, add salt, if need be, then take off the heat and leave covered.Heat a tablespoon of oil in a wide, nonstick pan and, when it’s hot, crack in as many eggs as you can fit comfortably into the pan. Fry until the whites are set and the yolks are runny. Meanwhile, warm the bread.To serve, spoon a quarter of the bean mix into four lipped plates or wide bowls, top each serving with a fried egg, then sprinkle over a little green chilli and as much of the leftover chopped red onion as you like. Put a lime quarter on each plate, then dig in, serving the bread on the side for mopping.Explore more on these topicsVegetablesMeera Sodha recipesFoodMalaysian food and drinkBeans, pulses and legumesVegetarian food and drinkEggsHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content
